bhaskara-wheel-1150.summary: Around 1150 Bhaskara II described a wheel with mercury in its spokes that would turn forever; the dream of perpetual motion had a design. As each spoke passed over its top, mercury was meant to flow outward, so that one side would stay heavier and keep it turning on its own. No such wheel has ever worked: whatever turning force its heavier side gains is cancelled as weights shift inward on its rising side. Bhaskara's design counts as history's first documented proposal for perpetual motion, and it drew imitators for centuries.

sources.title: Bhāskara's wheel - Wikipedia
White, Lynn, 'Tibet, India, and Malaya as Sources of Western Medieval Technology', The American Historical Review 65 (1960)
sources.author: White, Lynn
sources.confirms: The page gives no date or facts about Bhāskara II, mercury, or a perpetual-motion wheel. It identifies the article as Tibet, India, and Malaya as Sources of Western Medieval Technology, published 1 April 1960 in the April 1960 issue;
sources.qualifies: The page does not state whether the claim is accurate.

sources.title: 'Perpetual motion', Encyclopaedia Britannica

It also names later builders Edward Somerset (1601-67) and Johann Bessler (1680-1745).
sources.qualifies: The page attributes the first suggestion to Vilard, not Bhaskara II.

goryeo-sanggam-celadon-1150.summary: Kiln workers on Korea's southwest coast cut designs into leather-hard clay, filled grooves with white and iron-black slips, then glazed and fired at reducing heat so cranes, clouds and chrysanthemums appeared sharp beneath a jade-green surface. This sanggam technique matured around mid-twelfth century, after Song envoy Xu Jing praised Goryeo's plain green wares in 1123. Chemical analysis published in 2002 shows glaze compositions and firing conditions tuned to keep colour contrast crisp. Inlay turned a borrowed Chinese glaze tradition into a Korean signature, supplied court and monasteries, and ended with Mongol wars and kiln dispersal in later Goryeo.

sources.title: 'An archaeochemical microstructural study on Koryo inlaid celadon', Bulletin of the Korean Chemical Society 23 (2002)

hayy-ibn-yaqzan-1150.summary: Around 1150 Ibn Tufayl wrote of a boy raised by a gazelle alone on a desert island who, without meeting another human, reasons his way to science and God; it is counted the first philosophical novel. Edward Pococke the Younger's Latin translation, Philosophus Autodidactus, appeared in 1671 and Simon Ockley's English one in 1708; it sold widely across Europe, is thought to have inspired Locke's idea of infants as blank slates, and may have inspired Defoe's Robinson Crusoe.

parakrama-samudra-1153.summary: From 1153 Sri Lanka's king Parākramabāhu I built reservoirs so that, as he had said while ruling Dakkhinadesa before his accession, no drop of rain reached the sea unused. His largest, Parakrama Samudra, held some 25 square kilometres of water (sources give 2,400 to 2,550 hectares) for irrigation beside his capital Polonnaruwa. His saying, that not one drop of rain should reach the sea without first serving humanity, is still quoted.

tabula-rogeriana-1154.summary: In 1154 al-Idrisi finished a world map unmatched in accuracy for 300 years. He built it from travellers' reports checked against each other: he interviewed experienced travellers, kept only what they agreed on, discarded what conflicted, and drew seventy sectional maps with south uppermost, as Islamic cartographers did.

weavers-company-charter-1155.summary: In 1155 London's weavers got a royal charter, making theirs the oldest of London's guilds, bodies that decided who could ply a trade. Weavers' Company, formally The Worshipful Company of Weavers, is described as older than any other City of London livery company.

nur-al-din-bimaristan-1156.summary: In 1156 Damascus opened a hospital that treated anyone free and kept patient records. It ran for 700 years. Nur al-Din Zengi founded this bimaristan, as such hospitals were called. Bimaristans in Islamic lands admitted anyone regardless of religion, origin or gender, including people with mental illness, and their endowment deeds forbade turning patients away. Al-Nuri Hospital was first to keep medical records of its patients; Sultan Qalawun was treated there, and it inspired him to found his own great hospital in Cairo.

huizi-paper-money-1160.summary: In 1160 Song China began printing Huizi, which became the most heavily issued official paper money of its age. Its Ministry of Revenue issued these notes, overseen by a Paper Notes Office. Printed in three colours and backed by 280,000 strings of copper cash, they circulated widely; notes as small as 200 cash followed in 1163. As Mongol armies pressed south, military costs drove the government to print far more Huizi than it could back, so the notes lost value and people hoarded coins instead.

roman-de-troie-automata-1160.summary: Around 1160 to 1165 a French poem described four metal figures, golden in some tellings, guarding a chamber. Benoît de Sainte-Maure's 30,000-line Roman de Troie, dated between 1155 and about 1165, imagines these automata in a Chamber of Beauties: one holds a mirror showing those present their own appearance, and another plays music.

battle-of-caishi-paddle-ships-1161.summary: In 1161 Song paddle-wheel warships with gunpowder bombs sank a Jin fleet and saved the dynasty. Jin emperor Wanyan Liang had tried to cross at Caishi on 26 and 27 November to conquer Southern Song. Song commander Yu Yunwen met him with paddle-wheel warships driven by treadmills, whose crews hurled gunpowder bombs with trebuchets; Jin's fleet was destroyed. Liang's own officers assassinated him weeks later, Jin pulled back across the Huai River, and a peace in 1165 held for forty years.

prester-john-letter-1165.summary: Around 1165 a forged letter from Prester John, a Christian king in Asia, began circulating. Explorers sought him for centuries. Europeans later placed Prester John among Central Asia's Mongols, and Portuguese explorers came to assume he ruled Ethiopia; hope of finding him shaped diplomacy and exploration for three centuries.

al-zahrawi-surgery-latin-translation-117.summary: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (c.936 to c.1013), court physician at Madinat al-Zahra near Cordoba, wrote Kitab al-Tasrif, a 30-part medical encyclopedia whose final part is a surgical manual illustrated with more than 200 instruments: scalpels, cauteries, hooks, forceps, a concealed knife for tonsils, syringes and a vaginal speculum. Such illustration was new; earlier surgical texts described tools in words only. In Toledo, in the later twelfth century, Gerard of Cremona translated the surgical part into Latin as Liber Alsaharavi de cirurgia. Printed at Venice from 1497 and used at Salerno and Montpellier, it remained the standard surgical text in European universities for about five centuries, and Guy de Chauliac cited it more than 200 times.

sources.title: Al Aloul, Adnan, 'Al-Zahrawi surgical instruments and techniques: a milestone in the history of surgery', Medicine and Pharmacy Reports (2026)
sources.author: Al Aloul, Adnan

sources.title: 'Abu al-Qasim', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Confirms the Gerard of Cremona translation in the 12th century, the more than 200 instrument drawings, and roughly 500 years as the leading surgical text.

sources.title: National Library of Medicine, 'Islamic Medical Manuscripts: Catalogue, Surgery', NLM digital collections
sources.author: National Library of Medicine
sources.confirms: Confirms the Toledo translation and the illustrated instruments in the surgical part of al-Tasrif.

al-zahrawi-surgery-latin-translation-117.detail: No translation year is recorded; Gerard worked in Toledo from the 1140s until his death in 1187, so c.1170 is a midpoint estimate. Al-Zahrawi's own dates are approximate, and his Arabic original dates to around 1000. Arabic manuscripts of the surgical part with instrument drawings survive in Istanbul, Oxford and Paris, and drawings vary from copy to copy.

nur-ad-din-pigeon-post-1171.summary: In 1171 Nur al-Din Zengi set up a pigeon post across his Syrian domains, faster than any rider, fifteen years after pigeons had first linked Baniyas with Damascus; routes ran from Damascus to Cairo, Aleppo and Baalbek. Messages went on very thin paper tied to one wing feather; pigeon towers stood in major citadels, and relay stations along roads often shared sites with mounted courier posts. Caliph al-Nasir renewed the service around 1200, Mongol invasion disrupted it, and when it was abolished in the 15th century people pulled its relay stations down stone by stone.

gerard-of-cremona-translations-1175.summary: Around 1175 Gerard of Cremona translated Ptolemy from Arabic, one of 87 books returning Greek science to Europe. He had left Italy for Toledo to read the Almagest, then unavailable in Latin, and learned Arabic there. He went on to translate 87 Arabic books, including Euclid's Elements, Archimedes on measuring circles, Aristotle's On the Heavens and al-Khwarizmi's algebra, making Arab and ancient Greek learning in astronomy, mathematics and medicine available to Latin readers across Western Europe.

sources.title: Gerard of Cremona

sources.author: Burnett, Charles

It does not mention the Almagest, a date around 1175, 87 books, his departure from Italy, or learning Arabic in Toledo.
sources.qualifies: The page supports Gerard’s role in Toledo and a translation program, but does not state the specific claims above.

sources.title: 'Gerard of Cremona', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gerard went to Toledo to learn Arabic and remained there for life. His translation of Ptolemy’s Almagest “was finished in 1175” and was “printed in 1515.” About 80 translations, not 87, were attributed to him.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the Toledo, Almagest, 1175, and Euclid claims, but gives about 80 translations and does not mention al-Khwarizmi.

gerard-of-cremona-translations-1175.verification_note: Burnett, Science in Context 2001, describes Gerard's translation programme at Toledo in the later twelfth century; Britannica dates his Almagest translation to 1175 and credits about 80 translations, not 87.

al-hassar-fraction-bar-1180.summary: Abu Bakr al-Hassar, who taught arithmetic in twelfth-century Ceuta on Morocco's Mediterranean coast, set out in his Kitab al-Bayan wa-l-tadhkar a way of writing fractions with numerator above denominator and a horizontal line between them, using the Hindu-Arabic digits already current in the Maghreb. He extended the device to chains of numerators and denominators for compound fractions. Fibonacci took up this notation in chapter 5 of Liber Abaci in 1202, and Moses ibn Tibbon translated al-Hassar's manual into Hebrew at Montpellier in 1271. Mohamed Aballagh and Ahmed Djebbar identified a surviving part of his second book, al-Kamil, in 1987. This bar became standard notation for fractions.

sources.title: Aballagh, Mohamed and Djebbar, Ahmed, 'Découverte d'un écrit mathématique d'al-Hassar (XIIe s.): Le livre I du Kamil', Historia Mathematica 14 (1987)

sources.author: Pfeffer, Jeremy I.
sources.venue: Christ Church Library, University of Oxford
sources.confirms: Al-Hassar taught in twelfth-century Ceuta; his key contribution was a fractional notation with numerator and denominator separated by a horizontal bar, taken up by Fibonacci in Liber Abaci (1202); ibn Tibbon's Hebrew translation completed 12 May 1271 at Montpellier

al-hassar-fraction-bar-1180.detail: Al-Hassar's manual belongs to a Maghrebi school of calculation that ran from Fez and Ceuta to Marrakesh, later including Ibn al-Banna al-Marrakushi, whose Talkhis amal al-hisab summarised the tradition around 1300. Its oldest dated copy of Kitab al-Bayan comes from 1194. Exact dates for al-Hassar are unknown, so 1180 is approximate. Fibonacci's adoption carried it into Latin Europe, and printed arithmetics after 1478 fixed it as common notation.

picture.credit: Wikimedia Commons

ibn-al-awwam-kitab-al-filaha-1180.summary: In late 12th-century Seville, Abu Zakariya Ibn al-Awwam writes Kitab al-Filaha, 34 or 35 chapters covering 585 plants and more than 50 fruit trees, with sections on soils, manures, grafting, irrigation, pests and livestock. He cites 112 earlier authors about 1,900 times, drawing on Ibn Wahshiyya's Nabataean Agriculture, Greek and Byzantine writers and Andalusi predecessors Ibn Hajjaj, Ibn Bassal, Abu l-Khayr and al-Tighnari, yet insists: 'I put forward nothing that I have not first proved by experiment on repeated occasions.' Jimenez-Castillo and Camarero place his work on his own land in Aljarafe outside Seville. Josef Banqueri printed a Spanish translation in Madrid in 1802 and Clement-Mullet a French one in 1864 to 1867, feeding 19th-century European agronomy.

sources.qualifies: Dates him broadly to 12th to 13th centuries rather than to a single year.

ibn-al-awwam-kitab-al-filaha-1180.verification_note: Author flourished late 12th century; no exact composition year survives. Chapter count given as 34 or 35 by different sources.
ibn-al-awwam-kitab-al-filaha-1180.detail: Thirty chapters treat crops and grafting, four treat cattle, poultry and bees. British Library holds a manuscript as Add MS 10461. Nothing is known of the author beyond name and city; Al-Qantara dates him to the 12th to 13th centuries from authors he cites, so his date is approximate. His book sums up Andalusi irrigated horticulture that spread citrus, sugar cane, rice, cotton and eggplant through Iberia.

nan-madol-1180.summary: Around 1180 Pohnpei's rulers built Nan Madol, 92 artificial islands of basalt in a Pacific lagoon. No one knows how the columns were moved. Built off Pohnpei in Micronesia, its islets of stone and coral fill are separated by tidal canals. Islet building began by the 8th or 9th century, and its megalithic walls date from around 1180 to 1200, when large basalt columns were brought from a volcanic plug on Pohnpei's far side. How they were moved is not known. Nan Madol served as ceremonial and political seat of Saudeleur rulers, who united Pohnpei until about 1628.

sources.title: Nan Madol

sources.author: McCoy, Mark D.; Alderson, Helen A.; Hemi, Richard

sources.qualifies: The page does not state that there were 92 islands, that rulers moved the columns, or that tidal canals separated the islets.

sources.title: Earliest direct evidence of monument building at the archaeological site of Nan Madol (Pohnpei, Micronesia) identified using 230Th/U coral dating and geochemical sourcing of megalithic architectural stone | Quaternary Research | Cambridge Core
sources.confirms: The page dates the beginning of monument building at Nan Madol to AD 1180-1200, based on geochemical sourcing of basalt and high-precision ²³⁰Th/U dates on coral from “the tomb of the first chief of the entire island.” It describes Nan Madol as constructed over 83 ha of lagoon, with “artificial islets and other architecture”.
sources.qualifies: Timing and materials broadly align; the island count and other details are absent or differ.

sources.title: 'Nan Madol', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Nan Madol is “off the east coast” of Pohnpei and built around “a series of islets that were artificially constructed.” The page gives no number of islets and does not identify basalt. Construction began “about the 8th century,” while monuments date to “1180-1200.”

lalibela-rock-churches-1181.summary: From 1181 Ethiopians carved eleven churches down into rock at Lalibela, a pilgrims' Jerusalem. Tradition dates them to Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela's reign, around 1181 to 1221; most are thought to have been made in the 12th and 13th centuries, though dating is disputed. Their layout and names are widely read as a symbolic Jerusalem, which leads some experts to place construction after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187.

sources.title: Lalibela - Wikipedia
Fauvelle-Aymar, François-Xavier, 'Rock-cut stratigraphy: sequencing the Lalibela churches', Antiquity 84 (2010)
sources.author: Fauvelle-Aymar, François-Xavier; Bruxelles, Laurent; Mensan, Romain
sources.confirms: The page calls Lalibela a “famous site” with “rock-cut churches” and says their construction sequence is difficult to establish; it asks whether they belong to “one grand ceremonial monastic plan” or a “long-lived ritual centre” refashioned over time.
sources.qualifies: The page confirms rock-cut churches at Lalibela, but does not state the claimed number, ruler, or construction chronology.

sources.title: 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela', UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: The page states that “eleven medieval monolithic churches were carved out of rock” and attributes their building to King Lalibela, who set out “in the 12th century” to construct a “New Jerusalem.” It also describes them as the 13th-century “New Jerusalem.” It does not give King Lalibela’s reign dates or more specific.
sources.qualifies: It supports the eleven churches and 12th-century attribution, but does not state the claimed reign dates and also describes the churches as 13th-century.

lalibela-rock-churches-1181.verification_note: Fauvelle-Aymar et al., Antiquity 2010: construction sequence is hard to establish and these churches may be a long-lived ritual centre refashioned over time; UNESCO attributes them to King Lalibela in the twelfth to thirteenth century without reign dates, so 1181 is conventional.

joachim-of-fiore-1184.summary: In 1184 Pope Lucius III summoned Joachim of Fiore and urged him to press on with his biblical commentary, probably his Book of Harmony of New and Old Testaments, where he worked out his reading of history as three rising ages. Acclaimed as a prophet in his lifetime, Joachim was dimmed by condemnation at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215; Spiritual Franciscans and sects down to the 16th century took up his prophecy of a third age.

sources.title: Joachim Of Fiore
Reeves, Marjorie, 'The Originality and Influence of Joachim of Fiore', Traditio 36 (1980)
sources.author: Reeves, Marjorie
sources.confirms: The article examines Joachim's doctrine of three status of history and its later influence, and its notes record his exposition before Pope Lucius III in 1184.

sources.title: Gemeinhardt, Peter, 'Joachim the Theologian: Trinitarian Speculation and Doctrinal Debate', in A Companion to Joachim of Fiore (Brill, 2017), pp. 41-87
sources.author: Gemeinhardt, Peter
sources.confirms: A Brill companion chapter on Joachim's Trinitarian reading of history; bibliographic record confirmed, chapter text not read.

joachim-of-fiore-1184.detail:
Joachim was born about 1130 to 1135 at Celico and died in 1201 or 1202. He became a Cistercian monk at Sambucina and abbot of Corazzo in 1177; about 1191 he withdrew to contemplative life, and in 1196 Pope Celestine III let him form his disciples at San Giovanni in Fiore into their own order. His Book of Harmony worked chiefly in a pattern of twos, concords between Old and New Testaments; his pattern of threes grew from that, with a final age of the spirit proceeding from both earlier ages. He prophesied two new orders of spiritual men to guide that passage, hermits on the mountaintop and a mediating order, and the Franciscan and Dominican mendicants, hailed as those men, restored his standing as prophet.

The 1215 condemnation fell on his tract against Peter Lombard's doctrine of the Trinity. His Book of Figures, discovered in 1937, carried his ideas in drawings of flowering trees and geometric figures, and his double reputation as saint and heretic is still debated.

picture.alt: Tree diagram of the ages of history from a manuscript of Joachim of Fiore's Concordia, a medieval copy.
picture.credit: Deutsche Fotothek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Europeana

letter-of-toledo-1184.summary: In 1184 a letter credited to Toledo's astrologers, one of a genre of re-dated forgeries, foretold ruin in 1186, and Europe panicked over a forecast. People sought refuge, sold possessions and gathered in penance, in one of Europe's earliest recorded outbreaks of collective hysteria; when that week passed quietly, astrologers claimed prayer had turned disaster aside.

sources.title: The Letter from Toledo Unleashes Collective Hysteria, Canadian Library Association
Wikisource: Folk-Lore, Volume 13, The Letter of Toledo
Museum of Hoaxes: The Toledo Letter (1184)
Mentgen, Gerd, Astrologie und Öffentlichkeit im Mittelalter (Hiersemann, 2005), ch. 1 'Toledobriefe und ähnliche Prognostiken', pp. 17-135
sources.author: Mentgen, Gerd
sources.venue: Anton Hiersemann, Stuttgart (Monographien zur Geschichte des Mittelalters 53)
sources.confirms: The Letter of Toledo circulated as a forged astrological prophecy of disaster for 1186, and spawned a long series of later Toledo letters.
sources.qualifies: Mentgen treats the 1184 letter as one stage in a genre whose earliest versions and later re-datings (to 1229, 1395, 1472, 1479) spread over three centuries.

letter-of-toledo-1184.verification_note: Mentgen (2005) shows Toledo letters formed a genre of re-dated forgeries rather than one 1184 text; its 1184 to 1186 version is best known but one among several.

windmill-post-mill-europe-1185.summary: In 1185 northern Europe's earliest securely dated windmill stood at Weedley in Yorkshire, bringing power to country without streams; 1180s records also name Dinton and Amberley, and some scholars list Swineshead in 1170. Vertical windmills, sails turning in a vertical plane, appeared before 1200 across northern France, eastern England and Flanders. Europe's earliest type was the post mill: its whole body, holding all its machinery, balanced on one large upright post so it could turn to face north-western Europe's shifting winds. These first mills ground cereals.

sources.title: Windmill - Wikipedia
'Windmill', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page dates the earliest-known references to a Persian millwright to 644 CE and to windmills in Seistan, Persia, to 915 CE. It says windmill use spread in Europe from the 12th century, and calls the post mill “the earliest form of vertical mill.” The earliest-known illustration of a tower mill is dated about 1420.
sources.qualifies: Post mills are identified as the earliest vertical-mill form, but the specific northern European reference is absent.

sources.title: Bridge, Martin, Luke Bonwick, Martin Davies and David Pearce, 'What do dendrochronology and other timber-dating methods tell us about the history of English post mills?', Vernacular Architecture 53 (2022)
sources.author: Bridge, Martin; Bonwick, Luke; Davies, Martin; Pearce, David
sources.confirms: No windmills existed in England through the eleventh century, and three references from the 1180s, at Dinton, Amberley and Weedley in Yorkshire, show the post-mill design established by then.
sources.qualifies: Names three 1180s mills rather than a single first windmill, and says the origin of the post-mill design is unknown.

sources.title: Hough, Carole, 'Another Note on Windmills', Notes and Queries 53 (2006), p. 417
sources.author: Hough, Carole
sources.confirms: There is no evidence for windmills in Britain before the late twelfth century, and the Weedley mill near Beverley in the East Riding of Yorkshire is recorded in 1185.
sources.qualifies: States that the first windmill on record in England is at Swineshead, Lincolnshire, in 1170, with Weedley 1185 the next.

sources.title: Campbell, Bruce M. S., 'Adapting to change: English seigniorial agriculture, 1250-1450', in English Seigniorial Agriculture, 1250-1450 (Cambridge University Press, 2000), pp. 411-440
sources.author: Campbell, Bruce M. S.
sources.confirms: The first recorded reference to an English windmill is in 1185, and windmill construction spread widely between 1180 and 1300 after a breakthrough in woodworking.

windmill-post-mill-europe-1185.verification_note: Campbell (2000) and Bridge et al. (Vernacular Architecture 2022) treat 1180s references, Weedley among them, as England's earliest secure windmills, while Hough (Notes and Queries 2006), following Kealey and Breeze, lists Swineshead in 1170 as first on record; 1185 is therefore its earliest certain date among several candidates.

picture.alt: Great Gransden post mill in Cambridgeshire, a surviving seventeenth-century example of the type, photographed in 2014.
picture.credit: Barry Marsh from London, England, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

jayavarman-vii-hospitals-roads-1186.summary: A Sanskrit inscription at Ta Prohm, dated 1186, records that Khmer king Jayavarman VII endowed 102 arogyasala, or hospitals, dedicated to Bhaisajyaguru, each staffed with physicians, attendants and stocks of rice, honey and medicines. Another stele at Preah Khan (1191) lists 121 rest houses spaced along roads toward Phimai and Champa. Mitch Hendrickson's survey shows these routes developing from ninth century and formalised under Jayavarman with laterite bridges and stone way stations. Hospital chapels still stand at Say Fong in Laos and across northeast Thailand, which makes this one of few medieval state health networks visible in stone.

sources.title: Hendrickson, Mitch, 'Historic routes to Angkor: development of the Khmer road system (ninth to thirteenth centuries AD) in mainland Southeast Asia', Antiquity 84 (2010)
sources.author: Hendrickson, Mitch
sources.confirms: Khmer road system, rest houses, bridges; organic development across reigns
sources.qualifies: Warns against attributing whole network to Jayavarman VII

sources.title: Honda, Megumu, 'A Sanskrit inscription of Say Fong, Laos', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies 14 (1965)
sources.author: Honda, Megumu
sources.venue: Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies
sources.confirms: Hospital inscription text: staff, provisions, Bhaisajyaguru dedication

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jayavarman VII'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Crowned 1181; more than 100 hospitals and rest houses; roads radiating from capital

jayavarman-vii-hospitals-roads-1186.detail: Scholars read hospital numbers as programmatic claims rather than audited counts; some chapels may have been built in later reigns. Honda's 1965 reading of Say Fong inscription established staffing details that match Ta Prohm text. Hendrickson cautions that roads grew in stages and that attribution of every bridge to Jayavarman VII is unsafe.

picture.alt: Ta Prohm Kel, a hospital chapel of Jayavarman VII near Angkor Wat
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

mesa-verde-cliff-dwellings-1190.summary: By 1190 Ancestral Puebloans were building 150-room towns into Mesa Verde's cliffs. Within a century drought emptied them. Cliff Palace, with 150 rooms and 23 kivas, is one of North America's largest and housed about 125 people. By 1285, after severe and prolonged droughts, its people had migrated south into Arizona and New Mexico.

sources.title: Mesa Verde National Park
Varien, Mark D., The Mesa Verde Region (Oxford Handbooks Online, 2012)
sources.author: Varien, Mark D.; Kohler, Timothy A.; Ortman, Scott G.
sources.confirms: The page says Pueblo people “have not lived in the MVR since the late thirteenth century AD” and research there dates from 1874. It gives no dates or facts about cliff-dwelling construction, 1190, 1285, drought, Cliff Palace’s rooms or kivas, or its population.
sources.qualifies: The late-thirteenth-century departure is stated; the specific claims are not.

sources.title: 'Mesa Verde National Park', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says the Ancestral Pueblo peoples moved into canyon alcoves and began building cliff houses “between 1150 and 1200.” Cliff Palace had 217 rooms and 23 kivas and housed up to 250 people; 150 rooms describes Long House.
sources.qualifies: Cliff Palace’s room count differs, and the page does not state that the dwellings were built around 1190-1270.

mesa-verde-cliff-dwellings-1190.verification_note: Varien (Oxford Handbook 2012) places cliff dwelling construction in late 1100s to 1200s with depopulation by 1300; Britannica gives Cliff Palace 217 rooms, while 150 rooms matches Long House.

picture.alt: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde under its sandstone overhang, photographed in 2006.
picture.credit: Andreas F. Borchert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

qutb-minar-delhi-1199.summary: Qutb al-Din Aibak, Ghurid commander and later first Delhi Sultan, began a minaret in 1199 beside Quwwat al-Islam mosque, Delhi's first congregational mosque. His successor Iltutmish raised it to four storeys; later rulers repaired and capped it, reaching 72.5 metres, tallest masonry tower in India. Its shaft tapers from 14.32 metres at base to 2.75 metres at top, with alternating angular and rounded flutings in red and buff sandstone and bands of Quranic calligraphy. Indian masons used corbelled construction and carved motifs from local temple practice, while Persian inscriptions name Ghurid patrons. This complex set a template for Sultanate building in Delhi for three centuries.

sources.title: Anthony Welch, Hussein Keshani and Alexandra Bain, 'Epigraphs, Scripture, and Architecture in the Early Delhi Sultanate', Muqarnas 19 (2002)
sources.author: Anthony Welch; Hussein Keshani; Alexandra Bain
sources.confirms: Qutb complex epigraphy, Aibak and Iltutmish phases

sources.title: Nayanjot Lahiri, 'Qutb Minar', in Archaeology and the Public Purpose (Oxford University Press, 2021)
sources.author: Nayanjot Lahiri
sources.confirms: Qutb complex within Delhi's medieval archaeology

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi', World Heritage List 233
sources.confirms: 72.5 m height; 14.32 m base to 2.75 m top; red and buff sandstone; begun 1199; Alai Darwaza 1311

qutb-minar-delhi-1199.verification_note: UNESCO text read in full. Muqarnas article confirmed through publisher record and abstract.
qutb-minar-delhi-1199.detail: Welch, Keshani and Bain read the complex's epigraphy in Muqarnas to show how inscriptions project Ghurid and then Delhi Sultanate authority. Lahiri's Oxford monograph on Delhi archaeology sets the minar within its medieval cityscape. UNESCO gives 72.5 m height, tapering diameters and construction between 1199 and 1503 for later repairs. Alai Darwaza (1311) added a true arch and dome to this complex.

picture.alt: Qutb Minar, a fluted red sandstone tower in Delhi, seen past a neem tree
picture.credit: Shikhers

chimu-intervalley-canal-1200.summary: Chimú rulers at Chan Chan, on Peru's north coast, ordered an intervalley canal, known as La Cumbre, to bring Chicama river water across a desert divide into Moche valley fields and city reservoirs. Surveyors held gradients over more than 70 kilometres of open channel, built aqueduct embankments across dry ravines and shaped channel cross-sections to control flow speed. Ortloff, Moseley and Feldman's 1982 hydraulic analysis found many trial alignments near its lower end where tectonic tilt had altered slopes, and concluded construction stopped before Chicama water ever reached Moche. Kus answered in 1984 that parts did run water and that drought politics, not uplift, explain abandonment. Chimú canal networks nonetheless irrigated far more land than Moche valley farmers work today.

sources.title: Ortloff, Charles R., Moseley, Michael E. and Feldman, Robert A., 'Hydraulic Engineering Aspects of the Chimu Chicama-Moche Intervalley Canal', American Antiquity 47 (1982)
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.; Moseley, Michael E.; Feldman, Robert A.
sources.confirms: Computer analysis of channel design, trial alignments at the distal end and the conclusion that construction stopped before Chicama water reached Moche valley.

sources.title: Kus, James S., 'The Chicama-Moche Canal: Failure or Success? An Alternative Explanation for an Incomplete Canal', American Antiquity 49 (1984)
sources.author: Kus, James S.
sources.confirms: Chimú were skilled engineers and the canal functioned in a limited manner.
sources.qualifies: Argues drought politics rather than tectonic uplift explain abandonment and that the canal did carry some water.

sources.title: Ortloff, Charles R., 'Canal Builders of Pre-Inca Peru', Scientific American 259 (1988)
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.
sources.confirms: Overview of Chimú canal engineering, near-critical flow design and canal length.

chimu-intervalley-canal-1200.verification_note: Ortloff, Moseley and Feldman (1982) hold that construction stopped before any Chicama water reached Moche valley; Kus (1984) holds that sections functioned in a limited manner and that abandonment followed the end of a drought. Date is by ceramic association with Chimú expansion, so approximate.
chimu-intervalley-canal-1200.detail: Ortloff's computer modelling of channel sections showed Chimú builders varying width, depth and wall slope to hold water near critical flow, a design principle not written down in Europe until the eighteenth century. Pozorski and Pozorski's 1982 comment and Kus's 1984 article dispute how much water passed and why work ended. Dating rests on ceramic association with Chimú expansion, roughly 1000 to 1400; no single construction year is known.

picture.alt: Adobe walls of Chan Chan, Chimú capital near Trujillo, Peru; a modern photograph of the city whose fields the canals served
picture.credit: Håkan Svensson, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: resized to 1200 px long edge; converted to JPEG

dresden-codex-1200.summary: Around 1200 Maya astronomers made the Dresden Codex, whose tables predict Venus and eclipses. It is one of four Maya books to survive. It comes from Chichén Itzá's region. It dates to about 1200 to 1345, though estimates range from the 12th to 14th centuries. Its 78 pages of fig-bark paper fold screen-style to 3.7 metres and carry hieroglyphs with detailed Venus tables and lunar tables whose intervals match eclipses. Long thought to be the Americas' oldest surviving book, it ceded that place in 2018 to the Maya Codex of Mexico. Librarian Ernst Förstemann published its first full facsimile in 1880 and deciphered its calendar numerals, one key step in reading Maya writing.

sources.title: Dresden Codex - Wikipedia
B. The Dresden Codex: Description and Known History (Astronomy in the Maya Codices, 2011)
sources.confirms: The page describes the Dresden Codex as “a book of 39 physical pages,” thought originally to have formed “a single screenfold object.” Its contents list a “Venus Table in the Dresden Codex” and an “Eclipse Table in the Dresden Codex.” It gives no date or date range, creator, Chichén Itzá provenance, or claim that it is one of.
sources.qualifies: Table topics are listed; the other claims are not stated).

sources.title: [PDF] 33 IDENTIFICATION OF POSTCLASSIC MAYA CONSTELLATIONS ...
sources.confirms: The page says the Dresden Codex “tells us about the cyclic appearance of the Venus and lunar eclipses” (p. 36) and is one of “only four codices remaining in existence today”: Paris, Madrid, Dresden, and Grolier (p.
sources.qualifies: Venus and lunar eclipses and survival as one of four are supported; origin and production-date claims are not stated.

sources.title: 'Dresden Codex', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The codex is “thought to date from the 11th or 12th century,” not 1200-1300s. It contains “eclipse-prediction tables” and information on “the synodical period of Venus.” The page does not state that it has 78 pages or is made of bark paper.
sources.qualifies: The tables are confirmed, but the stated date differs and the page count and material are absent.

dresden-codex-1200.verification_note: Bricker and Bricker (2011) and the UNAM article confirm Venus and eclipse tables and this codex as one of four survivors; dating ranges from eleventh to twelfth century (Britannica) to a Postclassic first date of 1228, so 1200 is approximate.

picture.alt: Black and white reproduction of a Maya Dresden Codex page with figures and numeral tables, from SLUB Dresden.
picture.credit: SLUB Dresden / Deutsche Fotothek, Public domain, via Europeana

golem-eleazar-worms-1200.summary: Around 1200 the rabbi Eleazar of Worms wrote the first recipe for a golem, a clay man brought to life by words. The Rhineland mystic's instructions appear in his commentary on Sefer Yetzirah, an early Hebrew text on creation through letters. His recipe called for reciting letter combinations with God's name, 221 or 231 pairs in all, over shaped earth. In this tradition such rites were mystical practice and legend, not demonstrated beings; Prague's famous golem is a story first recorded centuries later.

sources.title: Golem - Wikipedia
[PDF] Jack Spira, Divine Speech in Sefer Yetzirah and Jābirean Takwīn
Idel, Moshe, Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid (State University of New York Press, 1990), ch. 'Ashkenazi Hasidic Views on the Golem'
sources.author: Idel, Moshe
sources.venue: State University of New York Press
sources.confirms: University-press monograph on medieval golem traditions, with a chapter on the Ashkenazi Hasidim including Eleazar of Worms's letter-permutation recipe in his commentary on Sefer Yetzirah.

sources.title: Scholem, Gershom, 'The Idea of the Golem', in On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, trans. Ralph Manheim (Schocken, 1965)
sources.author: Scholem, Gershom
sources.confirms: Scholem quotes Eleazar of Worms's instructions: two or three adepts take virgin mountain earth, knead it in running water, form a golem and recite the alphabet combinations derived from the gates of Sefer Yetzirah over it.

hanseatic-league-1200.summary: From around 1200 the Hanseatic League of northern trading towns pooled privileges and protection, running trade from London to Novgorod. Member cities shared trading privileges, defended their ships and ran foreign posts called kontors in Novgorod, Bergen, Bruges and London, carrying grain, fur, salt, timber and cloth in broad cogs. Its first formal diet met in 1356, and it dominated northern European trade for three centuries. Competition from Dutch and English merchants and rising territorial states wore it down, and its last diet met in 1669.

sources.title: Hanseatic League - Wikipedia
Zimmern, Helen, The Hansa Towns (T. Fisher Unwin, 1889)
sources.author: Zimmern, Helen
sources.confirms: The confederation of cities first met under the name Hansa in 1241, the year of the Lubeck-Hamburg alliance.
sources.qualifies: Zimmern dates the first use of the Hansa name to 1241, four decades after the record's 1200.

sources.title: 'Hanseatic League', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Lübeck became a base after its capture in 1158; town associations grew from the early 13th century, and by the 1280s the western merchants’ confederation was joined to the north German towns.
sources.qualifies: London and Bruges as kontors, and the 1356 first diet, are not stated.

hanseatic-league-1200.verification_note: Zimmern (and the Brill Companion chapter titles) place this league's formation in the 1200s, from 1241; 1200 marks only earlier Lubeck-Gotland trade.

lapphyttan-blast-furnace-1200.summary: At Lapphyttan in the Norberg mining district of central Sweden, peasant ironmasters smelt iron in a water-blown shaft furnace tall enough to produce liquid cast iron, which they then refine into wrought osmund bars. A 2011 Journal of Archaeological Science study of lake sediments and radiocarbon dates calls Lapphyttan Europe's oldest known blast furnace and finds mining and settlement there began as early as the 11th or 12th century. Jernkontoret, Sweden's steel producers' association, records 14th-century exports of osmund iron to Lubeck and Danzig at around 2,000 tonnes a year. Chinese founders had cast iron for more than a millennium; blast furnaces reached central Europe only by the mid-14th century and England around 1500.

sources.title: Bindler, R., Segerstrom, U., Pettersson-Jensen, I.-M., Berg, A., Hansson, S., Holmstrom, H., Olsson, K. and Renberg, I., 'Early medieval origins of iron mining and settlement in central Sweden: multiproxy analysis of sediment and peat records from the Norberg mining district', Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (2011), 291-300
sources.author: Bindler, Richard; Segerstrom, Ulf; Pettersson-Jensen, Ing-Marie; Berg, Anna; Hansson, Sophia; Holmstrom, Harald; Olsson, Kristina; Renberg, Ingemar
sources.confirms: Abstract read on the SLU repository page: Lapphyttan described as Europe's oldest known blast furnace; mining and settlement in the Norberg district as early as the 11th or 12th century.

sources.title: Jernkontoret, 'The history of the Swedish steel industry'
sources.author: Jernkontoret
sources.confirms: Osmund iron of about 3 hg per piece; 14th-century exports to Lubeck and Danzig of about 2,000 tonnes a year.

sources.title: 'Blast furnace', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Blast furnaces in central Europe by the mid-14th century and in England about 1500.

lapphyttan-blast-furnace-1200.verification_note: Archaeologists date Lapphyttan's operation broadly to the 12th and 13th centuries; 1200 is a midpoint, not a documented founding year.
lapphyttan-blast-furnace-1200.detail: Britannica dates blast furnaces in central Europe to the mid-14th century and in England to about 1500, two or three centuries after Lapphyttan, so Swedish finds moved Europe's origin of cast iron back by about two hundred years. Groups of peasant farmers rather than lords or monasteries ran the Norberg furnaces, and osmund iron refined from their cast product, sold in pieces of about 3 hectograms, became Sweden's main export through Hanseatic Baltic ports.

picture.alt: Information board and excavated house foundation at the medieval Lapphyttan blast furnace site, Norberg, Sweden.
picture.credit: Calle Eklund/V-wolf, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

motu-hiri-trade-voyages-1200.summary: Motu villages around what is now Port Moresby fired tens of thousands of clay pots each year and sailed them westward in lagatoi, multi-hulled craft lashed from dugout hulls with crab-claw sails, to Gulf of Papua villages 300 to 400 kilometres away. There Motu crews exchanged pots and shell ornaments for sago and canoe logs, waiting weeks for monsoon winds to carry them home. Excavations at Gulf sites found Motu-style pottery in deposits beginning after about 1200 CE, and traced shifting production centres across six centuries. Hiri shows a Melanesian maritime trade system built on seasonal wind knowledge, standardised ceramics and ritual exchange partnerships rather than on markets or money.

sources.title: Skelly, Robert John; David, Bruno, Hiri: Archaeology of Long-Distance Maritime Trade along the South Coast of Papua New Guinea (University of Hawai'i Press, 2017)
sources.author: Skelly, Robert John; David, Bruno
sources.confirms: Excavated Gulf of Papua sites document long-distance ceramic exchange from about 1200 CE
sources.qualifies: Dating of earliest Motu-style wares still being refined

sources.title: Allen, Jim, review of Skelly and David, Hiri, Antiquity 92 (2018)
sources.author: Allen, Jim
sources.confirms: Review confirms chronology and scale of Skelly and David's hiri archaeology
sources.qualifies: Review notes gaps in ceramic sequence

sources.title: Urwin, Chris; Lamb, Lara; Skelly, Robert, 'Rethinking agency in hiri exchange relationships on Papua New Guinea's south coast', Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 69 (2023)
sources.author: Urwin, Chris; Lamb, Lara; Skelly, Robert
sources.confirms: Oral traditions show Gulf partners as active agents in exchange
sources.qualifies: Ethnographic hiri of 1800s may differ from earlier forms

motu-hiri-trade-voyages-1200.verification_note: Start date is approximate; authors speak of hiri developing over several centuries rather than beginning in one year.
motu-hiri-trade-voyages-1200.detail: Lagatoi were assembled from several hulls for each voyage and taken apart afterwards; a single vessel could carry more than 1,000 pots and 20 to 30 tonnes of sago on return. Urwin, Lamb and Skelly argue from oral traditions that Gulf communities shaped exchange terms rather than acting as passive recipients. Earlier ceramic networks along this coast go back 2,000 years; hiri in its documented Motu form dates from roughly 1200 onwards. A 2018 review notes gaps in its ceramic sequence.

sweet-potato-polynesia-1200.summary: Charred sweet potato tuber from Tangatatau rockshelter on Mangaia, Cook Islands, dates to about 1000 to 1100 CE, centuries before any European ship entered Polynesia. Comparison of herbarium specimens collected on eighteenth-century voyages with modern landraces found a distinct Polynesian lineage descended from Ecuadorian and Peruvian varieties, separate from later Spanish and Portuguese introductions through Mexico and Manila. Genomic evidence added a single contact episode between Polynesians and Indigenous South Americans around 1150 to 1230 CE. Together these studies place kumara in Polynesian gardens by roughly 1200, carried by Polynesian canoes rather than drifting across an ocean on its own.

sweet-potato-polynesia-1200.detail: Polynesian names for sweet potato (kumara, kuumala) echo Quechua kumar, a linguistic link noted since Rivet. Hather and Kirch's Mangaia tuber remains a key direct date; later finds in Hawai'i and New Zealand are younger. Herbarium genetics cannot tell whether Polynesians sailed to South America and returned, or whether South Americans reached eastern Polynesia; Ioannidis's genomic signal favours contact near Marquesas or Tuamotu islands. Montenegro and others once argued for natural dispersal by seed, a view now seldom held.

tui-tonga-maritime-state-1200.summary: On Tongatapu, chiefs of the Tu'i Tonga line raised stone-faced house platforms, a trilithon at Heketa and a sequence of monumental tombs (langi) at Lapaha from about 1200 to 1400 CE, alongside a rock-cut canal for canoes. Geochemical sourcing found that 66 percent of stone adzes recovered from these central places came from Samoa, Fiji and even Tahiti, some 2,500 kilometres away. Tonga became one polity spanning an entire archipelago, drawing tribute and marriage partners from neighbouring island groups by canoe. Its rulers held exotic stone as political capital, giving archaeologists a rare material signature of long-distance power in Oceania.

tui-tonga-maritime-state-1200.detail: A 2008 survey dated Lapaha's monumental core to fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; later work at Heketa pushed early ceremonial architecture back toward 1200 to 1300. Tongan oral tradition lists Tu'i Tonga rulers over many generations, and archaeology now gives those traditions a chronology without treating them as literal king lists. Sourcing used trace elements and isotopes on basalt to match quarries in Samoa (Tutuila) and Society Islands. Kingdom structure persisted into Cook's visits in the 1770s.

al-jazari-ingenious-devices-1206.summary: In 1206 al-Jazari published 50 machines with building instructions, among them a crankshaft. His designs used camshafts and crankshafts, and some scholars count his musicians among history's earliest programmable machines.

mongol-empire-era-1206.summary: In 1206 Genghis Khan united the Mongols; the empire that followed carried paper, gunpowder and printing west. Temüjin, having united the nomadic tribes of Mongolia's steppe, was proclaimed Genghis Khan that year. Conquests under him and his successors stretched Mongol rule from Eastern Europe to Japan's sea, history's largest contiguous land empire. It brought about one century of relative order across Eurasia, in which trade routes, postal relays and travellers carried technologies, goods and ideas between China, Islamic lands and Europe. After Möngke Khan died in 1259 his empire split into four khanates.

magna-carta-1215.summary: On 15 June 1215, in a meadow at Runnymede between Windsor and Staines, King John sealed a charter of 63 clauses forced on him by his barons. It promised that no free man would be imprisoned, outlawed or exiled except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land, that justice would not be sold, delayed or denied, and that new taxes needed baronial consent, with a council of 25 barons to hold him to it. Papal annulment came within weeks and war followed, but reissues in 1216, 1217 and 1225 fixed it in English law. Three clauses still stand, and its principle that rulers are bound by law travelled into constitutions far beyond England.

paris-university-statutes-1215.summary: In August 1215 papal legate Robert de Courcon, acting on papal instruction, issued statutes for Paris's masters and students. They set the arts course: no one could lecture before his twenty-first year (an older translation gives twenty) or after fewer than six years of study, theologians needed eight years and age thirty-five, and every student had to have a regular master. They named books to be read, Aristotle's logic among them, and banned his natural philosophy and metaphysics. These statutes gave the university a legal shape, with rights to make its own rules and protect its members, a template later universities copied.

mapungubwe-1220.summary: Around 1220, by Huffman's chronology, Mapungubwe grew into southern Africa's first kingdom, rich on gold sold to Indian Ocean traders. It stood where the Shashe and Limpopo rivers meet in present-day South Africa; Huffman dates its K2 and Mapungubwe sequence to about 1000 to 1300, with Mapungubwe's own phase from about 1220 to 1290. Its rulers lived apart on a sandstone hilltop while commoners farmed and herded below, an early sign of class division in southern Africa. Its capital held about 5,000 people by 1250 and its territory probably covered 30,000 square kilometres, trading gold and ivory toward Indian Ocean ports. Mapungubwe was abandoned around 1300, as power shifted north to Great Zimbabwe.

sources.title: Kingdom of Mapungubwe
'Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape', UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: The page places Mapungubwe’s rise and fall between AD 900 and 1300, and says it was the “first indigenous kingdom in Southern Africa.” It locates it at the Limpopo-Shashe confluence and says it traded gold and ivory via East African ports with India and China.
sources.qualifies: 1220-1290 and a population or capital of about 5,000 are not stated; the page identifies three capitals.

villard-perpetual-motion-1225.summary: Around 1225 Villard de Honnecourt sketched a wheel he said would turn forever; no such wheel has ever worked. Between about 1225 and 1235 he drew some 250 subjects: church plans and elevations, figures, animals, one water-powered sawmill, one trebuchet and an overbalanced wheel with hinged mallets that he presented as perpetual motion. Whether he was working architect or lay draughtsman is debated.

sultan-han-caravanserai-1229.summary: Seljuk sultan Alaeddin Keykubad I commissions Sultan Han, finished in 1229 by architect Muhammad ibn Khawlan of Damascus, on the road between Konya and Aksaray in central Anatolia. Its walls enclose about 4,900 square metres: an open summer courtyard with a raised kiosk mosque, stables and lodging under arcades, a bath, and a vaulted winter hall lit through a domed oculus. Thirteenth-century Anatolian sultans and viziers endowed dozens of such hans along the routes from the Mediterranean ports to Sivas and Erzurum, spaced roughly a day's caravan march apart, each funded by a waqf so travellers, animals and goods could shelter without charge. Ayşil Tükel Yavuz's 1997 study classifies them by shelter and service spaces. A fire led to rebuilding in 1278.

yam-mongol-postal-relay-1234.summary: In 1234 Ögedei Khan set up relay stations every 25 miles, so messages crossed Eurasia in weeks. Yam stations had permanent staff who supplied remounts and fixed rations to post riders and envoys. Households attached to them were exempt from other taxes but paid a levy in goods to keep them stocked, and Ögedei barred nobles from issuing paizas, tablets that let bearers demand goods and services from civilians. He ordered Chagatai and Batu to run yams in their own domains separately.

mali-empire-1235.summary: Around 1235 Sundiata Keita founded Mali, which held West Africa's gold and made Timbuktu a seat of learning. He defeated Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina; his empire lasted until about 1610. It grew into West Africa's largest empire, controlling gold fields and trans-Saharan trade and spreading Mandinka language, law and customs. Its wealth became legendary under Mansa Musa, whose pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 carried so much gold it was noted across the Islamic world. Timbuktu grew into a centre of Islamic learning under Mali's rule.

Mongol invaders had burned Goryeo's first set in 1232; King Gojong, whose court had fled to Ganghwa Island, ordered a revised set carved to implore divine help against them. They are kept at Haeinsa temple to this day.

ibn-al-baytar-jami-pharmacopoeia-1240.summary: Diya al-Din Ibn al-Baytar, a Malaga-born herbalist who left Spain about 1220 and collected plants across North Africa, Syria and Anatolia, serves the Ayyubid sultans in Cairo and Damascus as chief of herbalists. In the 1240s he completes Kitab al-Jami li-mufradat al-adwiya wa'l-aghdhiya, an alphabetical guide to roughly 1,400 medicinal substances in 2,324 entries drawn from more than 150 earlier Arabic and Greek authors and his own field observations, with names in Greek, Berber, Persian and Spanish. He dedicates the companion al-Mughni to sultan al-Salih. He dies in Damascus in 1248. Eighty-six manuscript copies survive; Lucien Leclerc's French translation appeared in Paris between 1877 and 1883.

ibn-al-nafis-pulmonary-circulation-1242.summary: In 1242 Ibn al-Nafis worked out pulmonary transit of blood, centuries ahead of Europe. Galen had taught that blood passed from right to left ventricle through pores in their shared wall; Ibn al-Nafis denied such pores exist and reasoned that blood must pass from right ventricle through the lungs, where it mixes with air, into the left. His manuscript stayed unknown to Western scholars until one was found in Berlin in 1924.

qin-jiushao-mathematical-treatise-1247.summary: In 1247 Qin Jiushao published a method for finding a number from its remainders, now used in cryptography. He gave numerical methods for solving polynomial equations up to the tenth degree by nested multiplication, equivalent to what is now called Horner's method, and he applied mathematics to surveying, military matters and rainfall measured with gauges of his own design.

song-ci-forensic-handbook-1235.summary: In 1247 judge Song Ci wrote forensic medicine's first handbook: coroners could read a body for its cause of death. Song Ci, a judge in Southern Song high courts, wrote Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified as a handbook for coroners. It set out how to examine bodies and injuries and distinguish causes of death. Among its cases is a village stabbing of 1235: investigators matched wounds to sickle blades by testing them on animal carcasses, then had villagers lay their sickles in sunlight; flies gathered on just one blade, bearing traces of blood, and its owner confessed. Officials used Song's handbook for centuries, and it was translated into English, German, French and Japanese.

song-ci-forensic-handbook-1235.detail: Song Ci (1186 to 1249) was born into a bureaucrat family in Jianyang, in present-day Nanping, Fujian, and served several terms as presiding judge. While posted to a criminal court in Hunan he examined crime scenes himself whenever a homicide proved difficult. Sickles cut rice at harvest, which pointed suspicion at peasant workers. Generations of forensic scientists drew on his book, and translations extended to other languages beyond those four.

song-ci-forensic-handbook-1247.summary: Song Ci (1186 to 1249), a Southern Song judicial intendant, printed Xi Yuan Ji Lu (Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified, often translated as The Washing Away of Wrongs) in 1247. Written as a guide for magistrates conducting inquests, it tells officials how to examine a corpse, distinguish drowning from strangulation, read wounds to tell a weapon, estimate time of death from decay, and record findings on standard forms. It is the oldest surviving book devoted to forensic medicine. Reissued and expanded for six centuries, it was required reading for Chinese coroners into Qing times; Brian McKnight's English translation appeared from the University of Michigan in 1981.

tusi-couple-1247.summary: In 1247 al-Tusi made a straight line from two circles, a device Copernicus used to move Earth. In his Commentary on the Almagest, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi proposed one small circle rolling inside another of twice its diameter, so a point on its rim swings back and forth along a straight line. He offered it to account for inferior planets' motion in latitude, and later astronomers used it widely in place of Ptolemy's equant, an off-centre point that had troubled them for 1,000 years. Copernicus used this same construction, but no exact route by which it reached him has been identified.

gujarat-block-printed-cottons-fustat-125.summary: Dyers in Gujarat printed cotton with carved wooden blocks, using alum and iron mordants to fix madder reds and blacks, and wax or mud resists to hold whites against indigo vats. Fragments excavated at Fustat (Old Cairo) and Quseir al-Qadim on Red Sea coast, radiocarbon dated from tenth to early sixteenth century, show these cloths sold in Fatimid and Mamluk Egypt as cheap furnishing and dress fabric. Related pieces survived in Sulawesi and Sumatra as heirlooms. This was industrial scale export printing centuries before European calico workshops copied Indian technique, built on chemistry of mordants that European dyers did not master until the 1700s.

sources.title: Ruth Barnes, 'Indian Cotton for Cairo: The Royal Ontario Museum's Gujarati Textiles and the Early Western Indian Ocean Trade', Textile History 48 (2017)
sources.author: Ruth Barnes

Her 2017 survey of Indian block prints from Fatimid through Mamluk Egypt notes resist and mordant methods and Gujarat origins. Date here is approximate; finds span several centuries.

konark-sun-temple-1250.summary: Around 1250 India's Konark Sun Temple rose as a stone chariot whose 24 wheels are sundials. Much of it, including its great tower over the sanctuary, is now in ruins; what remains stands about 30 metres high.

land-of-cockaigne-1250.summary: In the 13th century poets described Cockaigne, a land with streets paved with pastry where no one worked. One French fabliau of that century and an English poem surviving in a 14th-century manuscript describe houses made of barley sugar and cakes and shops that give goods away; in English hands it also satirises monastic life. Its fantasy lived on in prints and paintings, including Bruegel's Land of Cockaigne of 1567.

land-of-cockaigne-1250.verification_note: Pleij (2003) confirms this motif; only its French fabliau is 13th century, while its English Land of Cokaygne survives in a 14th-century manuscript and is undated there.

moai-rapa-nui-1250.summary: From 1250 to 1500 Rapa Nui carved more than 900 moai, up to 80 tonnes each, and moved them without wheels. They were chiefly living faces of deified ancestors. Nearly half remain at Rano Raraku, their main quarry; hundreds were moved from there and set on stone platforms called ahu around the island's shore, gazing inland over clan lands. All had fallen before 1900, toppled in tribal conflicts or after European contact.

settlement-of-new-zealand-1250.summary: Around 1250 Polynesian voyagers reached New Zealand by canoe, the last large land on Earth to be settled. Māori oral history describes ancestors arriving from Hawaiki in waka; archaeology traces them to East Polynesia. Radiocarbon dating of rat bones in 2008 put arrival around 1280, and a 2022 study of more than 500 sites found settlement probably occurred in the North Island between 1250 and 1275 and in the South Island between 1280 and 1295. Many Polynesian crops failed in New Zealand's cooler climate, so settlers hunted native birds and sea life, driving some birds extinct.

florin-minted-1252.summary: In 1252 Florence minted its gold florin, a coin so stable in weight that Europe later used it as a common standard for big payments. Florence's florin held 3.5 grams of nominally pure gold and was struck to one standard until 1533; little used even in Florence before 1280, it was accepted across Europe after 1300 for larger transactions, including international trade, as the Byzantine solidus had been.

spinning-wheel-reaches-europe-1257.summary: Spinning wheels, which turn a spindle with a hand-driven wheel instead of twirling it by hand, are recorded in Persia by 1257 and in China by 1270; by 1298 Speyer guild laws regulate their use. They multiplied a spinner's output and fed growing wool and linen trades in Europe's cities. Where they were first invented is disputed. Britannica says probably India, reaching Europe through the Middle East. Dieter Kuhn, in a 1979 Early China article, argues from Han stone reliefs that spindle wheels were a Chinese invention of the Warring States period tied to silk reeling. A continuously working flyer wheel appears before 1500, ancestor of Saxony wheels and of Hargreaves's jenny.

sources.title: Kuhn, D., 'The Spindle-Wheel: A Chou Chinese Invention', Early China 5 (1979), 14-24
sources.author: Kuhn, Dieter
sources.confirms: Abstract read: the spindle wheel was a Chinese invention datable to the early Warring States period, linked to silk technology; the flyer spinning wheel was invented in 15th-century Europe.
sources.qualifies: Contradicts the Indian-origin account given by Britannica and the fashion encyclopedia.

sources.title: 'Spinning wheel', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Probably invented in India; reached Europe via the Middle East; Saxony wheel in the early 16th century.

sources.confirms: India about 750; Persia by 1257; China by 1270; Speyer guild laws 1298; flyer illustrated in the Waldburg Hausbuch about 1480.

spinning-wheel-reaches-europe-1257.verification_note: Persia's 1257 date and Speyer's 1298 regulation come from the fashion encyclopedia; place of origin is contested between India (Britannica) and China (Kuhn). approximate_year is set because this wheel's spread cannot be pinned to one year.
spinning-wheel-reaches-europe-1257.detail: Encyclopedia of Clothing and Fashion dates spinning wheels in India to about 750, Persia 1257, China 1270 and its first flyer illustration to Waldburg Hausbuch of about 1480. Kuhn's reconstruction of silk-based origins in China would push invention back more than a thousand years before India's date. Whichever origin holds, wheels reached Europe as Flemish and Italian cloth towns rose, and guild rules such as Speyer's show weavers at first distrusted wheel-spun yarn as weaker than hand-spun thread.

sack-of-baghdad-house-of-wisdom-1258.summary: In 1258 Mongol forces burned Baghdad's libraries, ending 500 years as Islam's seat of learning. Hulegu's army took this Abbasid capital after caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered on 10 February and began looting on 13 February. Estimates of dead range widely, 200,000 among them; Hulegu executed al-Musta'sim on 20 February. Baghdad had been Islam's intellectual capital, with centres of learning including the House of Wisdom; its fall is often said to end the Islamic Golden Age, though historians dispute that, and large libraries reopened within two years. Under Hulegu's Ilkhanate Baghdad prospered but declined relative to Tabriz.

maragheh-observatory-1259.summary: In 1259 Maragheh observatory opened in Persia after three to five years of building. It housed a large collection of astronomical instruments and books and taught students, becoming one of Eurasia's most advanced scientific institutions, and it served as model for Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand, Taqi al-Din's in Constantinople and Jaipur's Jantar Mantar.

mamluk-barid-1260.summary: From 1260 Baybars's relay post across Egypt and Syria brought Damascus news to Cairo in days. This Mamluk sultan, who ruled from 1260 to 1277, folded the barid into his military command. Earlier caliphs had used their barid both to carry official correspondence and as domestic intelligence, reporting on provinces and officials. Couriers on relay horses changed mounts at stations to carry Baybars's messages from Cairo.

yang-hui-triangle-1261.summary: In 1261 Yang Hui drew a number triangle Europe would name after Pascal 400 years later. His book Xiangjie Jiuzhang Suanfa carries China's earliest extant illustration of it. Each number in it is the sum of two above it, giving coefficients for expanding powers of binomials. Yang acknowledged that Jia Xian had invented this method and expounded it around 1100. Yang also worked on magic squares and magic circles.

assize-of-bread-and-ale-1266.summary: In 1266 England tied the weight of a farthing loaf to the price of wheat, a consumer law enforced for 600 years. Rather than fixing what a loaf cost, it fixed its weight: a farthing loaf of wastel, finest white bread, had to weigh 6 pounds 16 shillings by money-weight when wheat sold at 12 pence per quarter, and less at each higher price, so buyers paid a farthing whatever wheat cost. Coarser breads had to weigh more than wastel at each step.

roger-bacon-flying-machines-1267.summary: In the 1260s, by convention 1267, Roger Bacon wrote that ships without rowers, carts without horses and flying machines were possible by art, not magic. It argues that nature's powers worked by art can outdo anything claimed for magic, and foresees ships without rowers steered by one man, carriages moving without animals and flying machines with artificial wings: "instruments of navigation without men to row them, as great ships to brooke the sea, only with one man to steer them." It also sets out ways of hiding writing, an early treatment of cryptography.

roger-bacon-opus-majus-1267.summary: In 1267 Roger Bacon told the Pope that knowledge must be tested by experiment. He also described gunpowder in Latin for one of the first times. He sent his Opus Majus to Pope Clement IV at Clement's request. It surveyed learning from languages, optics and mathematics to alchemy and what he called experimental science, meaning that knowledge must be tested by experience. One passage in it, with one in his Opus Tertium, is usually regarded as among Europe's first descriptions of a mixture containing gunpowder's essential ingredients, long after China.

song-shipbuilding-bulkheads-1272.summary: Around 1272 Chinese shipbuilders divided hulls into watertight compartments; Western yards adopted them in the 1800s. A Song-dynasty merchant ship found in Quanzhou Bay in 1973 and excavated in 1974 was divided by 12 bulkheads into 13 compartments, among the strongest physical evidence for Song shipbuilding. Three-masted and about 34.6 metres long, average for long-distance trade of its day, it appears to have been scuttled in shallow water around when Mongols took Quanzhou, with its cargo left aboard. Archaeologists dated it from coins in its hull, latest from 1272.

sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling; Lu, Gwei-Djen
sources.confirms: Transverse watertight bulkheads are the fundamental characteristic of Chinese hull construction and could be made watertight, long before European adoption.
sources.qualifies: Needham's book (1971) predates the 1973-74 excavation of the Quanzhou ship, so that 1272 hull is documented in later archaeology such as Green, IJNA 1983.

siege-of-xiangyang-counterweight-trebuch.summary: In 1273 trebuchets hurling stones several feet across broke Xiangyang's walls, and Mongol conquest of China followed. Yuan forces had besieged this Han River city since 1267 without breaching its walls. In 1272 Kublai Khan had Ismail and Al al-Din, engineers sent by Abaqa, Ilkhan of Persia, build counterweight trebuchets, called Muslim trebuchets or hui-hui pao: later accounts credit them with stones of over 300 kilograms thrown some 500 metres with new accuracy, the only artillery able to reach Xiangyang's walls. Lu Wenhuan surrendered on 14 March 1273, which opened the Han and Yangtze rivers to Yuan forces and led to Southern Song's fall.

mongol-invasions-japan-bombs-1274.summary: In 1274 and 1281 Kublai Khan's fleets hit Japan with gunpowder bombs, after Korea's Goryeo kingdom became his vassal. Mongol troops advanced behind shields and threw paper- and iron-cased explosive bombs, frightening Japanese horses, in one of the earliest cases of gunpowder warfare outside China. Typhoons wrecked both fleets; Japanese called them kamikaze, divine wind. These failures set a limit on Mongol expansion and became nation-defining events in Japan.

ramon-llull-ars-magna-1274.summary: In 1274 Ramon Llull's paper wheels combined ideas into arguments mechanically, an ancestor of computing. He meant it as universal logic to prove Christian doctrine to people of every faith. It assigned letters to God's attributes and other principles, combined them mechanically with diagrams and rotating figures, and tested which statements held, giving it an algebraic cast. Llull refined it for decades, finishing Ars generalis ultima in 1308; later thinkers count it a forerunner of computation theory.

ramon-llull-ars-magna-1274.verification_note: Fidora and Sierra's volume confirms 1274 and the combinatorial figures; Bonner says the figures did not determine truth and the aim was conversion of Muslims and Jews.

fabriano-paper-watermark-1276.summary: In 1276 Fabriano in Italy began making paper, with watermarks, earliest of maker's marks pressed into a page. From then onward it earned renown for fine watermarked paper that it keeps today, and paper-making brought it prosperity through late medieval and Renaissance times.

fabriano-paper-watermark-1276.verification_note: Tsien dates Fabriano's mill to 1268 to 1276 and first watermarks to 1282; this entry ties watermarks to 1276.

gaocheng-observatory-1276.summary: In 1276 Kublai Khan ordered an observatory built at Gaocheng; its 12-metre gnomon measured the year to within 26 seconds of today's value. Guo Shoujing and Wang Xun designed it to track sun and stars and record time. Its brick-and-stone tower, 9.46 metres high, carries a horizontal bar as gnomon; its noon shadow falls along a 31.19-metre stone scale running north, so solstices and year length could be measured with new precision.

guo-shoujing-shoushi-calendar-1280.summary: In 1280 Guo Shoujing measured a solar year at 365.2425 days, a figure Europe's Gregorian calendar adopted three centuries later. At Kublai Khan's order, he, Zhang Wenqian and Wang Xun had built 27 observatories across China to gather observations. He also built astronomical instruments, including a simplified armilla and Ling Long Yi.

al-mansuri-hospital-1284.summary: In 1284 Cairo built a hospital that treated anyone free. Its building was finished in under six months, speed that drew accusations of forced labour. This hospital was the most lavish of its time, giving sick and poor people drugs, shelter, food and clothing as well as treatment, and it kept treating patients for more than 500 years until demolition in 1910.

beauvais-cathedral-collapse-1284.summary: In 1284 the tallest Gothic vaults ever built fell in at Beauvais: stone had found its limit. Part of its choir vaulting collapsed; one theory holds it was shaken down by resonant vibration in high winds. Builders rebuilt it at full height but with more columns and six-part vaults. Beauvais stayed incomplete: its nave was never built, and a 153-metre tower added in 1569 fell in 1573.

venetian-ducat-1284.summary: In 1284 Venice minted its gold ducat, a coin so trusted it stayed Europe's trade money for 500 years. Venice's Great Council ordered a pure gold coin after Byzantine emperors repeatedly debased their gold hyperpyron, copying size and weight from Florence's florin of 1252: 3.545 grams of 99.47% fine gold, as pure as medieval refining could make it. Ducats circulated beside florins from late medieval times into the 1800s.

spectacles-italy-1286.summary: Around 1286 a Tuscan made the first eyeglasses, giving scholars and craftsmen decades more working life. Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa said in 1306 that making eyeglasses was discovered about twenty years earlier, placing their first appearance in Pisa or Florence. Earlier readers held magnifying "reading stones" over their books; convex lenses mounted before both eyes corrected presbyopia, farsightedness from stiffening lenses in people past forty. Giordano's colleague Alessandro della Spina made glasses and shared his method openly. Venice became an early manufacturing center using Murano glass, and guild rules governed makers there by 1301.

three-sisters-agriculture-1070.summary: Around 1070 farmers in eastern North America were once thought to have begun growing maize, beans and squash together; direct dating now places their first co-occurrence in northern Eastern Woodlands in the late 13th century. Cahokia, at its peak from about 1050 to 1200, was fed by maize and Eastern Agricultural Complex crops. Each crop helps its neighbours: cornstalks serve as trellises for climbing beans, beans fix nitrogen in soil and steady maize in wind, and broad squash leaves shade ground, holding moisture and suppressing weeds. This mix gave more energy and protein than any single local crop. Over following centuries it became staple farming for many Indigenous peoples.

timbuktu-manuscripts-1290.summary: After 1200 Timbuktu's scholars filled manuscripts that survive by the hundred thousand. Scribes translated imported works by authors such as Plato, Hippocrates and Avicenna and local authors wrote on history, religion, law, medicine, astronomy and science, in Arabic and in African languages such as Songhay and Fula. During Mali's war of 2012 to 2013 some 4,203 were burned or stolen; about 350,000 were moved to safety in Bamako.

verge-and-foliot-clock-1290.summary: Late in the 13th century, clockmakers somewhere in western Europe replace water and sand with a falling weight checked by an escapement: a crown wheel, a vertical verge with two pallets and a horizontal foliot bar whose swing lets that wheel advance one tooth at a time. Britannica calls this escapement the key invention, probably made in 13th-century Europe, and J. D. North's 1975 study ties earliest clocks to monasteries that needed to ring canonical hours. Surviving examples come later: Salisbury's clock of 1386 and Wells's of 1392, now in the Science Museum, were both built with foliots and converted to pendulums after Huygens's invention of 1656. Verge escapements stayed in use for nearly four hundred years.

verge-and-foliot-clock-1290.verification_note: No source names the first clock or its year; 1290 is a placeholder inside the late-13th-century window that Britannica and North give. Dates of surviving clocks are confirmed.
verge-and-foliot-clock-1290.detail: De Vick's clock installed for Charles V in Paris in 1379 is the best documented of early examples and source of most textbook drawings. Astronomical showpieces followed soon after: Richard of Wallingford's clock at St Albans around 1327 and Giovanni de Dondi's astrarium of 1364. A foliot has no natural period of its own, so these clocks drifted by a quarter of an hour or more a day and were reset by sundial; 1656's pendulum cut that error to seconds.

murano-glass-decree-1291.summary: In 1291 Venice moved all its glass furnaces to Murano, whose guarded secrets made it Europe's glass capital. Venice's Republic ordered this move fearing fire in Venice's mostly wooden buildings.

McCray, W. Patrick, Glassmaking in Renaissance Venice (Routledge, 2017)

sources.qualifies: The page supports the move in 1291 and Murano’s role as a glassmaking centre, but does not say Venice ordered the move.

ram-khamhaeng-inscription-1292.summary: Inscription One, a four-sided stone found at Sukhothai in 1833 by Prince Mongkut, carries a date equivalent to 1292 and describes King Ram Khamhaeng inventing Thai letters in 1283, free trade without tolls, a bell for petitioners and rice fields and fish in rivers. Its script places vowels on one line with consonants, unlike later Thai writing. Michael Vickery and Piriya Krairiksh argued from 1987 that language and palaeography fit a nineteenth-century composition; defenders, including many Thai epigraphers, hold it authentic. Whatever its date, this stone shaped how Thailand narrates its earliest writing and kingship, and UNESCO placed it on Memory of World register in 2003.

sources.title: Vickery, Michael, 'Piltdown 3: further discussion of the Ram Khamhaeng inscription', Journal of the Siam Society 83 (1995)
sources.author: Vickery, Michael
sources.confirms: Linguistic and palaeographic arguments that inscription cannot be 13th or 14th century
sources.qualifies: One side of an unresolved debate

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ramkhamhaeng'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: 1292 inscription as earliest Thai-language text; reign c. 1279-1298

ram-khamhaeng-inscription-1292.verification_note: Authenticity and date are disputed: Vickery and Piriya argue for a 19th-century origin, while Thai epigraphers and reference works keep 1292. Vickery's article argues one side of that debate.
ram-khamhaeng-inscription-1292.detail: Vickery's 1995 article in Journal of Siam Society restates his case that terms and orthography are anachronistic for thirteenth century. Britannica and most survey histories keep 1292 as a working date. Authenticity is unresolved, and claims about a 1283 alphabet are inscription content rather than established fact.

gaykhatu-paper-money-tabriz-1294.summary: With Mongol herds decimated by cattle plague and his treasury empty, Ilkhan Gaykhatu authorises chav, block-printed paper notes copied from Yuan China, on advice from vizier Sadr al-Din Zanjani and Qubilai's envoy Bolad. First notes circulate in Tabriz on 12 September 1294 by Rashid al-Din's account. They carry Chinese characters, a shahada and Gaykhatu's Buddhist name, in values from a quarter dirham to ten dinars, and refusal is punishable by death. Merchants shut Tabriz's bazaar, prices rise more than tenfold, people flee and commerce halts; his edict is rescinded within about two months. Gaykhatu is overthrown and killed in 1295, and that spring Ghazan orders a consignment of notes bound for Mazandaran burned near Semnan.

sources.title: Fischel, W. J., 'On the Iranian Paper Currency al-Chav of the Mongol Period', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 71 (1939), 601-603
sources.author: Fischel, Walter J.
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society
sources.confirms: Translates Ibn al-Fuwati's account of the chav issue of 693 AH and its denominations.

sources.qualifies: Wassaf dates first circulation to Dhu'l-qa'da 693, September to October 1294; the duration of the episode is given only as about two months of disorder by Bar Hebraeus's continuator.

gaykhatu-paper-money-tabriz-1294.verification_note: Rashid al-Din and Wassaf differ on first circulation by a few weeks; this entry follows Rashid al-Din.
