huang-daopo-cotton-1295.summary: Returning around 1295 from Yazhou on Hainan, where Li women had long worked cotton, Huang Daopo taught villagers at Wunijing near Shanghai a roller gin for removing seeds, a large bow for fluffing fibre, a three-spindle treadle wheel and patterned weaving. Yuan writers Tao Zongyi and Wang Fengs record her arrival and a shrine raised after her death. Francesca Bray reads this transfer as a turning point that made Songjiang China's cotton cloth centre for five centuries and shifted women's textile labour from silk and hemp to cotton. Later Ming tax and market records show Songjiang cloth sold across north China.

sources.title: Bray, Francesca, Technology and Gender: Fabrics of Power in Late Imperial China (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1997)
sources.author: Bray, Francesca
sources.confirms: Huang Daopo's transfer of Hainan cotton technology to Songjiang and its consequences for women's work

sources.title: Review of Korean Studies 24:2 (2021), article on cotton diffusion in East Asia, pp. 173-204
sources.author: Review of Korean Studies (author not captured from PDF header)
sources.confirms: Huang Daopo returned from Yazhou to Wunijing and introduced ginning and spinning tools

huang-daopo-cotton-1295.verification_note: Biographical dates rest on Yuan notebooks, and 1295 is conventional; Bray's monograph is cited as supporting literature.
huang-daopo-cotton-1295.detail: Her birth date and exact year of return are uncertain; Chinese scholarship places her return between 1295 and 1296 and treats biographical details from Yuan notebooks as thin. A 2021 Korean study of cotton diffusion repeats this chronology. Bray's analysis situates her within Mongol-era movement of people and crops.

picture.alt: Gate of Huang Daopo's tomb and memorial, Xuhui district, Shanghai
picture.credit: Michele

hesdin-automata-park-1299.summary: Before 1300 Count Robert II of Artois filled his park at Hesdin with mechanical monkeys and trick fountains. His master of works Renaud Coignet oversaw this estate from 1292 to 1299. Later owners added mechanical birds and a mechanical king; poet Guillaume de Machaut praised its "engines". Charles V had the town and park destroyed after Hesdin surrendered in 1553.

Le Parc

ottoman-classical-era-1299.summary: Around 1299 Osman I founded the Ottoman state, which ruled three continents for six centuries. The Turkoman tribal leader began with a principality in northwestern Anatolia. His successors conquered most of Anatolia, crossed into Balkan Europe by mid 14th century, and under Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, ending Byzantine rule. Selim I's conquests brought Ottoman sultans their title of caliph. Ruled from Constantinople, this empire spanned three continents until its sultanate ended in 1922.

sources.title: Ottoman Empire - Wikipedia
Kafadar, Cemal, Between Two Worlds (University of California Press, 1995)
sources.author: Kafadar, Cemal
sources.confirms: The page gives no founding or conquest dates.
sources.qualifies: The general rise and regions are mentioned, but the specific dates and claims are absent.

sources.title: 'Ottoman Empire', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Osman I founded the dynasty and empire “about 1300,” and describes its beginnings as a “small northwestern Anatolian principality.” The Ottoman period “spanned more than 600 years” and ended in 1922. “Fall of Constantinople” appears as a major event, but the page gives no date for it.
sources.qualifies: The page says about 1300, not specifically 1299, and does not state that Constantinople was taken in 1453.

ottoman-classical-era-1299.verification_note: Kafadar (1995) and Britannica frame the Ottoman beginning as about 1300 under Osman, with 1299 a conventional date.

arte-della-lana-1300.summary: Around 1300 Florence's wool guild put 30,000 to work across the city, a factory without walls. Arte della Lana was one of seven greater guilds that governed trade and shared in ruling the commune. It controlled every stage from baled raw wool to finished cloth, woven on looms scattered through homes across Florence, and coordinated members who rarely owned those means themselves. At its height it employed 30,000 workers directly, kept about a third of Florentines in work and turned out 100,000 lengths of cloth yearly. From 1331 it ran construction of Florence's cathedral.

sources.title: Arte della Lana - Wikipedia
WHY WERE RENAISSANCE FLORENTINE WOOL INDUSTRY COMPANIES SO SMALL? (Quantitative Studies of the Renaissance Florentine Economy and Society, 2019)
sources.venue: Quantitative Studies of the Renaissance Florentine Economy and Society
sources.confirms: The page says Renaissance Florentine wool production used a “putting-out production system organized by a guild.” Its firms were profitable and “by far the largest employer in Florence,” with “dozens of firms” at any given time. It gives no specific year or date for these claims.
sources.qualifies: Guild-organized production is stated; the other details are absent.

sources.title: 'Florence', Encyclopaedia Britannica

sources.qualifies: It does not state that Arte della Lana was one of seven major guilds, employed 30,000 people, or controlled cloth production.

arte-della-lana-1300.verification_note: guild-organized production is stated; other details are absent; it does not state Arte della Lana was one of seven major guilds, employed 30,000 people, or controlled cloth production

baures-fish-weirs-moxos-1300.summary: In Llanos de Moxos, a seasonally flooded savanna of Bolivian Amazonia, communities around Baures laid out low earthen zigzag walls with funnel openings that trapped fish as floodwater drained, alongside straight causeways, canals, forest islands and ponds. Clark Erickson's 2000 survey identified these zigzags as weirs by form, orientation and comparison with weirs still used by local people, and mapped a connected network over 525 square kilometres. Fish, together with raised-field crops and palm groves on artificial mounds, fed dense settlements in a landscape that floods for months each year. Radiocarbon dates from mound settlements elsewhere in Moxos place that culture between about 500 and 1400.

sources.title: Erickson, Clark L., 'An artificial landscape-scale fishery in the Bolivian Amazon', Nature 408 (2000)
sources.author: Erickson, Clark L.
sources.confirms: Zigzag earthworks in Baures identified as fish weirs within a hydraulic network covering 525 square kilometres.
sources.qualifies: Gives no radiocarbon dates for the weirs themselves.

sources.title: Prümers, Heiko et al., 'Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon', Nature 606 (2022)
sources.author: Prümers, Heiko; Betancourt, Carla Jaimes; Iriarte, José; Robinson, Mark; Schaich, Martin
sources.confirms: Casarabe culture of Llanos de Mojos built mounds, causeways and canals between about 500 and 1400, dated by radiocarbon.

sources.title: Erickson, Clark L., 'The Domesticated Landscapes of the Bolivian Amazon', in Balée and Erickson (eds), Time and Complexity in Historical Ecology (Columbia University Press, 2006), ch. 8
sources.author: Erickson, Clark L.
sources.confirms: Synthesis of raised fields, causeways, canals, forest islands and weirs as a built landscape.

baures-fish-weirs-moxos-1300.verification_note: Erickson's Nature paper identifies weirs by form and ethnographic analogy and gives no direct dates; 1300 stands for a span of roughly 500 to 1400 taken from radiocarbon dating of Casarabe mound settlements in Prümers et al. (2022); Baures weirs may be later.
baures-fish-weirs-moxos-1300.detail: Erickson's identification rests on ethnographic analogy with weirs built by Baures and Itonama fishers rather than on direct dating of weir fill. A lidar survey of Casarabe mounds south-west of Baures gives occupation between roughly 500 and 1400, and the Jesuit missionaries who arrived in the 1680s found a reduced population still fishing with weirs. Causeways up to several kilometres long linked mounds and served as dikes.

egypt-sugar-refineries-1300.summary: Sugar cane spread from Lower Egypt into Upper Egypt after 1100, and by around 1300 plantations around Qus, Qift and Asyut fed pressing mills and refineries (matbakh al-sukkar) owned by sultans, amirs and merchant families such as the Kharrubis. In Fayyum a mid-thirteenth-century survey records 1,468 feddans of cane and villages where cotton and rice gave way to sugar. Boiling cane juice in copper vats and draining it in clay cones produced grades from red to white sugar, sold as medicine, festival sweets and an export to Italian merchants. Tsugitaka Sato reconstructed this industry from chronicles, cadastral surveys and al-Nuwayri's encyclopaedia.

sources.title: Sato, Tsugitaka, 'Sugar in the Economic Life of Mamluk Egypt', Mamluk Studies Review 8 (2004)
sources.author: Sato, Tsugitaka
sources.confirms: Spread of cane to Upper Egypt after the eleventh and twelfth centuries; 1,468 feddans of cane in Fayyum; Qift as a production centre; presses in districts surveyed in 1289; sugar as merchandise, medicine and festival goods

sources.title: Sato, Tsugitaka, Sugar in the Social Life of Medieval Islam (Brill, 2015)
sources.author: Sato, Tsugitaka
sources.confirms: Monograph chapters on expansion of cane from Lower to Upper Egypt and on production technology as described by al-Nuwayri

egypt-sugar-refineries-1300.detail: Sato's article lists districts granted after the 1289 cadastral survey whose revenue came from sugar presses, and notes al-sukkar al-Qifti prized for purity. Production contracted after 1400 as Mamluk monopolies, plague mortality and Cypriot and later Atlantic competition cut demand. Egyptian technology, including the use of lime and repeated boiling, passed along trade routes toward China and the Mediterranean. Anchor year 1300 marks a period of large-scale Upper Egyptian production.

picture.alt: Sugar cane growing at Qurna on the west bank of the Nile near Luxor, Upper Egypt
picture.credit: Marc Ryckaert (MJJR)

maori-kumara-storage-pits-1300.summary: Kumara, a tropical perennial, cannot survive a New Zealand winter in open ground. Maori gardeners, within decades of settling Aotearoa about 1250 to 1300, began harvesting tubers each autumn and storing them in rectangular pits (rua kumara) cut into well-drained ground, roofed and sealed to hold temperatures above 10 degrees. Seed tubers kept this way were replanted each spring in mounds, often on soils deliberately modified with added sand, gravel and charcoal to warm them and improve drainage. Excavations at Hokianga and on Banks Peninsula document these made soils and pits down to 43 degrees south, well beyond any other sweet potato cultivation zone of its time.

sources.title: Bassett, Kari N.; Gordon, Hamish W.; Nobes, David C.; Jacomb, Chris, 'Gardening at the edge: documenting the limits of tropical Polynesian kumara horticulture in southern New Zealand', Geoarchaeology 19 (2004)
sources.author: Bassett, Kari N.; Gordon, Hamish W.; Nobes, David C.; Jacomb, Chris
sources.confirms: Modified garden soils with gravel additions at southern limit of kumara cultivation on Banks Peninsula
sources.qualifies: Southern sites may date to late pre-contact centuries

sources.title: Jones, Kevin L., 'Dune soils and Polynesian gardening near Hokianga North Head, North Island, New Zealand', World Archaeology 16 (1984)
sources.author: Jones, Kevin L.
sources.confirms: Dune soils near Hokianga show deliberate sand and charcoal additions for Polynesian gardening
sources.qualifies: Single-site study

sources.title: Furey, Louise, Maori Gardening: An Archaeological Perspective (Department of Conservation, Wellington, 2006)
sources.author: Furey, Louise
sources.venue: Department of Conservation, Science and Technical Publishing
sources.confirms: Synthesis describes rua kumara pits, made soils and garden layouts across New Zealand
sources.qualifies: Grey literature report, not peer-reviewed journal

maori-kumara-storage-pits-1300.verification_note: Pits and made soils are securely documented; a 1300 start is inferred from settlement date and earliest garden deposits rather than a single dated pit.
maori-kumara-storage-pits-1300.detail: Storage pits are among the most common archaeological features in northern New Zealand, often on pa terraces. Garden sites keep borrow pits for gravel and stone-row boundaries alongside storage pits of several forms. At Okuora Farm, geophysics and soil chemistry showed deliberate gravel additions at the southern limit of gardening. These adaptations turned an annual crop cycle into a storable staple that supported dense settlement and later surplus trade with Europeans.

marco-polo-travels-paper-money-1300.summary: Around 1300 Marco Polo's account of China told Europe about paper money and porcelain. Columbus carried a copy. Polo returned to Venice in 1295 after 24 years in Asia and was soon captured by Genoa in its war with Venice. In prison he dictated his travels to cellmate Rustichello da Pisa, producing Europe's first detailed account of Mongol China around 1300, with first Western descriptions of paper money, porcelain and gunpowder. About 150 handwritten copies survive, differing widely because scribes altered text before printing existed. His narrative later inspired Christopher Columbus.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Marco Polo
Yule, Henry and Henri Cordier (eds.), The Book of Ser Marco Polo, 3rd ed. (John Murray, 1903), Book II ch. 24
sources.author: Polo, Marco; Yule, Henry; Cordier, Henri
sources.confirms: Chapter 'How the Great Kaan causeth the bark of trees, made into something like paper, to pass for money' describes Yuan paper currency; Yule dates the dictation at Genoa to 1298.
sources.qualifies: The text was dictated in 1298, two years before the record's 1300.

sources.title: 'Marco Polo', Encyclopaedia Britannica

It does not specify a 1295 return date or state that he was captured by Genoa, dictated his Travels to Rustichello around 1298-1300, or described China’s paper money.
sources.qualifies: The travel period and return to Venice are stated; the other details are absent.

muisca-tunjos-salt-1300.summary: On Colombia's eastern highlands, Muisca communities around Bogotá, Tunja, Zipaquirá and Nemocón ran two linked crafts. Goldsmiths modelled flat figures called tunjos in beeswax, coated them in clay and charcoal, burned out the wax and poured copper-gold tumbaga, leaving casting sprues and rough surfaces because the pieces were offerings for lakes and shrines rather than display. Salt makers at Zipaquirá and Nemocón boiled brine in large ceramic pots, broke the pots and traded hard salt loaves down to Magdalena valley for gold, cotton and shell. Martinón-Torres and Uribe-Villegas's analyses of several hundred tunjos in Bogotá's Museo del Oro show individual makers' habits and deliberate alloy choices across roughly 600 to 1600.

sources.title: Martinón-Torres, Marcos and Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia, 'Technology and Culture in the Invention of Lost-wax Casting in South America: an Archaeometric and Ethnoarchaeological Perspective', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 25 (2015)
sources.author: Martinón-Torres, Marcos; Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia
sources.confirms: Muisca lost-wax casting of tunjos as votive offerings with unfinished surfaces, analysed archaeometrically.

sources.title: Martinón-Torres, Marcos and Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia, 'The prehistoric individual, connoisseurship and archaeological science: The Muisca goldwork of Colombia', Journal of Archaeological Science 63 (2015)
sources.author: Martinón-Torres, Marcos; Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia
sources.confirms: Analysis of individual makers' habits and alloy choices in Muisca tunjos.

sources.title: Uribe Villegas, María Alicia and Martinón-Torres, Marcos, 'Typology, technology, composition and context of Muisca metalwork (Colombia, AD 600-1800): a database', Journal of Open Archaeology Data 1 (2012)
sources.author: Uribe Villegas, María Alicia; Martinón-Torres, Marcos
sources.confirms: Dated corpus of Muisca metalwork spanning 600 to 1800 with compositions and contexts.

muisca-tunjos-salt-1300.verification_note: Goldwork is dated by the Museo del Oro corpus to a span of 600 to 1800, so 1300 is a mid-point. Salt production at Zipaquirá and Nemocón is described by sixteenth-century chroniclers and archaeology; no single foundation date exists.
muisca-tunjos-salt-1300.detail: Spanish chroniclers of 1537 met Muisca markets where salt served as a currency alongside gold discs and cotton blankets. Archaeometric work shows tunjos were rarely polished or depletion-gilded, unlike display pieces from Calima or Quimbaya traditions. Muisca territory had no gold deposits of its own; metal arrived by exchange, with salt and emeralds as principal exports. Chronology spans Early and Late Muisca periods; 1300 is a mid-point, not an event.

picture.credit: Muisca, via Wikimedia Commons

polynesian-navigation-1300.summary: By 1300 Polynesians had settled nearly every habitable Pacific island, steering by stars and swells alone. Archaeologists believe the first settlers reached New Zealand no later than 1300 CE, from a region in East Polynesia later called Hawaiki by Māori.

sources.title: Story: Pacific migrations
J. M. Wilmshurst, A. J. Anderson, T. F. G. Higham and T. H. Worthy, 'Dating the late prehistoric dispersal of Polynesians to New Zealand using the commensal Pacific rat', PNAS 105 (2008), 7676-7680
sources.author: Janet M. Wilmshurst; Atholl J. Anderson; Thomas F. G. Higham; Trevor H. Worthy
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon dating of rat bones and gnawed seeds places human arrival on both main islands of New Zealand at about AD 1280.

sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Settlement of the remote East Polynesian islands, including New Zealand, happened in a rapid pulse around AD 1190-1290.

rapa-nui-lithic-mulch-gardens-1300.summary: Farmers on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) covered large tracts of ground with fist-sized broken basalt, built rock-ringed planting circles (manavai) and dug stone-lined pits to grow sweet potato, taro, yams and bananas on a windswept island with thin, nutrient-poor soils. Satellite mapping in 2013 estimated these rock gardens covered between 2.5 and 12.5 percent of island area. Soil chemistry showed garden plots held higher phosphorus and potassium than adjacent ground, because fresh rock weathering released nutrients while stone cover cut evaporation and wind damage. Lithic mulching let a small population feed its people for centuries on one of Earth's most isolated islands.

sources.title: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Flaws, Andrew; Stevenson, Christopher M., 'The distribution of rock gardens on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) as determined from satellite imagery', Journal of Archaeological Science 40 (2013)
sources.author: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Flaws, Andrew; Stevenson, Christopher M.
sources.confirms: Satellite mapping estimates rock gardens cover 2.5 to 12.5 percent of Rapa Nui
sources.qualifies: Range of estimates is wide

sources.title: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Stevenson, Christopher M.; Haoa, Sonia; et al., 'Soil nutrient analysis of Rapa Nui gardening', Archaeology in Oceania 45 (2010)
sources.author: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Stevenson, Christopher M.; Haoa, Sonia; Mulrooney, Mara; Puleston, Cedric; Vitousek, Peter M.; Chadwick, Oliver A.
sources.confirms: Garden soils carry higher nutrient levels than non-garden soils
sources.qualifies: Sampling limited to selected plots

rapa-nui-lithic-mulch-gardens-1300.verification_note: Garden chronology is bracketed by settlement around 1200 and forest clearance; 1300 is a rounded approximate start.
rapa-nui-lithic-mulch-gardens-1300.detail: Rapa Nui was settled about 1200 CE; gardens expanded as palm forest cleared in following centuries. These fields supported perhaps 3,000 to 4,000 people and remained productive into European contact in 1722. Rock mulch techniques appear elsewhere in Polynesia and in arid regions worldwide, but Rapa Nui's scale is unusual. Satellite estimates vary widely because scattered stone from natural rockfall is hard to separate from deliberate mulch.

picture.credit: Unknown author

renaissance-era-1300.summary: From around 1300 Italy's Renaissance revived Greek and Roman learning and put humans at the centre of thought. This name covers Europe's cultural rebirth between late medieval and early modern eras, variously dated 1400s to 1500s or more broadly 1300s to 1600s. Its first traces appear in Italy before 1300 in Dante's writing and Giotto's painting; Florence led, with Italy and then wider Europe following. Its basis was humanism, built on rediscovered Greek philosophy and Roman humanitas. Vernacular writing and metal movable type from late 15th century spread its ideas far beyond Latin readers.

sources.title: Renaissance - Wikipedia
Shapin, Steven, The Scientific Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
sources.author: Shapin, Steven
sources.confirms: The page gives no Renaissance dates or facts. It refers to the “crucial 17th century” and says “in the 1600s science emerged” from varied beliefs, practices, and influences.

sankore-madrasah-1300.summary: After 1300 Sankoré in Timbuktu drew scholars across the Sahara, and did for 300 years. It was built as Timbuktu took over trans-Saharan trade from declining Walata. Teaching grew around it under Mali and then Songhai rule, peaking in the 15th and 16th centuries under Songhai's Askia dynasty. It was never a centralized university on medieval European lines: individual scholars taught their own students, with some lectures held inside. Learning there declined after Songhai's defeat at Tondibi in 1591.

sources.title: Sankoré Madrasah - Wikipedia
Hunwick, John O., Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire: Al-Sa'di's Ta'rikh al-Sudan down to 1613 and Other Contemporary Documents (Brill, 2003)
sources.author: Hunwick, John O.
sources.confirms: Sankore mosque is associated chiefly with teaching, but there is no evidence of any institution called the University of Sankore; teaching took place in scholars' houses.

sources.title: 'Timbuktu', UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: Sankore Mosque was built in the 14th century and restored by Imam Al Aqib in 1578-1582; he demolished and rebuilt its sanctuary to the dimensions of the Kaaba.

tarascan-copper-bronze-1300.summary: Metalworkers in Michoacán and neighbouring west Mexico, from about 1300, began alloying copper with tin and with arsenic, casting thin-walled bells by lost wax and cold-working tweezers, needles, rings and axe-money. Dorothy Hosler's 1988 studies traced techniques to Ecuador and Colombia carried by sea, then showed west Mexican smiths choosing alloys for sound and colour over hardness: high-tin bronze gave golden bells with a clearer ring, arsenical copper gave silvery sheen. Tarascan rulers at Tzintzuntzan controlled copper ores of Balsas basin and workshops that supplied elites across their state, which Mexica armies never conquered. Spanish records of 1520s list copper tribute and smelting towns.

sources.title: Hosler, Dorothy, 'Ancient West Mexican Metallurgy: South and Central American Origins and West Mexican Transformations', American Anthropologist 90 (1988)
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Southern origins of west Mexican metallurgy and its transformation into a bronze technology chosen for sound and colour.

sources.title: Hosler, Dorothy, 'Ancient West Mexican Metallurgy: A Technological Chronology', Journal of Field Archaeology 15 (1988)
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Two-period chronology with bronze alloys appearing in Period 2, about 1200 or 1300 to 1521.

sources.title: Hosler, Dorothy, 'West Mexican Metallurgy: Revisited and Revised', Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009)
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Revised dating and ore sources in Balsas basin, Tarascan control of production.

tarascan-copper-bronze-1300.detail: Hosler defines Period 1 (about 600 to 1200) as copper only and Period 2 (about 1200 or 1300 to 1521) as bronze alloys, with mines near Churumuco and Inguarán. Bells carry up to 20 percent tin, far beyond any structural need, which Hosler reads as a cultural choice for tone and colour. Dating comes from stratified finds and radiocarbon at sites such as Tomatlán and Amapa, so 1300 marks an onset, not a single event.

zhu-shijie-jade-mirror-1303.summary: Zhu Shijie, a wandering teacher who had already issued a popular textbook in 1299, printed Siyuan yujian (Jade Mirror of Four Unknowns) in 1303. Its 288 problems in three volumes extend counting-rod algebra to equations with up to four unknowns laid out on a board around a central constant, eliminate variables step by step, and solve polynomial equations to degree fourteen by a method akin to Horner's scheme. He also gives summation formulas for stacked piles and a triangle of binomial coefficients to eighth power. Chinese algebra reached its peak here and then faded until Qing scholars recovered rod methods and Western readers met them through Martzloff and Needham.

sources.title: Martzloff, Jean-Claude, A History of Chinese Mathematics (Berlin: Springer, 2006)
sources.author: Martzloff, Jean-Claude
sources.confirms: Siyuan yujian's four-unknown elimination, polynomial solving and series

sources.title: O'Connor, J. J. and E. F. Robertson, 'Zhu Shijie', MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive
sources.author: O'Connor, J. J.; Robertson, E. F.
sources.confirms: 1303 publication; 288 problems in three volumes; four unknowns; equations to degree 14; 1299 Suanxue qimeng

zhu-shijie-jade-mirror-1303.detail: Jean-Claude Martzloff's history treats Zhu's elimination procedure as a general algebraic technique rather than isolated puzzles. MacTutor's biography summarises content and dating. Zhu's text survived through Korean and later Chinese editions; little is known of his life beyond prefaces.

picture.credit: Zhu Shijie, Siyuan yujian (1303)

sea-coal-ban-1306.summary: In 1307 Edward I banned burning sea coal in kilns in London and Southwark because of its smoke, the first recorded air pollution law; by 1321 to 1322 royal palace clerks were ordering coal for their king's own fires. Prelates, magnates and citizens had complained, and commissions had already inquired into lime kilns in 1285 and 1288.

[PDF] overview by ian williams - University of Southampton

sources.qualifies: Te Brake dates the proclamation to 1307 and limits it to kilns; he cites the Calendar of Close Rolls, Edward I (1302-7), p. 537, and mentions no parliamentary petition.

al-farisi-rainbow-explanation-1309.summary: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi, a student of Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi at Tabriz under Ilkhanid rule, writes Tanqih al-Manazir, a critical revision of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics; an autograph copy is dated Ramadan 708 AH (early 1309). In an appendix on halo and rainbow he treats a raindrop as a transparent sphere, places a water-filled glass globe in a dark chamber with one aperture, and traces sunlight through it. He shows that a primary bow comes from two refractions with one internal reflection and a secondary bow from two reflections between refractions, which also explains its reversed colour order. Theodoric of Freiberg reached identical geometry in Germany within a decade; Descartes repeated this sphere experiment three centuries later. Al-Farisi's account of why colours appear did not hold.

sources.title: Rashed, R., 'Le modèle de la sphère transparente et l'explication de l'arc-en-ciel: Ibn al-Haytham, al-Farisi', Revue d'histoire des sciences 23 (1970), 109-140
sources.author: Rashed, Roshdi
sources.confirms: Analyses al-Farisi's transparent-sphere model for the rainbow and its roots in Ibn al-Haytham's burning sphere.

sources.title: Rashed, R., 'Kamal al-Din al-Farisi', Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Scribner, 1973)
sources.author: Rashed, Roshdi
sources.confirms: Dark chamber with one opening and a water-filled sphere; primary arc from refraction, reflection, refraction; ring from two reflections; Wiedemann dates the final version between 1302 and 1311.
sources.qualifies: Gives Tabriz with a query as place of death in 1320 and dates completion to a range rather than one year.

sources.title: Sabra, A. I., 'Faresi, Kamal-al-Din', Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.author: Sabra, A. I.
sources.confirms: Correctly accounts for the arc, primary and secondary bows and colour reversal; glass sphere in a dark room with a single aperture; colour explanation unsuccessful.

al-farisi-rainbow-explanation-1309.verification_note: An autograph date of 708 AH is reported in secondary literature; Wiedemann's range 1302 to 1311 is standard scholarly dating, so approximate_year is set.

picture.credit: Kamāl al-Dīn al-Fārisī (1267-1319), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

rashid-al-din-rab-e-rashidi-scriptorium-.summary: Rashid al-Din Fadlallah, physician and vizier to Ilkhanid rulers, signs an endowment deed for his foundation in an eastern suburb of Tabriz on 9 August 1309 (1 Rabi I 709). Rab-e Rashidi holds a mosque, hospital, library, paper mill and book workshop with salaried scribes and painters. A codicil of 1313 to 1314 orders two copies a year of his own works, including Jami al-Tawarikh, one in Arabic and one in Persian, on large Baghdadi paper, collated against a master copy, bound in leather and sent to cities across Ilkhanid lands for anyone to consult or copy against a deposit. Painters cut page sizes and simplified scenes to keep pace. An Arabic copy dated 714 AH (1314) survives split between Edinburgh University Library and Khalili Collections. Rashid al-Din is executed in 1318 and his foundation is looted.

sources.title: Blair, S. S., 'Ilkhanid Architecture and Society: An Analysis of the Endowment Deed of the Rab'-i Rashidi', Iran 22 (1984), 67-90
sources.author: Blair, Sheila S.
sources.confirms: Analysis of the surviving waqf deed and the foundation's staff and functions.

sources.title: Edinburgh University Library, Heritage Collections, 'Jami al-tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), 714 A.H. (1314 C.E.)', Or Ms 20
sources.author: Rashid al-Din Tabib
sources.confirms: Arabic copy made in Tabriz by the author's own scribes and illustrators; the Khalili portion of the same manuscript is dated 714 AH (1314); 151 folios with 70 illustrated pages.

sources.title: Blair, S. S., 'Jame al-Tawarikh ii. Illustrations', Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.author: Blair, Sheila S.
sources.confirms: Deed dated 1 Rabi I 709 / 9 August 1309 in the patron's hand; addendum four years later requiring two copies a year in Arabic and Persian on Baghdadi paper, collated, bound and distributed; artists sped up production; execution in 1318.

wang-zhen-nong-shu-1313.summary: Yuan dynasty magistrate Wang Zhen (1271 to 1333) completes Nong Shu in 1313 after serving in Jingde, Anhui and Yongfeng, Jiangxi, where he saw northern dry farming and southern rice side by side. The book runs 22 or 37 chapters in three parts: general farming, individual crops, and Nongqi tupu, an illustrated catalogue of 273 tools from ploughs and seed drills to water-powered trip hammers, silk reels and polder fields, each with drawing, verse and notes on use. Bray calls his pairing of text with pictures a new method of encoding technical information, made possible by woodblock printing. He includes Chen Fu's rice methods and aims to carry southern wet-rice technique north and northern tools south.

sources.title: Bray, F., 'Science, technique, technology: passages between matter and knowledge in imperial Chinese agriculture', British Journal for the History of Science 41 (2008), 319-344
sources.author: Bray, Francesca
sources.venue: British Journal for the History of Science
sources.confirms: States Wang Zhen's Nongshu was completed in 1313, documented tools and methods from across China for north-south technology transfer, incorporated Chen Fu's rice techniques, and pioneered pairing text with illustrations.

sources.title: Bray, F., 'Thinking with Diagrams: The Chaine Operatoire and the Transmission of Technical Knowledge in Chinese Agricultural Texts', East Asian Science, Technology and Society 14 (2020), 199-223
sources.author: Bray, Francesca
sources.venue: East Asian Science, Technology and Society
sources.confirms: Dates the Nongshu to 1313 and attributes Wang's copious graphics to woodblock printing.
sources.qualifies: Editors' introduction to the same issue gives 1303 as the publication year.

sources.title: Chinaknowledge, 'Nongshu by Wang Zhen'
sources.author: Theobald, Ulrich
sources.confirms: Gives Wang Zhen's dates, posts in Jingde and Yongfeng, three-part structure, 273 illustrated tools in Nongqi tupu, and the movable type appendix.

wang-zhen-nong-shu-1313.detail: Nongqi tupu is the earliest systematic illustrated encyclopedia of agricultural machinery; later Ming compilers including Xu Guangqi copied its plates. An appendix describes wooden movable type Wang devised to print a county gazetteer, first such account anywhere. Wang's drawings of square-pallet chain pump, water-driven blowers and multi-tube seed drill reached Europe in 18th-century Jesuit reports. Some scholars cite 1303 for this treatise; Bray's 2008 and 2020 studies both give 1313.

picture.alt: Woodcut from Wang Zhen's Nong Shu: water wheels driving bellows for iron smelting
picture.credit: Wang Zhen, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

wang-zhen-wooden-movable-type-1313.summary: In 1313 Wang Zhen set wooden movable type on a revolving table of 60,000 characters, cutting typesetting time. His Nong Shu described the type he had pioneered as magistrate of Jingde in Anhui between 1290 and 1301. Bi Sheng had tried wood in the 11th century and rejected it as unsuitable; Wang added exact methods for cutting and finishing type and locked pieces firmly into one frame with wooden plugs before inking. His main gain was speed: all characters were sorted by tone and rhyme on two revolving tables so one seated compositor could find each piece.

sources.qualifies: Carter dates the description to 1314; the record uses 1313, the year Wang Zhen's Nong Shu was completed.

spondent-pariter-alchemy-ban-1317.summary: Around 1317, a conventional date since its decree is undated, Pope John XXII punished alchemists' fraud: they promised gold they could not deliver. His decree Spondent quas non exhibent, sometimes called Spondent pariter, targeted false metal without banning alchemy outright. Anyone making, ordering or selling false alchemical metal to pay debts owed one fine equal to what that weight of true gold or silver would cost, with prison possible. Using such metal to forge coins was condemned too, in a period when papal Avignon was awash in counterfeit currency.

'John XXII', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page states that John XXII issued the bull Execrabilis in 1317, increasing papal control over church-office distribution and recipients’ fees. It separately dates the decretals Ad Conditorem Canonum to 1322 and Cum Inter Nonnullos to 1323;
sources.qualifies: 1317 is stated for Execrabilis, but the named decretal and alchemy condemnation are absent.

ely-cathedral-tower-collapse-1322.summary: In 1322 Ely Cathedral's tower fell; in its place rose a timber octagon lantern like no other. Rather than rebuild on its old square plan, sacrist Alan of Walsingham's team removed all four tower piers and opened the crossing into one octagon absorbing adjoining bays, perhaps from distrust of soft ground under those piers. Its stone octagon carries timber vaulting and one glazed timber lantern that seems to float on slender struts. How much Walsingham designed remains debated.

mansa-musa-hajj-1324.summary: In July 1324 Mali's king Mansa Musa reached Cairo on his pilgrimage and gave away so much gold that its price fell for a decade. Al-Umari, who visited Cairo soon after, wrote that a mithqal of gold fell from 25 silver dirhams to under 22 and stayed there for at least twelve years. Historian Warren Schultz counters that this lay within normal swings in Mamluk Egypt's gold value. Most of what is known about Musa comes from such Arabic accounts written after his hajj.

tenochtitlan-founded-1325.summary: Around 1325 Mexica settlers founded Tenochtitlan on an island; in 200 years it was among the world's largest cities. Its exact founding date is unclear; 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 for 600th anniversary celebrations. Three raised causeways joined it to shore, cut by bridges that let canoes pass and could be pulled up in defense. It became capital of the expanding Aztec Empire and pre-Columbian America's largest city before Tlaxcaltec and Spanish forces captured it in 1521.

ibn-battuta-travels-1325.summary: In 1325 Ibn Battuta left Tangier for Mecca and kept travelling for 30 years across much of Africa, Asia and Iberia, some 117,000 to 120,000 kilometres by different counts, far beyond Marco Polo's 24,000. Near his life's end he dictated his account, A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities, known as the Rihla; most of what is known about him comes from it.

milemete-cannon-1326.summary: In 1326 an English manuscript drew Europe's first gun, a vase-shaped pot firing an arrow. It shows a vase-shaped pot-de-fer lying on its table, with one armored man about to touch its vent with red-hot iron. Such "iron pots" were bottles with narrow necks, loaded with powder and an iron-feathered bolt; they replaced spring-powered springalds. Through the 1300s tube-shaped barrels replaced them and grew into bombards.

djinguereber-mosque-1327.summary: In 1327 Timbuktu completed the Djinguereber mosque in mud brick; replastered yearly, it has stood 700 years. It is one of three mosques linked to the city's scholarly community. Ibn Khaldun credited its design to Andalusi scholar Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, reportedly paid 12,000 mithqals of gold dust; recent analyses trace its style instead to Saharan mosques and older African building, treating his influence as myth. Apart from a limestone minaret and some 1960s reinforcement, it is built of earth with straw, fibre and wood. UNESCO listed it in 1988.

wallingford-clock-1327.summary: In 1327 Richard of Wallingford described, in a treatise, a clock to show Moon phases and tides at London Bridge. William of Walsham finished it about 20 years after Richard died in 1336. His design showed mean time in equal and unequal hours and true solar time, lunar phases, positions of lunar nodes and tide height at London Bridge, almost certainly the most complex clockwork then in Britain. It was apparently destroyed when Henry VIII dissolved St Albans Abbey in 1539; modern reconstructions rest on Richard's surviving text.

vijayanagara-hampi-waterworks-1336.summary: From 1336 Hampi grew on aqueducts and tanks into what was probably India's richest city by 1500. Vijayanagara's rulers made this site on the Tungabhadra River, in today's Karnataka, its capital. Its fortified urban core held roads, an aqueduct, water tanks, gateways, monasteries and markets alongside temples. Persian and Portuguese travellers described prosperity, farms and trading markets; by 1500 it was also the world's second-largest city after Beijing. Armies of allied sultanates conquered, pillaged and destroyed it in 1565, and Hampi stayed in ruins.

vijayanagara-era-1336.summary: In 1336 two brothers founded Vijayanagara, which held southern India for three centuries against Deccan sultanates. This Hindu empire came to rule most of southern India, peaking under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529), when it pushed Deccan sultanates north of the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers. It survived until 1646, though central authority fell sharply after allied Deccan sultanates defeated it at Talikota in 1565.

bardi-peruzzi-bankruptcy-1344.summary: In the 1340s Florence's two largest merchant-banking companies, Bardi and Peruzzi, collapsed; Britannica dates the Bardi bankruptcy to 1345. Both traded wool cloth, grain, oil and wine between England and Mediterranean ports and lent to governments. Chronicler Giovanni Villani, whose brother held a Peruzzi partnership, blamed England's Edward III for repudiating war loans he put at 900,000 and 600,000 florins. Edwin Hunt (Journal of Economic History, 1990) showed both firms lacked resources to lend on that scale, that Edward never specifically repudiated their debts, and that they may have recovered part of their advances through channels absent from royal ledgers; overextension, including support for Florence's war with Lucca, brought them down. Acciaiuoli, Florence's third great company, failed too.

black-death-1346.summary: From 1346 plague killed a third or more of Europe; scarce labour raised wages for a century. Yersinia pestis bacteria spread mainly by flea bites and, in pneumonic cases, by breath. Its origin is unclear; it reportedly entered Europe in 1347 at Genoa's Crimean port of Caffa under Golden Horde siege, then travelled on rats aboard Genoese ships through the Mediterranean.

sources.author: Wheelis, Mark

sources.qualifies: The page does not support entry at Genoa in 1347.

sources.qualifies: Dates and mortality are broadly consistent; the page does not state the claimed 1346 start, Genoa entry, transmission routes, or wage effects.

sources.title: 'Black Death', Encyclopaedia Britannica

black-death-1346.verification_note: Wheelis, EID 2002, calls this Caffa transmission story anecdotal and gives European losses of a quarter to a third; Bos et al., Nature 2011, date this pandemic 1347-1351 with 30 to 50 percent mortality.

egypt-black-death-1348.summary: Plague arrived at Alexandria by ship in autumn 1347 and spread up the Nile through 1348. Al-Maqrizi reports deaths in Alexandria climbing to 200 a day and, at Cairo's peak in late 1348, counts of thousands a day recorded at mosques and city gates. Sultan al-Nasir Hasan and his amirs withdrew to Siryaqus from 25 September to 22 December 1348 while prayers and funeral processions filled Cairo. Michael Dols, working from Arabic chronicles, documented a demographic collapse that recurred with later waves; Stuart Borsch argued that depopulation broke the labour-intensive dyke and canal system of Egyptian agriculture, with consequences lasting into the fifteenth century.

sources.author: Dols, Michael W.
sources.confirms: Monograph on plague mortality and responses in Egypt and Syria from Arabic chronicles

egypt-black-death-1348.verification_note: Daily death figures follow al-Maqrizi as quoted by Borsch and Dols; chroniclers' numbers are not verifiable and scholars treat them as orders of magnitude.
egypt-black-death-1348.detail: Dols compared Muslim and Christian responses: Egyptian ulama framed plague as martyrdom for believers rather than divine punishment, and did not endorse flight or contagion theory. Fustat residents nonetheless fled east, leaving quarters in ruins. Borsch's comparison with England found that Mamluk landholding arrangements left Egypt unable to reallocate labour, so output fell while England recovered. Scholars differ on total mortality, often cited as a third of Egypt's population.

flagellants-1349.summary: In 1349 flagellants marched from town to town whipping themselves to avert plague; Pope Clement VI condemned them on 20 October that year. Spreading through northern and central Europe during the Black Death, they held plague to be God's punishment for sin; new members pledged thirty-three and a half days of pilgrimage, one for each year of Christ's life, under lay masters who heard confessions and dealt out whippings. France's king barred them on advice from Paris theologians.

black-death-jewish-persecutions-1349.summary: On 14 February 1349 Strasbourg burned 2,000 Jews alive, blamed for a plague that had not yet reached their city. As plague spread, Jewish communities across Europe were accused of poisoning wells, with confessions extracted under torture. Pope Clement VI had issued two bulls in 1348 declaring such accusations the work of "that liar" the devil, to little effect. Some 510 Jewish communities were destroyed between 1348 and 1351, driving large migration to Poland and Lithuania.

charkha-spinning-wheel-india-1350.summary: Isami's 1350 Futuh us-Salatin gives earliest unambiguous Indian reference to a spinning wheel, a hand-cranked wheel driving a spindle through a cord, replacing drop-spindle hand spinning. Irfan Habib argues it arrived from Iran with Turkish rule in thirteenth century and spread through Sultanate towns, multiplying a spinner's output several fold and lowering yarn cost for a cotton industry already dyeing and printing for export. A manuscript illustration of 1468 shows a woman at a wheel. By Mughal period, charkha spinning by women in households fed weaving across Gujarat, Bengal and Coromandel. Gandhi later took this wheel as emblem of self-reliance.

Smith and Cothren argued for earlier Indian use; Habib replies that no pre-Sultanate Indian text or image shows a wheel. Year 1350 marks the earliest secure Indian reference, not first use.

ibn-al-shatir-planetary-models-1350.summary: Ala al-Din Ibn al-Shatir (1305 to 1375), muwaqqit responsible for prayer times at Damascus's Umayyad Mosque, writes Nihayat al-sul fi tashih al-usul, in which every planet, Sun and Moon move on combinations of uniformly rotating circles with no equant point and no eccentric deferent. His lunar model removes Ptolemy's doubling of lunar apparent size, and his Mercury model uses a Tusi couple. His al-Zij al-Jadid turns these models into tables. E. S. Kennedy and Victor Roberts showed in Isis in 1957 and 1959 that Copernicus's lunar and planetary models in his Commentariolus, a century and a half later, are mathematically identical constructions. Ibn al-Shatir also built a sundial for his mosque in 1371 and an astronomical compendium instrument.

ife-bronze-heads-1100.summary: Around 1310 to 1350 Ife's artists cast brass heads so lifelike that Europeans later doubted Africans made them. This head was cast in heavily leaded zinc-brass by lost-wax casting, in which wax is modelled, coated in clay, melted out and replaced by molten metal. Museum curators date it to the 14th or early 15th century, while Blier places such heads around 1310 to 1350 on thermoluminescence dates, during Ife's long period as trade and religious centre. Its identity and function remain uncertain; its beaded headdress, possibly representing a crown, suggests association with an Ooni, ruler of Ife, rather than a portrait of one named person.

sukhothai-si-satchanalai-kilns-1350.summary: Along Yom river north of Sukhothai, potters at Si Satchanalai and Sukhothai town built hundreds of brick cross-draft kilns and fired celadon, underglaze-black and brown-glazed stoneware. Thermoluminescence dating by Barbetti and Hein shows stoneware production after about 900, with large-scale output from thirteenth to fifteenth centuries after kilns moved from pits to surface structures. Jars, bowls and figurines from these kilns turn up in shipwrecks and burial sites from Philippines to Indonesia, filling demand when Ming export restrictions cut Chinese supply. Production declined in sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and UNESCO listed Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai towns in 1991.

yuan-paper-money-inflation-1350.summary: In 1350 Mongol China printed money backed by nothing; and the hyperinflation that followed helped end Mongol rule. Paper money under Jin and Song had already run through cycles of overprinting, inflation and public flight to silver. Mongol rulers issued their own notes from 1227, first backed by silk; Kublai Khan's Zhongtong and Zhiyuan notes in turn suffered devaluation and hyperinflation. In 1350 Yuan's court issued its final series, Zhizheng Jiaochao, as pure fiat money, and people widely refused it. Marco Polo's chronicler, William of Rubruck and Ibn Battuta all described China's paper currency to outsiders.

statute-of-labourers-1351.summary: In 1351 England's first national labour law froze wages at pre-plague levels and barred moving for better pay. Parliament enacted the Statute of Labourers under Edward III in response to labour shortages after the Black Death. It set maximum wages at levels paid before plague, specifically those of 1346, and restricted labourers from moving to seek better conditions.

taghaza-salt-mines-1352.summary: Ibn Battuta left Sijilmasa on 13 February 1352 and after 25 days reached Taghaza, a mining settlement deep in the western Sahara where houses and a mosque were built of salt blocks roofed with camel skins. Enslaved Masufa workers cut rock salt into slabs; each camel carried two, and caravans hauled them south to Walata and Mali, where a load fetched 20 to 40 mithqals of gold against 8 to 10 at Walata. Nothing grew at Taghaza, so food came in from the south and water from brackish wells. His account is the earliest eyewitness description of this trade that underwrote Mali's gold exports.

taghaza-salt-mines-1352.detail: Taghaza supplied salt to Sahelian markets until Moroccan forces seized it in the sixteenth century and mining shifted to Taoudenni. E. Ann McDougall's work on Saharan salts traces how control of these deposits shaped relations between Saharan nomads, Mali and Songhay, and later Morocco's 1591 invasion. Ibn Battuta's travel narrative, dictated to Ibn Juzayy after his return, survives in manuscripts edited and translated in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

strasbourg-clock-rooster-1354.summary: In 1354 Strasbourg's cathedral clock was finished with a crowing rooster, made about 1349 and installed about 1352, the West's oldest surviving automaton. Its centerpiece was a gilded mechanical rooster of iron, copper and wood, taken as a symbol of Christ's Passion. At noon it flapped its wings, spread its feathers, opened its beak, put out its tongue and crowed through bellows and reed. Reused in Strasbourg's second clock, it survives in that city's Museum of Decorative Arts and is held to be the oldest surviving automaton in the West.

firuz-shah-yamuna-canals-1355.summary: Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq ordered canals from Yamuna and Sutlej rivers in 1355 to carry water to his new town Hisar-i Firuza and to dry tracts of Haryana. Engineers dug channels roughly 150 kilometres long with fall graded for gravity flow, and Firuz levied a water tax (haqq-i shurb) on irrigated fields. Contemporary chroniclers Barani and Afif report rising revenue, two crops a year and new villages along canal banks. A rebuilt line of his Yamuna canal became Mughal Nahr-i Bihisht to Delhi and then British Western Jumna Canal, making this one of South Asia's longest-lived irrigation works.

sources.title: Iqtidar Husain Siddiqui, 'Water Works and Irrigation System in India during Pre-Mughal Times', Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 29 (1986)

huolongjing-gunpowder-manual-1360.summary: Around 1360 Ming general Jiao Yu wrote the Fire Dragon Manual's earliest edition, finished by 1375, drawing on a now-lost illustrated text; its preface appeared only in Nanyang's edition of 1412. It guides use of gunpowder "fire weapons" China had used from the 1280s to 1350s: land mines, cast-bronze "eruptor" cannon about 130 centimetres long and fire arrows launched from hollow tubes, early rockets.

de-dondi-astrarium-1364.summary: In 1364 Giovanni de' Dondi finished a 107-gear clock that tracked the Sun, Moon and five planets on a tabletop. He, a scholar and physician, named it astrarium. Its 107 wheels and pinions combined timekeeping and calendar functions with displays of mean and sidereal time and of Sun, Moon and five then-known planets, following Ptolemy's Earth-centered model. Historians Bedini and Maddison call it the earliest astronomical clock with near-complete description and firm documentation. Its original was lost, perhaps in Mantua's sack of 1630, but de' Dondi's detailed account survives and has guided reconstructions.

ming-era-1368.summary: In 1368 the Ming expelled Mongol rulers and ruled China for 276 years, sending fleets to Africa, then turning in. This dynasty, officially Great Ming, ruled until 1644, China's last imperial dynasty ruled by Han Chinese. Founder Hongwu sought self-sufficient rural communities in fixed order. Yongle moved his capital to Beijing, built its Forbidden City, restored China's Grand Canal and sent eunuch Zheng He on seven Indian Ocean voyages. Beijing fell in 1644 to rebel Li Zicheng; Southern Ming remnants held out until 1662.

It gives no information about 1368, Mongol expulsion, the dynasty’s duration or end, fleets to Africa, or Hongwu’s policies.

haijin-sea-ban-1371.summary: In 1371 Ming rulers banned private sea trade; China turned from the ocean as Europe took to it. Founder Zhu Yuanzhang limited legal foreign trade to official tribute missions and placed overseas commerce under government monopoly. It answered Japanese piracy amid anti-Ming insurgency, but proved unenforceable: trade continued as smuggling, and piracy became endemic in waves, much of it by Chinese dispossessed by this policy. Piracy fell to negligible levels once this ban ended in 1567. It also slowed growth of China's domestic trade.

sources.title: Haijin - Wikipedia

da-ming-baochao-1375.summary: In 1375 the Ming issued paper money declared valid forever and printed too much of it; within a century these notes were worthless. A note of 1 guàn nominally equaled one thousand bronze coins. They had no backing in metal reserves, and officials set no limit on printing. Overprinting plus government reluctance to accept its own notes destroyed trust, driving silver's price upward. Later emperors abolished issue; by 1535 one guàn of paper was worth 0.28 of a coin. Qing rulers took that lesson and long avoided paper money.

sources.title: Great Ming Treasure Note - Wikipedia

sources.confirms: The page identifies a chapter, “Paper Money from the Yüan Dynasty to the End of the Ch’ing Dynasty,” on pages 62-70. It states none of the specific claims about Ming notes, including the 1375 date, overprinting, depreciation, guàn-to-coin value, metal backing, or issuance limits.

sources.title: 'Hongwu', Encyclopaedia Britannica

ibn-khaldun-muqaddimah-1377.summary: In 1377 Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah explained why states rise and fall by social forces, not God or chance. He wrote it as introduction and first book of his planned world history, Kitab al-ʿIbar. It proposed ʿilm al-ʿumrān, a new science of human society and its changes through history, ranging over historiography, economics, political theory and ecology. Its best-known idea is ʿasabiyyah, group cohesion: ruling houses rise on the edges of empires through strong solidarity, lose it in power and comfort, and fall to groups with stronger bonds. Many modern thinkers count it the first work of sociology.

sources.title: Muqaddimah - Wikipedia
Chapter 3 Ibn Khaldun the Statesman (Ibn Khaldun, 2010)
sources.confirms: The page identifies this as Chapter 3, “Ibn Khaldun the Statesman,” in a 2010 book (pp. 60-96).
sources.qualifies: The page does not state that he completed a draft in 1377, describe the Muqaddimah as the introduction and first book of Kitab al-ʿIbar, or mention ʿilm al-ʿumrān.

It does not explicitly say he completed it in 1377.
sources.qualifies: The other elements are supported, but completion in that year is not stated.

jikji-metal-type-1377-1377.summary: In 1377 Korean monks printed Jikji with movable metal type, 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible. This anthology of Zen Buddhist teachings, compiled by monk Baegun, was printed at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, three years after his death. His students Seoksan and Daldam, with Myodeok, published it in two volumes. Only its second metal-type volume survives, held in France's National Library. UNESCO confirmed it in 2001 as the world's oldest extant book printed with movable metal type.

It states that more than 14,000 types, including repeated uses, were used in the second volume, and that its typesetting was less regular than Joseon-period practice.
sources.qualifies: The metal-type and Goryeo claims are supported; the specific dates and other details are absent.

It does not state that it was printed at Heungdeok temple.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the year, Korea, Buddhist subject matter, and metal-type claim, but does not name Heungdeok temple.

ragusa-quarantine-1377.summary: On 27 July 1377 Ragusa's Great Council, ruling a trading republic on the Adriatic (now Dubrovnik), decreed that people and ships arriving from plague-infected places could not enter until they had spent a month on Mrkan islet or at Cavtat. This law, recorded in Ragusa's Liber Viridis, was the first municipal isolation rule of its kind; Venice set up a lazaretto in 1423 and stretched it to forty days, a wait from which quarantena takes its name. Ragusa followed with a permanent Health Office in 1390 and built its Lazareti outside its eastern gate in the 1620s. Trentino, this thirty-day rule, worked without any knowledge of plague's cause, by matching isolation to how long an infected traveller took to fall ill.

sources.title: Blazina Tomic, Zlata; Blazina, Vesna, Expelling the Plague: The Health Office and the Implementation of Quarantine in Dubrovnik, 1377-1533 (McGill-Queen's University Press, 2015)
sources.author: Blazina Tomic, Zlata; Blazina, Vesna
sources.confirms: Confirms that in 1377 Dubrovnik became the first city to adopt quarantine legislation and that it established a permanent Health Office in 1390.

sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Confirms the 27 July 1377 date, the thirty-day period, Mrkan and Cavtat as isolation sites, and the Liber Viridis record.

picture.credit: Lasta, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ciompi-revolt-1378.summary: In 1378 Florence's wool workers, with no guild and no vote, ran Florence's government for six weeks. These unrepresented labourers were called Ciompi; belonging to no guild, they had no voice in government yet owed heavy taxes. After minor guilds demanded more office in June, the Ciompi took up arms on 22 June and on 21 July seized government, forcing the Signoria to create three new guilds with political office. Their government fell late in August 1378; a regime after 1382 repealed its reforms and dissolved those new guilds.

salisbury-cathedral-clock-1386.summary: Around 1386 Salisbury Cathedral's clock began running; it still does and is said to be Earth's oldest working clock, though its dating and that claim are both disputed. Two descending stone weights power it, one for its going train, regulated by verge-and-foliot escapement of the earliest mechanical type, another for its striking train. Its usual date rests on a 1386 document naming a clock keeper; specialists dispute whether the surviving frame, identified by Howgrave-Graham in 1929, is that clock or a later one.

Howgrave-Graham, R. P., 'A Great Cathedral Clock Rediscovered', Practical Watch and Clock Maker (1929) 445-447
sources.author: Howgrave-Graham, R. P.
sources.venue: Practical Watch and Clock Maker (Antiquarian Horological Society document archive)
sources.confirms: Howgrave-Graham reports the rediscovery of the Salisbury Cathedral clock mechanism, a clock documented at the cathedral in 1386, and describes the foliot escapement later replaced by an anchor.
sources.qualifies: He treats the identification of the surviving mechanism with the 1386 clock as an inference from documents, not an established fact.

sources.title: Church of England, 'Salisbury Cathedral', Church Heritage Record 12031
sources.author: Church of England

salisbury-cathedral-clock-1386.verification_note: A 1386 document naming a clock keeper, not the surviving mechanism, supplies its date; Howgrave-Graham identified that mechanism in 1929, and specialists still dispute whether its frame is the clock of 1386 or a later one.
salisbury-cathedral-clock-1386.detail: Set aside in 1884 when its successor was installed, it was rediscovered in 1928 in Salisbury's central tower, by then fitted with a pendulum in place of verge and foliot. Restoration in 1956 gave it reproduction verge and foliot; it now stands in Salisbury's north nave aisle near its west front. Its original bell tower was demolished in 1790. Rival claimants to oldest working clock include Beauvais Cathedral's clock in France, said to date from 1305 and entirely preserved in its frame, Chioggia's clock tower in Italy and Comayagua Cathedral's clock in Honduras, said to be Moorish work of the 12th century though records are lost.

picture.credit: Arpingstone (Adrian Pingstone), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

dai-viet-firearms-1390.summary: In 1390 Vietnamese forces on Luoc river fired guns into Cham king Che Bong Nga's flagship and killed him, ending two decades of Cham raids on Thang Long. Sun Laichen traces how handguns and cannon moved from Ming China into Dai Viet in late fourteenth century through border trade and captured arms, then onward to Lan Xang, Lan Na and Ayutthaya during Ming occupation of Vietnam (1407-1427) and after. Vietnamese smiths adapted Chinese designs so well that Ming armies later copied Vietnamese guns. Tonio Andrade places this diffusion within a wider East Asian gunpowder age that predates Portuguese arrival.

sources.author: Sun, Laichen

Portuguese chroniclers found guns already in Melaka in 1511. Sun stresses overland and riverine transfer rather than maritime European routes.

kingdom-of-kongo-1390.summary: Around 1390 the Kingdom of Kongo arose in Central Africa; a century on it exchanged ambassadors with Portugal. It began with marriage between Nima a Nzima of Mpemba Kasi and Lukeni lua Nsanze of Mbata; their son Lukeni lua Nimi began its expansion. Ruled by its Manikongo, it stretched from Atlantic shores to the Kwango River. Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão arrived in 1483, and in 1491 King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised as João I. Kongo stayed independent until 1862, then served intermittently as Portugal's vassal until Portugal abolished its monarchy in 1914 after crushing one revolt.

stromer-paper-mill-nuremberg-1390.summary: On 24 June 1390 Nuremberg merchant Ulman Stromer starts making paper at Gleissmuhle mill on the Pegnitz, first paper mill in German lands, with Italian workmen he had hired and sworn to secrecy. His own chronicle records it: »Ich Ulman Stromer, hub an mit dem ersten papir zu machen zu sant johanns tag und der Clos Obsser war der erst der zu der arbait kam«. Paper had reached Europe through Xativa in Muslim Spain around 1100 and Fabriano in Italy by the 1270s; Stromer's mill carried papermaking north just as demand from chanceries, merchants and, sixty years later, Gutenberg's press began to climb. It appears in Schedel's Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493.

sources.author: Stadtarchiv Nurnberg

stromer-paper-mill-nuremberg-1390.detail: Lore Sporhan-Krempel's 1954 article in Archivalische Zeitschrift remains the standard archival study of that mill, and Wolfgang von Stromer's 1970 Business History Review article sets Stromer family businesses inside Nuremberg's late-medieval trading economy. Stromer's account survives in his Puchel von meim geslechet und von abentewr, a family chronicle begun in 1360, which also records that he made his Italian workers swear not to teach papermaking to anyone outside his mill.

chaucer-treatise-astrolabe-1391.summary: Geoffrey Chaucer writes A Treatise on the Astrolabe in Middle English for a ten-year-old, opening “Litell Lowis my sone, I have perceived wel by certeyne evidences thyn abilite to lerne sciencez touchinge noumbres and proporciouns”. Its worked examples are fixed to a date: “the yeer of oure lord 1391, the 12 day of March at midday, I wolde knowe the degree of the sonne”. It is English's earliest technical manual and shows how far an Islamic instrument had travelled: a Latin tradition descending from Arabic texts, now put into English for a London household. A 15th-century copy survives as British Library Sloane MS 314, and 14th-century English-made astrolabes survive in Cambridge's Whipple Museum.

chaucer-treatise-astrolabe-1391.detail: Walter Skeat edited it for the Early English Text Society in 1872 and again in Clarendon Press's Complete Works of 1900, quoted here. Chaucer worked from a 12th-century Latin translation of Messahala's Arabic astrolabe text. It explains its parts first and then gives forty short conclusions, each a procedure such as finding daytime hours or an ascendant at a given moment, so a child could follow it with astrolabe in hand.

joseon-era-1392.summary: In 1392 a new dynasty, Joseon, took Korea and ruled for 505 years, creating Korea's alphabet along the way. Taejo founded it after overthrowing Goryeo, moving his capital in 1393 to today's Seoul. His kingdom lasted until the Korean Empire replaced it in 1897. It pushed its northern border to the Amnok and Tuman rivers, made Neo-Confucianism state ideology while discouraging Buddhism, and saw classical Korean culture, trade, literature, science and technology reach their height. Failed Japanese invasions in 1592 and 1598, then Manchu invasions, severely weakened it.

ho-quy-ly-paper-money-1396.summary: In 1396 Vietnam issued its first paper money, Thông bảo hội sao, and made people hand in copper coins the state needed for weapons. Hồ Quý Ly, a Trần court official who held power behind the throne under king Trần Thuận Tông, ordered those notes on Vương Như Chu's proposal. They came amid his run of reforms after old king Nghệ Tông died in 1395: examinations for scholars and low officials, translation of Confucian classic Book of Documents into Nôm script, rules on official dress and, in 1397, a new capital in Thanh Hóa. In 1400 he deposed Trần rule and took power himself, founding his short-lived Hồ dynasty.

sources.title: Hồ Quý Ly - Wikipedia
Nguyen Thai Dung, 'Ong To cua tien giay Viet Nam', Bao tang Lich su Quoc gia (Vietnam National Museum of History), 25 July 2010
sources.author: Nguyen Thai Dung
sources.confirms: Quoting the Dai Viet su ky toan thu, the Thong bao hoi sao notes were printed and issued in the fourth month of 1396 on Le Quy Ly's order under Emperor Tran Thuan Tong, with copper coin banned.
sources.qualifies: The museum credits the proposal to the official Vuong Nhu Chu and gives the exchange rate as 1 quan of coin for 1 quan 2 tien of paper.

medici-bank-1397.summary: In 1397 the Medici Bank opened in Florence, a date usually taken as its founding, and became its century's most powerful bank. Its Rome branch handled Church deposits; further branches followed across Italy and Europe, and it improved general-ledger accounting through double-entry tracking of debits and credits. It became Europe's largest and most respected bank, and under Cosimo from 1434 its wealth made his family unofficial rulers of Florence. Branches collapsed with Medici political power in 1494.

sources.title: Medici Bank - Wikipedia
de Roover, Raymond, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank 1397-1494 (Harvard University Press, 1963), ch. 3
sources.author: de Roover, Raymond
sources.confirms: 1397 may be regarded as the founding date of the Medici Bank, when Giovanni di Bicci transferred his headquarters from Rome to Florence on 1 October 1397; the bank lasted until 1494.

sources.author: de Roover, Raymond

akan-goldweights-1400.summary: Akan communities in what is now Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire weighed gold dust on balances against small cast-brass weights, geometric at first and later shaped as animals, tools and proverb scenes. Timothy Garrard showed that their weight series derives from Islamic standards, the mithqal and the Islamic ounce, reaching Akan gold producers along Mande trade routes from Jenne and Begho. Akan smiths adopted this metrology about 1400 and used it until British colonial currency displaced gold dust around 1900. Hundreds of thousands of weights survive in museums, each a record of lost-wax casting skill and of a market system that priced gold against cloth, salt and later European goods.

sources.title: Garrard, Timothy F., 'Myth and Metrology: The Early Trans-Saharan Gold Trade', Journal of African History 23 (1982)
sources.author: Garrard, Timothy F.
sources.confirms: Akan made the Islamic weight standard the basis of their weight system from about 1400 to 1900; demolition of claims of a Roman-era trans-Saharan gold trade

sources.title: British Museum, Collection search: Akan gold-weights, Ghana (2,105 objects)
sources.confirms: 2,105 Akan gold-weights from Ghana in the collection, most dated 1700-1900

akan-goldweights-1400.detail: For his 1980 book Akan Weights and the Gold Trade, Garrard used metrological analysis of more than 8,000 weights to overturn earlier claims of Egyptian or Portuguese origin, and in 1982 he demolished the myth that Roman-era caravans supplied Mediterranean gold. Weights also served as teaching objects: figurative types encode sayings used in dispute and ceremony. Dating of adoption is inferred from weight standards and trade history rather than excavated contexts, so the year is approximate.

picture.credit: Unknown author

kohala-dryland-field-system-hawaii-1400.summary: On Hawai'i Island's leeward Kohala slopes, farmers laid out a grid of earth and stone embankments and trails covering about 60 square kilometres, planting sweet potato and dryland taro without irrigation. Mapping of walls from aerial photographs and GIS shows expansion from about 1400 CE, with subdivision of fields intensifying through 1600 and 1700s. Dating of residential complexes found household numbers grew in step with new field walls. Kohala fed a growing population and supplied surplus for chiefs during Hawai'i's transition to archaic states under rulers such as 'Umi and later Kamehameha, who was born in Kohala around 1758.

sources.author: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Graves, Michael W.; Jennings, Richard P.
sources.confirms: GIS mapping of Kohala walls and trails and controls on expansion
sources.qualifies: Early dates rest on few samples

sources.author: Field, Julie S.; Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Kirch, Patrick V.

kohala-dryland-field-system-hawaii-1400.detail: Embankments ran across slope to trap moisture and wind-blown soil; trails ran upslope dividing land units. Rainfall and soil age bounded field extent, with older, leached soils excluded. Later soil studies showed Hawaiian farmers targeted soils of intermediate age with the best nutrient supply. Production probably peaked around 1700 and declined after contact in 1778 as population collapsed from introduced disease.

madhava-kerala-school-1400.summary: Around 1400 Madhava in Kerala found infinite series for pi, 250 years before Newton. He is credited with deriving infinite series for π and for sine, cosine and arctangent, centuries before comparable work in Europe, and with correction terms that improve truncated series. Most of his writings are lost; later Kerala scholars, especially Nilakantha around 1500, name him as source, so attribution of some results is debated. His dates rest on circumstantial evidence from pupils' works.

sources.title: Madhava of Sangamagrama - Wikipedia
Madhava de Sangamagrama
sources.confirms: The page gives Madhava’s dates as “Environ 1350” (birth) and “1425” (death), not a finding dated around 1400 (p. 22).
sources.qualifies: The page gives Madhava’s dates as “Environ 1350” (birth) and “1425” (death), not a finding dated around 1400 (p. Cosine, Newton, and the “250 years” comparison are not stated.

mixtec-tomb-7-goldwork-1400.summary: Mixtec workshops in Oaxaca cast gold and tumbaga pectorals, rings, lip plugs and bells whose fine threads imitate wirework, using lost-wax moulds in which wax threads were laid over clay cores. Alfonso Caso's 1932 excavation of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, a Zapotec tomb reopened by Mixtec nobles in Late Postclassic times, yielded more than 120 gold objects alongside turquoise mosaics, carved bones, rock crystal and silver. Ceramic mould fragments from Mixtec sites show a two-part casting technique distinct from South American practice. Spanish conquerors melted most Mesoamerican gold; Tomb 7 survives as the largest intact set of Mixtec metalwork.

sources.title: Levine, Marc N., 'Ceramic Molds for Mixtec Gold: a New Lost-Wax Casting Technique from Prehispanic Mexico', Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory 26 (2019)
sources.author: Levine, Marc N.
sources.venue: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
sources.confirms: Ceramic mould fragments show a distinct Mixtec lost-wax casting technique for gold.

sources.title: Jansen, Maarten and Pérez Jiménez, Gabina Aurora, 'Tomb 7 at Monte Albán', in Time and the Ancestors: Aztec and Mixtec Ritual Art (Brill, 2017), ch. 1
sources.author: Jansen, Maarten; Pérez Jiménez, Gabina Aurora
sources.confirms: Account of Caso's 1932 excavation, contents and Late Postclassic Mixtec reuse of Tomb 7.

sources.title: Ortega-Avilés, M. et al., 'An archaeometallurgical study of Mixtec silver gold alloy foils from Tomb No. 7, Monte Alban, Oaxaca', Materials Chemistry and Physics 242 (2020)
sources.author: Ortega-Avilés, M.; Tenorio-Castilleros, D.; Segura-Venzor, I.L.
sources.confirms: Composition and working of silver-gold foils from Tomb 7.

mixtec-tomb-7-goldwork-1400.verification_note: Tomb 7's Mixtec reuse is dated by pottery association to roughly 1300 to 1500; 1400 is a mid-point. Object counts vary by source: Caso catalogued about 121 gold pieces among more than 500 objects.
mixtec-tomb-7-goldwork-1400.detail: Caso dated Tomb 7's reuse to about 1300 to 1500 by associated Mixteca-Puebla polychrome pottery; Jansen and Pérez Jiménez read its carved bones as a genealogical record of a Mixtec lady. Mould fragments come from Yucundaa and other Mixteca Alta sites and show goldsmiths pressing wax into fired clay matrices before investing, which allowed repeated motifs. A 2020 analysis of silver-gold foils from Tomb 7 found hammered, annealed sheets.

moa-extinction-new-zealand-1400.summary: Within roughly 100 to 150 years of Polynesian arrival in Aotearoa around 1280, every species of moa, flightless birds standing up to 3.6 metres, was gone. A 2000 population model showed a few thousand hunters taking eggs and adults could achieve this quickly. A 2014 study assembled 270 radiocarbon dates from moa bones and eggshell in archaeological middens and found hunting peaked within decades and ended by about 1400 to 1450. A genetic study that year estimated a human population below 2,500 at peak exploitation. Moa loss removed New Zealand's largest herbivores and a major protein source, pushing Maori economies toward kumara gardening, fishing and fern root.

sources.title: Perry, George L. W.; Wheeler, Andrew B.; Wood, Jamie R.; Wilmshurst, Janet M., 'A high-precision chronology for the rapid extinction of New Zealand moa (Aves, Dinornithiformes)', Quaternary Science Reviews 105 (2014)
sources.author: Perry, George L. W.; Wheeler, Andrew B.; Wood, Jamie R.; Wilmshurst, Janet M.
sources.confirms: 270 radiocarbon dates show rapid extinction within about a century, ending c. 1400 to 1450
sources.qualifies: Regional end dates differ by a few decades

moa-extinction-new-zealand-1400.verification_note: Studies agree on rapid extinction; estimates of final date range from about 1400 to 1450, hence approximate year.
moa-extinction-new-zealand-1400.detail: Moa-hunter sites such as Wairau Bar and Shag River Mouth contain remains of thousands of birds, often with only legs taken. Habitat burning of eastern South Island forest compounded hunting. Earlier scholars argued for extinction spread over several centuries; high-precision dating has narrowed it. Some bone dates still carry old-carbon problems, so exact end dates vary by region, with southern populations perhaps surviving a few decades longer.
