soroban-abacus-1400.summary: Around 1400, by one speculation, Chinese abacuses reached Japan as the soroban, merchants' calculator into the computer age. Smith and Mikami report historians usually assigning its importation to late sixteenth century, with Mori Kambei Shigeyoshi its first great teacher under Hideyoshi; merchants may have known its parent suanpan under Ashikaga shoguns. Early sorobans kept two upper and five lower beads per rod, as on the suanpan; Japanese makers cut them over time to a single five-bead above and four unit beads below, each rod holding one digit. Merchants used it from its arrival, but wide use came only after 1600, when mathematicians such as Seki Kōwa studied it and refined both device and methods. It is still taught in Japan.

sources.title: Soroban
Chen, Mark Yu-Shan, 'Mechanical Numeracy: Thinking With the Soroban Abacus in Modern Japan', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 47 (2025)
sources.author: Chen, Mark Yu-Shan
sources.venue: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing
sources.confirms: The page calls the soroban “a traditional arithmetic tool” in modern Japan and says it persisted in households, businesses, and bureaucracy. It gives the publication date as 23 September 2024 and journal issue as Jan.-March 2025.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the soroban’s role in Japan but does not verify the origin, date, route, or design claims.

sources.title: Smith, David Eugene and Mikami, Yoshio, A History of Japanese Mathematics (Open Court, 1914), ch. III, 'The Development of the Soroban'
sources.author: Smith, David Eugene; Mikami, Yoshio
sources.confirms: States that the importation and improvement of the Chinese suan-pan as the soroban is usually assigned to the close of the sixteenth century, names Mori Kambei Shigeyoshi as its first great teacher, and argues merchants may have known it earlier during the Ashikaga shogunate.
sources.qualifies: Places the soroban's arrival at the end of the sixteenth century, not around 1400, and traces it to direct China-Japan trade rather than Korea.

soroban-abacus-1400.verification_note: Chen (IEEE Annals 2025) treats abacus lineage without stating a 1400 arrival in Japan, a conventional date; Smith and Mikami (1914) report that historians usually assign soroban's importation to late sixteenth century, with Mori Kambei Shigeyoshi as its first great teacher under Hideyoshi, and only speculate that merchants knew suan-pan earlier under Ashikaga shoguns, so about 1400 and a route through Korea sit at an early edge of that speculation.
soroban-abacus-1400.detail: Around 1850 its upper pair of beads lost one member, and this Japanese configuration ran alongside the suanpan until Meiji times, after which suanpan use faded. In 1891 Irie Garyū removed one earth bead, giving today's pattern, reintroduced in 1930 and popular from the 1940s. Rods come in odd numbers, never fewer than seven; basic models have thirteen, practical ones 21, 23, 27 or 31. On 11 November 1946 in Tokyo, Kiyoshi Matsuzaki's soroban beat an electric calculator operated by US Army Private Thomas Nathan Wood 4 to 1 on speed and accuracy across all four arithmetic operations.

taino-conuco-cassava-1400.summary: Across Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico and Jamaica, Taíno communities planted bitter cassava cuttings in conucos, knee-high mounds of loosened earth that drained heavy rain and eased harvesting of tubers. Women grated roots on boards set with stone chips, squeezed out prussic acid in woven tube presses, then baked flat bread on clay griddles called burenes, producing a food that kept for months. Fields also carried sweet potato, beans, maize, peppers and cotton; fish weirs, corrals for hutia and sea turtle completed the diet. Irving Rouse's synthesis and Newsom's analysis of plant remains describe this system supporting towns of several thousand when Columbus arrived in 1492.

sources.title: Rouse, Irving, The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus (Yale University Press, 1992), ch. 1
sources.author: Rouse, Irving
sources.confirms: Conuco mound cultivation, cassava processing with graters, presses and griddles, and Taíno subsistence at contact.

sources.title: Newsom, Lee A., Native West Indian plant use (PhD dissertation, University of Florida, 1993)
sources.author: Newsom, Lee A.
sources.confirms: Archaeobotanical evidence for cassava, maize, sweet potato and other cultigens in Caribbean sites.

sources.title: Keegan, William F. and Hofman, Corinne L., The Caribbean before Columbus (Oxford University Press, 2017)
sources.author: Keegan, William F.; Hofman, Corinne L.
sources.confirms: Late Ceramic Age settlement, agriculture and population in Greater Antilles before 1492.

taino-conuco-cassava-1400.verification_note: Conuco agriculture is documented archaeologically from about 600 onward and in Spanish accounts after 1492; 1400 stands for the mature Taíno system at contact. Population figures for Hispaniola in 1492 are disputed across sources, so none is given.
taino-conuco-cassava-1400.detail: Las Casas and Oviedo, writing in the 1520s to 1550s, describe conuco mounds and cassava bread in detail; Spanish colonists adopted cassava bread as ship's biscuit. Archaeobotanical evidence from Puerto Rico and Hispaniola adds maize, yams and arrowroot. Griddle sherds and grater chips are common finds from about 600 onward, so 1400 marks the mature late Taíno system rather than an origin.

yap-rai-stone-money-palau-1400.summary: Men from Yap in western Micronesia sailed to Palau's limestone Rock Islands, negotiated quarry rights with Palauan clans, and carved aragonite and calcite disks with a central hole, some over three metres wide, using shell and stone tools. Finished rai were rafted and towed home behind outrigger canoes across roughly 400 kilometres of open sea. Survey and excavation of Omis Cave in 2001 gave radiocarbon dates showing quarrying by about 1400 CE, with far larger output after iron tools and European ships arrived in the 1870s. Rai value depended on size, quality and the story of each disk's voyage; ownership changed by public agreement while stones stayed in place.

sources.title: Fitzpatrick, Scott M., 'Archaeological investigation of Omis Cave: a Yapese stone money quarry in Palau', Archaeology in Oceania 36 (2001)
sources.author: Fitzpatrick, Scott M.
sources.confirms: Excavation of Omis Cave quarry with radiocarbon dates for pre-European quarrying
sources.qualifies: Earliest quarrying dates have wide intervals

sources.author: Fitzpatrick, Scott M.; McKeon, Stephen
sources.confirms: Describes 250-mile transport of rai and oral ledger of ownership
sources.qualifies: Analogy with cryptocurrency is interpretive

yap-rai-stone-money-palau-1400.verification_note: Fitzpatrick's dates indicate quarrying by at least 1400 CE; some sources place beginnings earlier, so year is approximate.
yap-rai-stone-money-palau-1400.detail: Scott Fitzpatrick and Stephen McKeon draw an analogy between rai ownership records, held in oral memory across a community, and distributed ledgers behind cryptocurrencies, while cautioning that rai were not currency in a strict sense. Omis Cave preserved unfinished disks, tool fragments and hearths. Captain David O'Keefe's trade in the 1870s enabled thousands of large stones, which deflated older values. Several thousand rai remain on Yap today.

zawar-zinc-smelting-1400.summary: By 1400 smelters at Zawar in Rajasthan made zinc by the ton, a method Europe did not master until the 1700s. Debris dates to the second millennium AD, with scale-up by 1300 to 1500. Zinc is hard to smelt because its ore, once reduced, leaves furnaces as vapour rather than molten metal. Zawar's answer was distillation: ore balled with organic matter went into clay retorts fitted with condenser tubes, set mouth-down in brick furnaces over water-filled vessels, where zinc vapour condensed and dripped down.

Craddock, P. T.; Gurjar, L. K.; Hegde, K. T. M., 'Zinc production in medieval India', World Archaeology 15, no. 2 (1983)
sources.author: Craddock, P. T.; Gurjar, L. K.; Hegde, K. T. M.
sources.confirms: The abstract reports a survey of the extensive ancient zinc mines and smelting remains at Zawar, Rajasthan, and a reconstruction of the original distillation process.

zawar-zinc-smelting-1400.detail: Retorts were aubergine-shaped, and bellows supplied their heat. Each furnace held 36 retorts, and a bank of seven furnaces ran 252 at once. Huge heaps of spent retorts remain on site.

act-against-multipliers-1404.summary: In 1404, in a parliament that met that January (regnal year 1403 to 1404), Henry IV made it a felony to multiply gold or silver by alchemy; the crown feared cheap gold more than it wanted it. It forbade "multiplying" gold or silver, meaning transmuting base metals, since such metal could feed counterfeit coin and debase currency, weakening royal authority. Four decades later Henry VI issued licences exempting alchemists from it in hopes of paying for wars. Robert Boyle lobbied for repeal, which came in 1689 with the Royal Mines Act of 1688.

Geoghegan, D., 'A Licence of Henry VI to Practise Alchemy', Ambix 6 (1957) 10-17
sources.author: Geoghegan, D.

city-of-ladies-1405.summary: In 1405 Christine de Pizan's City of Ladies argued that women lacked learning only because they were denied it. She wrote it in French as her formal reply to Jean de Meun's popular Roman de la Rose. It opens with Christine despairing over Matheolus's Lamentations and their claims about women; Reason, Rectitude and Justice then appear and help her build an allegorical city whose walls and houses are famous women, each adding to her case that women are valued members of society who should be educated as men are.

sources.title: The Book of the City of Ladies - Wikipedia
The Book of the City of Ladies.
Brown-Grant, Rosalind, Christine de Pizan and the Moral Defence of Women: Reading Beyond Gender (Cambridge University Press, 1999), ch. 4
sources.author: Brown-Grant, Rosalind
sources.pages: xiv + 224 pp.; ch. 4 on the Cite des Dames
sources.confirms: The Livre de la Cite des Dames (1405) mounts a full assault on medieval misogynist stereotypes and argues the moral equality of the sexes.

sources.title: Gower, Mark, 'Glorifying God: The Theological Notion of Women in Christine de Pizan's Livre de la Cite des Dames', Religion and Literature 54 (2022)
sources.author: Gower, Mark
sources.confirms: Dates the Livre de la Cite des Dames to 1405 and reads it as Christine's argument that women share men's capacities for intellect, virtue and teaching.

city-of-ladies-1405.detail: Her famous women are drawn largely from Boccaccio's On Famous Women. Its companion volume, Treasure of the City of Ladies, followed that same year.

picture.alt: Christine de Pizan presenting her collected works to Queen Isabeau of Bavaria, miniature from British Library Harley MS 4431, about 1410 to 1414.
picture.credit: Master of the Cité des Dames, public domain, via British Library (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

zheng-he-treasure-voyages-1405.summary: From 1405 to 1433 China's treasure fleets sailed as far as Africa; after 1433 no more were sent. Zheng He, a Muslim-born eunuch who had helped the Yongle Emperor seize his throne, commanded them under Yongle and his successor Xuande. Yongle meant them to establish a Chinese presence over Indian Ocean trade, impress foreign rulers and extend his tributary system; preparation included so many interpreters that Nanjing opened a language institute.

sources.title: Zheng He - Wikipedia
Church, Sally K., 'ZHENG HE: AN INVESTIGATION INTO THE PLAUSIBILITY OF 450-FT TREASURE SHIPS', Monumenta Serica 53 (2005)
sources.author: Church, Sally K.

yongle-encyclopedia-1408.summary: In 1408 Ming China completed its Yongle Encyclopedia in 11,095 volumes, a reference work unmatched in size until Wikipedia. The Yongle Emperor had commissioned this classified compendium of existing writings in 1403. Xie Jin's first version by 100 scholars was rejected as too small, and by 1405 some 2,169 scholars were gathering books across China. Never printed, it survived only as a 1562 to 1567 manuscript copy; most of that was lost in late 19th-century upheavals, leaving fewer than 400 volumes.

age-of-discovery-era-1418.summary: From 1418 Portuguese ships worked down Africa's coast, beginning voyages that joined every continent by sea. From about 1418 to 1620 seafarers from European states explored, colonised and conquered regions across the globe. Portugal began with Atlantic islands and West Africa's coast, reaching India by sea under Vasco da Gama in 1498; Spain backed Columbus's Atlantic crossings from 1492 and the Magellan-Elcano voyage that first circled the Earth in 1522. These routes spurred global trade and the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, peoples, including enslaved people, and diseases between hemispheres, and built European colonial empires with new centres of power beyond Europe.

ulugh-beg-observatory-1420.summary: In 1428 Ulugh Beg's Samarkand observatory charted stars better than anyone since Ptolemy. Its main instrument was a huge marble meridian arc, partly cut into rock so its building need not be tall, which measured solar altitude, star positions, year length, planetary periods and eclipses. Astronomers including Jamshid al-Kashi and Ali Qushji worked there and compiled Zij-i Sultani, tables and star catalogue listing about 1,000 stars, published in 1437. After Ulugh Beg's son had him murdered in 1449 this observatory was destroyed; its remains were found in 1908.

al-kashi-decimal-fractions-1427.summary: In 1427 al-Kashi used decimal fractions as routine, 150 years before Europe adopted them. Working at Ulugh Beg's observatory, he finished his Miftāḥ al-ḥisāb, Key of Arithmetic, that year. In it he used decimal fractions and base-sixty fractions with equal ease, a century and a half before Simon Stevin's De Thiende of 1585 made decimals common practice in Europe. The book also solves triangles from given sides and angles, so that in France the law of cosines is called al-Kashi's theorem. In 1424 he had computed 2π to 16 decimal places, unmatched for 180 years.

jang-yeong-sil-jagyeongnu-1434.summary: In 1434 Korea's Jang Yeong-sil completed the Jagyeokru, a water clock that struck the hours unattended. King Sejong, hearing of self-striking clocks abroad, had set his court technician to build one; after early failures Jang studied Chinese designs. Water rising in its lower vessel lifted floating rods that tipped small iron balls down pipes to release larger balls, which struck bell, gong and drum to sound each hour. Joseon used it as its standard of time. It did not survive; reconstructions follow written descriptions.

inca-chasqui-relay-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca relay runners carried messages and knotted records along 40,000 kilometres of road, covering 240 kilometres a day. Fresh runners at each station let a message travel up to 300 kilometres in one day. Chronicler Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa credited the service to Pachacuti, who began his reign about 1438 and wanted daily reports from his growing provinces; Juan de Betanzos credits his predecessor Viracocha Inca, and Martín de Murúa his son Topa Inca Yupanqui.

inca-empire-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca rulers under Pachacuti built an empire run by roads, storehouses and knotted cords, with no writing. He reorganized his Kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, Realm of the Four Parts. Through conquest and peaceful assimilation he and his son Topa Yupanqui brought most of today's Peru under Inca rule; by 1533 their empire ran from Ecuador to Chile, pre-Columbian America's largest, built, as anthropologist Gordon McEwan notes, without wheel, draft animals, iron or writing. Spanish conquest began in 1532.

inca-road-system-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca rulers ran an empire on 40,000 kilometres of road, without wheels or horses. As conquest spread from Cusco, they claimed exclusive right over routes many built centuries earlier by Wari and Tiwanaku peoples. They extended them into a single network of some 40,000 kilometres. Two north-south trunk roads, along the coast and through mountains, carried many branches, with paving where needed, stairways, retaining walls, drainage and bridges. Without wheels, these roads moved information, goods, soldiers and people across nearly 2,000,000 square kilometres holding about 12 million people.

quipu-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca officials kept census, taxes and stores on knotted cords called quipus, governing without writing. Specialists called quipucamayocs read these cords of cotton or camelid fibre. Pendant cords hang from one main cord; colour, order and knot type carry categories, while knots placed in decimal positions record numbers. Quipus appear in archaeological finds from the first millennium CE, probably under the Wari, and some features are thought to encode non-numeric information that remains undeciphered.

inca-stonecutting-sacsayhuaman-1440.summary: From Pachacuti's rebuilding of Cusco around 1440, Inca masons quarried andesite at Rumiqolqa and Huaccoto and limestone at Sacsayhuamán, dragged blocks on ramps and dressed them with river-cobble hammers of increasing fineness until each face met its neighbours with joints too tight for a blade. Jean-Pierre Protzen's experiments in the 1980s at Inca quarries showed a single worker shaping a block in hours by pounding and repeatedly test-fitting, with bedding joints cut concave to lock stones. Sacsayhuamán's zigzag terrace walls hold blocks weighing over 100 tonnes. Cieza de León, writing in 1553, recorded that twenty thousand workers served by rotation in its construction.

inca-stonecutting-sacsayhuaman-1440.detail: Protzen found no evidence for metal tools or abrasives; hammerstone pitting on finished faces and on quarry rejects matched his experimental marks. Blocks were moved by ropes over prepared ramps whose traces remain at Ollantaytambo's Kachiqhata quarry. Cusco's polygonal and coursed masonry served palaces, Qorikancha temple and kallanka halls; Sacsayhuamán's construction continued under Tupac Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac into early 1500s.

walls-of-benin-1440.summary: Around 1440 Benin City was rebuilt to a plan, with earthworks that grew into history's largest made before machines. Its inner earthwork ran about 12 kilometres, and in places a 17-metre drop separated rampart top from ditch floor, every basket of it dug and piled by hand. Villages across Ewuare's kingdom had been raising such banks since the seventh century; this whole network, estimated at 16,000 kilometres enclosing 6,500 square kilometres, holds a Guinness record as the longest earthwork built before machines.

cheugugi-rain-gauge-1441.summary: In 1441 Korea set standard rain gauges in every province, the earliest known national rainfall records. On 18 August 1441, by the lunar calendar, King Sejong ordered his Gwansanggam observatory to set an iron cylinder, two cheok tall and eight chon across, on a stone stand to catch rain; the Sejong Sillok credits this idea to his Crown Prince, later King Munjong. In 1442 dimensions were revised and standard procedure fixed, so provincial offices kept identical cheugugi and reported comparable totals.

cheugugi-rain-gauge-1441.detail: Under that 1442 procedure, offices measured depth with a ruler, recorded when rain began and ended, and reported totals. King Yeongjo revived this system in 1770, and surviving gauges date from then.

bahmani-cannon-deccan-1442.summary: Persian chronicler Shihab Hakim's Ma'asir-i Mahmud Shahi describes cannon (top) and gunpowder in Bahmani campaigns against Vijayanagara and Malwa from 1442, earliest clear textual evidence for firearms used in Indian warfare. Iqtidar Alam Khan's reading shows Deccan sultanates and their rivals acquired artillery through Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade and foundries staffed by Turkish and Persian gunners, decades before Babur's field guns at Panipat (1526). Gun founding then spread to Gujarat, Vijayanagara and Bengal. Surviving Deccan bronze guns at Bidar and Bijapur, including later Malik-i Maidan (1549), show large castings in copper alloy, a craft tied to local bell and icon metallurgy.

hangul-promulgation-1443.summary: In 1443 King Sejong gave Korean its own alphabet of 28 letters, so simple a reader could learn it in a morning. His court had been forcing Korean into Chinese characters built for another tongue. Each letter marks one sound, and five basic consonants are drawn as tongue, lips or throat making it, so a 1446 handbook could promise a sharp reader the whole set in a morning and a slow one in ten days. Officials kept writing Chinese for another four and a half centuries; in 1894 Korea's government made Hangul its preferred script for state papers, and both Koreas write with 24 of those original letters today.

nezahualcoyotl-dike-1449.summary: After floods in 1449 inundated Tenochtitlan, Mexica ruler Moctezuma Ilhuicamina asked Nezahualcoyotl, ruler of Texcoco, to design a remedy. Workers from allied cities drove twin rows of stakes across Lake Texcoco, packed them with stone and earth, and built a dike of about 16 kilometres from Atzacoalco to Iztapalapa, with sluices that let water pass. It separated brackish eastern water from fresh western water fed by springs, protected chinampa fields and the city's causeways, and kept lake levels workable for canoe traffic. Chroniclers Alva Ixtlilxóchitl and Torquemada describe its construction; archaeology and colonial maps confirm its line. Spanish forces breached it in 1521 and colonial Mexico City flooded repeatedly afterward.

sources.title: Cordova, Carlos E., 'Late Aztec Settlement, Hydraulic Management, and Environment', in The Lakes of the Basin of Mexico (Springer, 2022), ch. 13
sources.author: Cordova, Carlos E.
sources.confirms: Nezahualcoyotl's dike within Aztec hydraulic management of Lake Texcoco, with length and function.

sources.title: Candiani, Vera S., Dreaming of Dry Land: Environmental Transformation in Colonial Mexico City (Stanford University Press, 2014), ch. 1
sources.author: Candiani, Vera S.
sources.confirms: Prehispanic dikes and causeways as inherited infrastructure that colonial drainage projects replaced.

sources.title: Milhauser, John K., 'Aztec Use of Lake Resources in the Basin of Mexico', in Oxford Handbook of the Aztecs (Oxford University Press, 2016)
sources.author: Milhauser, John K.
sources.confirms: Dike separating saline and fresh water and its role for chinampa agriculture and lake transport.

nezahualcoyotl-dike-1449.verification_note: Construction date of 1449 or 1450 comes from chroniclers writing after 1600 (Alva Ixtlilxóchitl, Torquemada); length is given as 12 to 16 kilometres across sources.
nezahualcoyotl-dike-1449.detail: Palerm's 1973 survey of prehispanic hydraulic works and Cordova's 2022 synthesis treat the dike as part of a Basin-wide system with Chapultepec aqueducts, Coyoacán aqueduct and smaller dikes at Mexicaltzingo. Length estimates range from 12 to 16 kilometres. Chroniclers writing a century later give its date as 1449 or 1450; no contemporary record survives.

picture.alt: Coloured woodcut map of Tenochtitlan printed at Nuremberg in 1524, showing causeways and lake works; printed decades after the dike
picture.credit: Friedrich Peypus (1485–1534), probably after drawing made by one of Cortez' men., via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: resized to 1200 px long edge; converted to JPEG

bigo-earthworks-uganda-1450.summary: South of Katonga river in western Uganda, a community cut more than ten kilometres of ditches through laterite, some four metres deep, enclosing pasture and a central mound complex now called Bigo bya Mugenyi. It is one of about fifteen earthwork sites between the Katonga and Lake Albert; Munsa and Kibengo are next in size. Peter Robertshaw's radiocarbon and luminescence dates place digging at Munsa and Kibengo in the fifteenth or sixteenth centuries and Bigo at about the same time or a century earlier. He reads them as capitals of three contemporary polities built by cattle-keeping elites, not as evidence of a Cwezi empire of oral tradition.

sources.title: Robertshaw, Peter, 'The ancient earthworks of western Uganda: capital sites of a Cwezi empire?', Uganda Journal 48 (2002)
sources.author: Robertshaw, Peter
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon and luminescence dates place Munsa and Kibengo ditches in the fifteenth or sixteenth centuries, Bigo the same age or a century older; earthworks read as capitals of three contemporary polities rather than a Cwezi empire

sources.title: Robertshaw, Peter and Taylor, David, 'Climate change and the rise of political complexity in western Uganda', Journal of African History 41 (2000)
sources.author: Robertshaw, Peter; Taylor, David
sources.confirms: Palaeoecological and archaeological evidence linking earthwork construction at Munsa to climate shifts and growing political complexity

bigo-earthworks-uganda-1450.verification_note: Bigo's own dates are inferred from Munsa and Kibengo; Robertshaw allows a range from 1300s to 1500s.
bigo-earthworks-uganda-1450.detail: Merrick Posnansky excavated Bigo in 1960 and reported occupation debris, cattle bones and roulette-decorated pottery. Robertshaw's later fieldwork at Munsa linked earthwork construction to a period of drier climate and competition over grazing, and to a shift toward centralized power that preceded Bunyoro and Buganda. Dating of Bigo rests on few samples, and 1450 is a midpoint estimate.

picture.alt: Ditch at Bigo bya Mugenyi, Uganda, once about 8 m deep and 4 m wide, cut into laterite
picture.credit: Aishablue

chan-chan-chimu-1450.summary: Around 1450 Chan Chan, Chimu capital in northern Peru's Moche valley, was the largest mud-brick city on Earth, about 20 square kilometres fed by canals; the Incas took it within decades. Nine large rectangular compounds, independent units often called citadels or palaces, stand behind high thick earthen walls decorated with friezes, each holding temples, dwellings, storehouses, reservoirs and burial platforms. Moche valley canals irrigated its fields; an 80-kilometre canal meant to bring Chicama river water was abandoned unfinished.

sources.title: Chan Chan Archaeological Zone
Ortloff, Charles R.; Moseley, Michael E.; Feldman, Robert A., 'Hydraulic Engineering Aspects of the Chimu Chicama-Moche Intervalley Canal', American Antiquity 47 (1982), pp. 572-595
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.; Moseley, Michael E.; Feldman, Robert A.
sources.confirms: The abstract calls the Chicama-Moche (La Cumbre) intervalley canal the highest technical achievement of the Chimu empire's many canal systems and analyses its open-channel design.
sources.qualifies: It states the canal was abandoned before completion and never supplied the Moche Valley with Chicama water, so it did not irrigate Chan Chan's fields.

sources.title: Moseley, Michael E., 'Chan Chan: Andean Alternative of the Preindustrial City', Science 187 (1975), pp. 219-225
sources.author: Moseley, Michael E.
sources.confirms: The publisher page confirms the peer-reviewed article on Chan Chan as a preindustrial city; its text was not readable without subscription, so the twenty square kilometre figure and the nine compounds were not checked there.

chan-chan-chimu-1450.verification_note: Ortloff, Moseley and Feldman (American Antiquity 1982) show that Chicama-Moche intervalley canal construction was abandoned before completion and never carried Chicama water to the Moche valley; Moseley (Science 1975) is a standard account of Chan Chan's scale.
chan-chan-chimu-1450.detail: Around those nine compounds lay thirty-two smaller compounds and four craft sectors. Earthen walls make Chan Chan vulnerable to El Niño rains.

picture.alt: Chimú ceremonial knife, or tumi, of gold alloy with a figure handle, made on Peru's north coast between 1100 and 1470.
picture.credit: Chimú, CC0, via Art Institute of Chicago

gutenberg-press-1450.summary: By 1450 Gutenberg was printing with cast metal type; in 50 years Europe had 20 million books. His press printed from type cast in quantity, so a page could be set from reusable metal letters rather than carved or copied by hand. Movable type already existed in East Asia; his system joined type cast from a lead, tin and antimony alloy in his hand mould, oil-based ink and a wooden press adapted from screw presses used for wine and oil. Gutenberg, a goldsmith who had experimented with printing in Strasbourg during the 1430s, was funded by moneylender Johann Fust with 800 guilders; a second loan of 800 financed his 42-line Bible, completed in 1455 in about 180 copies, which showed the method working at scale.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Johannes Gutenberg
Fust and Gutenberg (Gutenberg, 2020)
sources.confirms: The page describes Gutenberg’s system: texts were broken into the Latin alphabet’s 26 letters, “cut and cast in metal once” and reused to print different texts, unlike copying whole texts by hand or carving them into wood. It identifies the Gutenberg Bible as dated 1454.
sources.qualifies: Reusable metal type is described; the other specifics are not stated.

sources.title: 'Johannes Gutenberg', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gutenberg was back in Mainz in October 1448. By 1450, his “printing experiments” had reached “a considerable degree of refinement.” The page says his method used movable type and likely involved a readily melting, quickly cooling metal alloy, “oil-based ink,” and a press likely adapted from presses for wine, oil, or paper.
sources.qualifies: Hand mould and the specific timing/location are not stated).

gutenberg-press-1450.verification_note: reusable metal type is described; other specifics are not stated; hand mould and specific timing/location are not stated

henry-the-navigator-caravel-1450.summary: Around 1450 Portugal refined the caravel, a ship that could sail into the wind and so come home from Africa. Prince Henry the Navigator, needing better ships for Atlantic and West African exploration, gathered experts in mapmaking, navigation, astronomy and ship design at Sagres. Their caravel, a small decked vessel descended from Iberian fishing craft, was rigged with triangular lateen sails or lateen and square sails together. Unlike square-rigged barcas and oared ships then standard, it could beat to windward and handle open ocean, and was easier to steer. Diogo Cão, Bartolomeu Dias and later Columbus sailed caravels, opening routes for Iberian spice trade.

sources.title: Caravel - Wikipedia
Unger, Richard W., Portuguese Shipbuilding and the Early Voyages to the Guinea Coast (The European Opportunity, 2019)
sources.author: Unger, Richard W.
sources.confirms: The page identifies a chapter titled “Portuguese Shipbuilding and the Early Voyages to the Guinea Coast,” by Richard W. Unger, first published in 1995.
sources.qualifies: The topic matches, but the claim’s specific details are absent.

sources.title: 'Caravel', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page describes the caravel as a 15th-, 16th-, and 17th-century ship used for long voyages, and says it is thought to have been developed by the Portuguese to explore Africa’s coasts, encouraged by Prince Henry the Navigator. Its ability to sail “to windward” helped sailors return despite opposing winds and currents;
sources.qualifies: Those details are missing.

henry-the-navigator-caravel-1450.verification_note: Unger (2019) and Britannica confirm Portuguese caravel development under Henry; a Sagres school of experts is a legend not stated in either.

inca-andenes-moray-terraces-1450.summary: During 15th-century expansion, Inca state labor builds stone-walled andenes that turn steep slopes into level, irrigated fields with drainage layers of gravel and sand, and at Moray near Cusco cuts concentric terraces with radii of 45 to 65 meters and walls 3 to 5 meters high. Microclimate gradients measured between top and bottom of Moray bowls support reading Moray as a space for adapting potato, oca, quinoa and maize to altitude bands. Potatoes freeze-dried into chuno stocked state warehouses. Terraces let the Inca feed several million people on mountain land Spanish observers later judged unfarmable, and many near Cusco remain in use.

sources.title: Esenarro, D., Hidalgo, C. and Vilchez Cairo, J., 'Microclimates, Geometry, and Constructive Sustainability of the Inca Agricultural Terraces', Heritage 9:2 (2026), 56
sources.author: Esenarro, Doris; Hidalgo, Celeste; Vilchez Cairo, Jesica
sources.confirms: Measures Moray terrace radii of 45 to 65 metres, wall heights of 3 to 5 metres, drainage construction and temperature gradients between terrace levels.
sources.qualifies: Treats Moray's role as an agricultural experiment site as an interpretation supported by microclimate data, not as documented Inca intent.

sources.title: BBC Travel, 'The innovative technology that powered the Inca'
sources.author: BBC Travel
sources.confirms: Describes andenes construction, drainage layers and continued use of Inca terraces near Cusco.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism (MINCETUR), tourism inventory record for Moray
sources.author: MINCETUR
sources.confirms: Official description of Moray's concentric terraces and depth.

inca-andenes-moray-terraces-1450.verification_note: Construction dates for Moray and most andenes are inferred from Inca expansion under Pachacuti and successors; no written date exists. Experimental-station reading is interpretation.
inca-andenes-moray-terraces-1450.detail: Andenes reduce erosion, store daytime heat in stone and lengthen growing seasons. Moray's purpose as experimental station is inferred from microclimates and geometry rather than from Inca records, which were oral and knotted in quipu. Terrace building predates Inca rule by centuries; they scaled and standardized it with mit'a labor service under Pachacuti and his successors after about 1438. Spanish chroniclers recorded state granaries holding years of reserves, and terrace walls still stand after five centuries of earthquakes.

picture.alt: Concentric Inca terraces at Moray near Cusco, Peru
picture.credit: Kenneth Moore, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

machu-picchu-1450.summary: Around 1450 Inca builders raised Machu Picchu with drains so good it has stood without mortar since. Its dry-stone walls and engineered terraces drained excess water and limited erosion.

sources.title: Machu Picchu - Wikipedia
Burger, Richard L., 'New AMS dates for Machu Picchu: results and implications', Antiquity 95 (2021)
sources.author: Burger, Richard L.; Salazar, Lucy C.; Nesbitt, Jason
sources.confirms: The page says Machu Picchu was occupied “from c. AD 1420-1532,” with activity beginning two decades before textual sources linking it to Pachacuti’s rise in AD 1438.
sources.qualifies: It does not state that the site was built around 1450 as a royal estate, or mention mortar, dry-stone walls, drains, terraces, or erosion.

sources.title: 'Machu Picchu', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Machu Picchu’s dwellings were “probably built and occupied from the mid-15th to the early or mid-16th century”; it gives no specific construction date of around 1450.
sources.qualifies: Royal-retreat/palace evidence and terraces are stated; the precise date and drainage, mortar, and erosion claims are not.

machu-picchu-1450.verification_note: Burger and colleagues (Antiquity 2021) report AMS dates showing occupation from about AD 1420 to 1532, two decades earlier than a 1438-based chronology, so around 1450 is a late estimate.

picture.alt: Terraces and stone buildings of Machu Picchu, built about 1450 under Pachacuti, photographed in 2009.
picture.credit: Martin St-Amant (S23678), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

yemen-sufis-coffee-drinking-1450.summary: By mid-fifteenth century Sufi circles in Aden, Zabid and Yemen's highlands drink qahwa brewed from roasted coffee beans during dhikr, their long night litanies. Arabic accounts collected by Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri in the 1550s credit Jamal al-Din al-Dhabhani, a jurist and Sufi of Aden who died in 1470 to 1471, with adopting this drink after seeing it in Ethiopia and finding it drove off fatigue. Ralph Hattox, reviewing every early source in 1985, concludes coffee entered common urban use in Yemen in the mid-1400s and no earlier reference exists. From Yemen both habit and commercial planting spread to Mecca by about 1500 and to Cairo soon after, and Yemeni terraces supplied almost all coffee sold worldwide for two centuries.

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses: The Origins of a Social Beverage in the Medieval Near East (University of Washington Press, 1985), ch. 2
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Coffee came into general use in Islamic lands in the mid-fifteenth century among Yemeni Sufis; al-Dhabhani died 875 AH (1470-71).

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses, full text (Internet Archive)
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Translates Ibn Abd al-Ghaffar's account of Sufi use in Yemen and al-Dhabhani's Ethiopian journey; conclusion that adoption by Sufi groups in Yemeni cities dates to the mid-fifteenth century.
sources.qualifies: Hattox treats the Ethiopian journey as legend and allows that others may have used coffee in Yemen slightly earlier.

yemen-sufis-coffee-drinking-1450.verification_note: No contemporary fifteenth-century text survives; dating rests on sixteenth-century Arabic accounts analysed by Hattox, who gives mid-fifteenth century. A 1454 date often quoted is unconfirmed.

picture.alt: View of Mocha, Yemen's coffee port, from Olfert Dapper's 1680 description of Arabia
picture.credit: Olfert Dapper / Jacob van Meurs, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hwacha-rocket-launcher-1451.summary: In 1451 King Munjong of Korea ordered stronger hwachas, carts firing up to 200 rocket arrows at once; Korean scientists including Yi To and Ch'oe Haesan had built the first in 1409. His Munjong hwacha, purportedly designed by king and brother together, had interchangeable modules firing 100 rocket arrows or 200 darts from 50 barrels. Fifty units guarded Seoul and 80 its northern border. In the 1590s, 40 hwachas helped 3,400 Koreans repel 30,000 Japanese at Haengju.

sources.title: Hwacha - Wikipedia
Cho, Sung-Jin, 'Lessons Learned: An Analysis of the Combat Effectiveness of the Joseon Singijeon Using a Ballistic Model', Journal of the KNST 9 (2026)
sources.author: Cho, Sung-Jin; Jung, Se-Youn
sources.confirms: The page states that the Joseon-era Singijeon was mounted on a Hwacha and could launch multiple projectiles simultaneously. It gives no date of 1451, no mention of King Munjong, and no figure of 100 or 200 rockets.
sources.qualifies: The launcher and simultaneous launches are stated; the claimed date, king, and rocket counts are not.

sources.title: 'Rocket and missile system', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page gives 1232 for Chinese defenders using weapons described as “arrows of flying fire,” but says there is “no explicit statement that these arrows were rockets.” It provides no information about Joseon, hwachas, Yi To, Ch’oe Haesan, King Munjong, 1409, 1451, or carts firing 200 rocket arrows.
sources.qualifies: It mentions an early rocket-related claim, but does not confirm the Korean names, dates, or figure.

hwacha-rocket-launcher-1451.verification_note: Cho, Journal of the KNST 2026, confirms singijeon mounted on a hwacha fired many projectiles at once; its 1451 date and 100-rocket count were not stated.

picture.alt: Reconstructed hwacha cart with its rack of launching tubes for singijeon rocket arrows, later photograph of a museum reconstruction.
picture.credit: Josh Berglund, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

fall-of-constantinople-orban-cannon-1453.summary: In 1453 Ottoman cannon brought down Constantinople's walls, which had resisted attack for 800 years. Sultan Mehmed II's army took the city after a 53-day siege. About 7,000 defenders held twelve miles of fifth-century Theodosian wall. Mehmed brought some 70 large guns from Edirne plus bombards cast on site, among them Hungarian engineer Orban's 8.2-metre "Basilica", which threw a 270-kilogram stone ball over a mile but took hours to reload. Repeated heavy shot opened breaches that infantry stormed.

sources.title: Fall of Constantinople - Wikipedia
Philippides, Marios, The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 (Routledge, 2017)
sources.author: Philippides, Marios; Hanak, Walter K.
sources.confirms: The page identifies the book as about “The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453.” It gives no details about cannon, Sultan Mehmed II, the siege’s duration, defenders, or the city walls.
sources.qualifies: The year 1453 is stated; the other claim details are absent.

sources.title: 'Fall of Constantinople', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page states the city fell on May 29, 1453, after a 55-day siege. Ottoman cannon bombardment began April 6 and “brought down a section of the wall”;
sources.qualifies: Cannon support and the fall are confirmed; the siege duration differs from 53 days, and the other claims are not stated.

fall-of-constantinople-orban-cannon-1453.verification_note: Philippides and Hanak (2011) and Britannica confirm its fall on 29 May 1453 after bombardment; Britannica gives a 55-day siege and land walls of 6.5 km, against 53 days and twelve miles in other accounts.

picture.alt: Dardanelles Gun, bronze bombard cast in 1464 on pattern of Orban's siege guns of 1453, photographed at Fort Nelson, Hampshire.
picture.credit: Tim Sheerman-Chase, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gutenberg-bible-1454.summary: In 1454 Gutenberg put the first printed Bibles on sale in Mainz; a book that took a scribe a year could be made by the hundred. Preparation probably began soon after 1450; his first precisely datable printing is a 31-line indulgence that existed by 22 October 1454. In March 1455 Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, wrote that he had seen pages displayed in Frankfurt and that all copies, 158 or 180, were already spoken for. Some sold for 30 florins, about 100 grams of gold. Forty-nine copies survive in substantial part.

sources.title: Gutenberg Bible - Wikipedia
The Gutenberg Bible (B 42) of 1454 (Gutenberg, 2020)
sources.confirms: The page identifies “The Gutenberg Bible (B 42) of 1454” and describes Gutenberg’s “master work of 1,282 pages - the Latin Bible.” It says he used the Vulgate, St Jerome’s “late-4th-century translation of the Septuagint,” in a Rhineland textual variant of a 13th-century Parisian revision.
sources.qualifies: Those claims are absent.

sources.title: 'Gutenberg Bible', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Gutenberg “completed it about 1455” at Mainz, Germany. It describes a three-volume Latin Bible printed in 42-line columns, with six compositors working simultaneously in its later stages.
sources.qualifies: The page gives about 1455, not 1454, and does not provide the other claimed details.

gutenberg-bible-1454.verification_note: A Brill chapter titles this Bible 'B42 of 1454' with 1,282 pages; Britannica gives completion about 1455, so 1454 marks when sales began and not completion.

picture.alt: Library of Congress's vellum Gutenberg Bible, printed in Mainz about 1454 to 1455, photographed on display in 2015.
picture.credit: MC BSU, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

bereguardo-canal-pound-locks-1458.summary: Bertola da Novate, ducal engineer to Francesco Sforza from 1451, completes a 19 km canal from Abbiategrasso to Bereguardo near Milan with 18 pound locks dropping 24 metres, Europe's first canal with a series of chambered locks. A single pound lock had been tried on the Naviglio Grande in 1438, and a lock at Vreeswijk in Holland in 1373 is probably Europe's first. China had built its first pound lock on the Grand Canal in 984, as Joseph Needham showed in a 1963 Newcomen Society paper. Milanese canals continued: Martesana in 1470, and in 1497 Leonardo da Vinci, as ducal engineer, fitted San Marco lock with the first mitre gates, V-shaped pairs still used on canals today.

sources.title: Needham, J., 'China and the Invention of the Pound-Lock', Transactions of the Newcomen Society 36 (1963), 85-107
sources.author: Needham, Joseph
sources.confirms: Landing page read: paper on the 10th-century Chinese pound lock and its European successors, read at the Science Museum on 1 April 1964; pages 85 to 107 confirmed, full text not opened.

sources.title: 'Bereguardo Canal', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: First European canal with a series of pound locks; 1438 lock on the Naviglio Grande; Bertola da Novate engineer from 1451, canal stopped at Bereguardo in 1458; 19 km, 24 m fall, 18 locks; Martesana 1470; Leonardo's San Marco lock 1497 with first mitre gates.

sources.title: 'Canals and inland waterways', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Vreeswijk lock of 1373 the probable first pound lock in Europe.

picture.alt: Remains of an old lock on the Naviglio di Bereguardo near Milan.
picture.credit: Yorick39, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

chapultepec-aqueduct-1449.summary: In 1466, under Moctezuma I, Tenochtitlan's new aqueduct had two channels, so water flowed while one was cleaned. Its two stone-masonry troughs kept water flowing while one was being maintained.

sources.title: Chapultepec aqueduct - Wikipedia
Solis Olguin, Felipe, 'Chapultepec, espacio ritual y secular de los tlatoani aztecas', Arqueologia Mexicana 57 (2002) 36-40
sources.author: Solis Olguin, Felipe
sources.confirms: Solis describes the Chapultepec aqueduct built in 1466 during the reign of Moctezuma I, with two channels so one could be cleaned while the other carried water, a design attributed to Nezahualcoyotl.
sources.qualifies: Solis dates the aqueduct to 1466, not 1449.

sources.title: Castaneda Gonzalez, Rocio, 'Water and the Aztec Empire', in Water Management in the Valley of Mexico (Springer, 2024) 3-16
sources.author: Castaneda Gonzalez, Rocio
sources.confirms: The chapter describes the aqueduct from the Chapultepec springs as the main fresh water supply of Tenochtitlan.
sources.qualifies: The chapter does not give a construction date.

chapultepec-aqueduct-1449.verification_note: Solis dates this Chapultepec aqueduct to 1466 in Moctezuma I's reign, with two channels and a design attributed to Nezahualcoyotl; an earlier aqueduct is sometimes placed in the 1420s or 1440s, and no peer-reviewed source gives 1449.

inca-qollqa-storehouses-1470.summary: Along Qhapaq Ñan roads and above provincial centres, Inca administrators built rows of round and rectangular stone storehouses, qollqa, on cool, windy hillsides. Floors raised on gravel and ventilation ducts kept chuño (freeze-dried potato), maize, quinoa, dried meat, cloth and weapons dry for years. At Hatun Xauxa in Peru's Mantaro valley, D'Altroy and Earle counted more than 2,000 qollqa with over 170,000 cubic metres of capacity; Cotapachi in Bolivia held about 2,400. Khipu keepers recorded contents. Stored staples fed armies, labour drafts under the mit'a system and relief after frost or drought, and Spanish armies in the 1530s lived off these stores for years.

sources.title: D'Altroy, Terence N. and Earle, Timothy K., 'Staple Finance, Wealth Finance, and Storage in the Inka Political Economy', Current Anthropology 26 (1985)
sources.author: D'Altroy, Terence N.; Earle, Timothy K.
sources.confirms: Counts and capacity of qollqa at Hatun Xauxa and the staple-finance model of Inca storage.

sources.title: LeVine, Terry Y. (ed.), Inka Storage Systems (University of Oklahoma Press, 1992)
sources.author: LeVine, Terry Y.
sources.confirms: Regional surveys of storehouse architecture, ventilation and contents across Inca provinces.

sources.title: Earle, Timothy, 'Staple Finance, Wealth Finance, and Storage in the Inka Political Economy', in Bronze Age Economics (Routledge, 2018), ch. 10
sources.author: Earle, Timothy
sources.confirms: Reprint and reassessment of the storage model.

inca-qollqa-storehouses-1470.detail: D'Altroy and Earle's 1985 model distinguishes staple finance (bulk food and cloth stored locally) from wealth finance (prestige goods moved to Cusco). Terry LeVine's 1992 volume gathers surveys of storage at Huánuco Pampa, Pumpu and Cuzco. Chuño production, freezing potatoes overnight at altitude and trampling out water, long predates the Inca but reached state scale in these depots. Construction dates follow Inca conquest of each province, roughly 1460 to 1530.

picture.alt: Row of stone qollqa storehouses on a hillside at Ollantaytambo, Peru; modern photograph
picture.credit: D. Gordon E. Robertson, via Wikimedia Commons

inca-tin-bronze-1470.summary: As Inca armies and administrators extended Tawantinsuyu under Pachacuti and Tupac Inca Yupanqui, they replaced local arsenical copper with tin bronze for chisels, axes, tumi knives, crowbars, mace heads and tupu pins, drawing tin from cassiterite deposits of Bolivia's altiplano. Heather Lechtman's 1984 analysis in Technology and Culture argued that Inca state policy, not metallurgical advantage alone, drove this shift: tin bronze cast well and could be standardised, and its distribution marked imperial reach. Sites from Ecuador to northwest Argentina show tin bronze appearing with Inca ceramics. Earlier Andean metallurgy had prized colour and surface; Inca practice added uniform alloy for utilitarian objects.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Andean Value Systems and the Development of Prehistoric Metallurgy', Technology and Culture 25 (1984)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Inca adoption of tin bronze as an imperial standard and its contrast with earlier Andean emphasis on colour and surface.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Andean Metallurgy in Prehistory', in Roberts and Thornton (eds), Archaeometallurgy in Global Perspective (Springer, 2014)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Chronology of arsenical and tin bronzes in the Andes and Inca-period distribution.

sources.title: Shimada, Izumi and Merkel, John F., 'Copper-Alloy Metallurgy in Ancient Peru', Scientific American 265 (1991)
sources.author: Shimada, Izumi; Merkel, John F.
sources.confirms: Arsenical bronze tradition on the north coast that Inca tin bronze displaced.

inca-tin-bronze-1470.detail: Lechtman's samples from Machu Picchu and provincial centres showed tin contents clustered around 5 to 8 percent, consistent with controlled alloying. Tin bronze had existed since Tiwanaku times around Lake Titicaca; Inca expansion from the 1460s made it empire-wide. Gold and silver remained state monopolies for cult and display, worked at Cusco by specialists drawn from conquered Chimú workshops after 1470.

picture.alt: Inca cast bronze tumi knife with figures on its handle, Metropolitan Museum of Art
picture.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. See the Image and Dat, via Wikimedia Commons

venetian-patent-statute-1474.summary: In 1474 Venice passed the first patent law: register a new device, get ten years' sole right. Its Senate's statute was Europe's first statutory patent system, possibly the world's earliest codified one. Its text argues that clever men gather in Venice and would invent more if others could not copy their works and take their honor. Anyone who perfected "any new and ingenious device, not previously made" in Venetian lands was to register it with the Provveditori di Comun; for up to ten years nobody else could make one without its inventor's consent. Some historians see it as codifying existing custom rather than founding modern patent law.

caxton-press-westminster-1476.summary: In 1476 William Caxton opened England's first press at Westminster, and his choices helped fix English spelling. Earlier, in 1473 or 1474, he had printed his own translation of the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, the first book printed in English. Heavy demand for it prompted his Westminster venture, where his first known book was Chaucer's Canterbury Tales. Printing in London's dialect across many works, he is credited with helping standardise written English.

ottoman-printing-ban-1483.summary: From 1483, by a tradition André Thevet first recorded in his 1580s writings, Ottoman sultans barred printing in Arabic script; no decree survives, though the Muslim world went without a press for 250 years. Later writers had Bayezid II and his successors enforcing it on pain of death; no documentary evidence supports such a ban. Printing in other scripts went on: Jewish presses from 1493 in Constantinople, and Greek, Armenian and other Christian presses in Salonica, Bursa, Belgrade and Smyrna. Arabic-script printing by non-Muslims began in Aleppo in 1706. In 1727 Sultan Ahmed III licensed the first Muslim-run press for secular Arabic-script works, religious texts still excluded, yet printing did not take off until the 19th century.

sources.title: Global spread of the printing press - Wikipedia

Scholarship is divided on whether any ban existed; this entry follows Schwartz.

malleus-maleficarum-1486.summary: In 1486 the Hammer of Witches was printed, and print spread a manual that fed two centuries of witch trials. Heinrich Kramer, a Dominican inquisitor expelled from Innsbruck in 1484 after failing to prosecute alleged witches there, published his Malleus Maleficarum in Speyer. It argued that witchcraft existed and denying it was error, classed sorcery as heresy for secular courts to prosecute, held that practitioners were more often women than men, and recommended torture to obtain confessions and death as its sure remedy. Printing carried it widely: 28 editions by 1600, used by Catholic and Protestant courts in witch trials.

ibn-majid-navigation-manual-1490.summary: Ahmad ibn Majid, born about 1432 in Julfar on a Gulf coast now part of Ras al-Khaimah and heir to a family of pilots, finishes his prose manual Kitab al-Fawaid fi usul ilm al-bahr wa'l-qawaid about 1490. Its chapters set out a 32-point sidereal compass rose, stellar altitude measured in finger-widths with a kamal, latitude sailing, monsoon seasons, and routes and landfalls from East Africa to Sumatra. He wrote some forty works, most in verse for memorising. A Meccan writer later claimed he piloted Vasco da Gama from Malindi to India in 1498; G. R. Tibbetts, who translated this manual in 1971, and later scholars reject that story, since Portuguese accounts name a Gujarati pilot and Ibn Majid was then in his sixties. A manuscript of his collected treatises is held by the Library of Congress.

taxis-imperial-post-1490.summary: In 1490 the Taxis family began an imperial relay post, the seed of Europe's first public mail. Innsbruck was its hub; its first main route ran to Mechelen in present-day Belgium. Stations about 15 km apart, with inns and stables, let riders and horses change without delay, raising travel speed from roughly 25 to 166 km a day. Meant for official traffic, it soon carried private letters, and the Taxis family ran posts for about 400 years.

columbian-exchange-1492.summary: After 1492 maize and potatoes crossed to feed Eurasia and smallpox crossed to empty the Americas, some transfers deliberate, many unintended. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, chili peppers and tobacco spread across Africa, Asia and Europe and supported population growth there; wheat, rice, sugar cane, horses, cattle, pigs and sheep went westward. Old World diseases cut Indigenous American populations by an estimated 80 to 95 percent and nearly wiped out Caribbean peoples. Millions of Africans were carried across in slavery.

sources.qualifies: The population-loss claim is overstated; intent is unspecified).

columbus-first-voyage-1492.summary: On 12 October 1492 Columbus landed on a Bahamian island, and two worlds unknown to each other were joined for good. Christopher Columbus made landfall on an island its people called Guanahani, having sailed west from Spain on 3 August in search of a sea route to Asia's spices. A Genoese navigator, he reckoned Japan lay about 2,400 nautical miles west of the Canaries, roughly a quarter of its true distance, and Spain's Catholic Monarchs backed him. Believing he had reached Asia's Indies, he returned on 4 March 1493; Caribbean islands are still called the West Indies.

trithemius-in-praise-of-scribes-1492.summary: In 1492 Abbot Trithemius argued that monks should keep copying books by hand because parchment outlasts paper, an argument he had printed. He sent it with a dedication letter to Abbot Gerlach of Deutz. It argued that copying books by hand remained useful work for monks, disciplining mind and body and preserving texts. In this dispute between scribes and printers he took a middle position: keep old practice and allow new. After months of stylistic revision he had it printed in 1494 by Peter von Friedberg in Mainz, which later writers have treated as a curiosity.

constantinople-hebrew-press-arbaah-turim.summary: Brothers David and Samuel ibn Nahmias, Sephardic refugees who left Spain after its 1492 expulsion and gathered type and paper in Naples, set up a press in Constantinople under Bayezid II. Their colophon dates completion of Jacob ben Asher's legal code Arbaah Turim, more than 800 folio pages, to 4 Tevet 5254, 13 December 1493, and blesses their sultan. Printing in Arabic script remained closed to Muslims, so for two centuries Hebrew, then Armenian (1567) and Greek (1627) presses carried this technology in Ottoman lands. Nahmias family members printed until 1518; Hebrew presses in Constantinople issued over 100 titles by 1530, more than Müteferrika's Arabic-script press produced in its eighteenth-century run. Bibliographers long doubted 1493; Adri Offenberg's 1969 study of colophon and paper confirmed it.

aldine-press-1494.summary: In 1494 Aldus Manutius founded his Venice press, whose first dated book appeared in 1495, and went on to print cheap pocket-sized classics; books became companions to carry as well as consult. He hired Francesco Griffo to cut type: a roman face first used in Pietro Bembo's De Aetna in 1496, then a cursive variant designed to save paper, used in his 1501 Virgil, the first book printed in italic. From April 1501, with that Virgil, he issued small octavo books sized for portability. Venice granted him sole right to print Greek, but counterfeits from Lyon undercut him abroad.

pacioli-double-entry-1494.summary: In Venice in 1494 Franciscan mathematician Luca Pacioli publishes Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalita, whose section Particularis de computis et scripturis gives the first printed account of double entry as Venetian merchants used it: journal, ledger, debit matched to credit, and a trial balance. Pacioli codified rather than invented double entry. Alan Sangster's 2016 article in The Accounting Review traces its emergence to early 13th-century Italy, most likely a Florentine bank answerable to Florence's bankers' guild. Print turned a craft passed between counting houses into a teachable technique, and translations spread it across Europe. Internet Archive holds a digitised 1494 copy.

leonardo-robot-knight-1495.summary: Around 1495 Leonardo drew a mechanical knight that sat and waved, the first humanoid robot. No complete drawing survives, but scattered sketches show pulleys driven through worm gears in its chest moving its arms, an external crank and cables working hips, knees and ankles, and a hinged jaw on its flexible neck, all hidden under German-Italian armour. Several researchers have since built working versions.

kano-indigo-dye-pits-1498.summary: At Kofar Mata inside Kano's city wall, Hausa dyers sank deep clay-lined pits in which indigo leaves, ash and potash ferment for weeks before cloth is dipped and beaten to a glossy blue-black. Dyers' guild tradition dates these pits to 1498, and Marisa Candotti's study of Hausa textile origins traces dyeing and weaving in Kano to this period of growth under Sarkin Kano Muhammad Rumfa. Dyed cloth and turbans moved by caravan to Tuareg and Kanuri buyers and across the Sahara, making Kano a textile capital that Heinrich Barth in 1851 saw clothing people from Timbuktu to Lake Chad. More than a hundred pits once worked at Kofar Mata; a few still do.

swahili-mtepe-sewn-ships-1498.summary: When Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored at Mozambique Island in March 1498, its chronicler described local vessels whose planks were stitched together with coconut-fibre cord instead of nails, with sails woven from palm matting. These were mtepe, sewn-plank ships that Swahili and Bajuni mariners sailed between Lamu, Zanzibar, Kilwa and Sofala, carrying mangrove poles, grain and goods for Indian Ocean exchange. Erik Gilbert traced this craft's survival into the twentieth century; a last mtepe left Lamu waters around 1935. In 2003 shipwrights in Zanzibar built a reconstruction, Shungwaya, documented by Bojakowski, Sarathi and Berrocal.

sources.title: Bojakowski, Katie; Sarathi, Akshay and Berrocal, Piotr, 'Mtepe: Documentation and Analysis of a Sewn-Boat Reconstruction from Zanzibar', African Archaeological Review 41 (2024)
sources.author: Bojakowski, Katie; Sarathi, Akshay; Berrocal, Piotr
sources.confirms: Sewn-plank boats sailed on the Swahili coast since at least the first century CE; the last mtepe vanished from Lamu in the mid-1930s; reconstruction Shungwaya built in Zanzibar in 2003

sources.author: Gilbert, Erik
sources.confirms: Study of mtepe trade and reasons for survival of sewn construction into the twentieth century
sources.qualifies: Landing page shows bibliographic record only

sources.author: Velho, Álvaro
sources.venue: Roteiro (journal of da Gama's first voyage)
sources.confirms: Fleet at Mozambique Island from 2 March 1498 met local sailing boats; description of vessels sewn with cord and sails of palm matting

swahili-mtepe-sewn-ships-1498.detail: Sewn boats had worked this coast since at least AD 100, as Periplus of the Erythraean Sea records. Mtepe hulls flexed over coral and could be unstitched and repaired, suiting shallow creeks and beach landings. Their square matting sail and curved stem carved with eyes made them distinctive to European observers. Metal fastenings and dhow types from Arabia and India gradually replaced them under British colonial regulation.

picture.credit: E. D. Ropes

vasco-da-gama-calicut-1498.summary: On 20 May 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India by sea, breaking Venice's hold on spices and opening Asia to Europe. He landed at Kappadu near Kozhikode, later called Calicut; the spice trade had reached Europe overland, largely through Venice. Bartolomeu Dias had rounded Africa's Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and spies sent via Egypt had scouted India's markets; da Gama's fleet joined those pieces. Sailing from Lisbon in 1497, he swung wide through the South Atlantic, worked up East Africa, and at Malindi hired a Gujarati pilot who used the monsoon winds to cross to India in 23 days.

sources.title: Vasco da Gama
Ravenstein, E. G. (ed. and trans.), A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (Hakluyt Society, 1898)
sources.author: Ravenstein, Ernest George
sources.confirms: The anonymous roteiro records that on the night of Sunday 20 May 1498 the fleet anchored two leagues from Calecut, with a convict sent ashore on 21 May.

sources.title: 'Vasco da Gama', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon on July 8, 1497, and reached Calicut on May 20, 1498, after a 23-day crossing of the Indian Ocean.
sources.qualifies: The arrival date and sea-route significance are supported, but the Venice claim differs from the page’s account.

vasco-da-gama-calicut-1498.detail: Returning against the monsoon took over 90 days and killed about half his crew.

picture.alt: Portrait of Vasco da Gama attributed to Gregório Lopes, painted about 1524, a quarter century after his first voyage to Kozhikode.
picture.credit: Gregório Lopes, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

atlantic-slave-trade-1500.summary: After 1500 Europeans began shipping enslaved Africans to the Americas, about 12.5 million embarked over four centuries by SlaveVoyages' estimate, with scholarly totals from 11.1 million to 15.4 million. Up to 2 million died at sea; most came from West and Central Africa. Europeans had bought enslaved people on Africa's coast since the 15th century; in American colonies, Indigenous workers were dying from overwork, disease and maltreatment, and colonists wanted labour for sugar, coffee, tobacco, cocoa and cotton plantations and for mines. Some voyages ran a triangular route whose middle leg, the Middle Passage, carried captives west.

sources.title: Atlantic slave trade - Wikipedia
Eltis, David and David Richardson (eds.), Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database: Estimates 1501-1866 (SlaveVoyages.org, Emory/Rice)
sources.author: Eltis, David; Richardson, David
sources.confirms: Estimates 12,521,354 people embarked 1501-1866, with 277,500 embarked in 1501-1600 and 5.69 million from West Central Africa.
sources.qualifies: Database total is 12.52 million embarked, against the record's 12.75 million.

sources.qualifies: The page’s total differs from 12.75 million; it does not state “up to 2 million” deaths at sea.

atlantic-slave-trade-1500.verification_note: SlaveVoyages estimates 12.52 million embarked and 10.7 million landed, Eltis (William and Mary Quarterly 2001) put departures at about 11.06 million and Inikori at 15.4 million; SlaveVoyages' difference of 1.8 million deaths at sea fits 'up to 2 million'.
atlantic-slave-trade-1500.detail: Spain at first relied on Portuguese ships and sailors; from 1525 slaves went directly from São Tomé to Hispaniola.

hawaiian-fishponds-1500.summary: By 1500 Hawaiians farmed fish in walled sea ponds, the Pacific's most developed fish farming; some still work. Heʻeia pond on Oʻahu is roughly 600 to 800 years old. Seawater ponds enclosed shallow reef flats behind low lava-rock walls, up to 1,920 metres long and cemented with coralline algae, which let water through but held fish. Keepers grew algae for mullet and other species to graze, and wooden grates in channels let small fish in while keeping mature ones from leaving. When James Cook arrived there were at least 360 ponds yielding some 2,000,000 pounds of fish a year.

sources.title: hawaiian-fishponds
Kikuchi, William K., 'Prehistoric Hawaiian Fishponds', Science 193 (1976)
sources.author: Kikuchi, William K.
sources.confirms: The page states that Hawaiian fishponds served as aquariums for raising selected fish “from the 14th to the 19th centuries,” changed little in design and function until the 1900s, and that by the 1930s most were archaeological remains.
sources.qualifies: It does not state that fish farming began by 1500, was the Pacific’s most developed, that any ponds still operate, or details about Heʻeia’s age, reef-flat locations, lava-rock walls, or their length.

sources.author: Costa-Pierce, Barry A.
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed survey of Hawaiian fishpond aquaculture as an integrated food-producing system supporting a large population on limited arable land; record and opening text read through OpenAlex.

hawaiian-fishponds-1500.verification_note: Kikuchi, Science 1976, dates Hawaiian fishpond building to the fourteenth to nineteenth centuries; 1500 is a mid-point.
hawaiian-fishponds-1500.detail: Sluice gates admitted nutrient-rich stream water from taro fields. At spawning time nets set at those grates caught fish heading for sea.

picture.alt: Aerial view of Kalokoeli fishpond on south shore of Molokai, Hawaii, its curved rock wall enclosing shallow water, a loko kuapa of the type built from around 1500, photographed in 2012.
picture.credit: Forest and Kim Starr, CC BY 3.0 US, via Wikimedia Commons

little-ice-age-1500.summary: From around 1500 the Little Ice Age cooled the North Atlantic world for three centuries. IPCC reviewers read it as largely independent regional changes with at most modest Northern Hemisphere cooling, no ice age of global extent. Convention dates it between 1500 and 1900; some experts prefer about 1300 to about 1850, and there is no consensus on its start. Proposed causes include low solar output, volcanic eruptions, ocean circulation shifts and population collapse.

sources.title: Little Ice Age - Wikipedia
Matthews, John A., 'The ‘little ice age’: re‐evaluation of an evolving concept', Geografiska Annaler: Series A, Physical Geography 87 (2005)
sources.author: Matthews, John A.; Briffa, Keith R.
sources.venue: Geografiska Annaler: Series A, Physical Geography
sources.confirms: The page identifies the article “The ‘little ice age’: re-evaluation of an evolving concept,” published in March 2005. It states no dates or facts about North Atlantic cooling, frozen rivers, harvest failures, frost fairs, global extent, or IPCC reviewers.
sources.qualifies: The topic is relevant, but the claim’s supporting details are absent.

sources.title: 'Little Ice Age (LIA)', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page dates the broader Little Ice Age to roughly 1300-1850 (early 14th to mid-19th century); some scientists use 1500-1850, when glaciers reached their greatest extent, not “three centuries” from around 1500.
sources.qualifies: Some scientists use 1500-1850, when glaciers reached their greatest extent, not “three centuries” from around 1500. It states crop failures and famines, but not frozen rivers or frost fairs.

little-ice-age-1500.verification_note: Matthews and Briffa (Geografiska Annaler 2005) define a Little Ice Age of roughly 1300 to 1850 with a glacial maximum phase from about 1500; a 1500 start follows that narrower definition.
little-ice-age-1500.detail: NASA notes three cold intervals beginning about 1650, 1770 and 1850. Cold European summers drove Alpine glaciers forward, with advances peaking around 1380 and again around 1590.

picture.alt: Hendrick Avercamp's Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters, painted about 1608 during one of the coldest stretches of the Little Ice Age.
picture.credit: Hendrick Avercamp, public domain (CC0), via Rijksmuseum

maori-pa-fortifications-1500.summary: From about 1500 CE, Maori began cutting ditches and banks across ridge spurs and headlands, terracing slopes and raising palisades of split timber to create pa. Roughly 6,000 to 7,000 pa sites survive, concentrated in North Island areas with kumara gardens. A reassessment of marine-shell radiocarbon dates put earliest defended sites near 1500, later than once believed. Archaeologists at Pouerua in Northland studied obsidian flows into a fortified volcanic cone to test whether population pressure explained fortification. Pa protected stored kumara in pits, served as refuges and statements of mana, and later in 1840s and 1860s evolved into gunfighter pa with trenches and bunkers that absorbed British artillery.

sources.title: Schmidt, Matthew, Radiocarbon Dating New Zealand Prehistory Using Marine Shell, BAR International Series 842 (Archaeopress, 2000)
sources.author: Schmidt, Matthew
sources.confirms: Re-evaluated radiocarbon dates place earliest pa around 1500
sources.qualifies: Marine shell dates require reservoir corrections

sources.title: McCoy, Mark D.; Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Codlin, Maria; Sutton, Douglas G., 'Does Carneiro's circumscription theory help us understand Maori history? An analysis of the obsidian assemblage from Pouerua Pa, New Zealand', Journal of Archaeological Science 42 (2014)
sources.author: McCoy, Mark D.; Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Codlin, Maria; Sutton, Douglas G.
sources.confirms: Obsidian assemblage from Pouerua pa used to test circumscription theory

sources.author: Allen, Mark W.
sources.confirms: Reviews pa and warfare beyond ecological explanations
sources.qualifies: Review article

maori-pa-fortifications-1500.detail: Ecological explanations tie pa to kumara storage and competition over gardens; Mark Allen argues that social and political motives mattered too. Pa design used natural slopes, with ditches up to several metres deep and fighting stages above palisades. Ruapekapeka and Gate Pa in 1845 and 1864 showed engineering adapted against muskets and cannon. Dating pa remains difficult because many were reoccupied and rebuilt over generations.

pounamu-greenstone-industry-1500.summary: Pounamu, nephrite jade from rivers such as Arahura and Taramakau on Te Tai Poutini (South Island's West Coast), is among Earth's toughest stones. Maori workers sawed boulders with sandstone and quartz sand, ground blanks for days on wet grinding stones (hoanga), and drilled holes with cord-driven stone-tipped spindles. Chapman's 1891 account to Otago Institute recorded these methods from Maori informants. Archaeological reviews show nephrite use rising sharply after about 1500, as earlier basalt and argillite adze sources fell from use. Pounamu toki (adzes), mere (clubs) and hei-tiki travelled by foot and canoe to every part of Aotearoa, carrying mana and genealogy with them.

sources.title: Moore, Phillip R.; et al., 'The pre-European utilisation of lithic resources in Aotearoa New Zealand', Archaeology in Oceania 61 (2025)
sources.author: Moore, Phillip R.; et al.
sources.confirms: Nephrite use rises in late period c. 1500 to 1800 as early adze materials decline
sources.qualifies: Chronology is broad; shift was gradual

sources.author: Chapman, Frederick Revans
sources.venue: Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute
sources.confirms: Nineteenth-century account of sawing, grinding and drilling methods and West Coast sources
sources.qualifies: Recorded from informants a century after contact

sources.author: Jennings, Chris; Weisler, Marshall; Walter, Richard
sources.confirms: Review places New Zealand nephrite within Polynesian adze-source networks
sources.qualifies: Review focuses on quarries generally

pounamu-greenstone-industry-1500.verification_note: Archaeology dates a marked increase in pounamu working to after about 1500; some use goes back to moa-hunter sites, so 1500 marks intensification rather than beginning.
pounamu-greenstone-industry-1500.detail: Nephrite occurs only in a few South Island districts; its spread to northern North Island sites demonstrates exchange networks spanning 1,000 kilometres. Ngai Tahu controlled main sources and crossing routes over Southern Alps passes. Today ownership of pounamu is vested in Ngai Tahu under a 1997 settlement. Chapman also described Te Koroka inland source near Lake Wakatipu, named in Ngai Tahu tradition, which later geologists confirmed.

picture.alt: Mere pounamu, a polished nephrite hand club, in Canterbury Museum, Christchurch
picture.credit: Szilas

spread-of-printing-1500.summary: By 1500 presses in 236 European towns, by Febvre and Martin's count, had printed some 20 million books for 70 million people. Before the press a book had to be copied by hand. After Gutenberg lost a lawsuit to his investor Johann Fust, his monopoly ended and his method ceased to be secret; emigrating German printers, then foreign apprentices, carried it outward: Cologne 1466, Rome 1467, Venice 1469, Paris 1470, Buda and Kraków 1473, London 1477. By 1481 the Netherlands had shops in 21 towns, Italy and Germany about 40 each; Buringh and van Zanden put 220 presses and about 8 million books by 1500, and output rose tenfold in the sixteenth century.

sources.title: Global spread of the printing press - Wikipedia

Buringh, Eltjo, 'Charting the “Rise of the West”: Manuscripts and Printed Books in Europe, A Long-Term Perspective from the Sixth through Eighteenth Centuries', The Journal of Economic History 69 (2009)
sources.author: Buringh, Eltjo; Van Zanden, Jan Luiten
sources.confirms: The article estimates manuscripts and printed books in Western Europe “over the course of thirteen centuries,” from the sixth through eighteenth centuries.
sources.qualifies: The page supports a general rise in production but does not state the claim’s specific details.

sources.author: Dittmar, Jeremiah E.

spread-of-printing-1500.verification_note: Febvre and Martin estimate 236 towns and 20 million books; Dittmar counts roughly 200 cities adopting printing before 1500, and Buringh and van Zanden give lower figures of about 220 presses and 8 million books.

nilakantha-tantrasangraha-1501.summary: In 1500, by his pupil's dating, Nilakantha in Kerala had planets circle a mean Sun, which in turn circled Earth, a model like Tycho Brahe's a century later. His Tantrasangraha, A Compilation of the System, covers planetary motion, eclipses, trigonometry and their underlying mathematics in 432 Sanskrit verses, drawing on Sangamagrama Madhava's work. In it he revised Aryabhata's model for Mercury and Venus; according to George G. Joseph, his equation of centre for those planets stayed most accurate until Johannes Kepler after 1600. Jyeshtadeva's Yuktibhāṣā commentary, around 1550, worked out its proofs. Western scholars learned of it through C. M. Whish's paper of 1835.

sources.title: Tantrasamgraha - Wikipedia
'Nilakantha (1444 - 1501) - Biography', MacTutor History of Mathematics
sources.confirms: Nilakantha was born on 14 June 1444. His Tantrasamgraha, written in 1501, comprises “432 Sanskrit verses divided into 8 chapters” and is “based on the epicyclic and eccentric models of planetary motion.” It covers planetary motions and longitudes, eclipses, and other astronomy topics.
sources.qualifies: The stated date, verse count, planetary motion, and eclipses are supported; the inner-planet claim is absent.

sources.title: Ramasubramanian, K.; Srinivas, M. D.; Sriram, M. S., 'Modification of the earlier Indian planetary theory by the Kerala astronomers (c. 1500 AD) and the implied heliocentric picture of planetary motion', Current Science 66:10 (1994), 784-790
sources.author: Ramasubramanian, K.; Srinivas, M. D.; Sriram, M. S.
sources.confirms: Nilakantha's Tantrasangraha (dated 1500 AD by his pupil) revised the planetary model so Mercury and Venus, like the outer planets, move on eccentric orbits around the mean Sun, which itself circles Earth.
sources.qualifies: Dates the work to 1500 rather than 1501.

sources.title: Ramasubramanian, K. and Sriram, M. S., Tantrasangraha of Nilakantha Somayaji (Springer and Hindustan Book Agency, 2011)
sources.author: Ramasubramanian, K.; Sriram, M. S.
sources.confirms: Full English translation with notes; publisher description confirms Nilakantha's major revision of the traditional planetary model and a better equation of centre for Mercury and Venus.

aztec-sun-stone-1502.summary: Between 1502 and 1521 Mexica sculptors carved their 24-tonne Sun Stone, a calendar now Mexico's national symbol. Moctezuma II's name glyph on its central disc dates it to his reign. It is 3.6 metres across, 98 centimetres thick and weighs 24,590 kg, cut from olivine basalt of Xitle volcano. Rings of day signs and glyphs for four earlier suns, or eras, surround a central deity; it uses calendar glyphs to express cyclical time rather than working as a calendar, and archaeologists now think it served as an altar for sacrifices.
