Clark, John E., 'The Aztec Calendar Stone, edited by Khristaan D. Villela & Mary Ellen Miller, 2010. Los Angeles (CA): The Getty Research Institute Publications Program; IS', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 21 (2011)
sources.author: Clark, John E.
sources.confirms: The page identifies a review of The Aztec Calendar Stone, published in 2010. It says the review was published online 06 June 2011 and appeared in Cambridge Archaeological Journal, Volume 21, Issue 2 (June 2011), pp.
sources.qualifies: The page names the Sun Stone topic but does not provide the claim’s supporting facts.

sources.title: 'Aztec calendar', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says the calendar stone was “uncovered in Mexico City in 1790,” is “about 12 feet (3.7 metres) in diameter,” and weighs “some 25 tons.” It is on display at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City; the caption calls it a basaltic monolith.
sources.qualifies: The page does not state carving dates, identify Mexica sculptors or Moctezuma II’s glyph, call it a national symbol, give its thickness or exact weight, or specify “oli.” Its approximate size and weight differ from the claim’s figures.

aztec-sun-stone-1502.verification_note: Clark, Cambridge Archaeological Journal 2011, and Britannica confirm the basalt monolith about 3.6 m across; Britannica gives about 25 tons and its 1502 carving date is inferred from Moctezuma II's glyph.
aztec-sun-stone-1502.detail: Its basalt block was probably dragged up to 22 kilometres by thousands of people. Buried after Spanish conquest, it was rediscovered on 17 December 1790 beneath Mexico City's main square.

picture.credit: Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

leonardo-codex-flight-1505.summary: In 1505 Leonardo filled a notebook with how birds fly and how a person might; he never flew, but he drew the problem correctly. Applying mechanics to observation, he compared wing to wedge and tail to rudder, used laws of equilibrium to explain how birds balance in air, studied air resistance, currents and wind, and sketched joints for an artificial wing. Smithsonian curators count among its notes early concepts that reappeared in successful airplanes four centuries later.

javanese-jong-1511.summary: When Portuguese fleets reached Melaka in 1511, they met Javanese jong: ships with hulls of three or four planking layers fastened by wooden dowels, two to four masts carrying lug sails, twin quarter rudders and cargo capacity that Portuguese observers put at several hundred tons, larger than their own carracks. Pierre-Yves Manguin's reading of Portuguese, Chinese and Javanese sources shows a Southeast Asian shipbuilding tradition that linked Java, Melaka, Pegu and Maluku in pepper, rice and cloth trade. Shipowners from Japara, Gresik and Tuban sent fleets to attack Portuguese Melaka in 1513. Within a century jong gave way to smaller hybrid vessels as Portuguese artillery and later Dutch monopolies changed Indonesian seas.

sources.title: Manguin, Pierre-Yves, 'The Southeast Asian ship: an historical approach', Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 11 (1980)
sources.author: Manguin, Pierre-Yves
sources.confirms: Jong construction, size and trade role as described in early 16th-century sources

sources.title: Manguin, Pierre-Yves, 'The vanishing jong: insular Southeast Asian fleets in trade and war (fifteenth to seventeenth centuries)', in Anthony Reid (ed.), Southeast Asia in the Early Modern Era (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1993)
sources.author: Manguin, Pierre-Yves
sources.confirms: Decline of large jong after Portuguese arrival

javanese-jong-1511.verification_note: Abstract and chapter metadata confirmed; tonnage estimates derive from Portuguese observers and Manguin treats them with caution.
javanese-jong-1511.detail: Manguin cautions that Portuguese tonnage figures may exaggerate and that no jong hull has been excavated intact. Archaeological wrecks in Gulf of Thailand show related lashed-lug and dowelled construction. His later chapter, 'The vanishing jong', traces decline through sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

picture.alt: Ship relief at Borobudur, Java, showing an outrigger vessel of an earlier Javanese tradition
picture.credit: Andreas Sihono

piri-reis-map-1513.summary: In 1513 the Ottoman admiral Piri Reis, at Gallipoli, mapped the Americas from captured Spanish charts. He presented it to Sultan Selim I after Egypt's conquest in 1517. About one third survives, its western part, on gazelle-skin parchment roughly 90 by 63 cm, showing Atlantic coasts of Europe, Africa and South America. It is a portolan chart: compass roses and radiating bearing lines for navigation by dead reckoning rather than a latitude and longitude grid, with long notes in Ottoman Turkish. Found at Topkapı Palace in 1929, it drew worldwide attention because its Caribbean copies a lost map by Christopher Columbus.

sources.author: McIntosh, Gregory

sources.qualifies: The title states 1513; the other claim details are absent.

piri-reis-map-1513.verification_note: Soucek (History of Cartography, 1992) confirms completion in 1513 at Gallipoli, presentation to Selim I in Cairo in 1517, a Columbus source obtained from a Spanish prisoner and rediscovery in 1929 by Deissmann; he gives 90 by 63 cm where other accounts give 87 by 63.
piri-reis-map-1513.detail: Columbus's map, as copied, merged Cuba into Asia. A 20th-century claim that it shows an ice-free Antarctica has been disproven.

picture.credit: Piri Reis, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

more-utopia-1516.summary: In 1516 Thomas More's Utopia, an island without property, named every later ideal society. The London lawyer, on embassy in Flanders, wrote it in Latin and had it printed by Dirk Martens in Leuven in December. It is framed as dialogue: More and his host Pieter Gillis meet a talkative Portuguese traveller, Raphael Hythlodaeus, whose name means roughly "peddler of nonsense", which let More disown his boldest claims. Hythlodaeus describes an island society holding goods in common, without money or gold, with religious freedom, a six-hour working day and no lawyers. More had called it Nusquama, Latin for "nowhere"; Erasmus suggested Greek coinage Utopia, "no place". Its title named a literary genre.

luther-95-theses-printing-1517.summary: In 1517 Luther sent out his Ninety-five Theses, and the press spread them across Germany. Luther, professor of moral theology at Wittenberg, had grown alarmed when parishioners returned from buying Johann Tetzel's indulgences believing they no longer needed to repent. The Theses argued that repentance was inward and lifelong, and that indulgences led Christians away from it and from works of mercy.

sources.author: McNally, Robert E.

It gives no details about printing or circulation, Luther’s 1517 actions or position, Tetzel’s indulgences, or parishioners’ beliefs.

luther-95-theses-printing-1517.detail: Printed forms included a four-page Latin pamphlet in Basel, placards in Leipzig and Nuremberg, several hundred copies across Germany that year, and Kaspar Nützel's German translation. Dispute with Johann Eck followed, then the 1519 Leipzig Debate.

fugger-charles-v-election-1519.summary: In 1519 Jakob Fugger lent 543,000 guilders to buy Charles V the empire: money, with dynastic politics, chose an emperor. When Emperor Maximilian I died, seven prince-electors chose his successor: three archbishops, Bohemia's king, and Palatinate's, Brandenburg's and Saxony's rulers. Francis I of France had already secured Trier and Palatinate and offered 300,000 guilders; Henry VIII and Frederick of Saxony also stood. Jakob Fugger of Augsburg, whose loans to Maximilian tied his fortune to Habsburg success, backed Maximilian's 19-year-old grandson Charles with more than 850,000 guilders transferred to electors. Charles was elected unanimously as Charles V, for political and dynastic reasons as much as for money, Cohn argues.

sources.title: Jakob Fugger - Wikipedia

fugger-charles-v-election-1519.detail: Of that sum about 550,000 guilders came from Fugger's own house, 150,000 from Augsburg's Welser family and the rest from three Italian bankers. In 1523 Fugger reminded Charles that without his help he could not have won.

magellan-elcano-circumnavigation-1519.summary: In September 1522 one ship and 18 men returned to Spain from humanity's first voyage around Earth. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought Victoria home three years after leaving with Ferdinand Magellan's five ships and some 270 men. Magellan, a Portuguese sailor in Spanish service, had set out on 20 September 1519 to reach the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, by sailing west. After mutinies and wintering on Patagonia's coast, his fleet entered the strait now named for him on 1 November 1520 and crossed an ocean he named Mar Pacifico in 98 days; Magellan was killed in the Philippines in April 1521.

It states that “one of his ships continued westward to Spain, accomplishing the first circumnavigation of Earth,” successfully completed by Juan Sebastián del Cano.

magellan-elcano-circumnavigation-1519.detail: During that Pacific crossing men died of scurvy and ate sawdust and rats. Magellan's ships reached those islands in November 1521.

smallpox-tenochtitlan-1520.summary: In 1520 smallpox reached Tenochtitlan and killed perhaps 40 percent of its people in months. It arrived while Hernán Cortés rebuilt his alliances after being driven out. Spanish sources trace it to Francisco de Eguía, an enslaved African in Narváez's force left ill at Cempoala. Smallpox had been endemic in Spain for centuries, so Spaniards had acquired immunity; Mexica had none. It broke out in Tenochtitlan in late October 1520 and ran about sixty days, until early December. Ruler Cuitlahuac died after eighty days in office. Historians count it as decisive in the 1521 siege.

No page numbers for those claims are visible.
sources.qualifies: The page identifies Robert McCaa’s article, “Spanish and Nahuatl Views on Smallpox and Demographic Catastrophe in Mexico,” published in 1995, but gives no specific epidemic date, mortality figure, account of Cortés’s alliances, or mention of Francisco de Eguía.

smallpox-tenochtitlan-1520.detail: Tlaxcalan chieftain Maxixcatl, Spain's ally, also died, but losses fell hardest inside crowded Tenochtitlan, where the Florentine Codex records people too sick to seek food.

first-battle-of-panipat-1526.summary: In 1526 Babur's 12,000 men with guns beat an army five times larger: gunpowder took India. He met Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Khan Lodi at Panipat, north of Delhi. Ibrahim reportedly fielded 50,000 to 70,000 men and 1,000 war elephants but no gunpowder arms; Babur had about 12,000, some with matchlock muskets, 15 to 20 cannons, and cavalry fighting as horse archers. Behind a line of tied wagons, musket and cannon pinned Ibrahim's centre while horse archers struck flanks and rear, and cannon noise panicked his elephants. Ibrahim and some 20,000 men died, opening Mughal rule in India.

first-battle-of-panipat-1526.detail: Babur tied 700 wagons in line with breastworks for musketeers between them and left gaps for cavalry sorties. He anchored one flank on Panipat town and dug a trench on the other, so Ibrahim's wider army could not deploy against that front.

mughal-empire-era-1526.summary: In 1526 Babur founded the Mughal Empire with cannon and muskets, and it ruled most of India for two centuries. This Timurid prince from Central Asia's Fergana Valley had ruled Kabul since 1504 and sought lands to its southeast. With assistance from Safavid and Ottoman empires, his outnumbered army used firearms and cannon to defeat Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526, then swept down northern India's plains. Conventionally that victory marks Mughal founding, though historians sometimes date its imperial structure to about 1600 under his grandson Akbar. Reduced to Delhi's surroundings by 1760, it was formally dissolved by Britain after 1857.

sources.qualifies: The battle date and invasion are supported; the other details are absent.

afonso-kongo-letters-1526.summary: Mvemba a Nzinga, baptised Afonso I, ruled Kongo from 1506 to about 1542 and ran a written diplomacy with Portugal through dozens of Portuguese-language letters drafted at his court in Mbanza Kongo. He asked Manuel I for ships, masons, carpenters, physicians and teachers, sent sons and nephews to study in Lisbon, and built a Kongolese church under his own authority. In letters of 1526 to João III he protested that Portuguese traders and their Kongolese partners were seizing free subjects, including nobles, and demanded that trade pass through his officials. John Thornton's work established the letters as a record of a literate African state negotiating with Europe on its own terms.

sources.author: Thornton, John K.

afonso-kongo-letters-1526.detail: Thornton's 1981 reinterpretation of early Kongo-Portuguese relations and his 2023 biography with Luís Madureira's translations show Afonso pursuing education and literacy campaigns, apprenticeships in carpentry, masonry and medicine, and control of the slave trade rather than its abolition. His letters survive in Lisbon's Torre do Tombo and in copies. Afonso's successors continued this correspondence with Rome and Lisbon for two centuries.

paracelsus-1500.summary: In 1527 Theophrastus von Hohenheim, called Paracelsus, became town physician and medical lecturer at Basel and taught that disease is chemical and should be treated with chemical remedies. He is believed to have taken his doctorate at Ferrara in 1516 (Britannica). At Basel he lectured and wrote in German rather than Latin so people outside universities could follow, and on 24 June 1527, in front of Basel's university, he reportedly burned books of Avicenna and Galen, pillars of academic medicine. He prepared remedies containing mercury, sulfur, iron and copper sulfate, uniting medicine with chemistry, and declared that what sickens in large doses can cure in small ones. Charles Webster (Social History of Medicine, 1995) shows how his medical system, first set out in full around 1531, was bound up with his theology and his attack on miraculous healing by saints.

sources.title: Paracelsus - Wikipedia
WEBSTER, CHARLES, 'Paracelsus Confronts the Saints: Miracles, Healing and the Secularization of Magic', Social History of Medicine 8 (1995)
sources.author: WEBSTER, CHARLES
sources.confirms: The page identifies Paracelsus as “Theophrast von Hohenheim, 1493-1541” and says his De causis morborum invisibilium followed Opus Paramirum (1531). It discusses his views on miraculous healing and secularizing magic.
sources.qualifies: Name and lifespan match; the other claims are not stated.

sources.title: 'Paracelsus', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Paracelsus was a German-Swiss physician and alchemist. The page says he helped establish “the role of chemistry in medicine” and used remedies containing mercury, sulfur, iron, and copper sulfate.
sources.qualifies: “illness is chemical” is not stated; the doctorate year differs.

paracelsus-1500.verification_note: Corrected in November 2026: date fixed at Paracelsus's Basel year, 1527, since 1500 was no event (he was born 1493); his Ferrara doctorate now reads 1516 and his book burning 24 June after Britannica, with Webster (Social History of Medicine, 1995) for his medical system.
paracelsus-1500.detail: His chemical and mineral remedies entered official pharmacopoeias; London's first Pharmacopoeia of 1618 records them. Students came from across Europe to hear him at Basel, and his quarrels with faculty and city drove him out within months.

picture.alt: Woodcut portrait of Paracelsus by Augustin Hirschvogel, 1538, made in physician's lifetime.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

yuktibhasa-1530.summary: Between about 1500 and 1530 (Singh and MacTutor give about 1500, Divakaran the early 1500s) Jyeṣṭhadeva wrote out proofs of Kerala's infinite series in Malayalam, the first to prove them. It consolidates discoveries of Madhava of Sangamagrama, Nilakantha Somayaji and others, and mainly supplies rationale for results in Nilakantha's Tantrasamgraha, giving proofs and derivations where earlier texts stated rules. Its topics include infinite series for π, sine, cosine and arctangent, techniques predating Newton and Leibniz by about two centuries, though it never unified them around derivative and integral. Written in a local language, it went largely unnoticed outside India until modern times.

yuktibhasa-1530.detail: It also gives second and third order approximations of sine and cosine.

iwami-ginzan-silver-1533.summary: In 1533 merchant Kamiya Jutei brought two refiners from Korea to Iwami Ginzan in western Honshu, where they introduced haifuki, a cupellation process that smelts silver ore with lead and then oxidises lead away on an ash bed. Output from Iwami and later Ikuno and Sado rose so sharply that Kobata Atsushi estimated Japan supplied up to a third of world silver in late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Portuguese and Chinese traders carried this silver to Ming China in exchange for silk, feeding Ming tax reforms and Manila galleon commerce. UNESCO listed Iwami Ginzan in 2007 as a mining landscape worked from sixteenth to twentieth centuries.

sources.author: Kobata, Atsushi

iwami-ginzan-silver-1533.detail: Kobata's 1965 article remains a base reference for production and export figures, though later work by Yamamura and Kamiki revised volumes. Daimyo and then Tokugawa shogunate controlled Iwami directly; thousands of shafts and settlements remain in forested hills. Haifuki came from Korean practice, with Chinese roots.

casa-de-moneda-mexico-1535.summary: In 1535 Spain opened a mint in Mexico City, America's first; its silver pesos served world trade as its coin for three centuries. It was built over Moctezuma's Casa Denegrida, his black house of meditation. Its silver coins of eight reales, and their successor, Mexico's silver peso, circulated widely across America and Asia well past 1800 and underlay several modern currencies, including the United States dollar, Japanese yen and Chinese yuan. Casa de Moneda still operates as Mexico's national mint, oldest in the Americas.

paracelsus-homunculus-1537.summary: In 1537 a text under Paracelsus's name gave a recipe for growing a tiny human in a glass, a dream of made life. A homunculus is an artificial miniature human that alchemists believed could be made. De natura rerum, dated 1537 in its text and of disputed authorship, gives this method: human semen sealed in a glass vessel and left forty days in venter equinus, warm fermenting horse dung, until something transparent and manlike forms; fed with human blood and kept at that even heat for forty weeks, it grows into a living child, like one born of a woman but much smaller.

sources.author: Newman, William R.
sources.confirms: The Paracelsian school asserted an artificial human, the homunculus, could be made; sixteenth-century debate over its status is treated in chapter 4.

paracelsus-homunculus-1537.detail: Such beings were credited with secret knowledge of their art. Later writers compared them to Jewish folklore's golem.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

mexico-city-printing-press-1539.summary: In 1539 the Americas' first printing press opened in Mexico City, a century before any in English America. Juan Cromberger, a Seville printer, had decided in 1536 to open a printing house in Mexico and sent Giovanni Paoli, a Lombard known as Juan Pablos, to run it. Pablos left Seville on 12 June 1539, reached Mexico City in October and set up shop in Cromberger's house. That year Pablos printed America's first known published book, Bishop Juan de Zumárraga's Breve y mas compendiosa doctrina Christiana, in Spanish and Nahuatl. After Cromberger died in 1540 Pablos secured permission to run his press as his own, printing at least 37 books and training Mexico's next printers.

mexico-city-printing-press-1539.detail: Cromberger's name appeared on all its early books until 1545, though he never crossed the Atlantic.

ardabil-carpet-woven-1540.summary: A knotted inscription on a pair of carpets made for Safavid shah Tahmasp's dynastic shrine at Ardabil records completion in 946 AH (1539 to 1540) as work of 'a servant of the court, Maqsud Kashani'. Each measures about ten by five metres, with wool pile in ten colours on a silk warp and weft, averaging 5,300 asymmetric knots per square decimetre; a single carpet holds roughly 26 million knots. A central sunburst medallion with two hanging lamps floats over a blue field of scrolling blossoms, a design shared with Tabriz manuscript illumination. Shrine authorities sold both carpets in 1888 through Ziegler and Company of Manchester to pay for earthquake repairs. London's South Kensington Museum bought one in 1893 for 1,750 pounds on William Morris's advice; its twin, trimmed to patch the first, reached Los Angeles County Museum of Art in 1953.

sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.confirms: Inscription dated 946H with Maqsud Kashani's name; 340 knots per square inch; wool pile on silk; bought 1893 for 1,750 pounds after Morris's advice; twin sold 1892 and given to LACMA 1953; Ziegler bought from shrine 1888.

sources.author: Melville, Charles

maize-west-africa-1540.summary: Maize crossed the Atlantic with Portuguese ships and by about 1550 was growing from Gambia's river to São Tomé and Congo's estuary, according to accounts that Marvin Miracle assembled in 1965. West African farmers folded it into existing systems: planted on cleared forest plots alongside yams, harvested early to bridge hungry months, and ground or roasted in ways borrowed from sorghum cooking. James McCann describes this as maize's 'invention' in West Africa, since Akan and Yoruba growers selected flinty, early-maturing types and gave it local names and ritual places. Maize spread inland slowly: it was unknown in Buganda in 1861.

sources.title: Miracle, Marvin P., 'The Introduction and Spread of Maize in Africa', Journal of African History 6 (1965)
sources.author: Miracle, Marvin P.
sources.confirms: Maize grown from the Gambia to São Tomé and the Congo mouth in the sixteenth century; Portuguese role undocumented; unknown in Buganda in 1861

sources.title: McCann, James C., 'Maize's Invention in West Africa', in Maize and Grace: Africa's Encounter with a New World Crop, 1500-2000 (Harvard University Press, 2005), ch. 3
sources.author: McCann, James C.
sources.confirms: Chapter on West African adoption and adaptation of maize
sources.qualifies: Chapter landing page gives title and pages; text not opened

maize-west-africa-1540.detail: Miracle found no documentary proof of Portuguese introduction and warned that early European observers often confused maize with sorghum. McCann's Maize and Grace follows the crop from coastal gardens to its twentieth-century dominance in eastern and southern African diets, when hybrid seed and colonial maize boards made it a staple. Provisioning of slave ships with maize meal tied it to Atlantic slaving. Anchor year 1540 is a midpoint of first reports.

picture.alt: Maize for sale at Sawla market, Northern Region, Ghana
picture.credit: CIAT

copernicus-de-revolutionibus-1543.summary: In 1543 Copernicus published a book that moved Earth from the universe's centre to orbit around the Sun. Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was printed in Nuremberg just before his death. He had sketched this system in his Commentariolus, a manuscript circulated to friends by 1514, but hesitated to publish for decades. In 1539 young Wittenberg mathematician Georg Joachim Rheticus came to study with him, printed a summary, Narratio Prima, in 1540, and its friendly reception persuaded Copernicus to release his book, dedicated to Pope Paul III, to printer Johannes Petreius. Kepler's 1609 ellipses refined its circles.

sources.title: Wikipedia: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
'Nicolaus Copernicus', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Copernicus “probably hit upon his main idea sometime between 1508 and 1514” and wrote a manuscript usually called the Commentariolus (“Little Commentary”). The final version, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium libri vi, “did not appear in print until 1543, the year of his death.” He died May 24, 1543.

sources.title: N. Copernicus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium libri VI (Nuremberg: Johannes Petreius, 1543), Boston Public Library copy, digitised on the Internet Archive
sources.author: Nicolaus Copernicus
sources.confirms: First edition printed at Nuremberg by Petreius in 1543, with 147 woodcut diagrams and the heliocentric system.

sources.title: O. Gingerich, An Annotated Census of Copernicus' De revolutionibus (Nuremberg, 1543 and Basel, 1566) (Brill, 2002)
sources.author: Owen Gingerich
sources.confirms: Describes all 560 located copies of the 1543 Nuremberg first edition and the 1566 Basel second edition from direct examination.

copernicus-de-revolutionibus-1543.detail: Lutheran preacher Andreas Osiander, supervising its printing, added an unsigned preface calling it mere computation; Kepler later exposed him.

picture.alt: Page from a 1543 De revolutionibus orbium coelestium showing Copernicus's diagram of the celestial spheres with Sun at centre.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

scientific-revolution-era-1543.summary: From 1543 Europeans tested nature by measurement and experiment instead of trusting ancient authors. Historians call this break with earlier natural philosophy across 1500 to 1700 the Scientific Revolution. Its new science departed from Greek traditions, read nature mechanically, leaned on mathematics, and prized gathering and interpreting fresh evidence over reverence for ancient authority. It is often dated from 1543, when Andreas Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica and Copernicus's De revolutionibus were printed, though some start it with 1572's supernova; it culminates in Isaac Newton's Principia Mathematica of 1687.

sources.title: Scientific Revolution - Wikipedia
Shapin, Steven, The Scientific Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
sources.author: Shapin, Steven
sources.confirms: The page says that “in the 1600s science emerged from a variety of beliefs, practices, and influences” and calls the 17th century “crucial.” It does not state that change began in 1543, describe measurement and experiment replacing trust in ancient authors, or specify a break with Greek tradition.
sources.qualifies: It supports the broad 17th-century emergence but omits those details.

sources.title: 'Scientific Revolution', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page dates the Scientific Revolution to c. 1400-1690 and describes it as a change in scientific thought during the 16th and 17th centuries.
sources.qualifies: It says science shifted toward “quantitative” views and an “experimental, scientific method,” with explanation emphasizing “how” rather than “why.” Copernicus published his heliocentric theory in 1543.

scientific-revolution-era-1543.verification_note: it supports broad 17th-century emergence but omits those details; it says science shifted toward “quantitative” views and an “experimental, scientific method,” with explanation emphasizing “how” rather than “why.” Copernicus published his heliocentric theory in 1543
scientific-revolution-era-1543.detail: Alexandre Koyré used this phrase last century and Herbert Butterfield popularised it. Francis Bacon's calls for progress inspired bodies such as London's Royal Society.

picture.alt: Heliocentric diagram in Copernicus's autograph manuscript of De revolutionibus, written before its 1543 printing, held by Jagiellonian Library, Kraków.
picture.credit: Nicolaus Copernicus, public domain, via Jagiellonian Library (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

tanegashima-arquebus-1543.summary: In 1543 two Portuguese muskets reached Tanegashima island, Japan, by chance; within decades Japan made thousands. Its lord, Tanegashima Tokitaka, bought both matchlocks, apparently of a type made at Portuguese Goa, and set swordsmith Yaita Kinbee Kiyosoda to copy barrel and firing mechanism. Most parts posed no difficulty, but drilling barrels helically so that their screw breech plugs fitted tightly was unknown in Japan; a Portuguese blacksmith brought back next year solved it. Guns named tanegashima spread through Japan's civil wars.

sources.title: Tanegashima (gun) - Wikipedia
Lidin, Olof G., 'The Arrival of the Portuguese', in Tanegashima: The Arrival of Europe in Japan (Routledge, 2002), pp. 16-41
sources.author: Lidin, Olof G.
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page shows title and chapter metadata only; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'Japan's encounter with Europe, 1573-1853'
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.confirms: 1543. The page says Portuguese matchlock guns arrived in Japan and Japanese guns were produced in large numbers within a decade.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sengoku period'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1543. The page supports the broad account that Portuguese firearms and construction knowledge reached Japan and that Japan adopted and produced matchlocks. It does not confirm the record’s specific copying story.

tanegashima-arquebus-1543.detail: Oda Nobunaga's 3,000 gunners fired volleys at Nagashino in 1575, and about one quarter of 1592's Korea invasion force were gunners.

picture.alt: Antique Japanese tanegashima matchlock guns, later photograph of surviving Edo period examples.
picture.credit: pdeaudney, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

vesalius-fabrica-1543.summary: In 1543 Vesalius published the first accurate atlas of human anatomy, from corpses he cut up. Andreas Vesalius, aged 28, published De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem in Basel: seven books with more than 250 woodcuts. Teaching at Padua, he had broken with practice by dissecting while lecturing; dissection had been left to barber surgeons under a doctor who did no manual work. Comparing what he saw with Galen's texts, he found Galen had worked from dogs and monkeys. Johannes Oporinus printed it, with a dedication to Charles V.

sources.title: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem - Wikipedia
Vesalius, Andreas, De humani corporis fabrica libri septem (Basel: Oporinus, 1543), digitized at BHL
sources.author: Vesalius, Andreas
sources.confirms: Catalogue of the original 1543 Basel edition printed by Oporinus in June 1543.
sources.qualifies: BHL description counts 204 illustrations; record says more than 250 woodcuts.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'De humani corporis fabrica libri septem'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1543. The page confirms that Vesalius’s major anatomy work was printed in 1543 and describes it as seminal; it does not call it the “first accurate atlas.”

vesalius-fabrica-1543.detail: He kept some of Galen's errors, such as veins and arteries carrying different kinds of blood. Its woodcuts are now attributed to Titian's studio.

picture.alt: Title page of Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica, Basel 1543, with a public dissection scene.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

gessner-bibliotheca-universalis-1545.summary: In 1545 Konrad Gessner catalogued every known author, some 10,000 works, and warned that printing was producing a confusing flood of books. He wrote in its preface of a confusing and harmful multitude of books since printing, and of fear that recent learning could vanish as Alexandria's library had. Authors are entered alphabetically by first name with life details, titles, places and dates of printing, and often extracts or his own judgement. It is counted as the first universal bibliography.

sources.title: Confusa e irritante multidão de livros: relações entre o contexto histórico-informacional da Europa Moderna e a estrutura documentária de Bibliotheca Universalis, de Conrad Gesner
Blair, Ann, 'Reading Strategies for Coping with Information Overload ca. 1550-1700', Journal of the History of Ideas 64, no. 1 (2003)
sources.author: Blair, Ann
sources.venue: Journal of the History of Ideas
sources.confirms: The abstract states the article surveys how early modern scholars responded to what they perceived as an overabundance of books; Blair opens with Gessner's 1545 complaint of a confusing and harmful multitude of books.

sources.title: Blair, Ann M., Too Much to Know: Managing Scholarly Information before the Modern Age (Yale University Press, 2010), ch. 1
sources.author: Blair, Ann M.
sources.confirms: University-press monograph whose first chapter treats Gessner's Bibliotheca universalis as the first universal bibliography and his preface on the harmful abundance of books; publisher record confirmed.

gessner-bibliotheca-universalis-1545.detail: His Pandectae of 1548 and 1549 then arranged the same material by subject. Gessner is called the father of bibliography on its strength.

picture.alt: Title page of Bibliotheca instituta et collecta primum a Conrado Gesnero, Zurich 1574, Simler's expansion of Gessner's 1545 universal bibliography.
picture.credit: Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler, John Carter Brown Library, public domain, via Internet Archive

potosi-silver-1545.summary: In 1545 Spaniards began mining silver at Potosí's Cerro Rico, a mountain whose ores, lake sediments show, Andean smelters worked at scale around 1000 AD. Tradition credits Andean prospector Diego Huallpa with its 1545 discovery. Potosí's silver paid for Spain's wars and swelled Spanish Empire tax returns; production peaked in 1592 after mercury amalgamation arrived in 1572. Earl Hamilton argued in 1934 that American silver drove Spain's 1520 to 1650 price revolution; historians still dispute how much it explains, since prices rose from 1516, before significant American silver reached Seville.

sources.title: Potosí
Tandeter, Enrique, 'Forced and Free Labour in Late Colonial Potosi', Past and Present 93 (1981), pp. 98-136
sources.author: Tandeter, Enrique
sources.confirms: OpenAlex bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Potosi Bolivia'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1545. The page says silver was discovered there in 1545 and the city quickly became famous for its wealth, but it does not explicitly say the discovery drove Potosí’s growth.

sources.title: Mark B. Abbott and Alexander P. Wolfe, 'Intensive pre-Incan metallurgy recorded by lake sediments from the Bolivian Andes'
sources.venue: Science, vol. 301, no. 5641, 26 September 2003, pp. 1893-1895; DOI 10.1126/science.1087806
sources.author: Mark B. Abbott, Alexander P. Wolfe
sources.confirms: 'Here, we reconstruct a millennium of metallurgical activity in southern Bolivia using the stratigraphy of metals associated with smelting (Pb, Sb, Bi, Ag, Sn) from lake sediments deposited near the major silver deposit of Cerro Rico de Potosí. Pronounced metal enrichment events coincide with the terminal stages of Tiwanaku culture (1000 to 1200 A.D.) and Inca through early Colonial times (1400 to 1650 A.D.). The earliest of these events suggests that Cerro Rico ores were actively smelted at a large scale in the Late Intermediate Period, providing evidence for a major pre-Incan silver industry.'

sources.title: Kris Lane, 'Potosí', in Mark Thurner and Juan Pimentel (eds), New World Objects of Knowledge: A Cabinet of Curiosities
sources.venue: University of London Press, 2021, Part 1 chapter 3 (open-access edition)
sources.author: Kris Lane
sources.confirms: 'Apparently discovered in 1545 by an Andean prospector named Diego Huallpa, the Cerro Rico, an eroded volcanic plug jutting up 4,782 m or nearly 16,000 feet above sea level, quickly captured the world's imagination.'; 'it was only with the construction of large-scale mercury amalgamation facilities after 1572 that the silver potential of these ores was unlocked'; 'attested to by soaring tax returns and Spanish government spending. Production peaked in 1592, after which the Cerro Rico began to lurch along in stair-step decline'; 'Figure 6. Potosí's registered silver production (yellow) and mint production (red) from discovery in 1545 to 1821.'

sources.title: John Munro, review essay on Earl J. Hamilton, American Treasure and the Price Revolution in Spain, 1501-1650 (Harvard University Press, 1934)
sources.venue: EH.Net, Classic Reviews in Economic History, January 2007
sources.author: John Munro
sources.confirms: 'His object was to validate the Quantity Theory of Money: in seeking to demonstrate that the influx of American silver was chiefly, if not entirely, responsible for the inflation of much of the Price Revolution era, from ca. 1520 to ca. 1650'; 'the Price Revolution had begun as early as the quinquennium 1516-20, long before, decades before, any significant amounts of Spanish American silver had reached Seville'; 'two most important silver mines were brought into production: those of Potosi in "Peru" (modern-day Bolivia) in 1545, and Zacatecas, in Mexico, the following year, 1546.' 'vast quantities of silver (and gold) thus undoubtedly flowed from Spain into the various military theaters, in payment for wages, munitions, supplies, and diplomacy'; 'Published by EH.Net (January 2007)'.

sources.title: Douglas Fisher, 'The Price Revolution: A Monetary Interpretation'
sources.venue: Journal of Economic History, vol. 49, no. 4, December 1989, pp. 883-902
sources.author: Douglas Fisher
sources.confirms: 'This article presents tests of the role of money in the price revolution'; 'The hypothesis is that American specie drove European prices, and that the mechanism was the quantity theory of money buttressed by the specie-flow mechanism.'

potosi-silver-1545.detail: Silver went by llama and mule train to Pacific ports, north to Panama and on to Spain. Spaniards still say valer un Potosí, to be worth a Potosí.

picture.alt: Woodcut of Cerro Rico and Potosí from Pedro de Cieza de León's Crónica del Perú, Seville 1553, eight years after silver was found there.
picture.credit: A.Skromnitsky, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

benin-brass-plaques-1550.summary: In Benin City, palace guild casters produced several hundred rectangular brass plaques, each about 40 by 30 centimetres, cast by lost wax and nailed to wooden pillars in palace courtyards. They show the Oba with mudfish legs holding leopards, warriors in coral regalia, Portuguese traders and court musicians, set against a stippled ground of river-leaf pattern. Kathryn Gunsch dates this series to around 1550 and argues it formed a single planned monument of royal history. Brass arrived as manillas traded by Portuguese ships for pepper and enslaved people. British forces removed them during their 1897 occupation; London's British Museum holds most.

sources.title: Gunsch, Kathryn Wysocki, The Benin Plaques: A 16th Century Imperial Monument (Routledge, 2017)
sources.author: Gunsch, Kathryn Wysocki
sources.confirms: Monograph dating the plaque series to the sixteenth century and treating it as an imperial monument
sources.qualifies: Publisher page shows title, author and dates only

sources.title: British Museum, Collection object Af1898,0115.30: plaque, Benin City, 16th-17th century
sources.confirms: Brass relief plaque of the Oba with mudfish legs holding leopards, made by Edo in Benin City by lost-wax casting, dated 16th-17th century, 38.5 by 32 cm, received via the Foreign Office after the 1897 occupation

benin-brass-plaques-1550.detail: British Museum's record for plaque Af1898,0115.30 gives a sixteenth- to seventeenth-century date, Edo manufacture by lost-wax casting in leaded brass, and arrival in London through the Foreign Office in 1898. Gunsch analysed composition, iconography and nail holes to reconstruct how plaques paired across pillars. Plaque production stopped by around 1700, though Benin casting continued in heads and figures. Restitution of Benin objects has been under negotiation since 2010.

picture.alt: Cast brass plaque with two court figures, Benin, 16th century, Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, Cambridge
picture.credit: SpeakingArch

leo-africanus-description-1550.summary: In 1550 Leo Africanus's account of Africa was printed; for some 300 years, until modern exploration, European scholars treated it as their most authoritative account of Africa. Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Wazzan, born in Granada about 1494 and raised in Fez, had travelled as a diplomat across North Africa and, around 1510, to Timbuktu in Songhai. Captured by Spanish corsairs in 1518, he was presented to Pope Leo X, freed, baptised in 1520 as Johannes Leo, and known as Leo Africanus. In Italy he wrote, in Italian, an account of Africa's geography, peoples and cities, finished in 1526. Giovanni Battista Ramusio published it in Venice in 1550 as Descrittione dell'Africa.

sources.title: Leo Africanus - Wikipedia
Leo Africanus, 'Della descrittione dell'Africa', in Marvels of the World (Penn Press), pp. 319-321
sources.author: Leo Africanus
sources.confirms: Contents page lists the Description of Africa excerpt; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Leo Africanus'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Descrittione dell’Africa was published in 1550; Leo Africanus completed it around 1526. The page gives 1550 for the work and says his writings were a principal European source for about 400 years.

leo-africanus-description-1550.detail: It was reprinted five times, with French and Latin editions in 1556 and English in 1600.

picture.alt: Title page of Leo Africanus's De totius Africae descriptione, Antwerp 1556, Latin edition of his description of Africa first printed in 1550.
picture.credit: Leo Africanus, John Carter Brown Library, public domain, via Internet Archive

mimar-sinan-suleymaniye-1550.summary: From 1550 Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye in Istanbul, a 53-metre dome above schools, a hospital and kitchen. Suleiman the Magnificent commissioned his imperial architect to build it on the Third Hill above the Golden Horn. An inscription dates its foundation to 1550 and inauguration to 1557, though work on parts of its complex probably continued for some years. Like other Ottoman imperial foundations it anchored a külliye, religious and charitable buildings with madrasas, public kitchen and hospital, whose staff and endowment deed served Suleiman's claim to lead Sunni Islam. Its layout deliberately echoes Hagia Sophia, Justinian's church turned mosque and Ottoman symbol of sovereignty.

sources.title: Süleymaniye Mosque - Wikipedia
Necipoglu-Kafadar, Gulru, 'The Suleymaniye Complex in Istanbul: An Interpretation', Muqarnas 3 (1985), pp. 92-117
sources.author: Necipoglu-Kafadar, Gulru
sources.confirms: OpenAlex bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Mainstone, Rowland J., 'Sinan's Suleymaniye Mosque and Justinian's Hagia Sophia', in Structure in Architecture (Routledge, 1999)
sources.author: Mainstone, Rowland J.
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mosque of Suleyman I the Magnificent'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates construction to 1550-57. It does not explicitly confirm an inauguration; it says the mosque was constructed during those years.

mimar-sinan-suleymaniye-1550.detail: Its dome rises 53 metres, exactly twice its 26.5-metre span. It remains Istanbul's largest Ottoman-era mosque and one of Sinan's masterpieces.

picture.alt: Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, designed by Mimar Sinan and built 1550 to 1557, photographed in 2013.
picture.credit: Arild Vågen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

oaxaca-cochineal-dye-trade-1550.summary: Mixtec, Zapotec and Nahua households in Oaxaca, Tlaxcala and Puebla bred Dactylopius coccus on cultivated nopal paddles, shielding egg-laying females in woven nests, brushing mature insects into baskets, killing them in hot water or ovens and drying them into grana. About 70,000 insects made one pound of dye. Spanish merchants shipped grana from Veracruz to Seville from the 1540s; by the 1570s it ranked second to silver among New Spain's exports and dyed scarlet for European courts, Ottoman carpets and later British uniforms. Raymond Lee's 1948 study traced production and trade to 1600; Jeremy Baskes showed how eighteenth-century Oaxacan growers financed harvests through repartimiento credit from Spanish magistrates.

sources.title: Lee, Raymond L., 'Cochineal Production and Trade in New Spain to 1600', The Americas 4 (1948)
sources.author: Lee, Raymond L.
sources.confirms: Indigenous breeding methods, Spanish export trade and cochineal's rank among New Spain's exports before 1600.

sources.title: Baskes, Jeremy, Indians, Merchants, and Markets: A Reinterpretation of the Repartimiento and Spanish-Indian Economic Relations in Colonial Oaxaca, 1750-1821 (Stanford University Press, 2000), ch. 2
sources.author: Baskes, Jeremy
sources.confirms: Repartimiento credit financing cochineal production by Oaxacan households in the eighteenth century.

sources.title: Marichal, Carlos, 'Mexican Cochineal and the European Demand for American Dyes, 1550-1850', in Topik, Marichal and Frank (eds), From Silver to Cocaine (Duke University Press, 2006)
sources.author: Marichal, Carlos
sources.confirms: Export volumes, European demand and the long cycle of the cochineal trade to 1850.

oaxaca-cochineal-dye-trade-1550.verification_note: Cochineal breeding predates 1521; 1550 marks the Atlantic trade's take-off per Lee. Export peaks and insect counts per pound vary by source (60,000 to 70,000 insects).
oaxaca-cochineal-dye-trade-1550.detail: Cochineal breeding predates conquest: Mixtec tribute lists in the Codex Mendoza record bags of grana owed to Tenochtitlan. Spain kept the insect's nature secret for two centuries; Europeans debated whether grana was seed or animal until microscopy settled it. Oaxaca exports peaked near 1.5 million pounds a year in the 1770s before synthetic dyes and Guatemalan and Canary Island competition cut prices after 1850.

picture.alt: Painting on vellum of a man brushing cochineal insects from a nopal cactus with a deer tail, from Alzate's 1777 memoir; later than the record year
picture.credit: José Antonio de Alzate y Ramírez (1737 – 1799)., via Wikimedia Commons

taqi-al-din-steam-turbine-1551.summary: In 1551 the Ottoman engineer Taqi al-Din described, by al-Hassan's reading of his treatise, a spit turned by steam blowing on vanes, a steam turbine for roasting meat. His book Al-Turuq al-samiyya fi al-alat al-ruhaniyya, The Sublime Methods of Spiritual Machines, explains it: steam from its boiler was directed onto vanes, turning a wheel fixed to one end of its axle, so that meat turned without anyone cranking it. Some historians count it as an early step in steam turbine history, though Hill's survey of his treatise mentions no steam. His influence stayed limited: few copies of his works survive, so they reached few readers.

sources.title: Taqi ad-Din Muhammad ibn Ma'ruf - Wikipedia
Hill, Donald R., 'Arabic Mechanical Engineering: Survey of the Historical Sources', Arabic Sciences and Philosophy 1 (1991) 167-186
sources.author: Hill, Donald R.
sources.confirms: Taqi al-Din's al-Turuq al-saniyya, written in 959 AH (1551 to 1552), describes several machines including a six-cylinder water-driven pump.
sources.qualifies: Hill lists the treatise's machines without mentioning a steam turbine or steam-driven spit.

sources.title: al-Hassan, Ahmad Y., Taqi al-Din and Arabic Mechanical Engineering (Institute for the History of Arabic Science, Aleppo, 1976)
sources.author: al-Hassan, Ahmad Y.
sources.venue: Institute for the History of Arabic Science, University of Aleppo
sources.confirms: Edition and study of al-Turuq al-saniyya, the treatise in which Taqi al-Din describes his machines.

taqi-al-din-steam-turbine-1551.verification_note: Hill (1991) confirms this treatise and its 959 AH date without mentioning steam; its steam-jack reading rests on al-Hassan's 1976 edition and later popular retellings.
taqi-al-din-steam-turbine-1551.detail: His book also described four water-raising machines, two driven by animals and two by paddle wheels.

picture.alt: Illustration of an astronomical sextant from Taqi al-Din's manuscript on observational instruments, 16th century, held at Topkapi Palace Museum.
picture.credit: Taqi al-Din, public domain, via Topkapi Palace Museum (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

badianus-aztec-herbal-1552.summary: At Colegio de Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco, outside Mexico City, Nahua physician Martin de la Cruz composed a herbal in Nahuatl in 1552 and Juan Badiano, a Nahua scholar from Xochimilco, translated it into Latin as Libellus de medicinalibus Indorum herbis. Its 185 colour paintings show more than 200 plants, each tied to a named ailment and a recipe, from headaches and sore eyes to wounds and childbirth. Sent to Spain for the viceroy's son, it lay unread in Vatican's library until 1929. No earlier medical book written in the Americas by Indigenous authors survives, and none records Nahua pharmacology so fully before Spanish practice displaced it. The Vatican returned it to Mexico in 1990.

sources.title: De Smedt, Johan; De Cruz, Helen, 'Cosmovision as Cognitive Technology: The Case of Mesoamerican Medicinal Knowledge', Topics in Cognitive Science 18 (2025)
sources.author: De Smedt, Johan; De Cruz, Helen
sources.confirms: Confirms Martin de la Cruz wrote the herbal in Nahuatl, Juan Badiano translated it into Latin in 1552 at Tlatelolco, and that it carries 185 illustrations.

sources.title: National Library of Medicine, 'The Badianus Manuscript: An Aztec Herbal of 1552', exhibition text
sources.author: National Library of Medicine
sources.confirms: Confirms the herbal as the first produced in the Americas and describes 204 plants with their uses.

sources.title: Smithsonian Libraries, catalogue record for The De la Cruz-Badiano Aztec Herbal of 1552
sources.author: Smithsonian Institution
sources.confirms: Confirms the 1552 date and the Emmart facsimile edition.

badianus-aztec-herbal-1552.verification_note: Plant counts differ between sources (about 185 paintings, 204 plant names) because several plants share a painting.

picture.alt: Folios 38v and 39r of the Libellus de medicinalibus Indorum herbis with painted plants
picture.credit: Martin de la Cruz, 1552, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

istanbul-coffeehouses-open-1554.summary: Ottoman historian İbrahim Peçevi, writing in the 1640s, records that in 962 AH (1554 to 1555) Hakam from Aleppo and Şems from Damascus each opened a kahvehane in Tahtakale, Istanbul's market quarter by the Golden Horn. Patrons sat on divans, drank coffee, played chess and backgammon, read poetry and talked politics, and Peçevi notes dismissed officials and judges among them. Coffee had reached Cairo's al-Azhar quarter about 1510 and Mecca's jurists tried to ban it in 1511. Within a generation Istanbul held hundreds of coffeehouses, giving men a gathering place outside mosque, home and tavern; preachers and sultans repeatedly tried to close them. Ralph Hattox's 1985 study traces this chain from Yemeni Sufi lodges to an urban trade in cups and conversation that reached Venice and London a century later.

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses: The Origins of a Social Beverage in the Medieval Near East (University of Washington Press, 1985), chs. 5-6
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Peçevi's account of two Syrians opening coffeehouses in Istanbul in 962 AH; social life of coffeehouses; Meccan ban of 1511.

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses, full text (Internet Archive)
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Translated passage from Peçevi on Hakam and Shams in Tahtakale, 962 AH, chess, backgammon, poetry and dismissed officials among patrons.

sources.author: Grehan, James
sources.confirms: Coffeehouses as centres of Ottoman urban sociability from the mid-sixteenth century and repeated attempts at closure.

picture.credit: Unknown Ottoman miniaturist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

patio-process-1554.summary: In 1554 Bartolomé de Medina used mercury to pull silver from poor ore, and Mexico's mines paid. By the 1550s New Spain's richest silver ores were running out, and smelting lower grades cost too much. Bartolomé de Medina, a Seville merchant, learned from an unknown German called Maestro Lorenzo that silver could be drawn from crushed ore with mercury and salt brine. In Pachuca in 1554 he built a model refinery and is credited with adding magistral, an impure copper sulfate, to speed its reaction. Amalgamation made remote Potosí viable; Spanish America produced three fifths of world silver before 1900.

sources.title: Patio process - Wikipedia
Probert, Alan, 'Bartolome de Medina: The Patio Process and the Sixteenth Century Silver Crisis', in Mines of Silver and Gold in the Americas (Routledge, 1997), pp. 96-130
sources.author: Probert, Alan
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'patio process'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates the process broadly to the 16th century through the early 20th century; it gives no specific year. It does not confirm that Medina introduced it in 1554.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pachuca'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives no specific year; it says the patio process was perfected in Pachuca in the 16th century. It supports the broad claim that Bartolomé de Medina perfected the process in Pachuca, but does not confirm 1554.

patio-process-1554.detail: Crushed ore was heaped with salt, water, magistral and mercury. Labourers or mules trod it in a shallow walled patio for six to eight weeks; it was then washed, and heated to drive off mercury.

agricola-de-re-metallica-1556.summary: In 1556 Agricola's De re metallica put the mining trade's guarded know-how in 292 woodcuts. It stayed the standard text for nearly 200 years. Georg Bauer, a physician who Latinised his name to Georgius Agricola, spent nine years in the Bohemian mining town of Joachimsthal and then lived in Chemnitz in Saxony's Ore Mountains, watching how metals were found, mined, refined and smelted. His De re metallica, in twelve Latin books, appeared in Basel in 1556, a year after his death. Latin let educated Europeans read it, and its detailed machinery made it a working reference for more than a century.

sources.title: De re metallica
Agricola, Georgius, De re metallica, trans. H. C. and L. H. Hoover (London: Mining Magazine, 1912), from the first Latin edition of 1556
sources.author: Agricola, Georgius; Hoover, Herbert Clark; Hoover, Lou Henry
sources.confirms: Catalogue states the translation is from the first Latin edition of 1556.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'De re metallica'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1556 and says the work was published posthumously. It confirms that De re metallica was a major mining and metallurgy text, described in cited coverage as the leading textbook for nearly two centuries; it does not confirm 292 woodcuts.

agricola-de-re-metallica-1556.verification_note: Published posthumously (Agricola died 1555). Title implies he published it.
agricola-de-re-metallica-1556.detail: Publication was delayed while its 292 woodcuts were cut from drawings by Blasius Weffring. Herbert and Lou Henry Hoover published its first English translation in 1912.

picture.alt: Woodcut from De re metallica, Basel 1556, page 131, showing a machine for drawing water out of a mine.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

cassava-africa-portuguese-1558.summary: Portuguese ships carry Brazilian cassava cuttings to Africa's Atlantic coast in the 16th century; FAO dates cassava's first African record to 1558. Dutch trader Samuel Brun saw it at Loango in 1611, and travelers found it a staple around Malebo Pool by 1698. Cassava tolerates poor soil and drought, stores in the ground for up to two years and resists locusts, so African farmers adopted it as famine reserve and then as staple, developing soaking and fermenting to remove cyanide. Jan Vansina showed in 1997 that adoption in Kongo, Angola and Loango took generations and varied by place. Nigeria now leads world output.

sources.title: Vansina, J., 'Histoire du manioc en Afrique Centrale avant 1850', Paideuma 43 (1997), 255-279
sources.author: Vansina, Jan
sources.confirms: Traces cassava's history in Kongo, Angola and Loango before 1850 and shows adoption as staple took variable time by locality.
sources.qualifies: Argues the supposed rapid cassava agricultural revolution in central Africa is far from proven.

sources.title: Guira, F. et al., 'Origins, production, and utilization of cassava in Burkina Faso', Food Science and Nutrition 5 (2016), 415-423
sources.author: Guira, Flibert; Some, Koussao; Kabore, Donatien; Sawadogo-Lingani, Hagretou; Traore, Yves; Savadogo, Aly
sources.confirms: States cassava was introduced into Africa from America by the Portuguese in 1558, citing Jones (1959) and Lebot (2003).

sources.title: FAO, 'Roots, tubers, plantains and bananas in human nutrition', ch. 1 (cassava in Congo basin 1558)
sources.author: FAO
sources.confirms: Gives Portuguese introduction into Congo basin as early as 1558.

sources.title: Carter, S. E. et al., 'Introduction and diffusion of cassava in Africa', IITA Research Guide
sources.author: Carter, Simon E.; Fresco, Louise O.; Jones, Peter G.; Fairbairn, J. N.
sources.confirms: Documents Brun's 1611 observation at Loango and cassava as staple around Malebo Pool by 1698.

cassava-africa-portuguese-1558.detail: Cassava also entered east Africa via Portuguese Mozambique and Indian Ocean trade in the 18th century. Its labour demands fell mostly on women, who processed roots into gari, fufu and chikwangue. Dependence brought risks: konzo paralysis from poorly processed bitter varieties, and mosaic virus epidemics in the 20th century that IITA breeding later addressed. Vansina argues claims of a cassava-driven transformation of central African farming are unproven.

picture.credit: Lebu Ayiga, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

index-librorum-prohibitorum-1559.summary: In 1559 Rome published a list of books Catholics could not print or read, censorship that lasted until 1966. Index Librorum Prohibitorum was the Church's changing list of books judged heretical or immoral; Catholic states could enforce it by law. A first Roman Index printed in 1557 under Pope Paul IV was withdrawn for unclear reasons. In 1559 his new Index appeared, banning every work of some 550 authors as well as individual titles, on a principle that an author's religious convictions contaminated all his writing. Even Catholic scholars found it too severe, and in 1564 the Council of Trent's Tridentine Index replaced it.

Barbierato, Federico, 'Index of Prohibited Books', in Encyclopedia of Renaissance Philosophy (Springer, 2022), pp. 1670-1676
sources.author: Barbierato, Federico
sources.confirms: Abstract: 'the first official Roman Index dates to 1559'; indices in force 1559 to 1966.
sources.qualifies: Legal force was 'in substance almost limited to the Italian territory'; France never received it, Spain and Portugal kept their own lists.

sources.title: Grendler, Paul F., 'Printing and censorship', in The Cambridge History of Renaissance Philosophy (Cambridge, 1988), pp. 25-54

index-librorum-prohibitorum-1559.detail: Later lists named Copernicus, Galileo, Descartes, Kant and many others.

huancavelica-mercury-mine-1563.summary: In 1563 and 1564 Amador de Cabrera registered cinnabar outcrops at Huancavelica, in Peru's central highlands, after an Andean worker named Ñahuincopa showed him its cinnabar. Within a decade, under Viceroy Toledo, Crown-controlled mines there supplied quicksilver to Potosí's refineries, where mercury amalgamation replaced smelting of low-grade ores from 1572. Indigenous mitayos drafted from surrounding provinces dug ore underground and roasted it in furnaces, inhaling mercury vapour; Kendall Brown's study documents tremors, tooth loss and early death that made Huancavelica notorious as 'mina de la muerte'. Output averaged several thousand quintals a year, and Huancavelica and Potosí together anchored Spain's American silver economy for two centuries.

sources.title: Brown, Kendall W., 'Workers' Health and Colonial Mercury Mining at Huancavelica, Peru', The Americas 57 (2001)
sources.author: Brown, Kendall W.
sources.confirms: Discovery in 1563 to 1564, mita labour, mercury poisoning symptoms and the mine's role in Andean silver refining.

sources.title: Robins, Nicholas A., Mercury, Mining, and Empire: The Human and Ecological Cost of Colonial Silver Mining in the Andes (Indiana University Press, 2011), ch. 2-3
sources.author: Robins, Nicholas A.
sources.confirms: Estimates of mercury emissions and health effects at Huancavelica and Potosí.

sources.title: Brown, Kendall, 'Mercury and Silver Mining in the Colonial Atlantic', Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History (Oxford University Press, 2017)
sources.author: Brown, Kendall
sources.confirms: Overview of mercury supply from Huancavelica, Almadén and Idrija to American refineries.

huancavelica-mercury-mine-1563.detail: Mercury was shipped by llama train to coastal ports, by sea to Arica and overland to Potosí, roughly 1,500 kilometres. Nicholas Robins estimates that Huancavelica released about 17,000 tonnes of mercury vapour into air and soil between 1564 and 1810, with Potosí's refineries adding far more. A 1786 gallery collapse cut production; Spain later imported Almadén and Idrija mercury to make up shortfalls.

picture.credit: LITOUS, via Wikimedia Commons

kirkcesme-water-supply-istanbul-1563.summary: Sultan Süleyman orders chief architect Sinan in 1554 to end Istanbul's water shortage. Sinan surveys streams in Belgrad Forest north of the city, gathers two branches of springs in covered masonry galleries and joins them at a deep collecting pool south of Kemerburgaz. A single gravity line then crosses valleys on aqueducts, among them Mağlova, 36 metres high and about 250 metres long with two tiers of arches, and Uzunkemer, before reaching distribution chambers at Eğrikapı and fountains across the walled city. Floods on 20 September 1563 wrecked Mağlova and damaged others; Sinan rebuilt them and water flowed again in 1564. A survey in 1568 counted 94 public fountains, 19 wells, 15 troughs, 13 baths and seven palaces served, and later dams raised supply to around 17,500 cubic metres a day. Parts remain in use.

sources.title: Uyumaz, A. and Dabanlı, İ., 'Architect Sinan's Kırkçeşme water supply system outside the city of Istanbul and city network', Water Supply 13 (2013), 626-637
sources.author: Uyumaz, Ali; Dabanlı, İsmail
sources.venue: Water Science and Technology: Water Supply
sources.confirms: Two branches fed from Kağıthane tributaries, collection at Başhavuz south of Kemerburgaz, crossing over Mağlova aqueduct, opening 1564, dams added 1620 to 1818.

sources.title: Kurt, B., 'The Ottoman State Between Urban Space and Environment: Preserving the Drinking Water of Istanbul', Belleten 85 (2021), 933-966
sources.author: Kurt, Burcu
sources.confirms: Süleyman ordered water from Belgrad Forest canals to new fountains; Kırkçeşme facilities built in response.

sources.title: Museum With No Frontiers, 'Kırkçeşme water-supply system', Discover Islamic Art
sources.author: Museum With No Frontiers
sources.confirms: Ordered 1554, completed 1563, flood damage rebuilt 1564; galleries about 55 km, 33 aqueducts, over 300 fountains at first.

manila-galleon-trade-1565.summary: In 1565 Spain found a way back across the Pacific, and galleons traded silver for silk. Augustinian friar Andrés de Urdaneta, and separately Alonso de Arellano, found this return route, the tornaviaje, by riding the Kuroshio Current north past Japan and then east. Spanish ships had crossed from Mexico to Asia for decades without finding a return; in 1552 Francis Xavier had asked that no more fleets try. From then until 1815 galleons made one or two round trips a year, carrying Chinese silk, porcelain and other Asian goods west to America and returning with New World silver for trade with China.

sources.title: Manila galleon - Wikipedia
Flynn, Dennis O.; Giraldez, Arturo, 'Silk for Silver: Manila-Macao Trade in the 17th Century', Philippine Studies 44.1 (1996)
sources.author: Flynn, Dennis O.; Giraldez, Arturo
sources.confirms: Landing page shows bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'The Manila Galleon Trade (1565-1815)'
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.confirms: The title gives 1565-1815; the page does not give a separate date for the route’s discovery. it confirms trade between China and Mexico involving Asian goods and New World silver.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Manila galleon'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1565-1815. The page says galleons made annual round trips between Manila and Acapulco, carrying Chinese silk and other goods west and Mexican silver back.

manila-galleon-trade-1565.detail: Galleons were mostly built at Cavite in Manila Bay, left Manila about July and took at least four months to reach Acapulco. Mexico's war of independence ended this route.

chinese-variolation-1567.summary: By the 1500s Chinese doctors gave children a mild case of smallpox to protect them: vaccination's root. Variolation deliberately infected a person with smallpox matter in hope of a mild case that would protect for life. About 1 to 2 percent of those variolated died, against about 30 percent of those who caught smallpox naturally. China's oldest documented practice dates to the 16th century, and sinologist Joseph Needham places its first use between 1567 and 1572. Practitioners chose donors with mild cases, dried their scabs for some time since fresh ones risked full infection, ground them to powder and blew it through a pipe into one nostril. Reports reached London's Royal Society in 1700.

sources.title: Variolation - Wikipedia
Boylston, Arthur, 'The origins of inoculation', Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 105.7 (2012), pp. 309-313
sources.author: Boylston, Arthur
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
sources.confirms: Full text: inoculation first practised in China between 1567 and 1572 by nasal insufflation; earliest written discussion in a 1549 book.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'variolation'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives the date as the 16th century; it does not give 1567 or a more precise date. broadly: it says 16th-century Chinese accounts describe nasal insufflation using powdered dried smallpox scabs blown through a pipe.

chinese-variolation-1567.detail: Three or four scabs were ground, sometimes with one grain of musk. Wan Quan and others recorded such methods, and the Kangxi Emperor later inoculated his children and troops.

potato-canary-islands-europe-1567.summary: On 28 November 1567 notary Lorenzo Palenzuela in Gran Canaria records three medium barrels of potatoes, oranges and green lemons shipped to Antwerp, the earliest known written record of potatoes in Europe. A second notary record of 24 April 1574 notes potatoes sent from Tenerife to Rouen, and Seville's Hospital de la Sangre bought potatoes on 27 December 1573, its first mention on mainland Europe. Tubers must have been planted in the Canaries by about 1562 to yield an export crop. A 2007 DNA study of Canary landraces finds both Andean and Chilean types, pointing to multiple introductions. Potatoes later fed Europe's population growth and, through blight in 1845, its worst 19th-century famine.

sources.title: Rios, D., Ghislain, M., Rodriguez, F. and Spooner, D. M., 'What Is the Origin of the European Potato? Evidence from Canary Island Landraces', Crop Science 47 (2007), 1271-1280
sources.author: Rios, Domingo; Ghislain, Marc; Rodriguez, Flor; Spooner, David M.
sources.confirms: States the potato was first recorded in Europe in the Canary Islands in 1567 and quotes the 1567 Palenzuela and 1574 Tenerife notarial records; DNA shows Andean and Chilean types among Canary landraces.
sources.qualifies: Argues the early European potato was selected from Chilean rather than only Andean introductions.

sources.title: Rios, D., Devaux, A. and Ruiz de Galarreta, J. I., 'Ancient Potato Varieties of the Canary Islands: Their History, Diversity and Origin of the Potato in Europe', Potato Research 67 (2024), 963-994
sources.author: Rios, Domingo; Devaux, Andre; Ruiz de Galarreta, Jose Ignacio
sources.confirms: Reviews the 1567 and 1574 shipping records, the 1573 Seville hospital purchase and the estimate of planting by about 1562.

sources.title: Hawkes, J. G. and Francisco-Ortega, J., 'The early history of the potato in Europe', Euphytica 70 (1993), 1-7
sources.author: Hawkes, J. G.; Francisco-Ortega, J.
sources.confirms: Argues potatoes were cultivated in the Canaries by about 1562 and documents the 1567 and 1574 shipments.

potato-canary-islands-europe-1567.detail: The Canaries sat outside Seville's monopoly on American trade, so they became a hub for plants moving between continents. Ancient Canary landraces still grown on Tenerife carry Andean genetics; Domingo Rios's group argues early European potatoes were selected from Chilean introductions long before the 1840s. Potatoes remained a garden curiosity in much of Europe until Prussia and France promoted them in the 18th century.

picture.alt: Papas antiguas, old potato landraces of Canary Islands
picture.credit: Koppchen, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

florentine-codex-1569.summary: By 1569 Nahua scholars with Sahagún had recorded Aztec life in 2,400 pages, in their own words. This Franciscan friar spent from 1545 until his death in 1590 compiling La Historia General de las Cosas de Nueva España. It was meant to help missionaries and to record a vanishing heritage. He worked with Nahua elders and with former students of his Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, crediting them by name, gathering testimony through questionnaires and writing in Nahuatl with Spanish alongside. Its Nahuatl text, completed in 1569 in a manuscript that does not survive, ran to 2,500 pages in twelve books with more than 2,000 illustrations by native artists.

sources.title: Florentine Codex - Wikipedia
Sahagun, Bernardino de, Historia general de las cosas de Nueva Espana (Florentine Codex, 1575-77), Library of Congress / World Digital Library
sources.author: Sahagun, Bernardino de
sources.confirms: The page says the complete copy was prepared in 1575-77; it gives 1577 as the publication year.

sources.title: Terraciano, Kevin, 'Three Texts in One: Book XII of the Florentine Codex', Ethnohistory 57 (2010), 51-72
sources.author: Terraciano, Kevin
sources.confirms: The Florentine Codex is a sixteenth-century manuscript of twelve books on Nahua culture in parallel Nahuatl and Castilian columns with many illustrations by Nahua artists.

florentine-codex-1569.verification_note: Terraciano (Ethnohistory 2010) describes twelve books in parallel Nahuatl and Castilian columns with Nahua illustrations; Library of Congress dates the surviving codex to 1575 to 1577, while 1569 marks Sahagún's completed Nahuatl text, whose manuscript is lost.
florentine-codex-1569.detail: Its books cover gods, society and natural history, and Book 12 tells the conquest as seen from Tenochtitlan. Its best manuscript, in Florence's Laurentian Library and made in 1575 to 1577, gives it its name.

picture.alt: Opening page of Book XI, on earthly matters and natural history, in Sahagún's Florentine Codex, completed about 1577, from Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana via World Digital Library.
picture.credit: Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua scribes, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, public domain, via Library of Congress World Digital Library (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

mercator-projection-1569.summary: In 1569 Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator published a world map, 202 by 124 cm in eighteen sheets, on which a straight line is a fixed compass course; it is still in use. Sailors follow rhumb lines, paths of constant bearing, which Portuguese cosmographer Pedro Nunes had analysed in 1537. Mercator titled his map a new description of Earth corrected for navigators' use. By spacing parallels ever wider toward both poles, it draws every rhumb line straight, so courses can be laid with a ruler. Its price is area: lands far from the equator swell, until Greenland looks as large as Africa, which is 14 times bigger.

sources.title: Mercator projection - Wikipedia
Monmonier, Mark, Rhumb Lines and Map Wars: A Social History of the Mercator Projection (Chicago, 2004)
sources.author: Monmonier, Mark
sources.confirms: Book page: Mercator's 1569 world map introduced the projection with straight rhumb lines.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mercator projection'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1569. The page says any straight line on a Mercator map is a line of constant true bearing, useful for plotting a straight-line course.

mercator-projection-1569.detail: Edward Wright published accurate construction tables in 1599. Mercator's projection became standard for navigation in the 18th century and returned in Web Mercator maps.

picture.alt: Composite of all sheets of Gerardus Mercator's 1569 world map Nova et aucta orbis terrae descriptio, from Basel copy.
picture.credit: Gerardus Mercator, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

potosi-mita-ingenios-1573.summary: Between 1572 and 1575 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo reorganised silver production at Potosí, in present Bolivia. He imposed a rotating labour draft, la mita, which obliged sixteen highland provinces to send about 13,500 men each year to mines and refineries, and he financed a chain of about 20 reservoirs in Kari Kari hills above town whose water drove more than a hundred ingenios, stamp mills that crushed ore for mercury amalgamation. Indigenous guayra wind furnaces, which had smelted rich ores since 1545, gave way to this water-powered industrial complex. Output climbed to over 200 tonnes of silver a year around 1592, flowing to Seville and, through Manila, to China.

sources.title: Bakewell, Peter, Miners of the Red Mountain: Indian Labor in Potosí, 1545-1650 (University of New Mexico Press, 1984), ch. 2-3
sources.author: Bakewell, Peter
sources.confirms: Toledo's mita quotas, reservoirs and ingenios, and the shift from guayra smelting to amalgamation.

sources.title: Saignes, Thierry, 'The Miners in Colonial Potosí' (review of Bakewell and Cole), Bulletin of Latin American Research 6 (1987)
sources.author: Saignes, Thierry
sources.confirms: Scholarly assessment of mita size and operation as reconstructed by Bakewell and Cole.

sources.title: Cook, Noble David, review of Bakewell, Silver and Entrepreneurship in Seventeenth-Century Potosí, Technology and Culture 32 (1991)
sources.author: Cook, Noble David
sources.confirms: Mill ownership and refining technology at seventeenth-century Potosí.

potosi-mita-ingenios-1573.verification_note: Mita quota figures range from about 13,000 to 14,000 men per year across sources; reservoir counts range from 18 to 32 depending on period. Toledo's ordinances date from 1572 to 1575, so 1573 is a mid-point of the reorganisation.
potosi-mita-ingenios-1573.detail: Peter Bakewell's Miners of the Red Mountain reconstructs labour arrangements and this shift from Indigenous smelting to amalgamation; Jeffrey Cole traces mita operations to 1700. A reservoir dam failure in 1626 destroyed many mills and killed hundreds. Mitayos walked up to two months from Cusco's hinterland with families and llamas; many stayed as paid mingas. Potosí's population reached about 160,000 around 1610.

picture.alt: Drawing of Cerro Rico above Potosí from Diego de Ocaña's account of about 1600, showing mine workings on the hill
picture.credit: José Fuertes, via Wikimedia Commons

li-shizhen-bencao-gangmu-1578.summary: In 1578 Li Shizhen finished a catalogue of every drug in Chinese medicine, 1,892 entries doctors still consult. The Ming physician's Bencao gangmu, Compendium of Materia Medica, took more than three decades of work. It lists every drug then known to Chinese medicine: 1,892 entries of plants, animals and minerals, 374 added by Li, with 11,096 prescriptions and 1,160 drawings across 53 volumes, each entry giving names, appearance, nature, uses and side effects. Ming emperors ignored it, and it was printed only in 1596 in Nanjing, three years after his death. It carries errors too, such as holding mercury non-toxic.

sources.title: Bencao Gangmu - Wikipedia
Tsai et al., 'Bencao Gangmu and the foundations of Chinese pharmacology', Frontiers in Pharmacology 17 (2026)
sources.author: Tsai et al.
sources.confirms: Full text: Li Shizhen completed the Bencao gangmu in 1578; first printed 1596.

sources.title: Metailie, Georges, 'Des mots et des plantes dans le Bencao gangmu de Li Shizhen', Extreme-Orient Extreme-Occident 10 (1988), pp. 27-43
sources.author: Metailie, Georges
sources.confirms: Full text on Persee discusses the work's nomenclature; gives no completion date.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bencao gangmu'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1578. It says the Bencao gangmu was completed in 1578 and described 1,892 drugs, but does not call it a first draft or say it listed every drug then known.

li-shizhen-bencao-gangmu-1578.detail: Entries are arranged in 16 divisions and 60 orders. Li drew on literary and historical texts as well as earlier herbals, and editions followed in 1603, 1606 and 1640.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

tamil-type-quilon-1578.summary: On 20 October 1578 a Jesuit press at Quilon (Kollam), Kerala, printed Thambiran Vanakkam, a sixteen page Tamil translation of a Portuguese catechism, using metal type cut for Tamil script. Henrique Henriques prepared text and Joao Gonsalves, a Spanish lay brother and former blacksmith, with Tamil assistants, cut and cast fifty or so sorts with ligatures for vowel signs. This was first book printed in an Indian script with movable type. A Goa printing of 1577 preceded it but no copy survives; one Quilon copy is held at Harvard. Printing in Tamil continued at Cochin and Punnaikayal with grammars and a dictionary, two centuries before Bengali type.
