sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a 1895 London edition published by William Heinemann; digitized full text is available, but the text was not read.

wells-time-machine-1895.detail: Modern readers take it as commentary on growing inequality and class division. It drew on Ray Lankester's theories of social degeneration and on William Morris's utopian News from Nowhere of 1890. Wells had tried time travel in his 1888 story "The Chronic Argonauts", which W. E. Henley, editor of National Observer, had him rewrite as seven anonymous essays in 1894; when Henley moved to Heinemann's New Review he serialised it there from January to May 1895, paying Wells £100. Henry Holt and Company published its first book edition on 7 May 1895 and Heinemann a textually different British edition on 29 May; nearly all modern reprints follow Heinemann's text.

picture.credit: William Heinemann, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

jagadish-bose-microwaves-1895.summary: In 1895 Jagadish Chandra Bose sent radio waves through walls and a body to ring a bell in Kolkata, a year before Marconi's patent. They also passed through a person, Lieutenant Governor Sir William Mackenzie. They reached apparatus he had set up to ring a bell and ignite gunpowder in a closed room. In 1897 he described his millimetre-wave research to London's Royal Institution: he used waveguides, horn antennas, dielectric lenses, polarisers and semiconductors at frequencies up to 60 GHz, and was first to use a semiconductor junction to detect radio waves.

sources.confirms: The article states that Bose demonstrated wireless transmission of millimeter waves at 60 gigahertz over 75 feet at Presidency College in 1895.
sources.qualifies: It locates the demonstration at Presidency College and does not mention transmission through walls or a person, a bell, or gunpowder.

The cited sources do not establish the claimed passage through walls or a person, or the bell and gunpowder details.
jagadish-bose-microwaves-1895.detail: Bose, a Bengali physicist, had studied natural sciences at Christ's College, Cambridge, and taught at Presidency College, Kolkata. He began his radio experiments in late 1894, when Marconi was developing wireless telegraphy and Popov his lightning detector. He submitted his first paper, on polarisation of electric rays by double-refracting crystals, to the Asiatic Society of Bengal in May 1895; his second, published by The Electrician that December, may have been the first by an Indian in Western scientific periodicals. He openly revealed his galena crystal detector in lectures and was not interested in patents.

picture.credit: Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

roentgen-x-rays-1895.summary: In 1895 Röntgen discovered X-rays and photographed his wife Anna Bertha Ludwig's hand bones, first X-ray of a human body part. He submitted "On a new kind of ray: A preliminary communication" to Würzburg's Physical-Medical Society on 28 December 1895, first paper on X-rays. He received the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics.

A Nature article provides related contemporary publication evidence, but its supplied text does not establish author or submission date. roentgen-x-rays-1895.detail: Crookes tubes, invented around 1875, produced cathode rays, energetic electron beams, when high voltage ionised residual air inside them. From 1888 Philipp Lenard had built tubes with thin aluminium windows to see whether those rays could escape into air, and found that something came through that exposed photographic plates. Röntgen burned his lab notes before his death, but his biographers' likely reconstruction is that he had wrapped a Crookes tube in black cardboard to block its visible light and noticed faint green glow on a fluorescent screen painted with barium platinocyanide about a metre away; invisible rays were passing through the cardboard, and also through books and papers on his desk.

picture.credit: Wilhelm Röntgen, Public domain, via Wellcome Collection

lumiere-cinematograph-1895.summary: On 28 December 1895 Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten short films to paying viewers in Salon Indien of the Grand Café on boulevard des Capucines, Paris, and cinema became public entertainment. Their Cinématographe, patented in 1895, served as camera, printer and projector, running perforated film at 16 frames per second. H. Mark Gosser (SMPTE Journal, 1996) calls it the first truly acceptable projection of film before a paying audience; earlier paid projections existed, since Max and Emil Skladanowsky had shown films to paying customers in Berlin with their Bioscop from 1 November 1895, and Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope of 1894 showed films to one viewer at a time through its peephole. Around 40 paying visitors attended, and Britannica marks this showing as cinema history's beginning.

sources.qualifies: The page does not establish that the showing was the first public screening or that it was paid.

lumiere-cinematograph-1895.detail: Auguste and Louis, born in Besançon to photographer parents, manufactured photographic plates in Lyon. Léon Bouly had patented an earlier cinématographe in 1892. On 22 March 1895 they privately screened Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory for members of Société d'encouragement pour l'industrie nationale. Their December programme included Le Jardinier, 49-second comedy later known as L'Arroseur arrosé.

picture.alt: Henri Brispot's 1895 poster advertising Lumière brothers' Cinématographe in Paris.
picture.credit: Henri Brispot, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

uganda-railway-1896.summary: In 1896 Britain began a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria; it cost 2,500 workers' lives and created Nairobi and Kenya's settler economy. It finished at its terminus, Kisumu on Lake Victoria's eastern shore, in 1901. In December 1890, months after Britain joined anti-slavery measures of the Brussels Conference Act, Britain's Foreign Office proposed a railway from Mombasa to Uganda to disrupt slave traffic from interior to coast; a bill introduced at Westminster in August 1895 became the Uganda Railway Act 1896. Its cost, estimated at £3 million to £5.5 million, and its casualties led critics to dub it Lunatic Line.

uganda-railway-1896.detail: George Whitehouse, experienced civil engineer who had worked across the British Empire, served as chief engineer from 1895 to 1903 and as its manager from its opening. Some 200,000 rail lengths, 1.2 million sleepers and steel for viaducts had to be imported from India, which required a modern port at Kilindini Harbour. Construction relied heavily on labour from British India under extremely harsh conditions; several thousand Indian labourers died from disease, famine, accidents and wildlife, most famously two Tsavo lions that killed at least 28 workers in 1898.

battle-of-adwa-1896.summary: In March 1896 Ethiopia destroyed an Italian army at Adwa with modern rifles it had bought; an African state kept its independence by force. Italy had tried to force Ethiopia to accept its version of their Treaty of Wuchale, whose interpretation was disputed, and so impose a protectorate. Italy recognised Ethiopia's sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa, Francesco Crispi's government fell, and Ethiopia stayed independent until Italy's invasion forty years later, alone among African countries to owe its independence to a military victory.

Britannica, "Battle of Adwa | Cause, Winner, Summary, & Consequences"
sources.confirms: The article dates the Battle of Adwa to March 1, 1896, and says the Treaty of Addis Ababa recognized Ethiopia's sovereign independence.

sources.title: "Listing toward Adwa," Chapter 2
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a chapter titled "Listing toward Adwa," published in 2011; text not read.

battle-of-adwa-1896.verification_note: Britannica confirms its battle date and Ethiopia's recognition as sovereign; other details rest on a chapter cited as supporting literature.
battle-of-adwa-1896.detail: Menelik mobilised a massive army, estimated at 73,000 to over 100,000 men and mostly equipped with modern rifles imported from France and Russia. Baratieri's much smaller force was unfamiliar with the terrain and hampered by poor reconnaissance; under pressure from Rome to act decisively, he launched his surprise attack on Ethiopian forces camped near Adwa, advancing in separate columns through difficult ground, where they became isolated and were overwhelmed by coordinated Ethiopian assaults despite their artillery. Over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and around 3,800 captured; Ethiopian losses were 4,000 to 7,000 killed.

becquerel-radioactivity-1896.summary: In 1896 Becquerel found that uranium fogged photographic plates in the dark: atoms give off energy on their own. He thought phosphorescent materials might emit penetrating X-ray-like radiation when lit by bright sunlight, so through February he wrapped photographic plates and coins in thick black paper, laid phosphorescent uranium salts on top and set them in sun for hours. By May, after experiments with non-phosphorescent uranium salts, he concluded that penetrating radiation came from uranium without excitation by any external energy source.

sources.confirms: The article dates Becquerel's discovery to 1896 and reports that he described uranium salts as active and photographic plates showing sample silhouettes.
sources.qualifies: The cited text does not establish the summary's details about the experiments through May or the conclusion that uranium emitted radiation without external excitation.

sources.title: Sagnac, G., "Les expériences de M. H. Becquerel sur les radiations invisibles émises par les corps phosphorescents et par les sels d'uranium," Journal de Physique Théorique et Appliquée 5 (1896)

Its Tier 1 contemporaneous article is confirmed bibliographically only; its text was not read.
becquerel-radioactivity-1896.detail: Becquerel, French experimental physicist, had long been interested in phosphorescence, emission of light of one colour after exposure to light of another. He had learned of Röntgen's X-rays when Henri Poincaré read Röntgen's paper to the French Academy of Sciences on 20 January. On 26 and 27 February skies were dark and overcast, so he left his layered plates in a dark cabinet, yet when developed object shadows were just as distinct as after sunlight. Intense research followed: thorium proved radioactive, and Marie and Pierre Curie found polonium and radium. Becquerel shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with the Curies.

marconi-radio-patent-1896.summary: In 1896 Marconi filed wireless telegraphy's first patent; messages could cross sea and sky without a wire. Wireless telegraphy had been tried before; no system had proved technically and commercially successful. His breakthrough came in summer 1895, when raising his antenna and grounding both transmitter and receiver, a technique borrowed from wired telegraphy, let signals carry about 2 km beyond Celestini hill. By March 1897 he had sent Morse signals about 3 miles across Salisbury Plain, and that year he founded The Wireless Telegraph & Signal Company.

marconi-radio-patent-1896.detail: British Patent 12039 was titled "Improvements in Transmitting Electrical impulses and Signals, and in Apparatus therefor". Marconi, born in Bologna in 1874, had studied Hertz's work through physics professor Augusto Righi, and at 20 began experiments in his family's Villa Griffone attic, building a spark transmitter and a receiver using a coherer, an early detector whose resistance changed when radio waves struck it. Italy's Ministry of Post and Telegraphs never answered his request for funding, so in early 1896 he went to London with his mother, where William Preece, Chief Electrical Engineer of the General Post Office, backed him.

braun-cathode-ray-tube-1897.summary: In 1897 Ferdinand Braun built a cathode-ray tube, a glass screen painted by an electron beam; it became television's screen. His cold-cathode diode was a Crookes tube modified with a phosphor-coated screen that glowed where electrons struck it. In cathode-ray tubes, electron guns fire beams that deflection coils or plates steer and an anode accelerates toward that screen, drawing images such as oscilloscope waveforms or television frames.

braun-cathode-ray-tube-1897.detail: Cathode rays were so named when first discovered, before anyone understood that electrons streamed from cathodes. Braun's paper appeared months before J. J. Thomson measured their mass-to-charge ratio and showed they were negatively charged particles smaller than atoms. In 1908 Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton described in Nature how "distant electric vision" could use Braun tubes as both transmitter and receiver. Western Electric's John Johnson and Harry Weinhart made the first hot-cathode tube, sold commercially from 1922, and Telefunken built the first commercial electronic television sets with cathode-ray tubes in Germany in 1934.

eijkman-beriberi-batavia-1897.summary: At a military medical laboratory in Batavia (Jakarta), Christiaan Eijkman noticed in 1889 that laboratory chickens fed cooked polished rice from hospital kitchen developed a nerve disorder resembling beriberi and recovered when fed unpolished rice. Through 1890s he and Gerrit Grijns ran feeding trials and prison surveys across Java showing that rice with its silver skin protected against beriberi, publishing a summary paper in 1897. Eijkman first proposed a toxin countered by a substance in bran; Grijns reframed it in 1901 as a dietary deficiency. Their work opened a path to vitamin B1, isolated from rice bran by Jansen and Donath in Batavia in 1926.

Eijkman's 1929 Nobel lecture recounts chickens falling ill after three to four weeks on polished rice and recovering on bran. Dutch East Indies prison data, gathered by Adolphe Vorderman in 1896, provided human evidence.

haffkine-plague-vaccine-bombay-1897.summary: When plague reached Bombay in 1896, Ukrainian-born bacteriologist Waldemar Haffkine, already known for a cholera vaccine tested in Calcutta, set up a laboratory in a corridor of Grant Medical College and grew Yersinia pestis in broth, killing that culture with heat. On 10 January 1897 he injected himself with 10 ml and ran a fever for days. Weeks later, during an outbreak in the Byculla House of Correction, he inoculated 147 prisoners who volunteered; among them two cases and no deaths followed, against twelve cases and six deaths among 172 who refused. The Government of India founded a Plague Research Laboratory under him, later the Haffkine Institute, which issued about 26 million doses across India between 1897 and 1925.

benin-expedition-1897-1897.summary: In 1897 British troops burned Benin City and carried off its bronzes to museums, exiled Oba Ovonramwen, and annexed Benin into the Niger Coast Protectorate. In late December 1896 James Phillips of that protectorate had led 250 people toward Benin City to discuss trade, without waiting for Ovonramwen's approval to enter; Benin forces attacked them on 4 January and killed or captured almost everyone.

benin-expedition-1897-1897.detail: Benin had kept its independence through the Scramble for Africa, and its Oba's monopoly over trade in his territories was seen as a threat by the Royal Niger Company. In 1892 Vice-Consul Henry Gallwey pressed a treaty on a hesitant Ovonramwen to open free passage of goods and develop palm oil. Rear-Admiral Harry Rawson then invaded with 1,200 men. After Benin City fell, houses, sacred sites and palaces were looted and burned, including Ovonramwen's palace on 21 February. Some 2,500 artefacts went to Britain; about 40 percent entered British Museum collections, and Britain's Admiralty auctioned others from May 1897 to defray expedition costs. Their repatriation is now an ongoing movement.

commercial-press-shanghai-1897.summary: In 1897 four young printers founded Commercial Press in Shanghai; it became China's largest publisher and schooled China. All four were Protestant Christians trained at American Presbyterian Mission Press, and they began by publishing books such as Bibles once financial backing arrived. From 1903 Zhang Yuanji, responding to China's move toward a new curriculum, created textbook and translation series, and from 1904 he launched popular periodicals including Dongfang Zazhi and Short Story Magazine.

commercial-press-shanghai-1897.detail: From 1903 to 1914 it ran as a joint venture with Kinkōdō, one of Japan's largest textbook publishers. Through Kinkōdō it obtained up-to-date printing technology, as well as lantern slides and cinema. Founder Xia was stabbed to death in January 1914. On 28 January 1932 Japan's Imperial Army bombed it, destroying its Zhabei headquarters, its Oriental Library with more than 500,000 books including tens of thousands of rare volumes, four printing presses and 80 percent of its assets. Its headquarters moved to Beijing in 1954, and it continues today as a publisher of dictionaries, textbooks and Chinese language materials.

thomson-electron-1897.summary: In 1897 J J Thomson found electrons, particles 1,000 times lighter than an atom and present in all matter: atoms had parts. Cathode rays were glowing beams seen in evacuated glass discharge tubes, then also called Lenard rays, and their nature was disputed; earlier investigators such as Heinrich Hertz had thought they could not be deflected electrically. He concluded that they were very light, negatively charged particles which were a universal building block of atoms, so atoms were divisible.

sources.confirms: The article says Thomson concluded in 1897 that matter contains particles now called electrons, based on his investigation of cathode rays.

sources.author: Falconer, Isobel
sources.venue: The British Journal for the History of Science
sources.confirms: The article says Thomson announced results on 30 April 1897, proposing that cathode rays were negatively charged subatomic particles he called corpuscles, later renamed electrons.

sources.author: Thomson, J. J.

thomson-electron-1897.verification_note: Britannica and Falconer confirm Thomson's 1897 electron-related conclusion, with Falconer dating his announcement to 30 April and describing these particles as corpuscles. These sources do not establish all additional details in this summary. His original paper is confirmed bibliographically only; its text was not read.
thomson-electron-1897.detail: Thomson found that they travelled much farther through air than expected for anything atom-sized. He estimated their mass by measuring heat generated when rays hit a thermal junction and comparing it with their magnetic deflection; his experiments suggested that they were over 1,000 times lighter than hydrogen atoms, and that their mass was the same whichever type of atom they came from. One month later he could reliably deflect them with an electric field by evacuating his tube to very low pressure. He called them corpuscles; later scientists preferred electron, a name George Johnstone Stoney had suggested in 1891. Thomson received the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics for his investigations of electrical conduction in gases.

marconi-company-1897.summary: In July 1897 Marconi founded a company to sell wireless telegraphy; radio became a business before it was a science. It opened the world's first radio factory on Hall Street in Chelmsford, northeast of London, in 1898, and went on to pioneer long-distance wireless communication and mass-media broadcasting. Isaacs then led it into radio broadcasting, where it was dominant in forming the British Broadcasting Company, while Marconi focused on research.

marconi-company-1897.detail: It founded American Marconi in 1899 and became Marconi's Wireless Telegraph Company in 1900. That year it set up Marconi International Marine Communication Company, and a training college followed in 1901. It sent transatlantic broadcasts between Clifden, Ireland, and Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, from 17 October 1907. When its finances faltered Marconi recruited Godfrey Isaacs as managing director, who turned it around and rode demand for maritime wireless after the Titanic sank in 1912; that year it moved to larger New Street Works in Chelmsford. It became one of Britain's most successful manufacturing companies.

ross-malaria-mosquito-1897.summary: Ronald Ross, an Indian Medical Service surgeon working in a tin-roofed hospital room in Secunderabad, had spent two years dissecting mosquitoes fed on malaria patients without result. On 20 August 1897 he examined "dapple-winged" mosquitoes (Anopheles) fed four days earlier on his patient Husein Khan and found pigmented cells in their stomach walls, the parasite's oocysts; a day later they had grown. He wrote in his Nobel lecture, "I counted altogether twelve of these cells in the insect." His paper appeared in the British Medical Journal on 18 December 1897. Transferred to Calcutta, he traced malaria's full cycle in birds in 1898, and Giovanni Grassi's team in Rome showed human transmission by Anopheles that same year. Ross received his Nobel Prize in 1902, and malaria control turned to draining, screening and killing mosquitoes.

maidstone-chlorination-1897.summary: Typhoid broke out in Maidstone, Kent, in August 1897 after hop-pickers contaminated springs feeding Maidstone's supply. By 9 October there were 1,200 cases; its final count was 1,847 cases and 132 deaths in a town of 34,000. On 20 September suspect Tutsham springs were cut off, and on 16 October pathologist German Sims Woodhead supervised dosing of Barming reservoir and mains with chloride of lime, about ten tons in 200,000 gallons, flushed through overnight. It was an emergency disinfection rather than continuous treatment, but it is the earliest documented chlorination of a public supply. Continuous chlorination began at Lincoln in 1905 after another typhoid outbreak and at Jersey City in 1908, where it survived a court challenge and spread across America.

curie-radium-polonium-1898.summary: In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie announced two new elements, polonium and radium, and Marie coined radioactivity. Using an electrometer, Pierre's sensitive device for measuring electric charge, she showed that pitchblende, a uranium mineral, was four times as active as pure uranium, so it must contain an element far more active.

curie-radium-polonium-1898.detail: Henri Becquerel had found in 1896 that uranium salts emitted rays, and Marie chose uranium rays as her thesis topic. They worked in a converted shed next to ESPCI that was poorly ventilated and not waterproof. Radium was elusive because it is chemically close to barium, which pitchblende also contains; from a tonne of ore they separated one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride in 1902, and Marie isolated pure radium metal in 1910. They shared 1903's Nobel Prize in Physics with Becquerel, and she won 1911's Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering and isolating these elements, the only person so far to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences.

picture.alt: Marie and Pierre Curie in their Paris laboratory, photographed about 1900.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public domain, via Wellcome Collection

garden-cities-1898.summary: In 1898 Ebenezer Howard proposed garden cities, planned towns of 32,000 ringed by farmland; suburbs and new towns worldwide follow his plan. He envisioned each garden city as a "third magnet" drawing residents and small businesses away from both too-crowded cities and too-isolated countryside. Howard founded the Garden City Association, later the Town and Country Planning Association, which created First Garden City Ltd in 1899 to build Letchworth, 34 miles outside London; Raymond Unwin and Barry Parker won its 1904 planning competition.

sources.title: Garden city movement
To-morrow : a peaceful path to real reform : Howard, Ebenezer ...
Miller, Mervyn, 'Garden Cities and Suburbs: At Home and Abroad', Journal of Planning History 1 (2002) 6-28
sources.author: Miller, Mervyn
sources.confirms: Ebenezer Howard published To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform in 1898, founding the garden city movement that built Letchworth from 1903.

garden-cities-1898.detail: It was reissued in 1902 as "Garden Cities of To-morrow". Howard drew on Edward Bellamy's utopian novel Looking Backward and Henry George's Progress and Poverty. His idealised city housed 32,000 people on 9,000 acres, laid out in his diagrams in concentric rings with open spaces, public parks and six radial boulevards 120 feet wide, and clusters of such cities would orbit a central city of 58,000 people, linked by road and rail and separated by green belts. Howard bought land at Welwyn for his second garden city in 1919. The movement's emphasis on planning fed Britain's post-war New Towns Act, and garden cities inspired by his model have since been built all over the world.

picture.alt: Ebenezer Howard's Diagram No. 1, Three Magnets, from his 1898 book To-morrow, which launched garden city movement.
picture.credit: Ebenezer Howard, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

war-of-the-worlds-1898.summary: In 1898 Wells's The War of the Worlds turned invasion by a superior technology against Britain, which practised it. Its unnamed narrator in Surrey, and his younger brother who flees to Essex, watch Martians invade London and southern England; their home planet has reached its "last stage of exhaustion", and they land on Horsell Common and lay waste to Woking with three-legged fighting machines armed with heat rays and toxic smoke.

sources.title: The War of the Worlds
Britannica, "The War of the Worlds (novel)"
sources.confirms: The article gives the novel's book publication year as 1898 and describes the Martians landing at Horsell Common and marching upon London.

sources.title: Wells, H. G., The War of the Worlds (William Heinemann, 1898)
sources.author: Wells, H. G.
sources.confirms: The archive catalogue confirms the 1898 publication by William Heinemann and the availability of digitized full text; the text was not read.

war-of-the-worlds-1898.verification_note: A reference article and an archive catalogue confirm 1898 publication and its invasion setting; detailed plot elements rest on general accounts.
war-of-the-worlds-1898.detail: Earthly bacteria, to which Martians had no immunity, save humanity where its armies fail. Wells, who had trained in biology, later said his inspiration was European colonisation's catastrophic effect on Aboriginal Tasmanians, and its plot has been read as commentary on evolution, imperialism and Victorian-era fears. It has never been out of print, is among science fiction's most discussed works, and is credited with establishing themes such as first contact and war between planets. Orson Welles's 1938 radio adaptation convinced part of its audience that a Martian invasion was under way.

picture.alt: Plate from page 279 of 1898 Harper and Brothers edition of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds.
picture.credit: Harper and Brothers, Internet Archive, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

aspirin-bayer-1899.summary: In 1899 Bayer began selling aspirin worldwide, the first mass-market synthetic drug. In 1897 Bayer scientists began studying it as a less-irritating replacement for common salicylate medicines, and Felix Hoffmann, or perhaps Arthur Eichengrün, first produced it in pure, stable form that year. Aspirin's popularity grew through the twentieth century's first half; Bayer lost its trademark in America and some other countries between 1918 and 1921 after letting other manufacturers use its name for years, so aspirin became a genericised trademark.

sources.title: Aspirin
Britannica, "Aspirin"
sources.confirms: The article states that aspirin is derived from salicylic acid, but gives no dates for its introduction or synthesis and does not mention Bayer or Hoffmann.

sources.title: Sneader, Walter, "The Discovery of Aspirin: A Reappraisal," BMJ 321 (2000)
sources.author: Sneader, Walter
sources.confirms: The article reports that pure acetylsalicylic acid was first prepared on 10 August 1897 and marketed in 1899.
sources.qualifies: The article says its analysis supports Eichengrün's claim, casting doubt on Hoffmann's credit for the preparation.

aspirin-bayer-1899.verification_note: A BMJ article reports preparation in 1897 and marketing in 1899, while Britannica's article provides no date or Bayer attribution. Sneader's account supports Eichengrün's claim and casts doubt on Hoffmann's credit. That BMJ page was access-gated, but its evidence reports these dates and finding.
aspirin-bayer-1899.detail: Salicin from willow bark, which human guts turn into salicylic acid, had been used for its health effects for at least 2,400 years. Charles Frédéric Gerhardt first made acetylsalicylic acid in 1853 by treating sodium salicylate with acetyl chloride. Its name blends a(cetyl) with spir, from Spirsäure, German for meadowsweet, from which salicylic acid was first isolated, plus drug suffix -in. Paracetamol in 1956 and ibuprofen in 1962 cut into its use, but John Vane showed in 1971 that it suppresses prostaglandins, winning a Nobel Prize in 1982, and trials established its anti-clotting value. Some 40,000 tonnes are consumed each year.

picture.alt: Bottle of Bayer aspirin powder from 1899, from Bayer archives.
picture.credit: Bayer AG Archives, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bolivia-patino-tin-llallagua-1900.summary: In 1900 Cochabamba-born storekeeper Simón Iturri Patiño, who had taken over La Salvadora claim at Llallagua in 1897, struck an exceptionally rich tin vein. As silver prices fell and canned-food and tinplate industries grew, Bolivian mines around Oruro and Potosí shifted to cassiterite, and Antofagasta railway wagons carried concentrates to Chilean ports. Patiño bought out neighbouring companies, built mills at Catavi and Uncía, acquired smelters in England and by 1924 controlled a large part of world tin production. John Hillman's study shows Bolivian output rising from about 1,000 tonnes in 1890 to nearly 20,000 tonnes in 1900, making tin Bolivia's main export for five decades, until nationalisation in 1952.

sources.title: Hillman, John, 'The Emergence of the Tin Industry in Bolivia', Journal of Latin American Studies 16 (1984)
sources.author: Hillman, John
sources.confirms: Rise of tin output around 1900, Patiño's Llallagua strike and consolidation.

sources.title: Hillman, John, 'The Mining Industry and the State: The Politics of Tin Restriction in Bolivia, 1936-1939', Bulletin of Latin American Research 21 (2002)
sources.author: Hillman, John
sources.confirms: Patiño group's dominance and relations with the Bolivian state.

bolivia-patino-tin-llallagua-1900.verification_note: Dates for the La Salvadora strike are given as 1900 in most accounts and 1899 or 1901 in some; export tonnage figures for 1900 vary with concentrate grades.
bolivia-patino-tin-llallagua-1900.detail: Mining at 4,000 metres relied on Quechua and Aymara workers who had served earlier silver mines; silicosis and low wages drove union militancy that shaped Bolivian politics. Patiño moved to Europe in 1912 and his group controlled smelting in Liverpool and Arnhem. Hillman's 2002 article follows state efforts to restrict output after 1931 under an International Tin Committee.

picture.credit: Carlillasa, via Wikimedia Commons

boxer-rebellion-railways-1900.summary: In 1900 Boxer fighters tore up railways and telegraph lines across north China as foreign tools; about 20,000 troops from eight nations marched on Beijing to crush them. Their movement had emerged in 1898 and 1899, and their rebellion ended in 1901 after that foreign invasion.

sources.author: Abdow, Emily
sources.confirms: The page says Boxers destroyed railroads, and that an eight-nation relief force reached Beijing on 14 August 1900.

sources.author: Klein, Thoralf

sources.author: Perdue, Peter; Sebring, Ellen

boxer-rebellion-railways-1900.verification_note: Sources place the movement's emergence in 1898 and 1899 and describe about 20,000 Allied troops marching on Beijing; they do not say those armies came by rail or that Qing troops guarded the Beijing-Tianjin line.

paris-exposition-1900-1900.summary: In 1900 fifty million visitors to the Paris Exposition rode a moving pavement and escalators and saw talking films. It set out to celebrate past achievements and speed development into a new century; Paris kept Métro Line 1 and new rail stations built for it.

sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.confirms: The Exposition Universelle ran from April to November 1900, drew over 50 million visitors and featured a moving electric walkway.

sources.author: Bureau International des Expositions
sources.confirms: Records 50.86 million visitors between April and November 1900 and the 3.5 km moving walkway, the Rue de l'Avenir, on the site.

sources.confirms: Film shot in July 1900 from the moving sidewalk at the Paris Exposition.

sydney-plague-rat-campaign-1900.summary: Bubonic plague reached Sydney in January 1900 aboard ships from Noumea and Hong Kong. Chief Medical Officer John Ashburton Thompson, following Simond's new hypothesis, treated rats and their fleas rather than human contact as main vector, and organised bounties that killed more than 100,000 rats, cleansing gangs that demolished and limewashed waterfront slums, and quarantine at North Head for contacts. By August 1900 there had been 303 cases and 103 deaths. Thompson's 1900 reports in Public Health and later Lancet papers were among first epidemiological demonstrations that rat plague preceded human plague, influencing global practice. Barr argues that dirt and fear framed political action ahead of Federation.

sources.title: Thompson, J. Ashburton, 'An account of the epidemic of plague at Sydney', Public Health 13 (1900)
sources.author: Thompson, John Ashburton
sources.confirms: Contemporary account of epidemic, case numbers and rat-focused control
sources.qualifies: Author's own perspective

sources.confirms: Comparative analysis of Sydney's plague response

sources.confirms: Argues uncertainty and emotion shaped plague response in 1900 Sydney
sources.qualifies: Cultural history focus

sydney-plague-rat-campaign-1900.verification_note: Case and death counts vary slightly between Thompson's reports and later tallies (303 cases and 103 deaths is widely cited).
sydney-plague-rat-campaign-1900.detail: Echenberg's Plague Ports compares Sydney to Honolulu, San Francisco and Cape Town, noting Sydney's relatively low mortality and lack of racial scapegoating compared with Honolulu's Chinatown fire. Photographs by John Degotardi Jr document resumption and cleansing of The Rocks and Darling Harbour. Plague returned in smaller outbreaks until 1925. Rat-proofing of wharves and sewers became standard. Tidswell's bacteriology confirmed Yersinia pestis in rats before human cases.

landell-de-moura-radio-1900.summary: In June 1900 Brazilian priest Landell de Moura sent voice without wires in Sao Paulo. Jornal do Commercio reported it from Alto de Sant Anna, naming British Consul P. C. P. Lupton and his family among the witnesses; Landell went on to patent his designs in Brazil and America.

zeppelin-lz1-1900.summary: In July 1900 Count Zeppelin's first rigid airship flew over Lake Constance carrying five people, 6 kilometres in 17 to 18 minutes, before its moveable weight jammed and one engine failed, forcing emergency landing; two more flights in October beat the French Army's electric airship speed record.

sources.confirms: Contemporary account in the Aeronautical Society's journal of Count Zeppelin's rigid airship and its 1900 trial on Lake Constance.

planck-quantum-1900.summary: In 1900 Max Planck proposed that energy comes in packets, quanta, the seed of quantum physics and of computer chips. That step made his black-body radiation law fit experiment. He first called quantization purely formal; physicists now regard it as where quantum physics began.

sources.author: Planck, Max
sources.confirms: Planck's published derivation of the black-body radiation law using energy elements, the paper that follows his December 1900 presentation to the German Physical Society.
sources.qualifies: The paper treats energy elements as a counting device; the physical reading of quanta came later.

sources.author: Klein, Martin J.

bengal-chemicals-ray-1901.summary: Chemist Prafulla Chandra Ray began making pharmaceutical chemicals in 1892 in his Calcutta home with Rs 700, and in 1901 incorporated Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Limited, first Indian-owned chemical manufacturer. His factory produced sulphuric acid, phosphates, tinctures and quinine preparations from local raw materials, and employed his students from Presidency College, where he had prepared mercurous nitrite in 1896. Ray saw chemical industry as swadeshi self-reliance and wrote A History of Hindu Chemistry to show Indian precedents. Bengal Chemicals grew into one of India's largest drug makers before independence and survives today as a public sector company.

sources.title: Dhruv Raina, 'Prafulla Chandra Ray and Marcelin Berthelot: Chemist-Historians', in Images and Contexts: The Historiography of Science and Modernity in India (Oxford University Press, 2010)

bengal-chemicals-ray-1901.detail: Ray gave founding details in his own hand in his 1932 autobiography, Life and Experiences of a Bengali Chemist. Founding is dated 1892 for first production and 1901 for incorporation.

picture.credit: Biswarup Ganguly

butantan-antivenom-serum-1901.summary: In 1901 physician Vital Brazil Mineiro da Campanha opened the Instituto Serumtherapico at Butantan farm outside São Paulo, set up to make plague serum, and began producing antivenoms from horses immunised with snake venom. Testing Albert Calmette's single cobra antiserum, he showed that it failed against Bothrops and Crotalus bites and that serum had to match venom species. He issued anti-bothropic and anti-crotalic sera, created a polyvalent serum, and distributed them to coffee plantations in exchange for live snakes shipped by rail in wooden boxes. Butantan became a centre for herpetology and venom research and later made vaccines; its 1911 treatise A defesa contra o ophidismo spread his methods across the Americas.

sources.title: Hawgood, Barbara J., 'Pioneers of anti-venomous serotherapy: Dr Vital Brazil (1865-1950)', Toxicon 30 (1992)
sources.author: Hawgood, Barbara J.
sources.confirms: Founding of Butantan in 1901, specificity experiments against Calmette's serum and polyvalent antivenom.

sources.author: Brazil, Vital
sources.confirms: Vital Brazil's own account of serum production, species specificity and snake exchange.

sources.author: Kalil, Jorge
sources.confirms: Continuity of antivenom production at Butantan since 1901.

butantan-antivenom-serum-1901.detail: Vital Brazil disputed serum specificity with Calmette and went on to found Instituto Vital Brazil in Niterói in 1919. Snakebite killed thousands of rural workers a year in coffee and sugar regions; serum distribution with Butantan's snake-exchange scheme cut mortality. The institute's serpentarium became a public attraction by the 1920s.

picture.credit: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net)., via Wikimedia Commons

landsteiner-blood-groups-1901.summary: Karl Landsteiner, an assistant at Vienna University's pathological-anatomical institute, mixed serum and red cells from himself and five colleagues and found that some combinations clumped and others did not. In a 1901 paper in the Wiener klinische Wochenschrift he sorted samples into three groups, A, B and C (later O); his students Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli added rare group AB in 1902. Transfusion had been tried since the 1660s with frequent deaths. Reuben Ottenberg in New York performed the first transfusion with compatibility testing in 1907 and showed by 1911 that typed transfusions were safe. Landsteiner received his Nobel Prize in 1930, and typing made 1930s blood banks and Second World War plasma programmes possible.

sources.title: Chandler, James G.; Chin, Theresa L.; Wohlauer, Max V., 'Direct blood transfusions', Journal of Vascular Surgery 56 (2012)
sources.author: Chandler, James G.; Chin, Theresa L.; Wohlauer, Max V.

picture.credit: Mfchris84, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

takamine-adrenaline-1901.summary: In 1901 Jokichi Takamine patented pure adrenaline, isolated in his laboratory by Keizo Uenaka after earlier impure forms; the first hormone purified, it stopped surgical bleeding and opened hormone studies. Drawn from animal glands, it became medicine's first effective drug for opening asthma sufferers' airways.

yawata-steel-works-1901.summary: In 1901 Japan lit its first modern blast furnace at Yahata; within decades it made steel for its ships, rails and guns. Its state-owned Imperial Steel Works had been set up in 1896 to feed growing shipbuilding, railway, construction and armaments industries. Poor output, high coke consumption and other failures led to suspension the following year; Japanese engineers, among them metallurgist Kageyoshi Noro, fixed those defects, and by 1912 Yahata made 80% of Japan's pig iron.

cape-town-plague-ndabeni-1901.summary: Bubonic plague reached Cape Town in early 1901 after infected forage arrived from Argentina for British army horses during the South African War; a first suspect ship, the Kilburn, had been quarantined in March 1900. Under public health powers Cape Colony's government forced some 6,000 to 7,000 African dock and railway workers out of inner-city districts to a fenced location at Uitvlugt on the Cape Flats, later Ndabeni. Maynard Swanson called this a sanitation syndrome: medical language of contagion turned into urban segregation, a pattern repeated at Port Elizabeth and Durban. Myron Echenberg's comparative study of plague ports shows Cape Town as the case where disease control most directly produced racial residential law.

sources.title: Swanson, Maynard W., 'The Sanitation Syndrome: Bubonic Plague and Urban Native Policy in the Cape Colony, 1900-1909', Journal of African History 18 (1977)
sources.author: Swanson, Maynard W.
sources.confirms: Plague in 1901 as pretext for removal of Africans from Cape Town and Port Elizabeth to locations; medical imagery shaping segregation policy

cape-town-plague-ndabeni-1901.detail: Echenberg's chapter opens with an 1899 Cape Times letter claiming whites were almost immune, then follows Chief Medical Officer John Gregory's quarantine at Saldanha Bay. Swanson showed how Native Reserve Locations Act of 1902 built on plague removals. Ndabeni residents resisted rents and conditions and were later moved to Langa after 1927. Plague killed 395 people in Cape Town in 1901, about half of those infected.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection

booth-vacuum-cleaner-1901.summary: On 30 August 1901 engineer Hubert Cecil Booth files British patent 17,433 for Improvements relating to the Extraction of Dust from Carpets, after testing his idea by sucking through a handkerchief laid on a restaurant chair. The Science Museum records his insight, that a cleaner should suck rather than blow, and his British Vacuum Cleaner Company's red horse-drawn vans, whose hoses ran through windows into drawing rooms; a visit cost about a junior maid's annual wages. In Ohio janitor James Murray Spangler filed his portable electric suction sweeper in 1907, granted in June 1908, and sold rights to his cousin's husband William Hoover. Household vacuums followed electricity into homes over the next thirty years.

Booth's vans cleaned Westminster Abbey's carpets before Edward VII's coronation in 1902, and his company moved into portable machines for households and ships before the First World War. Hoover's upright with rotating brush, the Model O, sold from 1908.

wardenclyffe-1901.summary: In 1901 Tesla began a tower on Long Island to send power and messages through the air worldwide; Morgan cut funding and it never worked. Investors' money went instead to Marconi's cheaper working system; Wardenclyffe's 187-foot tower was never completed as planned, operations closed in 1905, and it was demolished for scrap in 1917 to cover Tesla's debts.

marconi-transatlantic-1901.summary: In December 1901 Marconi heard a Morse S in Newfoundland, sent 2,200 miles from Cornwall without a wire, in competition with transatlantic telegraph cables. No recording was made and historians still debate whether he heard it; official wireless messages crossed the Atlantic between Poldhu and Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, in December 1902.

nobel-prizes-first-1901.summary: In 1901 the first Nobel Prizes were awarded from a dynamite fortune, making a few scientists famous each year since. His will left 94% of his estate to fund prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. Inaugural laureates included Wilhelm Röntgen, Jacobus van ’t Hoff, Sully Prudhomme, Emil von Behring, and Jean Henri Dunant and Frédéric Passy, who shared the Peace Prize.

philippines-cholera-1902.summary: Cholera arrived in Manila in March 1902, at close of Philippine-American War, and spread through provinces for two years. American military and civil health officers under Dean Worcester quarantined districts, burned Farola and other Manila neighbourhoods, banned sale of fresh vegetables and detained suspected carriers, measures that Filipinos often evaded or resisted. Ken De Bevoise estimates deaths at roughly 200,000 in 1902-1904, atop losses from war and famine. Warwick Anderson reads this campaign as a founding moment for American colonial medicine in Asia, with laboratories, sanitary codes and later Culion leper colony following from it.

sources.confirms: American sanitary campaign of 1902 and development of colonial public health

philippines-cholera-1902.detail: Mortality figures vary: official counts recorded about 109,000 deaths by 1903, while De Bevoise's demographic reconstruction gives higher totals. Anderson's work documents how hygiene became a tool of colonial rule and racial classification in Philippines.

picture.credit: Unknown author

carrier-air-conditioning-1902.summary: In 1902 Willis Carrier designed the first system to control both humidity and temperature. It answered a problem at Sackett-Wilhelms Lithographing & Publishing Company in Brooklyn, where humid summer air made paper expand and shrink and spoiled color printing. Carrier patented his spray-type apparatus in 1906 and founded Carrier Corporation in 1915.

pacific-cable-1902.summary: On 31 October 1902, cable ship Anglia spliced last section of a 12,900-kilometre telegraph cable linking Bamfield on Vancouver Island to Fanning Island, Suva, Norfolk Island and then Southport in Queensland and Doubtless Bay in New Zealand. Owned jointly by British, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand governments through Pacific Cable Board, it broke Eastern Extension Company's monopoly on Australasian traffic and completed an 'All Red Line' touching only British territory. Fanning to Bamfield section of 6,000 kilometres was longest single cable yet laid. Boyce's 2000 study traces two decades of lobbying by Sandford Fleming and colonial governments against Treasury and Eastern Extension resistance.

pacific-cable-1902.detail: Johnson's 1903 All Red Line compiles official documents and Fleming's advocacy. Cable stations at Fanning Island and Norfolk Island became isolated outposts; Fanning was raided by German cruiser Nurnberg in 1914. Rates fell as competition started, and traffic grew with newspapers. Board operated until 1929 when cables merged into Imperial and International Communications (later Cable and Wireless). Suva landing made Fiji a Pacific communications hub for a century.

aswan-low-dam-1902.summary: In December 1902 Aswan Low Dam opened, Earth's largest masonry dam. Its gates opened each year to pass flood and sediment, storing no water from year to year; found too small for Egypt's needs, it was raised in 1907-1912 and 1929-1933 and later fitted to generate electricity.

oswaldo-cruz-yellow-fever-1903.summary: From 1903 Oswaldo Cruz cleared yellow fever from Rio de Janeiro by hunting mosquitoes. Between 1897 and 1906, 4,000 European immigrants had died of yellow fever in Rio. In 1904 he proposed restoring compulsory smallpox vaccination, and popular resistance helped trigger the Vaccine Revolt; in 1907 Berlin's International Congress on Hygiene and Demography awarded him its gold medal for Rio's sanitation.

uganda-sleeping-sickness-1903.summary: From 1901 sleeping sickness spread along Lake Victoria's northern shore in Busoga and Buganda, killing well over 250,000 people within a decade as colonial transport, resettlement and ecological change brought people into tsetse habitat. A Royal Society commission reached Entebbe in 1902. On 12 November 1902 Aldo Castellani saw a living trypanosome in cerebrospinal fluid drawn by lumbar puncture from a patient, and reported further cases in early 1903. David Bruce, arriving in March 1903, confirmed the parasite's role and tsetse transmission, after which Uganda cleared lakeshore populations inland. Maryinez Lyons places this outbreak in the wider colonial disease history of Central Africa.

sources.author: Lyons, Maryinez
sources.confirms: Epidemic erupted in Uganda in 1901 killing well over 250,000 people

uganda-sleeping-sickness-1903.detail: Castellani had first favoured a streptococcus as cause and later fought a priority dispute with Bruce in the British Medical Journal. Lyons reads sleeping sickness in Belgian Congo and Uganda as an outcome of conquest and labour mobilisation. Forced depopulation of islands and lakeshore in 1906 to 1909 cut transmission but displaced tens of thousands. Case numbers are estimates from colonial records.

goldfields-water-supply-1903.summary: In 1903 water reached Kalgoorlie through about 560 kilometres of steel pipe from Perth (sources give 530 to 566); its engineer had killed himself a year earlier. Lady Forrest started pumping machinery at Pumping Station Number One on January 22, 1903, and water flowed into Mount Charlotte Reservoir on January 24. Designer C. Y. O'Connor, derided in parliament and press as attempting the impossible, had died by suicide less than 12 months earlier; it still supplies more than 100,000 people.

sources.author: Water Corporation (Western Australia)

baghdad-railway-concession-1903.summary: On 5 March 1903 Abdülhamid II's government signs a convention with Deutsche Bank's Anatolian Railway Company, led by Arthur von Gwinner, for a line from Konya through Taurus and Amanus ranges to Mosul, Baghdad and Basra, with kilometric revenue guarantees and rights to minerals and antiquities along its route. British and Russian objections turned financing into a decade of diplomacy; German crews reached Bulgurlu in 1904, tunnelled Taurus passes during World War I and used unfinished track to move troops, and in 1915 Armenian deportees were marched along it. Turkish, French and Iraqi successors completed remaining gaps, and a through train first ran from Istanbul to Baghdad in July 1940. Ottoman engineers trained on this project, and its alignment fixed routes of modern Turkish, Syrian and Iraqi railways.

sources.title: McMeekin, S., The Berlin-Baghdad Express: The Ottoman Empire and Germany's Bid for World Power, 1898-1918 (Harvard University Press, 2010), ch. 2 'Berlin to Baghdad'
sources.author: McMeekin, Sean

ford-motor-company-1903.summary: In 1903 Henry Ford founded Ford Motor Company with $28,000 from twelve investors. His earlier Henry Ford Company had become Cadillac when he left it. Between 1903 and 1908 Ford sold hundreds or a few thousand cars of each model per year, before its mass-produced Model T of 1908 sold millions.

wright-flyer-1903.summary: On 17 December 1903 Orville and Wilbur Wright made four controlled powered flights, history's first; their longest lasted 59 seconds over 852 feet. Their Flyer grew out of glider tests there from 1900 to 1902; gusts wrecked it minutes after its fourth landing and it never flew again.

fleming-valve-1904.summary: In 1904 Fleming invented a vacuum tube, electronics' first part; radio and early computers were made of it. His was the first practical vacuum tube and first thermionic diode, conducting current one way and blocking reverse flow.

nagaoka-saturnian-atom-1904.summary: In papers read to Tokyo Mathematico-Physical Society in December 1903 and published in Philosophical Magazine and Nature in 1904, Hantaro Nagaoka of Tokyo Imperial University modelled an atom as a large positive central mass circled by rings of electrons, by analogy with Maxwell's analysis of Saturn's rings. He used it to discuss spectral lines and radioactivity, in contrast to J. J. Thomson's model of electrons embedded in a diffuse positive sphere. Instability of such rings under electrostatic repulsion drew criticism and Nagaoka dropped it by 1908, yet Ernest Rutherford cited Nagaoka's paper in his 1911 article proposing a nuclear atom from alpha-scattering results.

His later career built Japanese physics at RIKEN and Osaka. Philosophical Magazine pages 445-455 carry full version.

casement-congo-report-1904.summary: Roger Casement, British consul at Boma, travelled up the Congo river in 1903 and in February 1904 Britain's Foreign Office laid his report before Parliament. He recorded villages near Lake Mantumba assessed at ten 25-kilogram bags of gum copal a fortnight, men at Bongandanga marched in under armed guards every two weeks to deliver three kilograms of rubber each to the ABIR company, and sentries of La Lulanga company holding women prisoner until husbands met their quotas. Robert Harms's study of ABIR shows how wild-rubber vines were exhausted by 1906, breaking the system. His report fuelled E. D. Morel's Congo Reform Association and Belgium's annexation of Leopold II's colony in 1908.

Casement's report named witnesses only by initials to protect them. Later estimates of population loss in the Free State range widely and remain disputed. Casement was executed in 1916 for his part in Ireland's Easter Rising.

vaccine-revolt-1904.summary: In 1904 Rio de Janeiro rioted for a week against compulsory smallpox vaccination, an early revolt against public health by force. Smallpox, bubonic plague and yellow fever were ravaging Brazil's capital. Rioters also drew on anger at public services and mayor Pereira Passos's urban reforms; 30 people were killed, 110 wounded, and 945 arrested, and on 16 November the government declared a state of emergency and suspended mandatory vaccination.

gillette-safety-razor-1904.summary: On 15 November 1904 King Camp Gillette receives US patent 775,134 for a razor using a thin double-edged blade stamped from sheet steel about 0.006 inch thick, held in a clamp and thrown away when dull. Gillette, a travelling salesman for Crown Cork, had his idea in 1895; MIT-trained engineer William Nickerson worked out how to harden and sharpen steel that thin, and American Safety Razor Company, founded 1901, began production in 1903. His blade made shaving a home task rather than a barber's trade and set a pattern of selling a cheap holder and a stream of consumable blades, later copied from ink cartridges to coffee pods. The Smithsonian holds early blades.

beijing-zhangjiakou-railway-1905.summary: In 1905 China began its first railway built without foreign money or engineers, Zhan Tianyou's line from Peking to Kalgan. Zhan had been educated in the United States. He laid a zigzag section near Qinglongqiao station to climb steep mountain grades and finished two years ahead of schedule and under budget, giving China its first railway built without foreign help.

broken-hill-froth-flotation-1905.summary: Broken Hill's silver-lead-zinc lode left mountains of tailings holding about 20 percent zinc that gravity separation could not recover. Between 1901 and 1905 Melbourne brewer Charles Potter and Broken Hill Proprietary's general manager Guillaume Delprat patented processes in which finely ground ore, hot acidulated water and gas bubbles lifted sulphide minerals into a froth that could be skimmed. BHP's plant ran from 1903; a 1905 Victorian Supreme Court case, Potter v BHP, fought over priority and ended in a combined Potter-Delprat name. Rival inventors including Minerals Separation's agitation-froth process soon followed. Flotation became standard worldwide for sulphide ores and today processes billions of tonnes of ore a year.

sources.qualifies: Technical practice, not origins

broken-hill-froth-flotation-1905.verification_note: Potter's patent dates to 1901 and Delprat's to 1902; 1905 anchors court judgement and full industrial operation. Priority remains disputed in sources.
broken-hill-froth-flotation-1905.detail: Eleven companies and dozens of individuals experimented at Broken Hill, making its field a collective laboratory. Lyster's 1912 selective flotation and xanthate collectors in 1925 completed modern technique. A 1918 review recorded a decade of practice. Zinc recovered from tailings supported smelters at Port Pirie and Risdon and Australia's role in First World War metal supply. Flotation chemistry drew on Haynes's 1860 oil patent and Elmore's 1898 bulk-oil process.

einstein-annus-mirabilis-1905.summary: In 1905 Einstein published four papers: light comes in packets, atoms exist, space and time stretch with speed, and mass is energy. The photoelectric effect paper earned his 1921 Nobel Prize.

sources.title: Annus mirabilis papers - Wikipedia
Einstein, Albert, 'Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper', Annalen der Physik (1905)
sources.author: Einstein, Albert
sources.confirms: The page identifies Einstein’s 1905 article “Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper” in Annalen der Physik, pages 891-921.
sources.qualifies: The source identifies the electrodynamics article, not all four papers in the record, and does not mention the Nobel Prize.

sources.confirms: The light-quantum paper of the 1905 series, published in Annalen der Physik volume 322; Crossref metadata confirmed, Wiley page did not open.

picture.credit: Lucien Chavan, Albert Einstein Archives, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

michell-thrust-bearing-1905.summary: Melbourne engineer Anthony George Maldon Michell solved Reynolds's lubrication equations for a sliding pad in 1905 and designed a thrust bearing whose segmental pads pivot to form a wedge of oil film, carrying loads many times those of older collar bearings with far less friction. His British patent 875 of 16 January 1905 and Australian patents followed. First installation ran a centrifugal pump at Cohuna on Murray River in 1907. Royal Navy adopted Michell bearings for propeller shafts during First World War, saving space and power; hydro and steam turbines worldwide followed. Cherry's Royal Society memoir calls it an invention that made large propeller drives and turbines possible.

sources.author: Cherry, Thomas Macfarland
sources.venue: Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society
sources.confirms: Memoir records invention of tilting-pad bearing and its importance for turbines and ships
sources.qualifies: Memoir by colleague

sources.title: Michell, A. G. M., British patent GB190500875, 'Improvements in thrust and like bearings' (1905)
sources.author: Michell, Anthony George Maldon
sources.venue: UK Patent Office via Google Patents

sources.qualifies: Patent abstract only

michell-thrust-bearing-1905.verification_note: Patent date and bearing description are confirmed by his primary patent; Kingsbury's independent claim is acknowledged.
michell-thrust-bearing-1905.detail: Albert Kingsbury in United States patented a similar bearing in 1910 after independent experiments; litigation and later agreements divided markets. Michell also invented a crankless engine (1920s) and wrote a lubrication textbook. He worked as a consulting engineer on irrigation and hydraulic schemes in Victoria. Bearing design still follows his analysis, with tilting pads in hydroelectric turbines and ship propeller shafts carrying thousands of tonnes.

necaxa-hydroelectric-plant-1905.summary: In December 1905 Mexican Light and Power Company, a Canadian-registered firm engineered by Frederick Stark Pearson, began generating at Necaxa in Puebla's Sierra Norte, where dams on Necaxa and Tenango rivers fed water through tunnels and penstocks dropping more than 400 metres to turbines. Transmission lines at 60,000 volts, then among Earth's longest and highest-voltage, carried power 150 kilometres to Mexico City's trams, lights and factories and to silver mines at El Oro and Pachuca. Capacity reached about 100 megawatts by 1910, and its earth-fill dams were among those of greatest volume yet built. Necaxa supplied most of central Mexico's electricity for three decades and remains in service.

sources.title: Pearson, F. S.; Blackwell, F. O., 'The Necaxa Plant of the Mexican Light and Power Company', Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers 58 (1907)

sources.confirms: Construction chronology from 1903, start of service in 1905 and later history of the complex.

necaxa-hydroelectric-plant-1905.detail: Pearson and Blackwell's 1907 paper in ASCE Transactions describes hydraulic works and hydraulic-fill dam construction; W. L. Hooper's 1911 AIEE paper covers transmission. Celina Peña Guzmán's 2011 study treats Necaxa as industrial heritage at risk. Mexico nationalised its owner as part of Compañía de Luz y Fuerza del Centro in 1960.

de-forest-audion-1906.summary: In 1906 Lee de Forest built his Audion and by 1908 had added a grid, making history's first triode; a weak signal could control a strong current. It found little use until about 1912, when researchers recognized it could amplify and built pioneering amplifying radio receivers and electronic oscillators.

picture.credit: Paul Thompson, published in Radio Broadcast 1922, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fessenden-broadcast-1906.summary: Fessenden claimed to have broadcast music and speech by radio on Christmas Eve 1906; proven or not, he had sent voice by radio since 1900. His claim has not been well documented. His proven firsts include transmitting speech by radio in 1900 and, in January 1906, two-way Morse exchange across the Atlantic, between his station at Brant Rock, Massachusetts, and Machrihanish, Scotland.

Belrose, John S., "A Fessenden Christmas Eve Broadcast Retrospective"
sources.author: John S. Belrose

sources.confirms: IEEE historical review of the evidence for and against Fessenden's claimed Christmas Eve 1906 voice broadcast from Brant Rock.
sources.qualifies: The only direct evidence is Fessenden's own 1932 letter; no contemporaneous log or press report has been found, which is why historians treat the broadcast as claimed rather than established.

sources.qualifies: The milestone citation treats the Christmas Eve broadcast as established, resting on Helen Fessenden's 1940 book; the record's doubt follows Belrose and others.

nauru-phosphate-mining-1906.summary: Albert Ellis identified a doorstop in Sydney as high-grade phosphate rock in 1899 and traced it to Nauru and Banaba (Ocean Island). Under German colonial rule, Pacific Phosphate Company began shipping Nauru rock in 1906 and 1907. After 1920 British Phosphate Commissioners for Britain, Australia and New Zealand took over, selling phosphate below world prices to farmers at home while paying Nauruans tiny royalties. Superphosphate from Nauru underpinned Australian wheat and New Zealand pasture through 1960s. Mining removed topsoil and left coral pinnacles across 80 percent of island. Nauru gained independence in 1968, bought the industry in 1970 and in 1989 sued Australia at International Court of Justice over rehabilitation.

sources.author: Viviani, Nancy
sources.confirms: Negotiations over phosphate and independence in 1960s

nauru-phosphate-mining-1906.detail: Viviani's 1968 article details negotiations by Head Chief Hammer DeRoburt leading to independence and phosphate purchase. Weeramantry's 1992 study, written for Nauru's case, documented environmental damage and trusteeship obligations; Australia settled in 1993 for 107 million dollars. Phosphate wealth briefly made Nauruans among world's richest per capita in 1970s, then collapsed through mismanagement. Reserves were largely exhausted by 2000s, and island later hosted Australian offshore detention centres.

san-francisco-earthquake-1906-1906.summary: In April 1906 an earthquake and three days of fire destroyed most of San Francisco and killed more than 3,000, the deadliest earthquake in United States history; San Francisco rebuilt in four years. Fires from ruptured gas mains burned for several days, destroying about 25,000 buildings on 490 blocks, more than 80% of its buildings, and causing at least 80% of all damage.

santos-dumont-14-bis-1906.summary: In October 1906 Alberto Santos-Dumont flew 50 metres before a crowd near Paris, the first powered flight witnessed in public and filmed. It won him the Aéro-Club de France's 3,000-franc prize for flying 25 metres or more. On 12 November he flew 220 metres and took its prize for passing 100 metres.

bakelite-1907.summary: In 1907 Leo Baekeland made Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, mouldable and hard for good once set. Resistant to heat and electricity, it went into insulators, radio and telephone casings, kitchenware and jewelry, and its success led to other synthetic plastics.

djenne-great-mosque-1907.summary: In 1907 Djenne's masons rebuilt the Great Mosque in mud brick, the largest earthen building on Earth; townspeople replaster it every year. An earlier mosque there fell into ruin after 1818 and a second went up in 1834 to 1836; Djenné, under French control since 1892, arranged its rebuilding in 1906. Its walls are sun-baked earth bricks and sand with earth-based mortar.

UNESCO, 'Old Towns of Djenné', UNESCO World Heritage

sources.confirms: The page states that reconstruction of the Mosque in 1906-1907 resulted in a monument representing local religious architecture.

sources.author: Editors, Britannica; McKenna, Amy

sources.qualifies: Britannica says the mosque had fallen into ruin after 1818, rather than placing the start of its ruin at least as late as 1828.

djenne-great-mosque-1907.verification_note: Britannica dates ruin of its first mosque to after 1818 and Khan Academy dates French control to 1892 and a second mosque to 1834-1836; other accounts give 1828 and 1893.

tata-steel-jamshedpur-1907.summary: In 1907 Tata family members founded India's first steel company at Jamshedpur, starting Indian heavy industry under colonial rule. It began producing pig iron in 1911 and steel in 1912, and through the First World War it supplied steel for India's war effort.

quebec-bridge-collapse-1907.summary: In August 1907 the Quebec Bridge collapsed during construction and killed 75 workers; engineers had ignored warnings that it was too heavy. Early calculations of its own weight had never been rechecked once design was finished, and distortions in key members seen that summer went unheeded. A Royal Commission inquiry followed; in 1916 its redesigned successor dropped its central span into the river, killing 13 more, and opened in 1917 with a 549-metre cantilever span that remains unmatched in length.

T. Hoke, 'The Importance of a Personal Pledge', Civil Engineering (ASCE), December 2012

sources.confirms: On 29 August 1907 the partly built cantilever bridge collapsed, killing 75 of 86 workers present, through defective design of the lower chords.

sources.author: Holgate, Henry; Kerry, John G. G.; Galbraith, John
sources.venue: Royal Commission on Quebec Bridge Inquiry, Ottawa
sources.confirms: States that the bridge collapsed on 29 August 1907 and finds that a grave error was made in assuming the dead load at too low a value and never revising it.

panic-of-1907.summary: In 1907 a run on New York's trust companies spread panic until J P Morgan organised a private rescue. Within a week Knickerbocker Trust Company, New York City's third-largest trust, failed, and stocks fell almost 50% from their 1906 peak. J. P. Morgan pledged his own money and rallied other bankers to shore up banking, which exposed how little cash Washington's Treasury could supply in a panic; Congress passed its Aldrich-Vreeland Act in May 1908 and, after its National Monetary Commission reported, the Federal Reserve Act in December 1913.

sources.title: Panic of 1907 - Wikipedia

sources.confirms: Shows the 1907 panic centred on New York trust companies, with Knickerbocker Trust's failure spreading runs that Morgan's clearing-house group contained.

sources.confirms: Knickerbocker Trust suspended on 22 October 1907 after depositors withdrew nearly 8 million dollars; Morgan organised the private rescue in the absence of a central bank.

picture.credit: L. M. Glackens, Puck, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, No known copyright restrictions, via Library of Congress

mauretania-blue-riband-1907.summary: In 1907 Cunard's Mauretania, driven by steam turbines, took the Atlantic speed record and held it for two decades. German liners had held it since 1897, so Britain's government lent Cunard £2,600,000 to build her and Lusitania at a guaranteed 24-knot service speed. On her return crossing of 30 November to 5 December she took the eastbound Blue Riband at 23.69 knots; she added a westbound record in September 1909 and held both until 1929.

sources.title: RMS Mauretania (1906) (Wikipedia)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Ship: Passenger liners in the 20th century"

mauretania-blue-riband-1907.verification_note: Sources agree on Parsons turbines, a maiden voyage of 16 November 1907 and an eastbound Blue Riband on her return crossing at 23.69 knots; a westbound record followed in September 1909.

hejaz-railway-1908.summary: In September 1908 the Hejaz Railway reached Medina, 1,300 kilometres from Damascus; pilgrimage time fell from 40 days to five. Sultan Abdul Hamid II had planned it to carry pilgrims toward Mecca and bind distant Arab provinces to Istanbul; World War I stopped it 400 kilometres short of Mecca, and during the Arab Revolt guerrillas led by T. E. Lawrence ambushed its trains.

sources.title: Hejaz railway - Wikipedia
Ochsenwald, William, The Hijaz Railroad (University Press of Virginia, 1980)

sources.confirms: The Hijaz Railway from Damascus reached Medina in 1908, cutting the pilgrimage journey from weeks to days.

ikeda-umami-msg-1908.summary: In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kelp and named its taste umami. Umami now counts among five basic tastes with sweet, sour, bitter and salty. He had noticed in 1907 that his family's dashi tasted better with kombu in it. By 1909 he had patented a process for mass-producing monosodium glutamate from wheat and soybeans, sold as Ajinomoto, 'essence of flavor'.

sources.confirms: Glutamate was identified as an umami substance by Japanese scientists beginning with Ikeda, and umami was recognised internationally as a fifth basic taste only late in the twentieth century.

jersey-city-chlorination-1908.summary: In 1908 Jersey City became the first American city to chlorinate its drinking water. Dilute chloride of lime at 0.2 to 0.35 parts per million killed bacteria that spread typhoid, cholera and dysentery. John L. Leal conceived it and George Warren Fuller designed its plant; within a few years chlorine disinfection spread to drinking water systems worldwide.

sources.title: Water chlorination (Wikipedia)
McGuire, Michael J., "Eight revolutions in the history of US drinking water disinfection", Journal AWWA 98, no. 3 (2006), pp. 123-149
sources.author: McGuire, Michael J.

thor-electric-washing-machine-1908.summary: Hurley Machine Company of Chicago puts its Thor on sale, a galvanised drum turned by an electric motor, which IEEE's engineering timeline lists as America's first commercially sold electric washer, in 1907. Hurley engineer Alva J. Fisher filed its drive mechanism on 27 May 1909 and received US patent 966,677 on 9 August 1910. Britannica notes that manually controlled electric washers reached a wide market in the 1920s and that the first automatic machine, a front loader cycling through wash, drain, rinse and spin without attention, appeared in 1937. Ruth Schwartz Cowan later argued such machines raised standards of cleanliness more than they cut hours women spent on laundry.

anglo-persian-oil-1908.summary: In May 1908 drillers struck oil at Masjed Soleyman in Persia, the Middle East's first oil field; this find became BP and remade the region. William Knox D'Arcy had bought a 60-year concession from Shah Mozaffar al-Din in 1901 and, deep in debt after years without a find, saw his interests taken over by a Burmah Oil syndicate in 1905. Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later BP, was founded in 1909 and by 1912 had piped Masjed Soleyman's oil to a refinery at Abadan, shipping its first cargo that March.

sources.qualifies: It describes Masjid Suleiman as the Middle East’s first oil field, not its first well; it says the Concessions Syndicate took over D’Arcy’s interests in 1905 and the pipeline connection was made in 1912.

ford-model-t-1908.summary: In 1908 Ford's Model T went on sale, the first car ordinary families could afford. Its low price came partly from moving assembly lines with fully interchangeable parts, which cut build time from 12½ hours to 93 minutes by 1914; its Runabout fell from $825 in 1909 to $260 by 1925. Ford built 15 million, and by its ten-millionth, half of all cars worldwide were Model Ts.

sources.author: Henry Ford; Samuel Crowther
sources.confirms: Ford's own account of the Model T, its 1908 introduction and the assembly-line time savings.
