picture.credit: Ford Motor Company advertisement in Life magazine, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

gandhi-hind-swaraj-1909.summary: In 1909 Gandhi's Hind Swaraj condemned machine civilisation, railways and doctors included, as a disease India should refuse. He repudiated Western civilization, arguing modern civilization was harming India.

sources.title: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule - Wikipedia
Gandhi, M. K., Hind Swaraj and Other Writings, ed. Anthony J. Parel
sources.author: M. K. Gandhi; Anthony J. Parel (ed.)
sources.venue: Cambridge University Press (Cambridge Texts in Modern Politics)
sources.confirms: Critical edition with Parel's introduction dating the text to November 1909 aboard the Kildonan Castle and its Gujarati serialisation in Indian Opinion; chapters on railways, lawyers, doctors and machinery carry the critique of modern civilisation.

sources.title: Gandhi, M. K., Indian Home Rule (Hind Swaraj), 1909, reprint (Madras: Ganesh, 1919), ch. IX 'Railways', p. 41
sources.author: M. K. Gandhi
sources.confirms: Gandhi's text states that railways, lawyers and doctors have impoverished the country and condemns modern civilisation as a disease.

picture.alt: Title page of Indian Home Rule, Gandhi's own English rendering of Hind Swaraj, in a 1919 Madras reprint of a text first published in 1909.
picture.credit: M. K. Gandhi, Indian Home Rule (Ganesh and Co., Madras, 1919), Public domain, via Internet Archive

haber-ammonia-1909-1909.summary: In 1909 Fritz Haber made ammonia from the nitrogen in air, the process behind fertiliser that feeds half of us. His assistant Robert Le Rossignol and he demonstrated it at laboratory scale that summer, producing ammonia drop by drop at about 125 mL per hour. Ammonia is nitrogen fertilizer's base; Carl Bosch scaled their process up for BASF, whose Oppau plant began industrial production in 1913.

sources.title: Haber process - Wikipedia
Haber, F. and Le Rossignol, R., 'Über die technische Darstellung von Ammoniak aus den Elementen', Zeitschrift für Elektrochemie 19 (1913) 53-72
sources.author: Haber, F.; Le Rossignol, R.
sources.venue: Zeitschrift für Elektrochemie und angewandte physikalische Chemie
sources.confirms: Haber and Le Rossignol's own account of high-pressure catalytic ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen, the process demonstrated to BASF in 1909.

sources.title: Haber, Fritz, 'The Synthesis of Ammonia from Its Elements', Nobel Lecture, 2 June 1920
sources.author: Haber, Fritz
sources.confirms: Haber's own account of the laboratory synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen under pressure with catalysts, work carried out with Le Rossignol in Karlsruhe before 1909.

indian-institute-of-science-1909.summary: In 1909 the Indian Institute of Science opened in Bangalore from Jamsetji Tata's bequest; India had a research university of its own. Jamsetji Tata had planned a research institute to advance India's scientific capabilities since meeting Swami Vivekananda on a ship in 1893; Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV gave about 371 acres of land and Tata gave buildings. Morris Travers, co-discoverer of the noble gases, became its first director, and its first students were admitted on 24 July 1911.

sources.title: Indian Institute of Science - Wikipedia
Indian Institute of Science, 'History' (institutional heritage page)
sources.author: Indian Institute of Science
sources.confirms: IISc records its establishment by a vesting order of 27 May 1909 from Jamsetji Tata's endowment with land from Mysore, Morris Travers as first director, and the first students in 1911.

sources.title: Balaram, P., 'The Indian Institute of Science: Marking a Centenary', Resonance 14, no. 5 (2009): 416-429
sources.author: P. Balaram
sources.confirms: Traces Tata's 1898 proposal, the deputation to Curzon on 31 December 1898 and the Institute's opening in 1909 in Bangalore.

sources.title: Ramdas, A. K., review of B. V. Subbarayappa, In Pursuit of Excellence: A History of the Indian Institute of Science (Tata McGraw-Hill, 1992), Science 262 (1993): 591-592
sources.author: A. K. Ramdas
sources.confirms: Points to the standard institutional history of the Institute, reviewed in Science.

futurist-manifesto-1909.summary: In 1909 Marinetti's Futurist Manifesto declared a racing car more beautiful than classical sculpture: art embraced its machine age. It launched an avant-garde movement founded in Milan that praised speed, technology, youth and violence, glorified objects such as cars, airplanes and industrial cities, and scorned museums and the past. Painters Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Luigi Russolo and others soon joined, and Futurists went on to issue manifestos on painting, architecture, music, cinema, fashion and cuisine.

sources.title: Futurism - Wikipedia
Le Figaro, 20 February 1909 (Gallica, Bibliotheque nationale de France), front page carrying F. T. Marinetti, 'Le Futurisme'
sources.author: Marinetti, F. T.
sources.confirms: The digitised issue of Le Figaro dated 20 February 1909, the issue in which Marinetti's founding manifesto of Futurism was printed on the front page.

sources.title: White, John J., 'Futurism', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: White, John J.
sources.confirms: Futurism was announced on 20 February 1909 when Le Figaro published Marinetti's manifesto, which glorified the automobile and the beauty of its speed and power.

picture.alt: Marinetti's Manifeste du Futurisme in its 1909 French printing, photographed on display in 2016.
picture.credit: JoJan (photograph of the 1909 printed manifesto), CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

chagas-disease-1909.summary: Sent in 1907 by Instituto Oswaldo Cruz to control malaria among workers extending the Central Railway at Lassance, Minas Gerais, Carlos Chagas worked from a railway carriage. Railway engineers showed him blood-sucking barbeiro bugs that infested mud-walled houses; in December 1908 he found a flagellate protozoan in their gut and named it Trypanosoma cruzi after his mentor. On 14 April 1909 he found the same parasite in the blood of a feverish two-year-old girl, Berenice. His 1909 paper in Memorias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz described agent, vector, human disease and reservoir animals in one stroke, a feat without parallel in parasitology. Chagas disease still infects an estimated six to seven million people, mostly in Latin America.

sources.title: Chagas, Carlos, 'Nova tripanozomiaze humana: estudos sobre a morfolojia e o ciclo evolutivo do Schizotrypanum cruzi n. gen., n. sp., ajente etiolojico de nova entidade morbida do homem', Memorias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz 1 (1909)
sources.author: Chagas, Carlos
sources.confirms: The original 1909 description of the parasite, its development in the triatomine bug and the new human disease.

sources.author: Coura, Jose Rodrigues
sources.venue: Revista da Sociedade Brasileira de Medicina Tropical
sources.confirms: Confirms the 1907 malaria assignment on the Central Railway, the first human case on 14 April 1909, and the 1909 publications.

sources.title: Instituto Oswaldo Cruz, 'Carlos Chagas', Fiocruz biography
sources.author: Fundacao Oswaldo Cruz
sources.confirms: Confirms the Lassance railway carriage, the December 1908 discovery in the bug, the naming after Oswaldo Cruz, and Berenice aged two on 14 April 1909.

picture.alt: Carlos Chagas at his bench in the Instituto Oswaldo Cruz
picture.credit: J. Pinto, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

bleriot-channel-flight-1909.summary: In July 1909 Blériot flew across the Channel in 36 minutes; Britain's sea moat no longer protected it from aircraft. He won Daily Mail's £1,000 prize for crossing by heavier-than-air aircraft. Some 10,000 people had gathered at Calais; he landed heavily in Northfall Meadow beside Dover Castle, breaking a propeller blade and damaging his undercarriage, but walked away unhurt and famous.

sources.title: Louis Blériot
National Air and Space Museum, 'Blériot XI', inventory A19500095000, collection record
sources.author: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.venue: National Air and Space Museum collection
sources.confirms: The museum's catalogue entry records that Louis Blériot flew a Type XI from Calais to Dover on 25 July 1909, covering 40 km in 36 minutes 30 seconds, the first aeroplane crossing of the Channel.

sources.title: Science Museum Group, 'Louis Charles Joseph Bleriot, 1872-1936', people record cp37014
sources.author: Science Museum Group
sources.confirms: The Science Museum's authority record states Blériot crossed the English Channel on 25 July 1909 in a heavier-than-air machine and links the surviving control mechanism of his monoplane.

picture.alt: Colour print by H. Delaspre showing Louis Blériot seated in his monoplane above the English Channel during his crossing on 25 July 1909.
picture.credit: H. Delaspre, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, No known copyright restrictions, via Library of Congress

forster-machine-stops-1909.summary: In 1909 E M Forster's The Machine Stops imagined people alone in cells, talking through screens, fed by a machine they worship. Humanity lives underground, each person in one cell, served by a giant Machine that provides everything and that people come to worship, until it fails and their society collapses with it. Forster wrote it to rebut H. G. Wells's A Modern Utopia of 1905, blaming technology rather than politics as humanity's controlling force; readers have since found instant messaging, social media and the Internet in it.

sources.title: The Machine Stops - Wikipedia
Forster's Other Cave
sources.author: Berman, Jeffrey
sources.confirms: Critical study of The Machine Stops (1909) as Forster's dystopia of isolated people served and finally failed by a worshipped Machine.

sources.title: The Machine Stops (1909)
sources.author: Forster, E. M.; Glenn, Joshua (ed.)
sources.venue: Voices from the Radium Age, MIT Press
sources.confirms: MIT Press scholarly reprint dating the story to 1909 and placing it among early science fiction.

picture.alt: Oil portrait of E. M. Forster painted by Roger Fry in 1911, two years after The Machine Stops
picture.credit: Roger Fry, 1911, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ehrlich-salvarsan-1910.summary: In 1910 Salvarsan, compound 606, went on sale as medicine's first modern antimicrobial agent; it cured syphilis. Paul Ehrlich had theorized that screening many compounds would turn up one that killed microbes without killing their host; his lab synthesized arsphenamine in 1907, and Sahachiro Hata found its effect on syphilis in 1909 while testing hundreds of arsenic compounds. Easier-to-prepare Neosalvarsan followed in 1912.

sources.title: Arsphenamine - Wikipedia
Williams, K. J., "The introduction of 'chemotherapy' using arsphenamine: the first magic bullet", Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 102, no. 8 (2009), pp. 343-348
sources.author: Williams, K. J.
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
sources.confirms: Reviews Ehrlich's screening programme, Hata's 1909 finding that compound 606 cured syphilis in rabbits, and Hoechst's marketing of Salvarsan in 1910 as the first synthetic antimicrobial drug.
sources.qualifies: Open access at PMC; confirmed from the article record.

sources.title: Bosch, Fèlix, and Laia Rosich, 'The Contributions of Paul Ehrlich to Pharmacology: A Tribute on the Occasion of the Centenary of His Nobel Prize', Pharmacology 82, no. 3 (2008), pp. 171-179
sources.author: Fèlix Bosch and Laia Rosich
sources.confirms: Describes Ehrlich's screening of arsenical compounds, Hata's 1909 finding on compound 606, and the 1910 introduction of Salvarsan against syphilis.

picture.alt: Manuscript sheet of chemical formulae in Paul Ehrlich's hand headed Salvarsanpraparate
picture.credit: Paul Ehrlich, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

taylor-scientific-management-1911.summary: In 1911 Frederick Taylor told managers to time and redesign every element of a job rather than leave method to workers. Its four principles were developing a science for each element of work, scientifically selecting and training workers, cooperating with them, and dividing responsibility between management and workers. Taylor, a mechanical engineer and former manufacturing manager, was by then consulting for industry; in 2001 the Academy of Management's Fellows voted it first among twentieth-century management books.

sources.title: The Principles of Scientific Management - Wikipedia
Taylor, Frederick Winslow, 'The principles of scientific management', Harper & Brothers (1911)
sources.author: Taylor, Frederick Winslow
sources.confirms: The page identifies the book as The principles of scientific management by Frederick Winslow Taylor and gives its publication date as 1911.
sources.qualifies: The source describes a special edition printed in February 1911 for confidential circulation among American Society of Mechanical Engineers members.

sources.title: Nelson, Daniel, 'Scientific Management, Systematic Management, and Labor, 1880-1915', Business History Review 48, no. 4 (1974): 479-500
sources.author: Nelson, Daniel
sources.confirms: Places Taylor's scientific management, and his 1911 book, within the systematic management movement and assesses its effect on labor through 1915.

picture.alt: Frederick Winslow Taylor in a 1911 photograph published in The World's Work, year of his Principles of Scientific Management
picture.credit: The World's Work, 1911, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

wu-lien-teh-manchurian-plague-1911.summary: Pneumonic plague spread from marmot hunters in Transbaikalia along new railways to Harbin in autumn 1910 and killed some 60,000 people across Manchuria within months. Qing government sent Wu Lien-teh, a Penang-born, Cambridge-trained physician, who performed an autopsy, identified airborne spread between people and ordered gauze-and-cotton masks for staff and public, isolation wagons, travel controls and, with imperial permission, cremation of frozen corpses in January 1911. Deaths ended by April. Wu chaired International Plague Conference in Mukden that year and led a Manchurian Plague Prevention Service until 1931. Christos Lynteris's study traces how Wu's mask became a template for epidemic protective equipment.

sources.title: Lynteris, Christos, 'Plague masks: the visual emergence of anti-epidemic personal protection equipment', Medical Anthropology 37 (2018)
sources.author: Lynteris, Christos
sources.confirms: Invention of anti-plague masks during 1910-11 Manchurian outbreak

sources.title: Summers, William C., The Great Manchurian Plague of 1910-1911: The Geopolitics of an Epidemic Disease (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Summers, William C.
sources.confirms: Course of epidemic, Wu Lien-teh's measures, Mukden conference

wu-lien-teh-manchurian-plague-1911.verification_note: Lynteris and Summers support this entry; death toll figures vary between 43,000 and 60,000.
wu-lien-teh-manchurian-plague-1911.detail: French physician Gerald Mesny, who dismissed airborne transmission and refused a mask, died of plague in Harbin, an episode that strengthened Wu's authority. William Summers's 2012 study sets outbreak within railway politics among China, Russia and Japan. Death tolls range from 43,000 to 60,000 across sources.

picture.alt: Anti-plague bureau at Fujiadian, Harbin, 1911, from a photograph album printed by Commercial Press
picture.credit: Harbin Fujiadian anti-plague photographs, Commercial Press (1911)

triangle-shirtwaist-fire-1911.summary: In 1911 a fire at the Triangle shirtwaist factory in New York killed 146 garment workers, 123 of them women and girls, behind locked doors. Exit doors had been locked to stop unauthorized breaks and theft, no sprinklers existed, and one flimsy fire escape collapsed, so many workers jumped from windows. New York's deadliest industrial disaster prompted legislation requiring improved factory safety standards.

sources.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire - Wikipedia
Kheel Center, Cornell University ILR School, 'Remembering the 1911 Triangle Factory Fire' (digital archive of primary sources)
sources.author: Kheel Center for Labor-Management Documentation and Archives
sources.confirms: Fire broke out on 25 March 1911 at the Triangle Waist Factory and 146 people were dead within 18 minutes; the site holds the original trial and investigation records.

sources.title: New York State Factory Investigating Commission, Preliminary Report, vol. 1 (Albany: Argus, 1912), digitised on the Internet Archive
sources.author: New York State Factory Investigating Commission (R. F. Wagner, chair)
sources.confirms: The commission created after the fire reported in 1912 on factory fire hazards, the basis for New York's safety laws.

picture.alt: Asch Building at Washington Place, New York, photographed by Bain News Service in March 1911 after the Triangle Shirtwaist Company fire that killed 146 workers.
picture.credit: Bain News Service, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, No known copyright restrictions, via Library of Congress

baro-kano-railway-1911.summary: Northern Nigeria's government built a 3 ft 6 in gauge line from Baro on Niger's bank to Kano, authorised in August 1907 and laid largely by Nigerian labour, about 15,000 workers at peak in early 1910. Railhead reached Zaria in January 1911 and Kano on 28 March 1911, 366 miles from Baro, at roughly £3,500 a mile. British planners expected cotton; instead Hausa farmers and Kano merchants shipped groundnuts, whose exports leapt from a few thousand tons to a cash crop that defined northern Nigeria's economy, as Jan Hogendorn documented. This line linked Kano's old caravan trade to Lagos and Atlantic shipping.

sources.title: Colonial Office, Northern Nigeria: Report for 1910-11, Colonial Reports Annual No. 704 (HMSO, 1912)
sources.author: Colonial Office
sources.venue: Colonial Reports Annual, University of Illinois digital collection
sources.confirms: Railhead at Zaria 20 January and first train into Kano 29 March 1911 (appendix gives 25 January and 28 March); 366 miles from Baro; cost roughly £3,500 per mile; groundnut exports via Idah £8,150 in 1910-11

sources.title: Mance, H. O., 'Baro-Kano Railway Construction', Royal Engineers Journal (April 1911)
sources.author: Mance, H. O.
sources.confirms: Construction authorised August 1907; 3 ft 6 in gauge recommended by Girouard; about 15,000 Nigerian workers employed January to March 1910; earthworks £200-£340 per mile

sources.title: Kwalam, Ibrahim Shua'ibu, 'The Impact of the Railway on Ringim from 1930 to 1972', MA dissertation, Bayero University Kano (2017), reviewing Hogendorn, Nigerian Groundnut Exports (1978)
sources.author: Kwalam, Ibrahim Shua'ibu
sources.venue: Bayero University Kano, Department of History
sources.confirms: Baro-Kano railway built 1908-1911; its completion stimulated groundnut exports from Kano rather than cotton, with booms in 1912-1914; Hogendorn stresses Hausa traders' role
sources.qualifies: Hogendorn's book is known here through this dissertation's literature review, not opened directly

baro-kano-railway-1911.verification_note: Covering letter of that Colonial Report gives 29 March 1911 for Kano; its railway appendix gives 28 March, used here.
baro-kano-railway-1911.detail: Captain H. O. Mance's account in Royal Engineers Journal gives earthwork costs of £200 to £340 a mile and describes plate-laying gangs of hundreds. A 1910-11 Colonial Report lists groundnut exports via Idah worth £8,150 before its effect showed. Hogendorn argued that Hausa traders and farmers, not colonial officials, chose groundnuts because prices and local credit networks favoured them. Kano's groundnut pyramids became an emblem of northern Nigeria until the 1970s.

picture.alt: Baro-Kano Railway 4-8-0 locomotive Emir of Bida, built for Northern Nigeria's 3 ft 6 in gauge line
picture.credit: Unknown author

kamerlingh-onnes-superconductivity-1911.summary: In 1911 Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury near absolute zero lost all electrical resistance, superconductivity, now used in MRI scanners. At 4.2 K he observed its resistance abruptly disappear. An ordinary metal's resistance falls gradually as it cools; a superconductor's drops to exactly zero, and it expels magnetic fields, behavior only quantum mechanics could later explain.

sources.title: Superconductivity
Dahl, Per F., "Kamerlingh Onnes and the Discovery of Superconductivity: The Leyden Years, 1911-1914"
sources.author: Per F. Dahl
sources.venue: Historical Studies in the Physical Sciences 15 (1), pp. 1-37
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed history of the April 1911 mercury measurements at Leiden in which resistance vanished near 4.2 K; JSTOR record confirmed title, journal and pages.

sources.author: Dirk van Delft
sources.confirms: Centenary article using the Leiden laboratory notebooks to reconstruct the 8 April 1911 experiment; Crossref record confirmed, page text not read.

picture.alt: Undated portrait photograph of Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, the Leiden physicist who found superconductivity in mercury in 1911.
picture.credit: Nationaal Archief, Public domain, via Europeana

rutherford-nucleus-1911.summary: In 1911 Rutherford proposed that an atom is mostly empty space around a tiny nucleus: nuclear physics began. He was interpreting experiments by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden in 1908 and 1910, in which alpha particles bounced off gold atoms far more sharply than J. J. Thomson's plum pudding model, with positive charge spread through whole atoms, could explain. That central region was later known as the atomic nucleus, though Rutherford did not use that term in his paper.

sources.title: Rutherford model - Wikipedia
Rutherford, E., 'The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom', Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911) 669-688
sources.author: Rutherford, E.
sources.confirms: Rutherford's 1911 paper deriving a concentrated central charge in the atom from alpha-particle scattering.

sources.title: Heilbron, J. L., 'The scattering of α and β particles and Rutherford's atom', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 4, no. 4 (1968): 247-307
sources.author: J. L. Heilbron
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: The standard historical study of the Geiger-Marsden scattering work and Rutherford's 1911 nuclear model; Springer page confirms title, volume and pages.

picture.alt: Portrait of Ernest Rutherford from Bain News Service glass negative, 1900s to 1910s
picture.credit: Bain News Service, No known restrictions on publication, via Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons

standard-oil-breakup-1911.summary: In 1911 America's Supreme Court broke Standard Oil into 34 companies, the first great monopoly dismantled under antitrust law. Standard had controlled US oil refining since the 1870s; Justice Department lawyers sued in 1906. On 15 May its decree separated 33 subsidiaries from their parent, 34 companies in all, while holding that only contracts restraining trade 'unduly' offended antitrust law, its 'rule of reason'; its largest descendants today are ExxonMobil and Chevron.

sources.title: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States - Wikipedia
Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)
sources.author: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.confirms: Decided 15 May 1911, the Court held the Standard Oil combination an unreasonable restraint of trade under the Sherman Act and affirmed the decree dissolving it.

sources.title: U.S. Reports: Standard Oil Co. v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (October Term 1910), Library of Congress
sources.author: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.confirms: The official report of the case in volume 221 of the United States Reports.

picture.credit: Udo J. Keppler, Puck, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, No known copyright restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons mirror

abadan-refinery-opens-1912.summary: After oil was struck at Masjed Soleyman in May 1908, Anglo-Persian Oil Company leased a square mile of Abadan island from Shaikh Khazal of Mohammerah in 1909 and shipped sixty miles of six-inch pipe from America to carry crude down to tidewater. Indian fitters and clerks, Chinese carpenters and Arab and Persian labourers built stills and tanks beside the Shatt al-Arab, and refining began in 1912 at about 2,400 barrels a day, 120,000 tons a year, though early runs broke down and product quality was poor. Britain's Admiralty bought a controlling stake in 1914 to fuel its oil-burning fleet, and capacity rose to a million tons by 1918, five million by 1930 and ten million by 1939, making Abadan the largest refinery anywhere and a company town of segregated bungalows and workers' lines whose strikes shaped Iranian politics.

sources.title: Ferrier, R. W., The History of the British Petroleum Company, vol. 1: The Developing Years 1901-1932 (Cambridge University Press, 1982)
sources.author: Ferrier, Ronald W.
sources.confirms: Abadan lease, pipeline, refinery construction and the troubled start of 1912.

sources.author: Encyclopaedia Iranica

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Abadan ii. Modern Abadan'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.confirms: APOC bought one square mile from Shaikh Khazal; refinery opened 1912 with 120,000 tons annual capacity, rising to 1 million in 1918, 5 million in 1930, 10 million in 1939; world's largest.

abadan-refinery-opens-1912.verification_note: Sources differ on whether first oil flowed in August or October 1912 and whether full operation came in 1913; all agree this refinery opened in 1912.

picture.alt: Abadan refinery, Iran
picture.credit: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

torres-quevedo-ajedrecista-1912.summary: In 1912 Leonardo Torres Quevedo built a machine that played a chess endgame against any human and won, with no hidden operator. It played a simplified endgame of white king and rook against black king, enforcing its rules mechanically and electromechanically with no hidden human, unlike earlier so-called automatons such as the Mechanical Turk. First demonstrated in 1913 and exhibited in Paris in 1914, it anticipated software chess programs by decades and was a precursor of computer chess.

sources.author: Marsh, Allison
sources.confirms: In 1912 Torres Quevedo built a chess-playing automaton that played king and rook against a human's lone king, with an algorithm that guaranteed a win, and upgraded it around 1920 with electromagnets under the board.

picture.alt: El Ajedrecista, Torres Quevedo's electromechanical chess endgame machine, with its board and mechanism, photographed in Madrid in 2013
picture.credit: Olea, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

wegener-continental-drift-1912.summary: In January 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that continents had once formed a single landmass, Pangaea, before breaking apart and drifting to their present locations; he expanded it into a book in 1915. Geologists largely rejected continental drift into the 1950s, partly because no plausible driving force was known; Wegener did not live to see it validated and absorbed into plate tectonics.

Alfred Wegener

sources.confirms: Wegener presented continental drift in lectures in 1912 and in Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane in 1915; the idea was widely rejected until the 1960s.

sources.author: Wegener, Alfred
sources.confirms: Wegener's first published statement of continental displacement, 1912, following his January 1912 lectures.

titanic-sinking-1912.summary: In April 1912 the Titanic, called unsinkable, hit an iceberg and 1,500 died for want of lifeboats; maritime law changed within two years. Watertight compartments and remotely closed watertight doors had given the White Star liner its 'unsinkable' reputation; under accepted practice, which treated lifeboats as ferries to nearby rescue ships, it carried boats for only about half of those aboard.

Report on the Loss of the S.S. Titanic (British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry)

sources.venue: HMSO, London; digitised by the Titanic Inquiry Project
sources.confirms: The official 1912 inquiry report records the collision with an iceberg on 14 April 1912, the loss of about 1,500 lives, lifeboat capacity for roughly half of those aboard, and recommendations on boats for all.

sources.title: International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), 1974
sources.author: International Maritime Organization
sources.confirms: The first SOLAS convention was adopted in 1914 in response to the Titanic disaster.

picture.alt: Titanic survivors in a crowded lifeboat rowing toward rescue ship Carpathia on 15 April 1912
picture.credit: Bain News Service, No known restrictions on publication, via Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons

radio-act-1912-1912.summary: In 1912 America required licences for radio transmitters. US radio had gone largely unregulated since the late 1890s, even after 1906's Berlin convention called for licensing; Titanic's sinking that April gave licensing new urgency. Radio then meant point-to-point maritime, transoceanic and amateur stations, and it proved inadequate once public broadcasting began.

sources.venue: United States Statutes at Large, vol. 37
sources.confirms: The statute, approved 13 August 1912, requires any person, company or corporation operating radio apparatus for interstate or foreign commerce to hold a licence from the Secretary of Commerce and Labor.

sources.confirms: Links the Titanic sinking of April 1912 to passage of the Radio Act that August.

haber-bosch-1913.summary: In 1913 BASF began making ammonia from air at factory scale; fertiliser lifted limits on how many could eat. Carl Bosch had scaled up Fritz Haber's 1909 laboratory process, Bosch's team, Alwin Mittasch prominent in it, had found a cheap iron catalyst still used today, and the Oppau plant reached 20 tonnes a day in 1914. Its ammonia fed nitrogen fertiliser and, once the First World War cut Germany off from Chilean nitrate, explosives.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Haber process

sources.author: Erisman, J.; Sutton, M.; Galloway, J.
sources.confirms: The page says that a century after Haber filed his 1908 patent, the world was transformed by and highly dependent on Haber-Bosch nitrogen.

ramanujan-hardy-letter-1913.summary: In 1913 a Madras clerk, Ramanujan, mailed Hardy pages of theorems; Hardy brought him to Cambridge, and his notebooks still yield results. Self-taught and working as a clerk in Madras, Ramanujan had failed to interest most professional mathematicians in results too novel and oddly presented for them. Hardy recognized his work as extraordinary and arranged for him to come to Cambridge; Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918, compiled nearly 3,900 results in his life, and died in India in 1920 aged 32.

sources.author: G. H. Hardy
sources.confirms: Hardy's first-hand published account of Ramanujan, the recipient of the 1913 letter.

picture.credit: Trinity College Library, Cambridge, Add. MS a.94.7, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

raja-harishchandra-phalke-1913.summary: Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, a trained lithographer and photographer, shot Raja Harishchandra over several months in Bombay and Nashik area and showed it at Coronation Cinematograph on 3 May 1913. He imported a Williamson camera and raw film from London, processed and printed footage himself and trained actors and technicians. Male actors played women's roles. He followed with Mohini Bhasmasur and Satyavan Savitri and set up Hindustan Film Company at Nashik in 1917. His choice of Puranic stories defined a mythological genre and his vertically integrated studio was template for Indian film industry, now largest in world by output.

sources.title: M. Sadiqur Rahman, 'Early Glocalization in Indian Cinema: An Analysis of Films of Dada Saheb Phalke and Himanshu Rai', Asiatische Studien 73 (2019)
sources.author: M. Sadiqur Rahman

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Dadasaheb Phalke'

raja-harishchandra-phalke-1913.verification_note: Rahman article confirmed through open access ZORA record; Britannica for exact date. Torne priority claim noted.

Some scholars argue Dadasaheb Torne's Shree Pundalik of 1912 deserves priority; it is generally treated as filmed stage play.

picture.credit: Dadasaheb Phalke

ford-assembly-line-1913.summary: In 1913 Ford's moving assembly line cut car build time from 12½ hours to 93 minutes: mass production. Ford's William Klann had brought that idea back from Swift & Company's Chicago slaughterhouse, where carcasses moved along a conveyor past butchers who each repeated one cut. It divided assembly into 45 steps and kept evolving through time and motion study.

sources.author: David A. Hounshell
sources.confirms: University-press monograph documenting the moving assembly lines at Highland Park from April 1913 and the fall in chassis assembly labour time from about 12.5 hours to 93 minutes.
sources.qualifies: The 93-minute chassis figure dates from spring 1914, after the line was raised and paced; 1913 saw the first moving sub-assembly lines, starting with the flywheel magneto in April.

sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed review confirming the book's standing as the standard account of Ford's Highland Park production system.

kingsbury-commitment-1913.summary: In 1913 AT&T agreed to connect rival phone companies and sell its Western Union stake to avoid being broken up: a regulated monopoly. Facing a government antitrust investigation, the company had spent months negotiating; president Theodore Vail wanted one unified telephone system, and its refusal to connect rivals to its long-distance network, by far the nation's finest, had alarmed regulators. The commitment came as a letter from Vice President Nathan Kingsbury and did not require AT&T to interconnect its local services with other local providers.

sources.author: Mueller, Milton L.

picture.credit: Harris and Ewing Collection, Library of Congress, No known restrictions on publication, via Library of Congress

federal-reserve-act-1913.summary: In December 1913 America created the Federal Reserve, a central bank to stop bank panics that had recurred every generation. America had gone nearly 80 years without a central bank, and 1907's panic had persuaded many that banking and currency needed reform. Introduced by Wilson, Congressman Carter Glass and Senator Robert Latham Owen, it created the Federal Reserve System: twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks that manage money supply, lend to banks, oversee them and serve as lender of last resort, under a seven-member Federal Reserve Board.

ford-five-dollar-day-1914.summary: In January 1914 Ford doubled his workers' pay to $5 a day; turnover fell and his workers could afford his cars. Ford said he meant to end turnover so heavy that some departments hired 300 men a year to fill 100 jobs, though Raff reads it as rent-sharing under union threat; the move proved profitable, forced Detroit competitors to raise wages, and came with conditions policed by a Social Department that frowned on drinking and gambling.

sources.title: Henry Ford
Raff, Daniel M. G. and Lawrence H. Summers, 'Did Henry Ford Pay Efficiency Wages?', Journal of Labor Economics 5:4 pt 2 (1987), S57-S86
sources.author: Raff, Daniel M. G.; Summers, Lawrence H.
sources.confirms: Ford introduced the five-dollar day in 1914 most plausibly in response to labour problems such as turnover; it produced queues for Ford jobs and rises in productivity and profits.

sources.title: Raff, Daniel M. G., 'Wage Determination Theory and the Five-Dollar Day at Ford', Journal of Economic History 48, no. 2 (1988): 387-399
sources.author: Raff, Daniel M. G.
sources.confirms: Examines Ford's five-dollar day of 1914, a wage well above the opportunity cost of the labor employed, and its link to the technical change at Highland Park.
sources.qualifies: Argues that efficiency-wage explanations such as cutting turnover are implausible and that the wage was rent-sharing driven by the threat of collective action.

ford-five-dollar-day-1914.verification_note: Raff (1988) confirms a January 1914 five-dollar day but judges a turnover explanation implausible, reading this wage as rent-sharing under threat of labor organization.

picture.credit: Ford Motor Company, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activated-sludge-1914.summary: At Manchester Corporation's Davyhulme works, chemists Edward Ardern and William Lockett, under Gilbert Fowler, bubbled air through sewage in 80-ounce bottles in 1913 and, instead of discarding settled solids, kept them for each new batch. After five weeks of recycling, a batch cleared in 24 hours instead of weeks. On 3 April 1914 they read "Experiments on the oxidation of sewage without the aid of filters" to the Society of Chemical Industry at Manchester's Grand Hotel, naming those solids "activated sludge". Worcester built the first full plant in 1916 and Davyhulme ran one million gallons a day by 1921. Patents by Jones and Attwood slowed uptake in Britain while American cities such as Milwaukee adopted it; it remains standard at urban treatment plants worldwide.

panama-canal-1914.summary: In 1914 the Panama Canal opened, cutting 13,000 kilometres between America's coasts; 27,000 workers had died. France had begun digging in 1881 and gone bankrupt in 1889 after engineering failures and an estimated 22,000 deaths from disease and accidents. America took over in 1904; Colonel William Gorgas's campaign against mosquitoes nearly eliminated yellow fever and malaria, though about 5,600 workers, mostly West Indian labourers, still died.

sources.author: Sutter, Paul S.

picture.credit: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, No known restrictions on publication, via Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons

agote-citrated-blood-transfusion-1914.summary: On 9 November 1914 Luis Agote, director of Instituto Modelo de Clínica Médica at Hospital Rawson in Buenos Aires, transfused 300 millilitres of blood mixed with sodium citrate from hospital porter Ramón Mosquera into a patient, with press photographers present. Citrate stopped clotting, so blood no longer had to pass directly from donor vein to recipient vein. Agote cabled his results to European governments at war and published them in Anales del Instituto Modelo in January 1915. Albert Hustin in Brussels had used citrate in March 1914 and Richard Lewisohn in New York set safe doses in 1915; Agote's demonstration drew publicity none of them had. Citrated, refrigerated blood made blood banks possible within two decades.

sources.title: Lefrère, Jean-Jacques; Danic, Bruno, 'A historic picture: the first transfusion of citrated blood', Transfusion 51 (2011)
sources.author: Lefrère, Jean-Jacques; Danic, Bruno
sources.confirms: Date of 9 November 1914, Hospital Rawson setting and photographic record.

sources.author: Mollison, P. L.
sources.confirms: Priority of Hustin, Agote and Lewisohn and significance of citrate for stored blood.

agote-citrated-blood-transfusion-1914.verification_note: Hustin's March 1914 transfusion predates Agote's; sources disagree over whether Agote knew of it. Lewisohn's 1915 work fixed the citrate dose that made the method safe.
agote-citrated-blood-transfusion-1914.detail: Lefrère and Danic's 2011 note in Transfusion reproduces a staged photograph of this procedure. Mollison's 2000 history in British Journal of Haematology weighs priority among Hustin, Agote and Lewisohn and notes Agote's claim to independence. Agote, also a national deputy, later campaigned on child welfare law.

picture.alt: Staged photograph of Luis Agote's citrated blood transfusion at Hospital Rawson, Buenos Aires, 1914
picture.credit: Unknown photographer, via Wikimedia Commons

second-ypres-chlorine-gas-1915.summary: In April 1915 Germany released 168 tons of chlorine along four miles of front at Ypres, the first mass use of poison gas. Chemist Fritz Haber had proposed heavier-than-air chlorine in place of tear gas and supervised installation of 5,730 cylinders. French troops in its path suffered 2,000 to 3,000 casualties and fled, opening a 6-kilometre gap in Allied lines, but German infantry dug in rather than advance on Ypres; Canadian troops identified chlorine by its smell and held their flank.

sources.title: Second Battle of Ypres - Wikipedia

sources.author: Fitzgerald, Gerard J.
sources.confirms: Describes the 22 April 1915 German chlorine cloud attack at Ypres, organised by Fritz Haber, as the first large-scale use of a weapon of mass destruction, and the medical response.

picture.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

chuquicamata-mine-1915.summary: In May 1915 the Guggenheims opened Chuquicamata, 2,850 metres up in Chile's Atacama near Calama, with a leaching plant planned to yield 50,000 tons of electrolytic copper a year; output reached 4,345 tonnes in its first year. Anaconda Copper bought it in 1923, Chile nationalized its copper around 1971 and state company Codelco now runs what is described as the world’s largest open pit by excavated volume.

einstein-general-relativity-1915.summary: In November 1915 Einstein submitted general relativity's field equations, published on 2 December, gravity as curvature of space and time by mass; a 1919 eclipse expedition confirmed its predicted light deflection. It explained Mercury's anomalous orbit without any fudge factors; GPS satellites correct for its effects today.

picture.credit: Henri Manuel, Public domain, via Wellcome Collection

sarnoff-radio-music-box-1916.summary: In 1916, by his own later account, David Sarnoff proposed a radio music box for homes, point-to-mass when radio was seen as point-to-point; Louise Benjamin dates that memo to 1920. He said Nally deferred it during World War I, and he revived it in 1920 at RCA.

sources.title: David Sarnoff
Britannica Money

sources.author: Benjamin, Louise M.
sources.venue: Journal of Broadcasting and Electronic Media
sources.confirms: Abstract: new evidence suggests the oft-cited Radio Music Box memo was written in 1920, not 1915, when broadcasting was already around the corner, so historians must revise their assessment of Sarnoff's early contributions.
sources.qualifies: Benjamin dates the memo to 1920 and treats the 1915 (or 1916) claim as Sarnoff's later self-presentation.

sarnoff-radio-music-box-1916.verification_note: Benjamin (1993) finds Sarnoff's Radio Music Box memo as cited was written in 1920; a 1916 date comes from his own later account, and no contemporaneous memo is known.

sonar-langevin-1916.summary: In 1916 Paul Langevin patented an ultrasonic submarine detector using quartz crystals as U-boats sank Allied ships. One design used electrostatics, another thin quartz crystals that vibrate under voltage, drawing on piezoelectricity, which Langevin's teacher Pierre Curie had found; each timed its signal's round trip to calculate submarine distance. An operational active system had been built by 1918, as World War I ended.

sources.title: Paul Langevin
Kane, D.; Grassi, W.; Sturrock, R.; Balint, P. V., 'A brief history of musculoskeletal ultrasound: ‘From bats and ships to babies and hips’', Rheumatology (2004)
sources.author: Kane, D.; Grassi, W.; Sturrock, R.; Balint, P. V.
sources.confirms: The page says Paul Langevin and Constantin Chilowsky constructed an underwater sound generator using quartz crystals and two steel plates, considered a prototype of modern ultrasound devices, and that the first recorded detection and subsequent sinking of a German U-boat using a hydrophone occurred on 23 April 1916.
sources.qualifies: It dates Fessenden’s patent to 1912 and the first sonar apparatus to 1914, rather than dating Langevin’s patent to 1916.

sources.author: Editors, Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says an early passive system was used to detect submarines by 1916, an operational active system had been built by British and U.S. scientists by 1918, and sonar transducers can use piezoelectric crystals such as quartz.
sources.qualifies: It says an operational active system had been built by 1918, rather than only after World War I ended.

sonar-langevin-1916.verification_note: Kane et al. (2004) date Fessenden's patent to 1912, a first sonar apparatus to 1914 and a U-boat detection in 1916; Britannica says an operational active system existed by 1918.

tank-somme-1916.summary: In September 1916 British tanks first crossed trenches at the Somme. Britain and France had developed tanks separately to break trench warfare's deadlock on Europe's Western Front. Mark I grew from Little Willie, William Foster & Co.'s 1915 prototype built in Lincoln; for secrecy its hulls were described in shop orders as water carriers, hence tanks.

sources.author: Robin Prior; Trevor Wilson

sources.confirms: Forty-nine Mark I tanks were earmarked for the first tank attack on 15 September 1916, and eighteen went into action.

addis-djibouti-railway-1917.summary: In 1917 Djibouti's railway reached Addis Ababa after 20 years of building; Ethiopia had a link to the sea it did not own. Begun in 1897, a year after Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa, its single meter-gauge track stretched 784 km and replaced six weeks of camel and mule caravan from Djibouti. It gave landlocked Ethiopia its only access to the sea, and towns grew along its line as trade expanded.

A. Mehretu, 'Ethiopia: Economy', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Assefa Mehretu
sources.confirms: The Djibouti to Addis Ababa railway was built between 1897 and 1917 by a French company.

sources.author: Bar-David, Sharon; Schler, Lynn

fordson-tractor-1917.summary: Henry Ford and Son, organized 27 July 1917 in Dearborn, ships its first Fordson Model F tractor on 6 October 1917 against a British government order for 7,000 to replace horses and farmhands lost to war; 254 leave by year end and 6,000 plus 1,000 in parts by April 1918. Its frameless design uses engine and transmission castings as chassis, weighs about 1,230 kilograms and costs 750 dollars, falling to 395 dollars in a 1922 price war with International Harvester. Fordson number 100,000 rolls out on 21 February 1920; about 740,000 are built in the United States by 1928. Olmstead and Rhode's 2001 study finds tractor diffusion across American farms was more rapid than historians had thought, even as horses and tractors coexisted for decades.

sources.title: Olmstead, A. L. and Rhode, P. W., 'Reshaping the Landscape: The Impact and Diffusion of the Tractor in American Agriculture, 1910-1960', Journal of Economic History 61 (2001), 663-698
sources.author: Olmstead, Alan L.; Rhode, Paul W.
sources.confirms: Analyzes the tractor's impact on rural America 1910 to 1960 and finds diffusion faster than generally thought, with long coexistence of horses and tractors.

sources.author: Museums Victoria

sources.title: Farm Collector, 'Early history of Fordson tractors'
sources.author: Farm Collector

fordson-tractor-1917.detail: Fordson's faults were serious: its worm-drive rear end ran hot, its light front end reared over if a plow snagged, killing drivers, and there was no power take-off. Farmall of 1924 and Ferguson's three-point hitch answered those. Cork, Ireland production ran from 1919 and Soviet plants built licensed copies. Within three decades tractors freed cropland once devoted to feeding draft animals for food crops. Olmstead and Rhode count tractors replacing some 23 million draft animals in the United States by 1960.

picture.credit: Père Igor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

radium-girls-1917.summary: From 1917 women painting watch dials with radium were told to lick their brushes; their deaths won workers the right to sue employers. They had been told to point their brushes on their lips, because rags or water rinses wasted time and paint, and that it was harmless. Workers in Illinois and Connecticut faced similar exposure in the 1920s; by 1927 more than 50 had died, five New Jersey women won a settlement in 1928, and their cases helped establish occupational disease labor law.

sundback-zipper-1917.summary: On 20 March 1917 Swedish-born engineer Gideon Sundback, working for Hookless Fastener Company in Meadville, Pennsylvania, receives US patent 1,219,881 for a Separable Fastener: rows of cupped metal teeth on cloth tapes that a slider meshes and parts. Whitcomb Judson had shown a clumsy clasp locker at Chicago's 1893 fair; Sundback's Hookless No. 2, on sale from 1914, stayed shut and could be made by machine, a first. US Army flying suits and money belts used it; B. F. Goodrich named it the zipper in 1923 for its rubber galoshes, and clothing adopted it in the 1930s. Sundback also designed machines that stamped and set its teeth.

spanish-flu-1918.summary: Between 1918 and 1920 influenza infected about 500 million people, a third of humanity, and killed between 17 million and 50 million by competing estimates, some running to 100 million. It was caused by an H1N1 subtype of influenza A and broke out as the First World War ended; wartime censors suppressed bad news while newspapers in neutral Spain reported freely, so it was misnamed Spanish flu. Unlike most influenza, it killed young adults at unusually high rates, with its deadliest wave from late August 1918.

shu-zhendong-chinese-typewriter-1919.summary: Engineer Shu Zhendong, working at Commercial Press in Shanghai, refined a design by MIT-trained Zhou Houkun into a machine with a tray bed of about 2,500 common-usage characters in metal type, picked one at a time by a lever that lifted and struck each slug against paper. Commercial Press put Shu-style typewriters into production around 1919 and sold them to banks, government offices and newspapers through 1920s and 1930s. Thomas Mullaney's research shows how typists rearranged tray beds by frequency and adjacency, an early form of predictive text that continued under Maoist offices and anticipated input methods for Chinese computing.

Rival common-usage and combinatory designs failed commercially. Mullaney's 2012 article and 2017 book document production, training schools and tray-bed layouts.

great-molasses-flood-1919.summary: In January 1919 a tank in Boston burst and a wave of molasses killed 21 people; the court case made companies answer for their engineering. Holding 2.3 million US gallons, about 13,000 short tons, it loosed a wave 25 feet high moving at an estimated 35 miles per hour; 21 people died and about 150 were injured. It had been poorly built, insufficiently tested and leaking since 1915. 119 residents brought one of Massachusetts' first class-action suits against owner United States Industrial Alcohol, which was found responsible, a milestone in modern corporate regulation.

alcock-brown-transatlantic-1919.summary: In June 1919 Alcock and Brown made history's first nonstop transatlantic flight, 1,890 miles in 15 hours 57 minutes, eight years before Lindbergh, carrying nearly 200 letters, its first airmail. Winston Churchill presented them Daily Mail's £10,000 prize for crossing in under 72 hours, and King George V knighted them a week later.

scadta-colombia-airmail-1919.summary: On 5 December 1919 Colombian and German investors in Barranquilla founded Sociedad Colombo-Alemana de Transportes Aéreos. From 1920 its Junkers F 13 floatplanes, flown by German pilots such as Hellmuth von Krohn and managed by Austrian Peter Paul von Bauer, carried mail and passengers along Magdalena river between Barranquilla and Girardot, cutting a journey of a week or more by steamer to a few hours. SCADTA built its own airfields and radio stations, printed its own stamps under a government concession, and extended routes to Bogotá, Medellín and Ecuador. Pan American Airways secretly bought control in 1931; SCADTA merged into Avianca in 1940, and Avianca counts among airlines with longest continuous operation anywhere.

scadta-colombia-airmail-1919.detail: Colombia's mountains and rivers made aviation pay earlier than in flatter countries; Magdalena steamers formed Bogotá's main artery and steamers were slow and seasonal. US fears of German influence near Panama's canal shaped diplomacy over SCADTA, described in Stephen Randall's study of Colombian-American relations. A 2020 Banco de la República volume documents fleet, routes and 1919 to 1925 'grandes hazañas'.

saha-ionization-equation-1920.summary: Working at University College of Science in Calcutta, Meghnad Saha applied thermodynamics and quantum theory to gas ionisation and published in 1920 an equation relating degree of ionisation to temperature and pressure. Applied to Sun and stars, it explained why spectral lines of different elements appear at different temperatures, turning Harvard's spectral sequence into a temperature scale. Astrophysicists including Fowler, Milne and Payne built on it to measure stellar temperatures and composition. Saha later founded Institute of Nuclear Physics in Calcutta, promoted river planning and sat in parliament. His equation remains basic to plasma physics and astrophysics.

we-zamyatin-1920.summary: In 1920 Zamyatin's We imagined a glass city where its state watches everyone and numbers replace names, Orwell's model for 1984. It depicts the OneState, an urban nation built almost entirely of glass for surveillance and run on Frederick Winslow Taylor's principles of scientific management, where citizens' lives are controlled and its protagonist, spacecraft engineer D-503, rebels. First published in English translation in New York in 1924, it did not appear in Soviet Russia until 1988; George Orwell said Brave New World must partly derive from it and acknowledged its influence on Nineteen Eighty-Four.

argentina-radio-broadcast-parsifal-1920.summary: On 27 August 1920, after dark, Enrique Telémaco Susini, César Guerrico, Luis Romero Carranza and Miguel Mujica, medical students and radio amateurs later called 'los locos de la azotea', used a five-watt transmitter and a war-surplus Telefunken valve on Teatro Coliseo's roof to broadcast a performance of Parsifal to a few dozen receivers in Buenos Aires. They continued nightly with opera and concerts, forming Radio Argentina, and sold receivers through a company they founded. Within a decade Buenos Aires had more than a dozen stations, tango orchestras and radio theatre, and by 1930 Argentina counted among highest radio ownership rates outside North America. Andrea Matallana's study traces how Argentine governments regulated this new medium from 1920 to 1946.

sources.title: Matallana, Andrea, 'Entre el mercado y el Estado: primeros pasos de la radiodifusión en Argentina (1920-1946)', Dixit 39 (2025)
sources.author: Matallana, Andrea
sources.confirms: The 1920 Coliseo broadcast and early regulation and growth of Argentine radio.

sources.confirms: Claxton's account of the Parsifal broadcast and the industry's growth to the 1940s.

argentina-radio-broadcast-parsifal-1920.verification_note: Claims that this was the world's first regular broadcast are contested; Dutch (PCGG, 1919) and US experimental stations preceded it. Transmitter power figures range from 5 to 15 watts across accounts.
argentina-radio-broadcast-parsifal-1920.detail: Argentine accounts describe this Coliseo transmission as a scheduled broadcasting service predating KDKA's election broadcast in Pittsburgh by two months; that claim rests on continuity of nightly programming rather than on any earliest transmission of speech or music. Robert Claxton's From Parsifal to Perón follows Argentine radio through commercial networks to Perón's use of radio. Susini later directed films and founded Argentina's first television station in 1951.

picture.credit: Unknown photographer, via Wikimedia Commons

kdka-broadcast-1920.summary: On 2 November 1920 Westinghouse broadcast election results by radio from Pittsburgh: one voice in many homes. Publicity staffer Leo Rosenberg was the announcer. The broadcast used a temporary 8ZZ call sign, its “special amateur” grant allowing frequencies away from crowded 200-meter amateur bands, and included music between election updates. Newspapers reported returns that came through clear and distinct, and this station, licensed as KDKA, is counted by many historians as America's first commercially licensed broadcaster.

kdka-first-broadcast-1920.summary: In November 1920 Pittsburgh's KDKA broadcast election returns to about 1,000 listeners, starting scheduled radio broadcasting. Westinghouse engineer Frank Conrad had been broadcasting from his home station 8XK, and stood by to take over if Westinghouse's East Pittsburgh transmitter failed. Using temporary call sign 8ZZ, it is often called the first broadcast by a commercially licensed station, though other stations also aired returns that night; KDKA gained national prominence once it offered regular programming.

lenin-electrification-1920.summary: In December 1920 Lenin defined communism as Soviet power plus electrification of the whole country. His line made electrification an emblem of Bolshevik plans for recovery after civil war; Lenin argued only electricity could lift Russia out of being a small-peasant country.

soviet-goelro-plan-1920.summary: In 1920 Russia's GOELRO plan set out to electrify Russia, history's first national economic plan and a template for Soviet five-year plans. Drawn up by electrical engineers on a commission chaired by Gleb Krzhizhanovsky, championed by Lenin and approved by the Communist Party in December 1920, it aimed to restructure the Soviet economy through nationwide electrification. It called for 30 regional power plants, including ten large hydroelectric stations, to raise annual output to 8.8 billion kWh from Imperial Russia's 1.9 billion in 1913; that goal was reached in 1931, and GOELRO became Gosplan's prototype for its Five-Year Plans.

banting-best-insulin-1921.summary: In 1921 Banting and Best isolated insulin, and diabetes stopped being a death sentence. On 30 July 1921 their extract from a duct-tied dog's islets lowered a diabetic dog's blood sugar. Biochemist James Collip purified it, and on 11 January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old dying of diabetes at Toronto General Hospital, received the first injection; purer doses from 23 January cleared his symptoms. Eli Lilly began large-scale production that year, and Banting and Macleod shared their 1923 Nobel Prize money with Best and Collip.

poj-2878-sugarcane-1921.summary: At Proefstation Oost-Java in Pasuruan, breeders led by Jacob Jeswiet crossed noble sugarcane with wild Saccharum spontaneum through a hybrid called Kassoer, a process he named nobilisation, to carry resistance to sereh and mosaic diseases that were ruining Java's estates. From 2,266 seedlings of a 1921 cross between POJ 2364 and EK 28, Jeswiet selected POJ 2878, which was tested and released in 1925. Within a decade it covered most of Java's cane land, lifted sugar yields and was planted from India to Louisiana and Brazil. Most commercial canes bred since carry it in their pedigrees, which earned it name 'wonder cane of world'.

urea-stibamine-brahmachari-1922.summary: Physician Upendranath Brahmachari, working at Campbell Medical School in Calcutta with almost no laboratory, prepared urea stibamine, a pentavalent antimony compound, in 1920 and reported clinical trials in 1922. It cured over ninety percent of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) cases, a disease then killing tens of thousands a year in Assam and Bengal. Earlier tartar emetic treatments needed many painful injections and often failed. Assam's health department adopted urea stibamine in mass campaigns from 1923 and kala-azar deaths fell steeply. Brahmachari was nominated for Nobel Prize in 1929, and pentavalent antimonials remained standard leishmaniasis drugs for decades.

ypf-founded-1922.summary: In 1922 Argentina created YPF, the first state oil company to run everything from wells to petrol pumps, a model many countries copied. It handled exploration, production, refining and sales. First director Enrique Mosconi sought national control of oil supplies to strengthen Argentina's independence; its La Plata refinery, opened in December 1925, then ranked tenth largest worldwide.

bbc-founded-1922.summary: In 1922 Britain formed the BBC as a single licensed broadcaster, a model for public service radio and television worldwide. It made its first official broadcast in November, and Scottish Calvinist John Reith became general manager in December. On 1 January 1927 it became the British Broadcasting Corporation, a public body under royal charter funded by licence fees.

bose-statistics-1924.summary: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose sent Einstein a paper counting photons in a new way; Einstein extended it, and bosons bear his name. Einstein translated it into German and arranged publication; it came out in 1924. Bose had derived Planck's radiation law by treating light quanta as identical, indistinguishable particles that could crowd into the same state; Einstein extended the method to atoms. Particles that obey Bose-Einstein statistics are now called bosons.

hubble-andromeda-galaxy-1924.summary: In 1924 Hubble showed Andromeda lay far outside the Milky Way, a galaxy of its own; our universe grew by a factor of billions. Astronomers then mostly held that our Milky Way was the entire universe. Cepheids pulse at rates tied to their true brightness, as Henrietta Swan Leavitt had found in 1908, so they serve as distance markers; Hubble's observations, begun with an October 1923 plate and announced in January 1925, showed Andromeda was far too distant to be part of our galaxy and was an entire galaxy outside it.

technion-opens-1924.summary: In 1924 Technion opened in Haifa after a fight over whether to teach in German or Hebrew. Zionist delegates had first discussed such an institute at their Fifth Congress in Basel in 1901. Choosing Hebrew, in what was called the War of the Languages, helped establish Hebrew as Israel's official language; Technion is now Israel's oldest university and underpins its high-tech industry.

walker-southern-oscillation-1924.summary: As Director General of Observatories in India from 1904, Gilbert Walker set teams of Indian computers in Simla and Pune to calculate correlations between rainfall, pressure and temperature records worldwide in search of monsoon predictors after famines of 1890s. In 1924 he named a see-saw of surface pressure between Indian Ocean and eastern Pacific the Southern Oscillation. Later work by Bjerknes linked it to El Nino, giving ENSO, now central to seasonal forecasting for farmers across tropics. Walker's statistical method, including what became Walker's test for significance of periodogram peaks, grew from a practical need: forecasting rains that decided harvests for hundreds of millions.

Oxford Dictionary of National Biography entry gives career dates. Walker's own 1920s papers were calculated by Indian staff whose names are not recorded in his publications.

electricity-half-1925.summary: In 1925 electricity reached half of American homes, 43 years after Edison's first power station; farms waited another generation, with nine in ten urban homes electrified in 1930 and about one farm in ten.

gezira-scheme-1925.summary: In 1925 Sennar Dam began irrigating the Gezira plain in Sudan for cotton; a colony's economy was built on one crop and one dam. Egyptian-type long-staple cotton had grown there since 1904, promising raw material for British textile mills, and irrigation began on 24 square kilometres in 1914; after the lowest Nile flood in 200 years, Sennar's 3-kilometre dam was built, financed first by Sudan Plantations Syndicate and then guaranteed by Britain. Cotton remained the region's main crop, and by 2008 irrigation covered 8,800 square kilometres.

sources.confirms: Irrigated areas centred on the Gezira Scheme between the Blue and White Niles produce the bulk of Sudan's commercial crops.

heisenberg-matrix-mechanics-1925.summary: In 1925 Heisenberg wrote the first consistent quantum mechanics, atoms as arrays of numbers, which Born and Jordan completed with him in 1926. It represented physical observables as matrices that evolve in time and described quantum jumps without Bohr's sharply defined electron orbits. Erwin Schrödinger's wave mechanics, published months later, proved equivalent to it; Heisenberg received physics' 1932 Nobel Prize.

scopes-trial-1925.summary: In July 1925 a Tennessee teacher was tried for teaching evolution and fined $100; the trial was broadcast live on radio, the first to be. Town boosters staged his trial to draw publicity, with American Civil Liberties Union lawyers defending; Scopes was unsure he had ever taught evolution but incriminated himself so that there was a defendant. William Jennings Bryan prosecuted against defense lawyer Clarence Darrow; Scopes was fined $100, overturned on a technicality, and radio's first nationally broadcast trial publicized America's fundamentalist-modernist controversy.

gandhi-charkha-spinners-association-1925.summary: In September 1925 Mohandas Gandhi founds the All-India Spinners' Association (Akhil Bharat Charkha Sangh) to organise hand spinning and production and sale of khadi, hand-spun and hand-woven cloth. Its constitution, printed in Young India on 1 October 1925, declares that an expert organisation to develop hand-spinning and khaddar is now needed, "a permanent organisation, unaffected and uncontrolled by politics". Charkhas, low portable spinning wheels, had appeared on a prototype Congress flag since 1921, and Congress members were asked to spin half an hour a day. Lisa Trivedi's Journal of Asian Studies article shows how 1920s khadi exhibitions turned a household tool into a visual map of a nation. A folding charkha Gandhi sent Henry Ford in 1941 survives in the Henry Ford museum.

gandhi-charkha-spinners-association-1925.detail: Where jenny and power loom had moved thread making from household to mill, charkha spinning moved it back, as a daily act of economic self-reliance against imported cloth. Congress repealed its spinning franchise after most members ignored it, and Gandhi's association became a service body independent of party politics, running khadi stores, schools and a yarn certificate scheme until independence.

baird-televisor-1925-1925.summary: In October 1925 Baird transmitted the first television picture with shades of grey, a ventriloquist's dummy's head, in his London attic. It showed a head belonging to a ventriloquist's dummy called Stooky Bill in a 32-line image at five pictures per second. Earlier that year he had shown only moving silhouettes, at Selfridges department store in London; he now fetched office worker William Edward Taynton, 20, who became television's first human subject, and on 26 January 1926 gave his first public demonstration of true television images.

lilienfeld-fet-patent-1925.summary: In 1925 Lilienfeld patented a solid-state device to control current with an electric field, the transistor's idea 22 years early. It described a solid-state device in which an electric field controls current through semiconductor material, doing vacuum tubes' work. Without high-purity semiconductors he was never able to build a working device, and he published nothing in journals, so his patent won little notice. US Patent 1,745,175 was granted in 1930; when Bell Labs' Brattain and Bardeen sought patents on their 1947 transistors, most of their claims were rejected because of Lilienfeld's.

toyoda-automatic-loom-1925.summary: In 1925 Toyoda's loom changed its own shuttle and stopped when a thread broke; its sale to Britain funded Toyota's first cars. Kiichiro Toyoda's design changed shuttles without stopping, and the workshop introduced limit gauges so that replacement parts were interchangeable. By the end of March 1926, its Kariya plant had added 240 Type G looms, and 520 were operating by September's end; Hioki-cho built 1,023 before Toyoda Automatic Loom Works took over.

car-half-1926.summary: In 1926 by one series, and by 1929 by others, half of American households owned a car, 40 years after Benz's first; Ford's Model T and moving assembly line had done it. By 1929 there were more than 27 million on the road, nearly one per household.

csir-founded-1926.summary: In 1926 Australia founded a national science council; as CSIRO it later gave the world Wi-Fi and plastic banknotes. CSIR strengthened national science leadership and grew rapidly. In 1949, legislation renamed it Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO); its later developments include atomic absorption spectroscopy, essential components of early Wi-Fi, and the first commercially successful polymer banknote.

nbc-founded-1926.summary: In 1926 RCA formed NBC, a national radio network following AT&T's earlier venture; stations nationwide carried identical programmes simultaneously. Federal regulators forced NBC to divest a network in the early 1940s; NBC pioneered commercial television in 1939 and aired all its programmes in colour from 1966.

vitaphone-don-juan-1926.summary: In 1926 Don Juan became cinema's first feature film with a recorded score on synchronised discs. Sound came from phonograph discs played in step with its projector. It premiered August 6, 1926, at New York's Warner Theatre after Vitaphone shorts, and earned $1,258,000 domestically.

wallace-hybrid-corn-hi-bred-1926.summary: Editor and plant breeder Henry A. Wallace incorporates Hi-Bred Corn Company in Des Moines on 20 April 1926, the first firm devoted to hybrid seed corn. His Copper Cross hybrid had won the 1924 Iowa Corn Yield Test, and he built on Donald Jones's double-cross method of 1917 to 1918 at Connecticut's experiment station, which made inbred-line hybrids commercially viable. Farmers must buy new seed each year because hybrid vigor collapses in saved seed, so Wallace's business model holds. Iowa hybrid acreage rises from under 1 percent in 1933 to 6 percent in 1935, 50 percent in 1938 and near 100 percent by 1942. Zvi Griliches's 1957 Econometrica study fit logistic curves to this spread and explained timing by profitability, founding diffusion economics.

wallace-hybrid-corn-hi-bred-1926.detail: Griliches reduced state-by-state differences to origins, slopes and ceilings of logistic curves and tied each to seed firms' entry and farmers' gains. Wallace served as Secretary of Agriculture from 1933 and Vice President from 1941. Hybrid breeding moved to sorghum, sunflower and, in China under Yuan Longping, to rice. Hi-Bred becomes Pioneer Hi-Bred, later DuPont Pioneer. Corn Belt yields, flat near 26 bushels an acre for 60 years, roughly tripled by the 1970s.

yagi-uda-antenna-1926.summary: At Tohoku Imperial University in Sendai, Shintaro Uda, working under Hidetsugu Yagi, found in 1925-26 that parasitic metal rods placed near a half-wave dipole, slightly longer behind as reflectors and shorter in front as directors, focused short-wave radio into a narrow beam without any feed to those rods. Uda published a series of Japanese papers from 1926, and Yagi presented a summary in English to Institute of Radio Engineers in 1928, which carried design abroad. Japanese military showed little interest, while British and American radar sets in Second World War used Yagi arrays; rooftop television aerials later made it familiar worldwide.

It was history's first public demonstration of mechanical television, following his October 1925 greyscale picture of Stooky Bill, his dummy. His Baird Television Development Company achieved transatlantic television transmission in 1928.

Snopes rates this attribution correct; Collier's also had him predicting unmanned radio-guided aircraft and long-distance power transmission.

goddard-liquid-rocket-1926.summary: In 1926 Robert Goddard flew a liquid-fuelled rocket, 41 feet up, ancestor of every rocket to space. Burning gasoline with liquid oxygen, it rose 41 feet and flew 184 feet in 2.5 seconds. Liquid propellants can be throttled and carry far more energy than gunpowder, which had powered rockets for centuries. Ridiculed by press and fellow scientists for his spaceflight theories, Goddard grew secretive; he was recognized after his death as one of the founding fathers of modern rocketry.

gernsback-amazing-stories-1926.summary: In April 1926 Hugo Gernsback launched Amazing Stories, the first magazine devoted to science fiction; its genre had a name and a readership. He called its contents "scientifiction" in the style of Jules Verne, H. G. Wells and Edgar Allan Poe; such stories had appeared only occasionally in general magazines, and nobody had yet coined science fiction as a term. Circulation reached 150,000, and Gernsback added readers' discussion pages in 1927 and Amazing Stories Quarterly in 1928, helping define his genre.

air-commerce-act-1926.summary: In May 1926 America began licensing pilots and aircraft and marking airways. Civil aviation had grown from Post Office airmail routes begun in 1918, and aviation leaders had pressed for federal safety regulation. It created an Aeronautic Branch in the United States Department of Commerce with powers to test and license pilots, certify aircraft, make and enforce safety rules, establish airways, maintain navigation aids and investigate accidents. William P. MacCracken Jr. was its first head; it became the Bureau of Air Commerce in 1934.

takayanagi-electronic-television-1926.summary: On 25 December 1926 at Hamamatsu Technical College, Kenjiro Takayanagi scanned a katakana character painted on mica with a Nipkow disc and reproduced it as a stable 40-line image on a Braun cathode-ray tube, which he regarded as first electronic display of a television picture. He continued with photoelectric cells and vacuum tubes, built an iconoscope camera in 1935 and demonstrated an all-electronic system that November. His group at NHK began test broadcasts in Tokyo in 1939 and ran weekly experimental programmes until war stopped them in June 1941. After 1945 he led television development at Victor Company of Japan.

Mechanical scanning remained on transmitting side in 1926, so claims to 'first all-electronic television' belong to 1935 system.

cbs-founded-1927.summary: In 1927 a Chicago talent agency became the Columbia Broadcasting System, a radio network that grew into one of America's three TV giants. It began as United Independent Broadcasters, founded in Chicago by New York talent agent Arthur Judson on January 27, 1927; that April Columbia Phonograph Company invested and gave it its name.

davisson-germer-1927.summary: In 1927 Davisson and Germer showed electrons bouncing off a nickel crystal made interference patterns; diffraction is wave behaviour, so electrons, until then treated as particles, behave as waves too. This confirmed Louis de Broglie's 1924 hypothesis that all matter shows wave-particle duality and supported Schrodinger's wave mechanics.

ge-monitor-top-refrigerator-1927.summary: In 1927 General Electric introduces its Monitor Top, a steel cabinet with its sealed compressor mounted in a round housing on its lid, the first electric refrigerator to become widely popular in American homes, Smithsonian curators say. Until then most households kept food in an icebox supplied by ice deliverymen; DOMELRE of 1914 and Kelvinator's unit of 1918 had shown an electric alternative but sold in small numbers. Kelvinator, founded in Detroit in 1916, held about 80 per cent of that market by 1923. Its hermetic unit needed no servicing, and GE sold over a million. Cheap Freon refrigerant from 1930 and New Deal appliance loans from 1935 completed this shift.

kenya-radio-1924.summary: In 1927 radio reached Kenya with shortwave for settlers relaying BBC news; Africans waited decades for programmes of their own. A Nairobi station started regular English-language service in November 1928, drew only several hundred licence holders, and within twelve months was taken over by Imperial and International Communications, later Cable and Wireless, which ran Kenyan broadcasting under its 1931 agreement. That service passed through colonial-era Kenya Broadcasting Service to become Kenya Broadcasting Corporation in 1961.

lemaitre-expanding-universe-1927.summary: In 1927 the priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre argued that receding galaxies meant an expanding universe, two years before Hubble's data. Einstein told him his calculations were correct but his physics abominable. An English translation appeared in 1931, with Eddington's endorsement, and his work led to his primeval atom hypothesis, now regarded as Big Bang theory's first formulation; in 2018 astronomers voted to rename Hubble's law as Hubble-Lemaitre law.

negative-feedback-amplifier-1927.summary: In 1927 Harold Black sketched the negative-feedback amplifier on his newspaper; it made long-distance calls clear and machines stable. Long-distance telephone lines needed chains of amplifiers, and each added distortion. Feeding part of an amplifier's output back to oppose its input sacrifices gain but makes output far more linear, stable and broadband, and less sensitive to component drift. Patented in 1937, his principle underlies modern electronics and control systems.

transatlantic-radiotelephone-1927.summary: In January 1927 telephone calls crossed the Atlantic by radio at $75 for three minutes; voices spanned an ocean before any cable could. Submarine cables had carried telegraph traffic since 1858, but voice needed amplifiers along its route, and a telephone cable, discussed from the 1920s, required advances that arrived only two decades later. Radio telephony remained Europe's and North America's only voice link until TAT-1, laid between Oban in Scotland and Clarenville in Newfoundland, opened on September 25, 1956 with 36 channels.

uncertainty-principle-1927.summary: In 1927 Heisenberg showed a particle's position and momentum cannot both be known exactly, a limit on knowledge built into nature. He had realised in March 1926, at Bohr's institute, that his quantum mechanics made such quantities non-commuting, and worked out his idea in letters to Wolfgang Pauli. Earle Kennard that year and Hermann Weyl in 1928 proved that position and momentum spreads multiply to at least half Planck's reduced constant.

metropolis-1927.summary: In 1927 Lang's Metropolis put a robot on screen, a machine woman who leads workers to ruin, the image behind a century of film robots. Shot over 17 months in 1925 and 1926 at more than five million Reichsmarks, it depicts a futuristic city divided between industrialists and underground workers, with a robot duplicate of activist Maria helping drive conflict toward revolt. Reviews were mixed, with praise for its technical achievements and complaints about its story; in 2001 it became UNESCO's first film on its Memory of the World register.

radio-act-1927.summary: In February 1927 America created a Federal Radio Commission to assign frequencies. Court rulings in 1923 and 1926 had found that 1912's Radio Act gave Commerce officials no power to refuse licences or assign frequencies, so stations such as Zenith's WJAZ broadcast wherever they liked. Stations henceforth had to show they served "the public interest, convenience, or necessity" to hold licences; 1934's Communications Act replaced it.

att-hoover-television-1927.summary: In April 1927 AT&T sent live television of Commerce Secretary Hoover by wire from Washington to an audience in New York. Ives led Bell Labs' television research with a team of more than 50; by 1930 his two-way television-telephone, the ikonophone, was in regular experimental use.
