massey-harris-self-propelled-combine-193.detail: Self-propulsion dates to Sunshine Harvester Works in Australia and to 1920s hillside experiments; Carroll, who had worked on Sunshine headers before joining Massey-Harris in Argentina, made it reliable and affordable. Brigade machines saved 333,000 man-hours and 500,000 gallons of fuel by Massey-Harris count, and custom cutters still follow ripening wheat each summer. Within a decade pull-type combines fell from favour in the North American grain belt. Thresher crews of 20 men were replaced by two. Such machinery underwrote postwar yield gains on Kansas farms.

owens-corning-fiberglas-1938.summary: In 1938 two glass companies formed Owens-Corning to make glass fibre; it insulated houses and reinforced boats and car bodies. Games Slayter of Owens-Illinois, with John Thomas and Dale Kleist, whose 1932 accident at Corning produced fine glass fibres, developed glass wool between 1932 and 1933 as thermal building insulation, filing his patent in 1933, and commercial production began in 1936. Fiberglass traps many small air cells with a bonding agent, giving light, low-density insulation. Owens-Corning introduced continuous filament glass fibres, which reinforce plastics in boats, pipes and other composites, and Fiberglas became a genericised trademark; Owens-Corning remains glass fibre's major producer.

volkswagen-beetle-1938.summary: In 1938 Hitler laid a foundation stone for a people's car factory; the Beetle became the postwar world's best-selling car. On 26 May that year Hitler laid that stone at Fallersleben, now Wolfsburg. In May 1934 he had demanded a car for two adults and three children using no more than seven litres of fuel per 100 km, and Ferdinand Porsche's team designed it. Manufacture began on 27 December 1945 under British control and ran to 2003, reaching 21.5 million cars, the longest run for any single automobile generation.

volkswagen-beetle-1938.detail: Renamed KdF-Wagen, it was sold through a scheme urging workers to save five marks a week, but war stopped series production.

wells-world-brain-1938.summary: In 1938 H G Wells proposed a World Brain, a permanent world encyclopaedia on microfilm open to everyone. He first set it out in a Royal Institution lecture on 20 November 1936, describing "a sort of mental clearing house for the mind, a depot where knowledge and ideas are received, sorted, summarized, digested, clarified and compared". He argued such an intellectual project would do more for peace than any political movement.

zuse-z1-1938.summary: In 1938 Konrad Zuse finished the Z1 in his parents' living room in Berlin, a mechanical computer that read programs from punched film. It was a binary, electrically driven mechanical computer, financed completely by private funds, reading instructions from perforated 35 mm film and working on 22-bit floating-point numbers with a 16-word memory. Some 20,000 thin metal sheets, cut with a jigsaw, formed its logic; it was freely programmable but unreliable in operation. Allied bombing destroyed it in December 1943.

zuse-z1-1938.detail: Its mechanical memory carried over into his Z2 and Z3, which replaced its arithmetic with relays.

burgan-oil-discovery-1938.summary: In 1938 oil was found at Burgan in Kuwait. Kuwait Oil Company, owned by American and British interests, began commercial production there in 1946, after World War II. Greater Burgan, a group of fields including Burgan, is described as Earth's second-largest oil field after Saudi Arabia's Ghawar, with recoverable oil estimated at 66 to 75 billion barrels. Production peaked at 2.4 million barrels per day in 1972, stood near 1.7 million in 2005, and in 2010 still supplied half of Kuwait's oil.

dammam-no-7-saudi-oil-1938.summary: In March 1938 well number 7 at Dammam struck oil in commercial quantity, Saudi Arabia's first. Bahrain's 1932 oil strike had spurred Saudi exploration, but when drilling began in the 1930s nobody knew whether oil lay there, and American geologist Max Steineke, assisted by Saudi Bedouin Khamis Bin Rimthan, persisted in drilling deeper. From this well Saudi Arabia grew into a leading oil exporter.

mexico-oil-expropriation-1938.summary: In March 1938 Mexico nationalised its oil industry and founded Pemex, the first major expropriation of foreign oil companies. Oil workers had struck in 1937 over pay, an arbitration board ruled for their union on December 18, and Mexico's Supreme Court rejected companies' appeal and ordered higher wages, which they refused to pay. On June 7, 1938, Cárdenas created Petróleos Mexicanos with exclusive rights over oil, and companies and foreign governments boycotted Mexican oil. After those sanctions Mexico paid compensation near asset value, settled as World War II's alliance formed, and March 18 is now a Mexican civic holiday.

teflon-ptfe-1938.summary: In April 1938 DuPont chemists trying to make a new chlorofluorocarbon refrigerant at Chambers Works in New Jersey found a gas had turned into a waxy solid nothing would stick to; Teflon coated bombs, then frying pans. Sawing its cylinder open, they found its interior coated with a waxy, slippery white powder: polytetrafluoroethylene, polymerised with its iron walls as catalyst. Kinetic Chemicals patented PTFE in 1941 and registered Teflon as trademark in 1945. Chemically inert, it coated valves and seals holding uranium hexafluoride at Manhattan Project's K-25 plant, and its very low friction later gave non-stick cookware.

action-comics-superman-1938.summary: In April 1938 Action Comics #1 introduced Superman, the first superhero; its creators were paid $130 for the story. Publisher Jack Liebowitz ran their Superman story as lead feature of his new anthology, paying them $10 per page, $130 in all. Its 200,000-copy print run sold out, and once National Allied Publications realised Superman drove sales, circulation approached a million a month, launching superhero comics. On April 4, 2024, a copy sold at Heritage Auctions for $6 million, a record for any comic.

fair-labor-standards-act-1938.summary: In 1938 the United States set its first minimum wage, 25 cents an hour, capped weekly hours and banned child labour. This law covered industries employing about one fifth of America's labour force. Labor Secretary Frances Perkins had fought for such legislation almost all her working life, and the Supreme Court had stood as its major obstacle, voiding state and federal wage laws.

food-drug-cosmetic-act-1938.summary: In 1938 the United States required new drugs to be shown safe before sale, replacing 1906's Pure Food and Drug Act after 107 patients died from Elixir Sulfanilamide, a medication dissolved in toxic diethylene glycol. Manufacturers now had to show FDA that new drugs were safe before marketing, through what became its New Drug Application process, and medical devices were later sorted into three classes with premarket approval for those sustaining life. It remains FDA's governing statute.

trans-iranian-railway-completed-1938.summary: Iran's Majles voted a state monopoly on tea and sugar in 1925 and a railway law in February 1927 so that a north-south line could be built without foreign loans, a condition shaped by memories of Qajar concessions. An American-German syndicate began at both ends in 1927; after payment disputes Danish firm Kampsax took over supervision in 1933 and split construction into 43 lots for contractors from a dozen countries and Iran. Crews cut about 230 tunnels and built 4,100 bridges through Alborz and Zagros mountains, with spirals and Veresk viaduct lifting single track to 2,220 metres. Reza Shah tightened a final bolt in Lorestan on 26 August 1938, eleven years after breaking ground, linking Bandar Shah on the Caspian with Bandar Shahpur on the Gulf via Tehran. Allied forces used this line to carry supplies to the Soviet Union after occupying Iran in 1941.

xerography-1938.summary: In October 1938 Chester Carlson made the first photocopy in a rented room in Queens; twenty companies turned it down before Xerox was born. Carlson worked in a patent department and had copied law books longhand because he could not afford them, so he wanted better ways to copy documents. Kornei wrote "10.-22.-38 ASTORIA." in India ink on a glass slide, charged his sulfur-coated zinc plate by rubbing it with his handkerchief, and exposed it through that slide. Haloid's Xerox 914 copier later made plain-paper copying routine.

war-of-the-worlds-broadcast-1938.summary: In October 1938 Orson Welles broadcast his War of the Worlds radio play as fake news bulletins. Its first half ran as realistic breaking-news bulletins: explosions on Mars, something falling at Grovers Mill, New Jersey, Martians emerging with heat rays. Listeners' nerves were raw weeks after September's Munich Pact, and some who tuned in late believed an invasion had begun. Newspapers, hostile to radio, reported mass panic, which later research found exaggerated. Welles apologised next morning; his notoriety carried him to Hollywood.

nuclear-fission-discovery-1938.summary: In 1938 Hahn and Strassmann split the uranium atom; within seven years that energy had levelled two cities. They had found barium, an element about half uranium's mass, among their products. Lise Meitner, who had fled Berlin for Sweden in July 1938, and her nephew Otto Robert Frisch explained it theoretically in January 1939, and Frisch named it fission after cell division. One uranium-235 atom's fission releases about 100 million times more energy than burning one carbon atom. Because fission emits further neutrons, it can sustain a chain reaction, which led to nuclear reactors and atomic bombs.

dakar-yellow-fever-vaccine-1939.summary: At Institut Pasteur de Dakar, Jean Laigret, Max Peltier and Constant Durieux developed a yellow fever vaccine from a virus strain isolated in Senegal in 1927 and attenuated by passage through mouse brains. Their freeze-dried single dose could be scratched into skin together with smallpox vaccine, letting a team immunise up to 800 people an hour. Mass campaigns across French West Africa began in 1939; about 14 million people were vaccinated in wartime and 56 million by 1953, and urban yellow fever epidemics there stopped. Cases of encephalitis, mostly in children, were recorded but poorly reported, as Aro Velmet shows, and use in children was restricted in 1961 and ended in the 1980s.

sources.author: Frierson, J. Gordon
sources.venue: Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine

dakar-yellow-fever-vaccine-1939.detail: Frierson's history notes that this French neurotropic vaccine lacked the human serum used in early Rockefeller preparations and risked febrile and nervous-system reactions, but suited large campaigns. Velmet documents 17 deaths after about 100,000 vaccinations in Brazzaville and a later cluster of 57 encephalitis cases, reports that stayed inside colonial administration. Rockefeller's rival 17D vaccine, grown in chick embryos, replaced it worldwide.

ddt-insecticide-1939.summary: In 1939 Paul Muller found DDT killed insects; it stopped typhus and malaria for millions and then poisoned birdlife. Armies used it in World War II's second half to limit malaria and typhus, and it went on public sale in the United States by October 1945. He received 1948's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this discovery. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring focused opposition to its environmental harm in 1962, and its agricultural use has been banned worldwide under the Stockholm Convention since 2004.

elektro-robot-1939.summary: In 1939 Westinghouse showed Elektro at the New York World's Fair, a seven-foot robot that walked on voice command and spoke 700 words. J.M. Barnett, Jack Weeks Sr., Harold Gorsuch, and other engineers built it at Westinghouse Electric Corporation's Mansfield, Ohio, facility. Seven feet tall and 265 pounds, it walked by voice command, spoke about 700 words from a 78-rpm record player, smoked cigarettes and blew up balloons; its steel gear, cam and motor skeleton wore an aluminum skin, and photoelectric eyes told red light from green. A robot dog, Sparko, joined it in 1940. Restored, Elektro is displayed at Mansfield Memorial Museum.

futurama-exhibit-1939.summary: In 1939 General Motors' Futurama ride showed fairgoers a 1960 of motorways and suburbs; the American future was sold as a car trip. It grew from his 1937 Shell Oil City of Tomorrow model and presented his vision of 1959 to 1960, 20 years ahead, with automated highways and vast suburbs. Futurama first put a nationwide expressway network before mass audiences, and GM built a working automated-highway prototype by 1960.

new-york-worlds-fair-1939.summary: In 1939 New York's World's Fair sold its World of Tomorrow to slightly over 45 million visitors across two seasons; television was demonstrated publicly there. President Roosevelt opened it on April 30, 1939, with 62 nations and more than 1,400 organizations and companies exhibiting around Trylon and Perisphere, its theme center. RCA and NBC ran television demonstrations, among them the first televised Major League Baseball game; Westinghouse showed Elektro, General Motors ran Futurama, and nylon made its debut. War in Europe four months later closed or shrank several exhibits.

voder-1939.summary: In 1939 Bell Labs' Voder spoke in a synthetic voice played by an operator at a keyboard, the first machine to talk from scratch. It grew from Bell Labs' vocoder work on compressing voice for copper wires. Its operator chose with a wrist bar between a buzz tone for vowels and nasals, pitch set by foot pedal, and hiss for sibilants, then shaped each sound through filters with fifteen keys; the console demanded highly trained operators.

hydramatic-transmission-1939.summary: In October 1939 General Motors announced the first mass-produced automatic gearbox, shipping 1940-model Oldsmobile Series 60 and 70 cars with it at $57 for the option; driving no longer needed a clutch. Cadillac engineers under Earl Thompson had worked on "shiftless" transmissions since 1932; Hydra-Matic paired hydraulically shifted planetary gears with a fluid coupling in place of a friction clutch, so drivers never declutched, and offered four forward speeds plus reverse. Almost 200,000 had sold when passenger car production stopped for war work in February 1942.

einstein-szilard-letter-1939.summary: In August 1939 Einstein signed Szilard's letter warning Roosevelt fission could make bombs; the Manhattan Project grew from it. Szilard visited Einstein at Cutchogue, Long Island, on July 12, 1939; Einstein, who had not considered fission as a weapon, said "Daran habe ich gar nicht gedacht" and agreed to sign, doing so on August 2. Germany's invasion of Poland delayed Alexander Sachs's meeting with Roosevelt until October 11, 1939, after which Roosevelt authorized the Advisory Committee on Uranium under Lyman Briggs.

heinkel-he-178-jet-1939.summary: In August 1939 Heinkel's He 178 made the first flight on turbojet power, days before the Second World War began. It flew on Hans von Ohain’s engine, which Heinkel developed in secrecy, concealed even from Luftwaffe leaders. That flight lasted six minutes and almost ended in disaster during its unpowered landing approach. With 598 km/h top speed and short endurance, it failed to impress Nazi officials at a demonstration on 1 November 1939, and German jet development passed to other programmes.

sikorsky-vs-300-helicopter-1939.summary: In September 1939 Sikorsky flew his VS-300, the first helicopter with the single-main-rotor and tail-rotor layout every helicopter now uses. He had convinced United Aircraft's directors in 1938 that his years of rotary-wing research would pay off; this first experimental machine used a single three-blade main rotor driven by a 75 horsepower engine. Its first free flight took place on 13 May 1940, making it America's first successful single lifting rotor helicopter.

blood-for-britain-plasma-1940.summary: In 1940 Charles Drew's Blood for Britain shipped 5,000 litres of plasma from New York to England. Plasma, blood's cell-free fluid, treats shock and keeps without refrigeration, so it suited combat; dried plasma shipped as two tin cans, one holding distilled water, and was ready about three minutes after mixing. Planned as a rehearsal for national blood banking, it led to the American Red Cross National Blood Donor Service in November 1941.

blood-for-britain-plasma-1940.detail: Bernard Fantus had opened America's first hospital blood bank at Cook County Hospital in Chicago on March 15, 1937, and coined the term blood bank. Charles Drew, whose 1940 dissertation was titled “Banked Blood,” served as full-time medical supervisor of Blood for Britain and developed its first mass production methods.

cavity-magnetron-1940.summary: In 1940 Randall and Boot built a cavity magnetron; in mass production by early 1941, it made radar small enough for aircraft, and it now heats food in microwave ovens. Wartime radar needed high power at about 10 cm wavelength, far shorter than existing tubes could manage at 50 to 150 cm. Their tube swept electrons past small open cavities cut in a metal block, under a magnetic field, and made them ring at microwave frequencies. It produced about 400 watts, unprecedented output at 10 cm. After 1945 this same device came to power microwave ovens.

walkie-talkie-1940.summary: In 1940 Motorola built its SCR-536 Handie-Talkie, a handheld radio for infantry. Canadian inventor Donald Hings had built a portable "packset" in 1937 and Alfred J. Gross worked on similar technology from 1938 to 1941; both are sometimes credited with inventing the walkie-talkie. Galvin's engineers, including Dan Noble, who proposed frequency modulation, built vacuum-tube sets powered by high-voltage dry cells. Their backpack SCR-300, proposed to the Army in early 1942 so a squad could talk to its commander, followed in 1943.

walkie-talkie-1940.detail: Galvin's SCR-300 team comprised Marion Bond, Lloyd Morris, Bill Vogel, Dan Noble and Henryk Magnuski. Surplus sets reached ham radio operators after World War II.

gonzalez-camarena-color-tv-1940.summary: On 19 August 1940 Guillermo González Camarena, a 23-year-old engineer at Mexico City radio station XEFO, filed a Mexican patent for a 'sistema tricromático secuencial de campos', a colour television method using a rotating disc of red, green and blue filters synchronised at camera and receiver. The US Patent Office granted him patent 2,296,019 in 1942. He built cameras and receivers in his own workshop from salvaged parts, demonstrated colour pictures to Mexican officials, and in 1946 opened experimental station XE1GC. Camarena's station XHGC, channel 5, broadcast from 1952; Mexico's first colour transmissions followed in 1963. Andrés Burbano's study places his work alongside parallel field-sequential systems by Baird and CBS's Peter Goldmark.

gonzalez-camarena-color-tv-1940.detail: Field-sequential colour was compatible with mechanical scanning and simple receivers but flickered and suited only small screens; electronic shadow-mask systems displaced it in the 1950s. Camarena later developed a simplified bicolour system in the 1960s and died in a road accident in 1965. His receivers and documents survive in Mexican collections.

stibitz-remote-computing-1940.summary: In September 1940 George Stibitz ran a computer in New York from a teletype in New Hampshire, a computing machine's first live remote use. Stibitz, who researched at Bell Labs, had built his relay-based binary adder on his kitchen table in November 1937, later called Model K; Bell Labs then backed a full programme, and his Complex Number Calculator, finished in November 1939, computed with complex numbers using electromagnetic relay circuits in place of counting wheels or gears.

stibitz-remote-computing-1940.detail: His audience was the American Mathematical Society and the Mathematical Association of America.

pennsylvania-turnpike-1940.summary: In October 1940 the Pennsylvania Turnpike opened, America's first long-distance controlled-access motorway with no speed limit, branded "America's First Superhighway"; its Interstate Highway System copied it. Its 1930s design carried cars across Pennsylvania's mountains, reusing seven tunnels bored for South Pennsylvania Railroad in the 1880s; its feasibility study, proposed in April 1935, led to bonds and federal grants. Treated as a yardstick for limited-access roads, it became a model for later toll roads.

tacoma-narrows-bridge-collapse-1940.summary: In November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted apart in a 40 mile an hour wind on film; bridges have been tested in wind tunnels since. Leon Moisseiff’s design used shallow, narrow plate girders that left its deck too flexible. Textbooks often call this failure resonance, but moderate wind set off aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting twist that grew without bound above about 35 mph. It collapsed into the strait, and its central span fell into the water, five days after Frederick Farquharson’s wind-tunnel study had proposed fixes. Its collapse drove research into bridge aerodynamics that has shaped long-span bridge design since.

tacoma-narrows-bridge-collapse-1940.detail: This suspension bridge across Puget Sound had opened on July 1, 1940, and its deck had heaved in wind from construction onward, earning it the nickname Galloping Gertie.

pet-polyester-1941.summary: In 1941 two British chemists patented PET, the polyester of drink bottles and fleece; a fabric and a package came from one molecule. It is a polyester-family thermoplastic resin. ICI commercialized its fibre as Terylene in the 1940s; DuPont first produced Dacron fibre in 1950 and trademarked Mylar film in June 1951. Known as polyester in clothing and PET in packaging, it fills soft-drink bottles and blends with cotton in apparel; it is now the most common polyester thermoplastic, with global production of 31 million tons in 2025.

velcro-hook-and-loop-1941.summary: In 1941 Swiss engineer George de Mestral, after a hunting trip in the Alps, studied burdock burs stuck to his clothes and his dog's fur and designed a fastener of hooks and loops; Velcro took a decade to make. Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks catching in loops of fabric and fur. He named it velcro, from the French velours and crochet, velvet and hook. Clothing makers resisted its appearance at first; its first break came in aerospace, helping astronauts in and out of bulky space suits.

willys-jeep-1941.summary: In 1941 Willys-Overland and Ford put the Jeep into production as the Willys MB and Ford GPW, a light four-wheel-drive car for America's army; under Ford's Charles E. Sorensen they built about 640,000, and off-road vehicles trace to it. Bantam's Karl Probst had drafted full plans in two days against a 49-day Army deadline, and Bantam's bid went in on July 22, 1940, using mostly stock parts with Spicer four-wheel drivetrains.

ntsc-monochrome-standard-1941.summary: In March 1941 the NTSC set America's black-and-white television standard at 525 lines, based on the Radio Manufacturers Association's 1936 recommendation; it lasted until digital switch-off in 2009. It selected 525 scan lines as its compromise between RCA's 441-line system, used by its NBC network, and Philco and DuMont's push for 605 to 800 lines, with 30 frames per second sent as two interlaced fields of 262.5 lines each. NTSC's second standard, in December 1953, added color while remaining compatible with existing black-and-white sets.

zuse-z3-1941.summary: In 1941 Konrad Zuse's Z3 ran programs on 2,600 telephone relays in Berlin, the first working programmable digital computer. Designed in 1938, it was presented on May 12, 1941, and used 2,600 relays operating at about 5–10 Hz with 22-bit floating point words, exception handling and a square root instruction; programs were stored on punched film and initial values entered by hand. Never put into everyday use, it ran a matrix program to solve aircraft wing flutter problems, and Zuse's request for funding to replace relays with electronic switches was denied.

zuse-z3-1941.detail: Allied bombing destroyed it on 21 December 1943; its 1961 replica stands in Munich's Deutsches Museum. In 1998 Raúl Rojas showed it was, in principle, Turing-complete.

first-tv-commercial-bulova-1941.summary: In July 1941 a Bulova watch ad ran before a Dodgers game, the first paid television commercial; Bulova paid $9, $4 in airtime fees and $5 in station charges. Accounts differ: Guinness describes a 10-second clock over a map of America captioned "America runs on Bulova time"; others describe WNBT's test pattern modified into a clock with Bulova's logo, its second hand sweeping for one minute. WNBT later became WNBC. Britain's first television advertisement did not air until September 22, 1955, on ITV.

smith-putnam-wind-turbine-1941.summary: In October 1941 a 1.25-megawatt turbine on a Vermont hilltop fed wind power into a grid, the first megawatt-scale wind machine. The S. Morgan Smith Company built it as history's first megawatt-size wind turbine. Two eight-ton steel blades spanned 175 feet downwind of its 120-foot lattice tower, and its synchronous generator fed loads up to 700 kW. It ran about 1,000 hours before bearing failure in February 1943; on March 26, 1945, one blade broke at a known weak point left unreinforced by wartime shortages.

smith-putnam-wind-turbine-1941.detail: Palmer Cosslett Putnam, struck by high winds at Cape Cod, had enlisted General Electric, Vannevar Bush and Central Vermont Public Service by 1937. Testing was cut short as war approached.

atanasoff-berry-computer-1942.summary: In 1942 the Atanasoff-Berry Computer in Iowa solved equations electronically with binary digits; a court later called it the first computer. John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built it in the basement of Iowa State College's physics building, where construction and testing took place from 1939 to 1942. Designed only to solve systems of up to 29 simultaneous linear equations, it was the first to do arithmetic with vacuum tubes, computed in binary and stored numbers on two rotating drums of 1,600 capacitors each, refreshed every turn, an early regenerative memory; it was not programmable, and its paper card storage for intermediate results proved unreliable.

grand-coulee-dam-1942.summary: In 1942 Grand Coulee Dam was completed, the largest concrete structure on Earth; its power smelted the aluminium for America's warplanes. Built between 1933 and 1942, this concrete gravity dam on Washington state's Columbia River was designed to produce hydroelectric power and pump irrigation water; 1920s debate between a gravity canal and a high dam with pumps ended with dam supporters winning in 1933. Its power fed growing Pacific Northwest industries during World War II. Its reservoir, Franklin Delano Roosevelt Lake, forced over 3,000 people from their homes, including Native Americans whose lands were flooded, and it was built without fish passage.

grand-coulee-dam-1942.detail: A third powerhouse completed in 1974 made it America's largest power station.

manhattan-project-1942.summary: From 1942 the Manhattan Project put 130,000 people and $2 billion into the first nuclear weapons; in July 1945 one bomb could level a city. Major General Leslie Groves directed it, while J. Robert Oppenheimer ran Los Alamos, which designed two bombs: Little Boy, an enriched uranium gun-type weapon, and Fat Man, a plutonium implosion device.

manhattan-project-1942.detail: Groves was an Army Corps of Engineers officer; Los Alamos lay in New Mexico. Its Manhattan District, active from 1942 to 1946, was disbanded on 15 August 1947, after control of American atomic weapons research and production had passed to civilian hands, under its new Atomic Energy Commission, in January 1947.

sikorsky-r-4-helicopter-1942.summary: In 1942 Sikorsky's R-4 became the first helicopter built in quantity; it rescued downed airmen in Burma before the war ended. Developed from Igor Sikorsky's experimental VS-300 as his VS-316, it received Army designation XR-4, first flew on 14 January 1942 and was accepted on 30 May 1942. A two-seat light helicopter with a single three-bladed main rotor driven by a radial engine, it was first among helicopters used by United States Army Air Forces, Navy and Coast Guard units and by Britain's Royal Air Force and Royal Navy.

sources.author: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.confirms: The XR-4 was the world's first mass-production helicopter and the first successful production single-rotor rotorcraft.

sources.confirms: The Sikorsky R-4, whose experimental version first flew in 1942, was the world's first production helicopter and served US and British forces in the Second World War.

sikorsky-r-4-helicopter-1942.detail: In January 1944 Coast Guard Commander Frank Erickson flew blood plasma to casualties of USS Turner, America's first helicopter rescue. That April Lieutenant Carter Harman made the first combat rescue by helicopter, in Burma.

us-synthetic-rubber-program-1942.summary: In 1942, cut off from Asian rubber, the United States built 51 synthetic rubber plants in two years. Rubber was needed for tires, hoses, seals and belts on military vehicles and aircraft, so America turned to synthetic elastomers made from petroleum byproducts, above all styrene-butadiene rubber. With government sponsorship, a consortium of rubber and oil companies agreed with federal representatives on March 26, 1942, on a "mutual recipe" for GR-S (Government Rubber-Styrene). Annual output of general purpose synthetic rubber rose from 231 tons in 1941 to about 920,000 tons in 1945.

us-synthetic-rubber-program-1942.detail: Styrene-butadiene rubber is formed by copolymerizing styrene and 1,3-butadiene. The recipe was 75 percent butadiene and 25 percent styrene, with potassium persulfate as initiator, soap as emulsifier, water and a dodecyl mercaptan modifier. It drew on German Buna S research, because Buna S could be mixed with natural rubber and milled on existing machines. The Baruch Rubber Survey Committee's September 1942 report called for one rubber director with full authority and for 51 plants to make its monomers and polymers; Firestone, B. F. Goodrich, Goodyear, Standard Oil of New Jersey and United States Rubber took part, and 85 percent of 1945 output was GR-S.

voice-of-america-1942.summary: In February 1942 Voice of America began broadcasting in German to counter Axis propaganda. Before Pearl Harbor, America's Coordinator of Information office had fed war news to private shortwave stations through Robert E. Sherwood's Foreign Information Service; VOA used shortwave and shared BBC medium-wave transmitters in Britain. Control passed in mid-1942 to Office of War Information staff, in 1945 to State Department officials and in 1953 to the U.S. Information Agency.

voice-of-america-1942.detail: Its first broadcast opened with “The Battle Hymn of the Republic” and promised listeners truthful war news. Its 1976 charter requires accurate, objective reporting.

asimov-runaround-three-laws-1942.summary: In 1942 Asimov's story Runaround stated the Three Laws of Robotics; fiction began asking how to make machines safe. On Mercury, engineers Powell and Donovan send robot Speedy to fetch selenium for their failing life support; a weakly worded order under Asimov's Second Law collides with a strengthened Third Law of self-preservation near a dangerous pool, so Speedy circles it until Powell exposes himself to danger and the First Law breaks that standoff. Collected in I, Robot in 1950, its Laws have shaped fiction and debate about robot ethics since.

chicago-pile-1-1942.summary: In December 1942 Fermi's team started the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in a graphite pile under a Chicago stadium. About 30 people assembled it in November 1942; hired high school dropouts machined 45,000 graphite blocks enclosing 19,000 pieces of uranium, graphite slowing neutrons so natural uranium could sustain fission.

chicago-pile-1-1942.detail: Leo Szilard, Leona Woods, Herbert L. Anderson and Walter Zinn were among its builders. Moved to Site A near Chicago in 1943 as Chicago Pile-2, it ran until 1954.

biro-ballpoint-pen-1943.summary: In 1943 Hungarian journalist Laszlo Biro and his brother Gyorgy, refugees in Argentina since 1941, put their Birome on sale in Buenos Aires: a pen whose tiny rotating ball draws viscous, rapid-drying newspaper ink from a sealed tube. Biro had patented the idea in Britain in 1938; an Argentine filing of 17 April 1943 became US patent 2,390,636 in 1945. The Royal Air Force ordered 30,000 because they did not leak at altitude. In New York, Milton Reynolds copied it and sold 30,000 at Gimbels in a week from 29 October 1945 at 12.50 dollars each. Marcel Bich's Cristal of 1950 made it a disposable; by 2006 Bic had sold 100 billion.

hou-debang-soda-1943.summary: Chemical engineer Hou Debang, who had run Yongli Chemical Industries' Solvay-type plant at Tanggu before Japanese occupation forced a move inland, worked at Wutongqiao in Sichuan during war on a process that feeds ammonia and carbon dioxide into brine to produce sodium carbonate and crystallises ammonium chloride as fertiliser, instead of discarding calcium chloride waste as Solvay plants do. He described this 'Hou process' in 1943 and patented it abroad; Chinese plants adopted it after 1949 and it remains in use for soda and fertiliser in China. Yongli's effort, financed by Fan Xudong, trained a generation of Chinese chemical engineers.

Pilot plant ran in Sichuan; full-scale production came in 1950s.

kolff-dialysis-1943.summary: In 1943 Willem Kolff built a kidney machine from sausage casing and orange juice cans in Kampen during Germany's occupation of the Netherlands, where he was also active in resistance work, to filter waste from blood of patients whose kidneys had failed; a 22-year-old patient dying slowly of kidney failure had prompted his research. He treated his first patient in 1943 and successfully treated a patient with the machine in 1945.

kolff-dialysis-1943.detail: He moved to America in 1950, improved his dialysis machine and worked on heart-lung machines at Cleveland Clinic. From 1967 he led artificial organ research at the University of Utah, where surgeons implanted their first artificial heart in 1982.

mcculloch-pitts-neuron-1943.summary: In 1943 McCulloch and Pitts described a nerve cell as a unit that sums its inputs, each multiplied by its own weight, and fires when the sum passes its threshold. Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron added adjustable weights to it, and neural networks build on both.

sigsaly-1943.summary: In 1943 SIGSALY encrypted Churchill's and Roosevelt's calls by turning speech into digits, the first digital voice link. Existing telephone scramblers were cracked by both sides, so Bell Telephone Laboratories built a prototype under A. B. Clark, assisted by British mathematician Alan Turing, and won an Army contract for two systems in 1942. It encoded speech digitally, in history's first transmission of speech by pulse-code modulation: its vocoder reduced voice to a dozen slow signals, which were masked with random noise recorded on phonograph records used as one-time pads and played on precisely synchronized turntables at both ends.

teleology-paper-1943.summary: In 1943 Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow argued that purpose in animals and machines is feedback toward a goal. Rosenblueth was lead author. Their paper classified behavior as active or passive, active behavior as purposeful or random, and purposeful behavior as guided or not by negative feedback, so that machines steering toward targets and animals pursuing prey could be described in one language. Wiener said it set the bases for cybernetics, and he dedicated his 1948 book Cybernetics to Rosenblueth, "for many years my companion in science."

watson-five-computers-myth-1943.summary: In 1943 IBM's Thomas Watson supposedly said the world might want five computers; no record shows he said it, and the line lived on anyway. In 1943 computer usually meant a person who calculated, and biographer Kevin Maney found no speech, document or contemporary article containing those words. Its earliest known attribution appeared in Der Spiegel on May 22, 1965, describing an estimate of maximum demand of five in America's economy as commercial machines appeared in the early 1950s. Described as myth by 1973, it survives as a favorite example of failed prediction.

lockheed-constellation-1943.summary: In January 1943 Lockheed's Constellation first flew, pressurised and swift; after the war it carried passengers across the Atlantic daily. It was designed as a pressurized airliner after Transcontinental and Western Air, pushed by major stockholder Howard Hughes, asked in June 1938 for a transcontinental airliner with a 6,000-pound payload and 3,500 mile range. With America at war, TWA's order became C-69 military transports. Its triple tail, dolphin-shaped fuselage and four 18-cylinder Wright R-3350 engines became familiar after 1945, when Constellations became the first civil airliner family in widespread use with pressurized cabins, flying above most bad weather.

lockheed-constellation-1943.detail: Lockheed built 856 at Burbank between 1943 and 1958.

abc-network-founded-1943.summary: In October 1943 ABC began as a radio network after NBC was forced to sell one of its two, making Blue, which NBC had operated since 1927, independent. It kept its Blue Network name until June 1945, when it became American Broadcasting Company. ABC extended into television in 1948, following CBS and NBC, and merged with United Paramount Theatres in 1953 to form American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres, later American Broadcasting Companies, Inc.

streptomycin-1943.summary: In October 1943 Albert Schatz, working in Selman Waksman's soil-screening programme at Rutgers, isolated streptomycin, the first drug to cure tuberculosis; sanatoria emptied. A PhD student in a project funded by Merck and Co., he drew it from soil bacterium Streptomyces griseus. Streptomycin binds bacterial ribosomes' 30S subunit and blocks protein synthesis, acting on both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and it was tuberculosis's first antibiotic cure. Rutgers researchers published in January 1944, and from 1946 to 1948 Britain's Medical Research Council ran what is often cited as history's first randomized curative trial.

sources.author: Albert Schatz, Elizabeth Bugie, Selman A. Waksman

streptomycin-1943.detail: Rutgers soon worked with William Feldman and H. Corwin Hinshaw of the Mayo Clinic toward human trials. Streptomycin remains on WHO's List of Essential Medicines.

borlaug-mexico-wheat-program-1944.summary: Norman Borlaug arrives in Mexico in September 1944 to lead wheat research in the Rockefeller Foundation's cooperative program with the Mexican Ministry of Agriculture, when Mexico imports half its wheat and stem rust ruins harvests. He grows two generations a year by shuttling seed between Chapingo and Sonora's Yaqui Valley, 10 degrees of latitude and 2,600 meters apart, which breaks photoperiod sensitivity and yields widely adapted lines. Rust-resistant varieties make Mexico self-sufficient in wheat by 1956. After learning in late 1952 of Orville Vogel's Norin 10 crosses, Borlaug obtains seed in 1953 and releases semi-dwarf Pitic 62 and Penjamo 62 in 1962, which carry heavy fertilizer without lodging and later seed India and Pakistan.

sources.title: Lumpkin, T. A., 'How a Gene from Japan Revolutionized the World of Wheat', in Advances in Wheat Genetics: From Genome to Field (Springer, 2015)
sources.author: Lumpkin, Thomas A.

borlaug-mexico-wheat-program-1944.detail: Shuttle breeding defied received wisdom that seed should be bred where it will be grown; Borlaug's wide adaptation became central to CIMMYT, founded from the program in 1966. Jonathan Harwood's 2009 study in Agricultural History shows the early Rockefeller program served peasant farmers before turning to high-input varieties for commercial growers. Mexican wheat yields rose from about 750 kilograms per hectare in 1944 to over 3,000 by the 1970s.

picture.credit: Ben Zinner, USAID, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

jet-age-era-1944.summary: In 1944 jet aircraft first entered combat; by the 1950s jets carried passengers across oceans in hours. In civil aviation it reached Britain in 1952 with scheduled de Havilland Comet flights and America later that decade. De Havilland's Comet was history's first jet airliner to fly, in 1949, and its first to offer regular transatlantic service, in 1958, while Tupolev's Soviet Tu-104 was the only jet airliner operating anywhere between 1956 and 1958.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jet Age
'Messerschmitt Me 262 A-1a Schwalbe (Swallow)', National Air and Space Museum

sources.qualifies: Covers the Allied jet programme at the start of 1944, not the German Me 262's entry into combat later that year.

picture.credit: US Army Air Forces photo 342-FH-3A1971, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

colossus-computer-1944.summary: In 1944 Colossus began breaking German cipher traffic at Bletchley Park, the first electronic digital computer, kept secret for 30 years. It became operational in January and successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944. General Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers designed it from plans by mathematician Max Newman to break the Lorenz cipher, which German high command used for teleprinter traffic British codebreakers called Tunny. Using thermionic valves for Boolean and counting operations against message tapes read at 1,000 to 2,000 characters per second, Colossus is regarded as history's first programmable electronic digital computer.

sources.venue: Annals of the History of Computing

colossus-computer-1944.detail: Mark 2, five times faster, ran on 1 June 1944, in time for D-Day; ten machines were in use by war's end, and their existence stayed secret until the mid-1970s.

avery-macleod-mccarty-1944.summary: In 1944 Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA, not protein, carries heredity. Frederick Griffith had shown in 1928 that some "transforming principle" could change one pneumococcal type into another, and most scientists assumed proteins carried heredity. Treatments that destroyed protein or RNA did not eliminate the extract's transforming power, while a DNA-degrading preparation did. Acceptance came slowly; Erwin Chargaff's finding that base composition varies by species and Hershey and Chase's 1952 experiment moved geneticists to accept DNA as genetic material.

sources.author: Oswald T. Avery, Colin M. MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty

avery-macleod-mccarty-1944.detail: Phoebus Levene's tetranucleotide hypothesis had cast DNA as a dull repeating molecule.

picture.credit: Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, National Library of Medicine, Public domain, via National Library of Medicine

messerschmitt-me-262-1944.summary: In 1944 the Me 262 became the first jet fighter in service, reaching a trials unit in April and combat on 25 July, 100 miles an hour faster than anything Allied. Its design began in April 1939, and it first flew on jet power on 18 July 1942, but engine problems, metallurgy and interference from Göring and Hitler, who in 1943 demanded it be built as a high-speed bomber, delayed service. Among that war's most advanced combat aircraft, it proved an effective dogfighter; German pilots claimed 542 Allied aircraft, though shortages of strategic materials left it unreliable.

National Air and Space Museum, 'Messerschmitt Me 262 A-1a Schwalbe (Swallow)', collection object A19600328000
sources.author: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.confirms: The Me 262 was the first jet fighter to enter operational service, in 1944, and outpaced every Allied fighter.

sources.author: RAF Museum
sources.confirms: Me 262s were the first operational jet fighters to enter Luftwaffe service, in April 1944, and shortages of special metals and fuel limited them.

messerschmitt-me-262-1944.detail: Captured examples influenced North American's F-86 Sabre, Mikoyan's MiG-15 and Boeing's B-47 Stratojet.

harvard-mark-i-1944.summary: In May 1944 Harvard's Mark I began computing for the Navy; Grace Hopper programmed it. Howard Aiken had proposed it to IBM in November 1937, drawing on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, and IBM built it at Endicott, New York: 765,000 switches, relays, shafts and clutches in a frame 51 feet (15 metres) long, doing three additions per second and one multiplication in six seconds, reading instructions from 24-channel punched paper tape. Its first programs included John von Neumann's March 1944 check on implosion for the atomic bomb.

sources.title: Harvard Mark I - Wikipedia
'Mark I, Harvard', in Encyclopedia of Computer Science (Wiley, 2003)
sources.author: Encyclopedia of Computer Science
sources.confirms: The Harvard Mark I, originally the IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator, was the first large-scale automatic computer completed in the USA, unveiled in August 1944.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, 'Grace under pressure'
sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.confirms: Hopper went to Harvard's Cruft Laboratory to work on the Mark I under project director Howard Aiken.

sources.title: Chapter on Howard Aiken and the Harvard machines, in Springer volume on the history of computing, ch. 5
sources.author: Springer
sources.confirms: Aiken began planning an automatic computing machine at Harvard in 1937 to solve differential equations numerically.

harvard-mark-i-1944.detail: It had been shipped to Harvard in February 1944 and was officially presented there on August 7, 1944. Aiken's press release named himself sole inventor, enraging IBM chairman Thomas J. Watson. It was disassembled in 1959.

v2-rocket-1944.summary: In September 1944 Germany began firing V-2 rockets at London, history's first long-range guided ballistic missiles; the same rockets later reached space. Designated A4 by its builders, it ended a series of prototypes developed after Germany's Army noticed Wernher von Braun's graduate research; Hitler had ordered attacks to begin as soon as possible on 29 August 1944. From September 1944 the Wehrmacht launched more than 3,000 at Allied targets, first London and later Antwerp and Liège.

sources.title: Wikipedia: V-2 rocket
Neufeld, Michael J., The Rocket and the Reich: Peenemünde and the Coming of the Ballistic Missile Era (Harvard University Press, 1996)
sources.author: Neufeld, Michael J.
sources.venue: Free Press 1995; Harvard University Press paperback 1996
sources.confirms: The A-4/V-2 campaign against London and Antwerp began in September 1944 after development at Peenemünde.

sources.title: 'V-2 rocket', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: States that the A-4, developed under Wernher von Braun from 1936, was fired against Paris on 6 September 1944 and two days later began a campaign of more than 1,100 launches against Britain.
sources.qualifies: Places the first operational firing against Paris on 6 September, two days before the first against Britain.

v2-rocket-1944.detail: One rocket launched on 8 September caused modest damage near Porte d'Italie; that evening another, fired from The Hague, struck London. A 2011 BBC documentary estimated 9,000 deaths from these attacks and 12,000 forced laborers and camp prisoners killed building them.

picture.alt: V-2 rocket lifting off its launch stand at Peenemünde in a 1943 test, one year before combat use.
picture.credit: Bundesarchiv, Bild 146-1978-Anh.026-01, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons

chicago-convention-icao-1944.summary: In December 1944 fifty-two states signed the Chicago Convention, rules of the air that let airlines fly across borders. It set rules for airspace, aircraft registration, safety and security, and Article 1 gave every state complete and exclusive sovereignty over airspace above its territory. It established the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which came into being on April 4, 1947, after its 26th ratification on March 5, 1947; ICAO became a United Nations specialized agency that October.

Convention on International Civil Aviation, Doc 7300, signed at Chicago on 7 December 1944 (International Civil Aviation Organization)

chicago-convention-icao-1944.detail: Revised eight times since, it had 193 state parties as of March 2019, every UN member except Liechtenstein, which is covered through Switzerland.

operation-paperclip-1945.summary: From 1945 America brought 1,500 German scientists over, Wernher von Braun among them, under Joint Intelligence Objectives Agency oversight; their rockets took Americans to the Moon. As Allied armies advanced into Germany in 1945 they found research behind V-2 rockets, jet aircraft and other wartime advances; SHAEF's T-Force, set up in February 1945, examined 5,000 German targets. Washington wanted that expertise kept from neutral countries and, as Cold War tensions emerged, from the Soviet Union, and several recruits were confirmed former Nazi Party, SS or SA members.

Slayton, Rebecca, review of Jacobsen, 'Our Germans: Project Paperclip and the National Security State', Journal of American History 105, no. 4 (2019), 1078-1079
sources.author: Slayton, Rebecca
sources.confirms: The review states that more than 1,600 scientists and engineers from Nazi Germany came into the US national security state under Project Paperclip.

operation-paperclip-1945.detail: Beyond rocketry, Paperclip transferred aerodynamics and aviation medicine; von Braun's team at Redstone Arsenal turned V-2 technology into American missiles and launch vehicles. Valued at $10 billion in patents and processes, it remains controversial.

edvac-report-1945.summary: In June 1945 von Neumann's EDVAC report, circulated under his name alone, described a computer whose instructions sit in the same memory as its data, a design later called stored-program. This 101-page draft was incomplete; Goldstine circulated it more widely on 30 June. Distribution bred bitter acrimony: courts later ruled it a public disclosure that made EDVAC's patent unenforceable, and Moore School engineers argued that stored-program ideas predated von Neumann's consulting.

sources.author: von Neumann, John
sources.venue: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing
sources.confirms: The First Draft report, a first draft in the usual sense, had a pervasive influence when written and was cited by Turing as the definitive source on the design of the general-purpose digital computer.

sources.qualifies: Haigh and colleagues argue that the 'stored-program concept' is a later label and that the First Draft's influence should be described in terms of its specific ideas, not a single concept.

sources.author: Aspray, William
sources.confirms: Standard scholarly account of von Neumann's computing work including the EDVAC report; press page confirms the bibliographic data.

bush-as-we-may-think-1945.summary: In 1945 Vannevar Bush imagined the memex, a desk that stored everything a person read and linked it by association: hypertext in outline. It described a proposed personal device for storing and consulting records and linking related items through associative trails. Bush, who had directed America's wartime science effort, urged scientists turning to peacetime work to make humanity's growing store of knowledge accessible, since inventions had so far extended physical powers more than powers of mind. It anticipated hypertext, personal computers and online encyclopedias; Douglas Engelbart read it soon after publication and kept its memex in mind in work leading to the mouse and hyperlinks.

picture.credit: Office for Emergency Management, Library of Congress, Public domain, via Library of Congress

bush-science-endless-frontier-1945.summary: In 1945 Bush's Science, the Endless Frontier argued government should fund basic research; a National Science Foundation followed. Bush, who headed America's Office of Scientific Research and Development, which produced radar and proximity fuzes, answered that scientific progress was essential to national security, health, jobs and living standards, and proposed a National Research Foundation to fund university research. His centralized model shaped modern American science policy.

atomic-age-era-1945.summary: In July 1945 Trinity exploded the first nuclear weapon in New Mexico. Robert Oppenheimer named that test Trinity; New York Times journalist William L. Laurence, who witnessed it as Manhattan Project official journalist, wrote its first accounts and popularised talk of an atomic age. Early visions promised near-limitless power: science writer David Dietz foresaw cars running for a year on a vitamin-pill-sized pellet of atomic energy. By the late 1970s, though, nuclear power faced economic difficulties and public opposition, culminating in Three Mile Island in 1979 and Chernobyl in 1986.

trinity-nuclear-test-1945.summary: On 16 July 1945 America exploded the first atomic bomb in New Mexico, with explosive force of 25,000 tonnes of TNT. It detonated a plutonium implosion-design device yielding 25 kilotons of TNT. Its “gadget” shared its design with Fat Man, dropped on Nagasaki: following John von Neumann's September 1943 proposal, layers of faster and slower high explosives sent a single compressive wave into its plutonium core. President Truman wanted results before the Potsdam conference opened on July 16, so testing went ahead on that earliest date.

US Department of Energy, Office of Scientific and Technical Information, 'The Trinity Test, July 16, 1945', Manhattan Project History (OpenNet)
sources.author: US Department of Energy (after F. G. Gosling)
sources.confirms: The plutonium implosion device was detonated at 5:30 a.m. on 16 July 1945 with a calculated yield of 21 kilotons.

trinity-nuclear-test-1945.detail: Fired at 05:29 Mountain War Time in the Jornada del Muerto desert, on ground renamed White Sands Proving Ground just before, it was planned and directed by Kenneth Bainbridge. Some 425 people were present; its site became a National Historic Landmark in 1965.

picture.credit: Berlyn Brixner, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hiroshima-nagasaki-1945.summary: In August 1945 American atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing over 100,000. At about 8:15 a.m. the B-29 bomber Enola Gay released “Little Boy” over Hiroshima, where about 350,000 people were present that morning; President Truman then threatened further bombings unless Japan surrendered under his July 26 Potsdam Declaration, and “Fat Man” followed over Nagasaki. Japan accepted Potsdam's terms on August 15 and formally surrendered on September 2, 1945. These remain history's only uses of nuclear weapons in war.

One set puts deaths in subsequent months at 90,000 to 166,000 in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki, while Hiroshima City estimates about 140,000 dead there by December 1945 and about 74,000 in Nagasaki. Acute radiation effects, keloid scars and later disorders afflicted survivors, hibakusha, for decades.

clarke-geostationary-satellite-concept-1.summary: In 1945 Arthur C Clarke proposed satellites parked over the equator to relay radio worldwide; communications satellites orbit there today, above all for satellite television. Herman Potočnik had described such orbits in 1928, but Clarke expanded on them: a satellite in circular orbit 35,786 km above Earth's equator circles once per sidereal day, so it appears fixed in the sky and ground antennas never have to track it.

fao-founded-1945.summary: In October 1945 44 governments founded the Food and Agriculture Organization to lead international efforts against hunger and improve nutrition and food security. Its first conference, led by Sir John Boyd Orr, ran to 1 November 1945. It succeeded the International Institute of Agriculture, created in Rome in 1905, urged by Polish-born American agriculturalist David Lubin, and dissolved in 1948, when its functions passed to FAO.

fao-founded-1945.detail: Headquarters moved from Washington to Rome in 1951. FAO now has 194 members, 193 countries plus the European Union, and operates in over 130 countries.

ethiopian-airlines-founded-1945.summary: In December 1945 Ethiopia founded an airline managed by TWA; it became Africa's largest and most profitable carrier. Ethiopia's government provided its initial investment, and TWA managed it. Its first revenue scheduled service began on 8 April 1946, flying the Addis Ababa-Asmara-Cairo route. After Ethiopia's liberation, Emperor Haile Selassie I had asked the United States, Britain and France to help establish an airline as part of his modernisation effort. International flights began in 1951, Ethiopian staff took over management in 1971, and the carrier joined Star Alliance in December 2011.

ethiopian-airlines-founded-1945.detail: Ethiopia's government held all 25,000 shares, worth ETB 2.5 million, while American pilots, technicians and managers ran operations with five Douglas C-47 Skytrains bought from the US government. A February 1946 flight to Nairobi carrying East African currency preceded scheduled service.

macy-conferences-1946.summary: From 1946 the Macy conferences brought mathematicians, biologists and engineers together to study feedback and control: cybernetics. Warren McCulloch chaired them, with responsibility for seeing that disciplinary boundaries were crossed, and they brought together researchers to discuss feedback, circular causality, and biological and social systems. The first met on 8–9 March 1946; participants discussed research still in progress rather than finished papers, and widely circulated transcripts spread their conversation. Aiming at a general science of how human minds work, these meetings spawned breakthroughs in systems theory, cybernetics and what became cognitive science.

Frank and Frank Fremont-Smith of the Josiah Macy Jr. Foundation motivated this series, whose first meeting was titled “Feedback Mechanisms and Circular Causal Systems in Biological and Social Systems.” Participants included Claude Shannon, Margaret Mead, Gregory Bateson and Walter Pitts.

telephone-half-1946.summary: In 1946 half of American homes had a telephone, 70 years after Bell's first call, a slower spread than any other great invention. Its diffusion ran slowest of all: a tenth of homes in 1903, a half in 1946, more than nine in ten by 1990.

tupperware-1946.summary: In 1946 Earl Tupper moulded his first airtight polyethylene container; sold at home parties from 1948, it put plastic in every kitchen. His airtight, food-safe plastic containers were aimed at consumers. From 1951, with former Stanley Home Products saleswoman Brownie Wise as vice president of Tupperware Home Parties, Tupperware sold mainly through home “Tupperware parties”, promoted since 1948, which let women of the 1950s earn income without holding a regular job; parties reached Europe in 1960. Parent company Tupperware Brands filed for bankruptcy in September 2024, and Party Products LLC, formed by its lenders, bought the brand that November.

volta-redonda-csn-1946.summary: In 1946 Brazil's state steelworks at Volta Redonda, in Rio de Janeiro state, began production with American wartime loans under President Eurico Gaspar Dutra, initially making coke, pig iron castings and long products. Brazil and America had agreed, in the Washington Accords, that its Presidente Vargas Steelworks would supply steel to Allied forces in World War II and support Brazil's development afterward. Brazil's government privatized it in 1993 and early 1994, and CSN is now Brazil's largest fully integrated steel producer.

eniac-1946.summary: In 1946 ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, appeared, a thousand times faster than any rival. John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert had designed the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer to calculate artillery firing tables for the Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory, under a contract signed on 5 June 1943, though its first program studied a thermonuclear weapon's feasibility. It weighed more than 30 tons, consumed 150 kW and cost $487,000.

Its six primary programmers, including Kay McNulty and Ruth Lichterman, learned to trace bugs to single failed tubes. Moved to Aberdeen Proving Ground in 1947, it ran until 1955.

mobile-telephone-service-1946.summary: In June 1946 the first car telephone service opened in St Louis; a handful of calls at a time could be made from the road. Bell System's service needed operators in both directions: landline callers reached a mobile operator who announced each call over its shared channel, and mobile users asked that operator to place outgoing calls. Improved Mobile Telephone Service replaced it from 1964, though MTS stayed in use in places into the 1980s.

bikini-atoll-operation-crossroads-1946.summary: In February 1946 US Navy Commodore Ben Wyatt asked 167 Bikinians to leave their atoll 'for the good of mankind'; they were moved to Rongerik, where they nearly starved, and later to Kili. On 1 July 1946 Test Able dropped a 23-kiloton bomb over 95 target ships in Bikini lagoon, and on 25 July Test Baker exploded underwater, drenching fleet in radioactive spray that could not be decontaminated. Shurcliff's official 1947 report recorded results; Weisgall's history documents how Baker's contamination surprised planners. Bikini hosted 23 nuclear tests through 1958, including Castle Bravo. Niedenthal's 1997 account traces islanders' displacement, brief return in 1970s, re-evacuation in 1978 and continued exile.

bikini-atoll-operation-crossroads-1946.detail: Crossroads was staged for press and foreign observers to show atomic weapons against navies; 42,000 personnel took part. Radiation safety chief Stafford Warren halted work after Baker because of plutonium contamination. Bikinians received compensation through a trust fund and Nuclear Claims Tribunal awards, most unpaid. Marshall Islands Compact of Free Association in 1986 settled claims against US while leaving health and resettlement questions open. Bikini became UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010.

atomic-energy-act-1946.summary: In 1946 America put the atom under civilian control in a new Atomic Energy Commission; the bomb's makers answered to civilians, though a Military Liaison Committee kept considerable military influence. When it took effect on January 1, 1947, this Commission took over from the Manhattan Project. Its control-of-information section made all data on weapon design “restricted data,” classified from birth. By cutting off nuclear information to other countries it opened a rift with Britain and Canada, Manhattan Project partners, and pushed Britain to build its own weapons.

atomic-energy-act-1946.detail: Senator Brien McMahon of Connecticut sponsored it after scientists, Leo Szilard and Harold Urey among them, attacked an earlier May-Johnson bill for leaving room for military administrators. Senators passed it by unanimous voice vote, representatives by 265 to 79, and President Truman signed it on August 1, 1946. A 1954 amendment under Atoms for Peace opened private nuclear development.

celorio-tortilla-machine-1947.summary: In 1947 Mexican inventor Fausto Celorio receives Mexican patent 45,792 for a machine that presses masa into discs and carries them on a conveyor belt through a gas-fired cooking tunnel, as a later US patent in this lineage describes. Earlier machines from 1904 had cut and cooked tortillas but jammed on dough; Celorio's rollers and continuous belt made production reliable. He built about one machine a month in the early 1950s, then forty a week in partnership with Alfonso Gandara, and in 1963 introduced a duplex model producing 132 kg an hour. Corner tortillerias with clattering belts became part of Mexican urban life, and machines like his are exported across the Americas.

first-computer-bug-1947.summary: In 1947 operators of Harvard's Mark II traced a fault to a moth in a relay and taped it into the log as the first actual case of a bug. They removed it and taped it into their log book with this note: “First actual case of bug being found.” Engineers had called defects bugs long before electronic computers; Thomas Edison used it in an 1878 letter. Hopper, later a U.S. Navy rear admiral, popularized her moth story, and that log page is remembered as computing's first literal bug, though that word came first.

houssay-pituitary-nobel-1947.summary: In 1947 Bernardo Alberto Houssay shared a Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work done at Universidad de Buenos Aires's Instituto de Fisiología since 1924: removing anterior pituitary tissue from dogs made with diabetes by pancreatectomy relieved their diabetes, and pituitary extracts caused it. These experiments, published with Alfredo Biasotti from 1930, showed that a pituitary hormone opposed insulin and placed hormonal regulation of carbohydrate metabolism on an experimental footing. Houssay's institute trained a generation including Luis Leloir and Eduardo Braun-Menéndez. Dismissed from his chair in 1943 by a military government, he worked on at a privately funded institute until reinstatement in 1955.

No Latin American scientist had received a science Nobel before; Leloir, his student, followed in 1970. He founded Argentina's research council CONICET in 1958.

microwave-oven-1947.summary: In 1947 Raytheon sold the first microwave oven after radar melted an engineer's chocolate bar; it cost $5,000 and weighed 340 kilograms. Percy Spencer, Raytheon's self-taught engineer from Maine, had noticed in 1945 that microwaves from an active radar set melted his pocketed candy bar; microwave ovens feed magnetron power into a closed metal box, where it makes polar molecules in food rotate and produce heat (dielectric heating), and Raytheon filed for a patent on his cooking process on October 8, 1945. Tappan sold a licensed home model in 1956, and Raytheon, which bought Amana in 1965, introduced countertop ovens in 1967.

tukey-bit-1947.summary: In 1947 John Tukey coined the word bit for a binary digit, information theory's unit of information since. Claude Shannon's 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" first used it in print, crediting Tukey. Tukey is also credited with first using "software" for computer programs, in his 1958 American Mathematical Monthly article, and is best known for the Cooley–Tukey algorithm for computing Fourier transforms, developed with James Cooley.

woomera-range-1947.summary: In 1947 Britain and Australia set up a rocket range at Woomera, the Western world's largest land test range. Britain was too densely populated to test safely, so it asked Australia for a sparsely peopled site offering long firing corridors. Under their Anglo-Australian Joint Project of 1946, Woomera in South Australia was declared a prohibited area in 1947, an RAF Dakota landed at its airfield on 19 June 1947, and its first trial ran that December. Missile testing began in 1949, and Australia's first satellite, WRESAT, went up from Woomera in 1967, making Australia the fourth nation to orbit a satellite from its own territory.

automation-term-ford-1947.summary: In April 1947 Ford set up an Automation Department, and the word entered English; within ten years it named a national anxiety. Harder is credited with coining “automation.” Five staff grew to fifty within a year, working first on engines and later on sheet metal, wheels, axles and frames; relay controls modernized transfer lines that moved engine blocks between machining stages. Usage spread widely after John Diebold's 1952 book Automation: The Advent of the Automatic Factory; American audiences were fixated on this new word for nearly two decades after 1947.

doomsday-clock-1947.summary: In 1947 atomic scientists set the Doomsday Clock at seven minutes to midnight, a gauge of how close humanity stood to destruction. Manhattan Project scientists in Chicago had founded that magazine in 1945, and Langsdorf, whose husband Alexander Langsdorf Jr. had worked on that project, chose a clock to convey urgency: midnight stands for human-made global catastrophe, and she set its hands at seven minutes to midnight. Its publishers have reset it 27 times since, as far back as 17 minutes in 1991 and, in 2026, to 85 seconds, its closest setting yet.

pulqui-jet-1947.summary: On August 9, 1947 Argentina flew the Pulqui I prototype, the first jet designed and built in Argentina and in Latin America, with test pilot First Lieutenant Osvaldo Weiss at its controls. Designed in 1946 at Argentina's Instituto Aerotécnico by engineers led by Frenchman Émile Dewoitine, it carried a Rolls-Royce Derwent 5 turbojet with its air intake in its nose; ducting around its cockpit left so little fuselage room that fuel tanks went into its wings, cutting range. Only one was completed, its performance was judged unsatisfactory, and work shifted to the more advanced Pulqui II.

bell-x1-sound-barrier-1947.summary: In October 1947 Chuck Yeager flew Bell's X-1 faster than sound; the barrier was a myth and supersonic flight followed. His aircraft, nicknamed Glamorous Glennis for his wife, was rocket-powered and shaped like a .50-caliber machine gun bullet, known to be stable at supersonic speed; it was drop launched from a B-29 bomber's bomb bay and glided down to a dry lake bed once its engine burned out. News stayed secret until Aviation Week and the Los Angeles Times reported it in December 1947.

bell-x1-sound-barrier-1947.detail: Larry Bell, Yeager and NACA's John Stack won 1948's Collier Trophy.

picture.credit: NASA Langley Research Center, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cellular-concept-1947.summary: In 1947 a Bell Labs memo proposed splitting a city into cells with their own transmitters so frequencies could be reused: mobile networks. In such a network, service territory is divided into cells, each served by its own base station, and a switching system developed by Amos Joel at Bell Labs lets many callers share one frequency by handing calls to the nearest tower with that frequency free, so scarce radio spectrum is reused across cells. Japan's NTT launched history's first commercial cellular network in Tokyo in 1979; regulatory battles delayed AT&T's commercial service until 1983.

sources.title: Cellular network (Wikipedia)
V. H. MacDonald, 'Advanced Mobile Phone Service: The Cellular Concept', Bell System Technical Journal 58 (1979), 15-41
sources.author: V. H. MacDonald
sources.confirms: Describes frequency reuse, cell splitting and hexagonal cell geometry as implemented in AMPS.
sources.qualifies: Does not itself date the idea to 1947.

sources.author: Young, W. R.
sources.confirms: Bell System history of mobile radio preceding AMPS, outlining the cellular concept and the events and legal decisions that led to it.

cellular-concept-1947.detail: The Bell System ran cellular networks in Chicago and Dallas before 1979; Illinois Bell offered its commercial service in 1983.

transistor-1947.summary: In 1947 Bell Labs demonstrated the transistor, a switch with no moving parts, the building block of every chip. John Bardeen, Brattain and William Shockley had built on wartime work to make ultra-pure germanium for radar diodes; two gold contacts pressed very close together onto germanium made it amplify, and in that trial it worked as a speech amplifier with power gain of 18. Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared 1956's Nobel Prize in Physics, and transistors went on to replace vacuum tube triodes.

sources.author: Computer History Museum

sources.title: 'The Nobel Prize in Physics 1956', NobelPrize.org

sources.confirms: Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain shared the 1956 physics prize for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect.

transistor-1947.detail: John R. Pierce's name “transistor” won Bell's internal ballot over “Crystal Triode” and others; Shockley's improved junction transistor of 1948 entered production in the early 1950s.

picture.alt: Replica of Bell Labs' 1947 point-contact transistor, a germanium slab under a plastic wedge, beside a later 2N43 transistor, photographed 2019
picture.credit: Mister rf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cable-television-origins-1948.summary: In 1948 towns with no reception put an antenna on a hill and ran cable to homes; cable television began as a fix for mountains. They put large antennas on hills and mountaintops and ran coaxial trunk lines from them, to which homes in the community below connected. Local cable networks had relayed broadcasts before, in London (Rediffusion) and Berlin in 1936, and Switzerland also began in 1948, but in the United States cable grew into a commercial business in the 1950s. By 1968, 6.4 percent of American households had cable service, rising to 62.4 percent in 1994.

Tabron, Sheila, 'Community Antenna Television and the Law', North Carolina Central Law Review (1979)
sources.author: Tabron, Sheila

sources.qualifies: It describes homes connecting to a trunk line rather than cable running directly from the antenna to each home.

sources.author: Editors, Britannica

cable-television-origins-1948.detail: Penetration reached 52.8 percent in 1988, and cable systems later carried FM radio, high-speed internet and telephone service.

cybernetics-book-1948.summary: In 1948 Norbert Wiener published Cybernetics, naming the study of feedback and control in animals and machines. He traced its ideas to Harvard Medical School meetings where physicians discussed method with mathematicians and engineers, and to his work with Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer.

sources.title: Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine
Mindell, David A., '1948: Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics', in A New Literary History of America (Harvard University Press, 2012), pp. 795-799
sources.author: Mindell, David A.
sources.confirms: Wiener's Cybernetics (1948) defined control and communication in animal and machine and became an unexpected bestseller.

sources.title: Wiener, Norbert, 'Cybernetics', Scientific American 179 (November 1948) 14-19
sources.author: Wiener, Norbert
sources.confirms: Wiener's own 1948 popular statement of cybernetics.

cybernetics-book-1948.detail: Public interest led Wiener to write The Human Use of Human Beings for general readers in 1950, and its second edition, with two added chapters, appeared in 1961.

ghawar-oil-field-1948.summary: In 1948 Ghawar was found in Saudi Arabia, the largest oil field on Earth; it has produced more than half of Saudi oil since. Measuring about 280 by 30 kilometres (some 8,400 square kilometres), it is by far the world's largest conventional oil field and is owned and operated by Saudi Aramco, the state oil company. Roughly 60 to 65 percent of all Saudi oil produced between 1948 and 2000 came from Ghawar, and cumulative output passed 65 billion barrels by early 2010.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghawar Field
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Al-Ghawar'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Al-Ghawar, discovered in 1948, is the world's largest conventional oil field, running about 260 km north to south.

sources.title: Arabian American Oil Company staff, 'Ghawar Oil Field, Saudi Arabia', AAPG Bulletin 43, no. 2 (1959): 434-454
sources.author: Arabian American Oil Company staff
sources.confirms: Reports that Ghawar was discovered in 1948 by a wildcat well at Ain Dar and that later wildcats proved one accumulation along at least 140 miles of the En Nala anticline.
sources.qualifies: Gives a 1959 conservative estimate of 875 square miles for the oil accumulation, smaller than the roughly 8,400 square kilometres the record cites from later measurements.

ghawar-oil-field-1948.detail: Aramco's 2019 bond prospectus put its maximum at 3.8 million barrels per day, below earlier outside estimates of more than 5 million. Since 1965 operators have pumped in seawater to sustain production (waterflooding), reportedly around 7 million barrels of water per day.

grey-walter-tortoises-1949.summary: In 1949 Grey Walter built Elmer and Elsie, robot tortoises that sought light and avoided obstacles with two brain cells' worth of circuitry. He wanted to show that rich connections among a small number of brain cells could produce very complex behavior, that is, that how a brain worked lay in how it was wired. Three-wheeled and slow, hence nicknamed tortoises, they steered toward light (phototaxis) and could find their way to a recharging station when batteries ran low.

sources.title: William Grey Walter
Walter, W. Grey, "An Imitation of Life"
sources.author: W. Grey Walter
sources.confirms: Walter's own description of Elmer and Elsie, the light-seeking, obstacle-avoiding tortoises built with two valves; Crossref record confirmed, page text not read.

sources.title: Holland, Owen, 'Exploration and high adventure: the legacy of Grey Walter', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 361, no. 1811 (2003): 2085-2121
sources.author: Owen Holland
sources.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A
sources.confirms: Detailed peer-reviewed study of Walter's tortoises, their design principles and their 1948-51 construction, from the researcher who rebuilt them.

grey-walter-tortoises-1949.detail: Walter mounted a light on one robot's nose and let it approach a mirror. It “began flickering,” he wrote, “twittering, and jigging like a clumsy Narcissus,” and he argued that, had animals shown such behavior, it might be accepted as evidence of some degree of self-awareness.

information-theory-1948.summary: In 1948 Claude Shannon defined information as bits and set limits on what any channel can carry; every modem rests on it. It introduced channel capacity, entropy and redundancy, and the bit as its unit, a name Shannon credited to John Tukey.

sources.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
Shannon, C. E., 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication', Bell System Technical Journal 27 (1948), pp. 379-423
sources.author: Shannon, Claude E.

sources.author: Verdu, Sergio
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed retrospective on Shannon's 1948 paper and the theory it founded; Crossref confirms the bibliographic data (IEEE page would not open).

information-theory-1948.detail: Its 1949 book version appeared as The Mathematical Theory of Communication, its new definite article marking its generality, and included Warren Weaver's overview for general readers.

picture.alt: Claude Shannon at his desk at MIT in September 1958, ten years after A Mathematical Theory of Communication
picture.credit: MIT Photo Service, MIT Museum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

polaroid-instant-camera-1948.summary: In 1948 Edwin Land's Model 95 went on sale, the first camera to hand over a finished print a minute after its shutter clicked. His Model 95 Land Camera, introduced in 1948, a year after he unveiled instant film in New York City, is often called history's first commercial instant camera. It used roll film loaded as two rolls, one holding its negative and another its positive and developing agent, so that pictures developed inside the camera rather than in darkrooms. Polaroid filed for bankruptcy in February 2008 and stopped making instant film, but the Impossible Project took over one of its factories that year and revived film for its cameras.

sources.author: Land, Edwin H.
sources.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America
sources.confirms: Land's 1947 paper describing the one-step process sold in the Model 95 camera from November 1948.
