adaline-1960.summary: In 1960 Widrow and Hoff built ADALINE, a neuron that learned by adjusting weights to reduce error, a rule that still trains networks. Based on the perceptron, it was an early single-layer neural network built as a physical device, its weights set by rheostats and later memistors; it differed from Rosenblatt’s perceptron in how it learned. ADALINE found wide use in adaptive signal processing, especially filtering noise.

irri-founded-1960.summary: In 1960 Ford and Rockefeller foundations, with Philippine government, set up International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) on University of Philippines campus at Los Banos, Laguna, to apply plant breeding and agronomy to Asia's staple grain. Breeders crossed Indonesian tall variety Peta with Taiwanese dwarf Dee-geo-woo-gen and released IR8 in 1966, a short-strawed, fertiliser-responsive rice that doubled yields where irrigation allowed. IRRI trained thousands of Asian scientists and seeded national programmes from Indonesia to Vietnam. Nick Cullather's history places its founding within Cold War food politics and American development thinking as much as within agronomy.

loeb-sourirajan-reverse-osmosis-1960.summary: Charles Reid at the University of Florida had shown in the 1950s that dense cellulose acetate films reject salt under pressure, but flow through them was far too slow to matter. At UCLA, Sidney Loeb and Srinivasa Sourirajan cast cellulose acetate from an acetone solution with magnesium perchlorate, quenched it in ice water and annealed it in hot water. The result, reported in UCLA Engineering Report 60-60 in July 1960, was an asymmetric membrane with a thin dense skin on a porous support that passed ten times more water at the same salt rejection. Their 1963 paper gave 5 to 11 gallons per square foot per day of 0.05 percent salt water from a 5.25 percent brine. Spiral-wound and thin-film composite membranes built on this work supply most desalinated water today, including Sorek in Israel.

scarp-tubewells-indus-salinity-1960.summary: Canal irrigation in West Pakistan raised water tables until salt crust spread over fields. From 1960-61 WAPDA runs Salinity Control and Reclamation Project 1 in Rechna Doab, pumping groundwater with large public tubewells to lower water tables, flush salts and add irrigation supply. A WAPDA master plan calls for 31,000 tubewells across 26 project areas covering 30 million acres. A White House panel under Roger Revelle, reporting in 1964, endorses vertical drainage by tubewells in million-acre blocks. Ghulam Mohammad's 1964 analysis in Pakistan Development Review weighs public against private wells; farmers soon sink private tubewells by the hundred thousand, and groundwater pumping becomes central to Punjab farming.

shuwaikh-msf-desalination-kuwait-1960.summary: Kuwait had shipped drinking water by dhow from Shatt al-Arab until Westinghouse submerged-tube stills began at Shuwaikh in 1953 and a four-stage flash evaporator followed in 1957. Robert Silver, chief engineer at Weir in Glasgow, patents in 1957 a multi-stage flash process in which heated brine passes through many low-pressure chambers, each flashing vapour that condenses on tubes carrying incoming seawater. Weir Westgarth builds two units of 4,546 cubic metres a day at Shuwaikh with 19 stages and a performance ratio of 5.6, commissioned in 1960 alongside a smaller Guernsey plant. Within a decade Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Qatar pair MSF stills with power stations, and this design supplies most Gulf municipal water until reverse osmosis spreads after 2000.

sr52-hybrid-maize-1960.summary: In 1960 breeders at Salisbury Research Station released SR52, a single-cross hybrid maize developed from a programme H. C. Arnold began in 1932. Single-cross hybrids are made from two inbred lines rather than four, giving uniform, higher-yielding plants; SR52 reached commercial farmers before comparable hybrids anywhere and yielded about 46 percent more than open-pollinated varieties in trials. White commercial farms adopted it first; smallholders in Zimbabwe took it up after 1972, when seed and credit reached communal areas, and it spread to Zambia, Malawi and Kenya. Zimbabwe's post-independence smallholder maize surge of the 1980s rested on SR52 and its successors.

Southern Rhodesia's breeding programme worked alongside maize research at Salisbury from 1932 and shared inbred lines with Kenya's Kitale station. Smallholder uptake in Zimbabwe's communal areas depended on hybrid seed sales through Seed Co-op, credit from Agricultural Finance Corporation and depot expansion after 1980, which together drove a maize surplus in good years.

television-majority-1960.summary: By 1960 87 percent of American homes had a television, more than had a bathtub; the set had become furniture in a decade. More households owned a set than an automobile or a telephone (41.6 million each), a washing machine (39 million) or air conditioning (6.6 million). By 1965 it was 93 percent.

singapore-hdb-founded-1960.summary: Singapore's new self-governing administration sets up its Housing and Development Board on 1 February 1960 under Lim Kim San, replacing a colonial trust that had built about 23,000 units in 32 years. HDB completes 54,430 flats in its first five years, rehouses squatters after a 1961 Bukit Ho Swee fire, and from 1964 sells 99-year leases that buyers pay for with Central Provident Fund savings. Chua Beng Huat's analysis shows how state land acquisition, compulsory savings and ethnic quotas made home ownership a tool of governance. By 2020 about 80 percent of residents live in HDB estates and roughly nine in ten of those own their flat.

reggane-gerboise-bleue-1960.summary: On 13 February 1960 France exploded a 70-kiloton plutonium device near Reggane in southern Algeria, during Algeria's war of independence. Three more atmospheric shots followed at Reggane and thirteen underground tests at In Ekker until 1966; Evian accords of 1962 let testing continue after independence. African governments protested: Nigeria expelled France's ambassador in January 1961, and Ghana convened a positive action conference. Fallout and buried waste remain contested between Algiers and Paris. Roxanne Panchasi places these tests inside colonial war rather than apart from it.

reggane-gerboise-bleue-1960.detail: Debate over French tests became Nigeria's first foreign-policy quarrel before formal independence. France evacuated Reggane and In Ekker in 1967; health and environmental effects have lasted. Algerian, Moroccan, Nigerian and Ghanaian press reactions and Frantz Fanon's commentary set Saharan tests alongside Algeria's independence struggle. France's 2010 compensation law has recognised few Algerian claimants, and Algeria still seeks maps of waste burial sites.

It described close cooperation between people and computers, with people setting goals and evaluating results while computers handled routinizable work.

tiros-1-weather-satellite-1960.summary: In April 1960 TIROS-1 sent back the first television pictures of clouds from orbit. It operated for 75 days until June 15, 1960 and returned 23,000 television pictures of cloud cover, 19,000 of them usable for weather analysis, opening an era of satellite storm tracking.

He warned that a machine whose action is too swift and irrevocable for people to intervene must be given a purpose that is what they want, not some colourful imitation of it.

laser-ruby-maiman-1960.summary: In May 1960 Maiman fired the first laser, a flash-pumped ruby rod; its beam now cuts steel, reads discs and carries the internet. His design pumped its synthetic ruby rod with a flashtube, with mirrors at each end bouncing light back through it until it emerged as pulses of coherent deep red light at 694.3 nanometres.

After 1954's Atomic Energy Act let private companies own reactors, Commonwealth Edison had contracted General Electric in 1955 to build its 192 MWe unit for 45 million dollars; it ran until 1978.

It carried no electronics; that day microwaves sent from JPL's Goldstone facility in California were reflected off its surface to Bell Laboratories at Holmdel, New Jersey.

It is an intergovernmental body often called a cartel, though Colgan finds little or no effect on members' output. Its members, now eleven, produced 38 percent of world oil in 2022 and hold an estimated 79.5 percent of proven reserves.

indus-waters-treaty-1960.summary: Nehru and Ayub Khan signed Indus Waters Treaty in Karachi on 19 September 1960 after nine years of World Bank mediation. India received unrestricted use of eastern rivers Ravi, Beas and Sutlej; Pakistan received western rivers Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, with India allowed limited non-consumptive and run-of-river uses. An Indus Basin Development Fund paid for Mangla and Tarbela dams and link canals that moved western river water to lands formerly fed from eastern rivers cut off at Partition. A Permanent Indus Commission handles data and disputes. The treaty survived three wars; India placed it in abeyance in April 2025 after Pahalgam attack.

dimona-reactor-disclosed-1960.summary: On 21 December 1960 David Ben-Gurion tells Knesset that Israel is building a 24 megawatt research reactor near Dimona 'for peaceful purposes', days after American intelligence and press identify a secret site in Negev. France had agreed in 1957 to supply a heavy-water reactor and, in unwritten protocols, a reprocessing plant; Saint-Gobain engineers and some 2,500 French staff work at site from 1958. Reactor reaches criticality by 1963 or 1964 and plutonium separation follows. Dimona becomes core of a weapons programme Israel neither confirms nor denies, a posture fixed in Nixon-Meir understandings of 1969. It also sets template for later regional reactor projects and strikes, from Osirak to Bushehr.

agent-orange-vietnam-1961.summary: From 1961 to 1971, under Operation Ranch Hand, American C-123 aircraft and helicopters sprayed herbicides over forests and crops in South Vietnam to strip cover from guerrilla routes and deny food. A 2003 reconstruction of flight records raised earlier estimates by more than seven million litres, to roughly 77 million litres, and put dioxin (TCDD) contamination in Agent Orange at almost double prior figures. Application rates exceeded domestic weed control by more than an order of magnitude. Vietnamese communities near sprayed zones and former airbases such as Da Nang and Bien Hoa carry elevated dioxin exposure, and veterans' health claims led to US Institute of Medicine reviews from 1994.

Hydraulically driven and programmable, with five degrees of freedom, its 4,000-pound arm moved die castings and welded parts on car bodies.

It reported 5,400,000 people out of work, noted that 50 Census Bureau staff had done tabulations that took 4,100 statisticians in 1950, and said Labor Secretary Arthur Goldberg had set up a special group to find how much technological change was to blame.

vostok-1-gagarin-1961.summary: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, circling Earth once in 108 minutes. Vostok 1 launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome and his orbit peaked at 327 kilometres. He was first to reach orbital velocity and complete an orbit of Earth. His single orbit peaked at 327 kilometres and took 108 minutes from launch to landing; Gagarin ejected at 7 kilometres and parachuted down separately from his capsule. His flight beat America’s Project Mercury to the first human spaceflight.

United Nations experts were appointed to run it alongside local officers, and it was fully operational by 24 November; EDB offered free advice to electrical industries, spearheaded development works at the 9,000 acre Jurong industrial estate and in 1962 began courting overseas industrialists, starting with Japan.

Designed by KB-11 for 100 megatons and backed by Nikita Khrushchev in July 1961, it dwarfed America's largest test, Castle Bravo, at 15 megatons.

thalidomide-scandal-1961.summary: In 1961 thalidomide, a sedative sold to pregnant women, was tied by William McBride in Lancet and Widukind Lenz in Germany to over 10,000 babies born with severe malformations, many of limbs. Drug testing laws were rewritten. Sold from 1957 as a sedative and for morning sickness without testing on pregnant women, it had been prescribed in 46 countries. FDA reviewer Frances Oldham Kelsey had kept it off America's market, and this scandal led to stronger drug regulation in many countries.

It popularized “global village,” his term for mass communication letting a village-like mindset apply worldwide.

ogas-1962.summary: In 1962 Viktor Glushkov proposed OGAS, a nationwide computer network to run the Soviet economy; it was never built. Anatoly Kitov’s similar plan had been rejected in 1959 over military objections to sharing data with civilian planners. OGAS called for a computer centre in Moscow, 100 to several hundred regional centres, and up to 20,000 local centres at firms and organisations, communicating live over existing and new telephone lines; its draft reached government in 1964. Costed at no less than 100 billion rubles, it was denied funding in 1970.

rinderpest-tcrv-muguga-1962.summary: Walter Plowright and R. D. Ferris at Muguga, Kenya passed Kabete O rinderpest virus about ninety times through calf kidney cell cultures from 1956 and published a stable attenuated vaccine in 1962. Tissue culture rinderpest vaccine gave lifelong immunity from one dose, could be produced in bulk and did not spread. Joint Project 15, launched in 1961 and run 1962 to 1979 across 22 countries at a cost near USD 16 million, vaccinated hundreds of millions of cattle and drove rinderpest out of most of Africa. After a 1980s resurgence and renewed campaigns, Kenya saw its last outbreak in 2001 and global eradication was declared on 28 June 2011.

Rinderpest had crossed Africa in 1890s, killing most cattle and wildlife from Eritrea to the Cape and causing famine. JP15 campaigns moved west to east, then OAU's Pan-African Rinderpest Campaign from 1986 and a Global Rinderpest Eradication Programme from 1994 finished work with thermostable vaccine variants.

rogers-diffusion-of-innovations-1962.summary: In 1962 Everett Rogers showed that every new idea spreads along a bell curve from innovators to laggards. It sorts adopters into innovators (2.5 percent), early adopters (13.5 percent), early majority (34), late majority (34) and laggards (16), and shows cumulative adoption tracing an S-shaped curve. By the mid-2000s it ranked second among most-cited social science books.

From mid-1962 its public-domain code spread to other universities and institutions among a few dozen PDP-1 installations and was recreated elsewhere; it was the first video game played at multiple computer installations and directly inspired later games, including the first commercial arcade game.

Earlier carrier systems multiplexed analog calls by frequency division; T1 instead digitized voice with pulse-code modulation and time-division multiplexing at 1.544 megabits per second. Later T2 and T3 carried multiples of that rate.

cuba-polio-mass-vaccination-1962.summary: Between 26 February and 4 March 1962 Cuba's health ministry delivered Sabin oral polio vaccine to about 87.5 percent of children aged one month to fourteen years, using Committees for Defense of the Revolution, Federation of Cuban Women and farmers' associations to map households and hand out doses. A second round followed in April. Cuba had recorded 3,939 paralytic cases from 1932 to 1961 and 342 cases in a 1961 epidemic; after 1962 no epidemic recurred, and annual campaigns in two short rounds became routine. Pan American Health Organization declared Cuba polio-free in 1994 alongside the rest of the Americas. The campaign showed that a mass, time-limited oral vaccine drive could interrupt transmission, a model later used in national immunisation days elsewhere.

cuba-polio-mass-vaccination-1962.detail: MEDICC Review's history gives campaign dates, coverage and case counts; Más Lago's WHO Bulletin paper reviews surveillance and the later eradication certification. Earlier Soviet trials of Sabin vaccine on a national scale in 1959 to 1960 preceded Cuba's. Cuba's approach differed from routine clinic immunisation used in United States and Western Europe: whole age cohorts received drops within days, so virus found few susceptible hosts. Vaccine came from Soviet Union after Cuba's 1961 break with Washington. PAHO later adopted national immunisation days as a central tactic of its 1985 regional polio eradication drive.

telstar-1-1962.summary: In July 1962 Telstar relayed transatlantic live television, a first; events could be watched on two continents at once. Unlike 1958’s SCORE, a passive reflector, it amplified signals before relaying them. On July 23 at 3:00 p.m. EDT it carried the first publicly available live transatlantic signal, shown by Eurovision in Europe and NBC, CBS, ABC and CBC in North America. Radiation from Starfish Prime, a nuclear test, killed it after seven months.

Prompted by USDA’s 1957 aerial spraying against fire ants, it documented harm from indiscriminate use of DDT and other synthetic pesticides and accused chemical companies of disinformation. Despite fierce industry opposition it swayed public opinion, led to a nationwide ban on DDT for agriculture and fed a movement that produced America's Environmental Protection Agency.

Before his term ended in 1964 he had set in motion computer science departments at several universities, time-sharing and networking, and his promotion of networking inspired ARPANET by decade’s end.

engelbart-augmenting-human-intellect-196.summary: In 1962 Engelbart proposed using computers to augment human intellect rather than replace it; the mouse and windowed screens came from it. By augmenting intellect he meant “increasing the capability of a man to approach a complex problem situation, to gain comprehension to suit his particular needs, and to derive solutions to problems.” His hypothesis: intellectual effectiveness could be significantly improved by redesigning changeable components of systems people work within, their language, artifacts, methodology and training, with computers handling symbols; SRI was already turning his recommendations into experimental research plans.

Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework - 1962 ...

led-holonyak-1962.summary: In October 1962 Nick Holonyak made the first visible LED, a red one, at General Electric. It emitted coherent visible light at low temperatures and functioned at room temperature as an LED, forerunner of first-generation commercial light-emitting diodes.

kefauver-harris-amendment-1962.summary: In 1962, after thalidomide, America for the first time required drug makers to prove a medicine effective as well as safe before marketing it; advertising had to disclose side effects, and generics could no longer be sold as costly new “breakthrough” medicines.

cuban-missile-crisis-1962.summary: In October 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers within days of nuclear war; a hotline and test ban followed. After U-2 spy planes photographed Soviet missile sites in Cuba, matching US Jupiter missiles placed in Italy and Turkey in 1961, President Kennedy rejected advice to bomb and invade and ordered a naval blockade on 22 October. Kennedy and Khrushchev then agreed: Soviet missiles left Cuba under UN verification, Washington pledged not to invade and secretly agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey.

ascii-1963.summary: In 1963 ASCII assigned a seven-bit code to each letter and symbol; computers could exchange text, and the standard lives inside Unicode. Unlike earlier telegraph codes such as Baudot, it was ordered for convenient sorting; the 1963 edition left 28 code positions unassigned, lowercase letters came in later revisions, and today it encodes 128 code points in seven bits, 95 printable characters and 33 control characters.

intergalactic-network-1963.summary: In 1963 Licklider wrote to colleagues about an Intergalactic Computer Network open to all, an idea ARPANET set out to build.

iran-qanat-decline-pumped-wells-1963.summary: From late 1950s diesel and electric pumps spread across Iranian villages, drawing water from deep wells faster than gravity-fed qanat tunnels can deliver it. A survey in 1971 records tens of thousands of qanats still in use but many drying as water tables fall under pumped fields nearby. Land reform after 1962 breaks up landlord estates that had paid for qanat maintenance, and government credit favours wells. Over two decades a hydraulic system refined for 2,500 years, which could not overdraw an aquifer, is replaced by one that can and does. Groundwater decline across Iran's plateau and later subsidence of Tehran and Isfahan plains are traced to this shift, and qanat restoration returns as policy after 2000.

measles-vaccine-1963.summary: In 1963 America licensed a measles vaccine; a disease that infected nearly every child became rare where it was used. Live attenuated means a living virus altered so that it no longer causes disease but still trains immunity. Maurice Hilleman’s 1968 version attenuated its virus further, causing fewer reactions such as fever while protection held, and has been America’s only measles vaccine since. Before vaccination, America recorded 3 to 4 million cases and 400 to 500 deaths each year.

measles-vaccine-1963.detail: One dose is about 93 percent effective and two doses about 97 percent. By one World Health Organization report, vaccination averted 57 million deaths worldwide between 2000 and 2022.

sketchpad-1963.summary: In 1963 Sutherland's Sketchpad let a user draw on a screen with a light pen and move the shapes. Users could fix geometric constraints, such as a line’s length or an angle between lines. It pioneered human-computer interaction, is considered ancestor of modern computer-aided design programs and inspired graphical user interfaces; Sutherland received his 1988 Turing Award for it.

stanford-ai-lab-1963.summary: In 1963 John McCarthy founded Stanford's AI Lab; its students built robots, time-sharing and the first computer music. Lester D. “Les” Earnest, also from MIT, served as its executive officer from 1965 to 1980, and from 1966 to 1979 SAIL occupied the D.C. Power building, named for General Telephone chief Donald Clinton Power. Its researchers created WAITS, an operating system for DEC PDP computers, and, in 1970, SAIL, a programming language.

sources.confirms: The Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory run by John McCarthy was one of three Stanford-area labs that shaped modern computing.

syncom-geostationary-1963.summary: In 1963 Syncom 2 became the first satellite to hover over one spot on Earth; a fixed dish could now reach a fixed point overhead. Syncom 3, launched on August 19, 1964, was first into geostationary orbit; parked near the International Date Line with a wideband television channel, it telecast Tokyo’s 1964 Summer Olympics to America, and in 1965 it carried Defense Department communications for Vietnam.

picture.credit: NASA, GPN-2002-000123, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ziegler-natta-nobel-1963.summary: In 1963 Ziegler and Natta won the Nobel for catalysts that build plastics molecule by molecule; polypropylene came from their work. Ziegler had found titanium tetrachloride with an organoaluminium compound polymerized ethylene; Natta used crystalline titanium trichloride to make the first isotactic polypropylene. Their catalysts have made polyolefins commercially since 1956, and by 2010 output of plastics and rubbers from them and related catalysts exceeded 100 million tonnes.

picture.credit: Mondadori Publishers, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

astro-boy-tv-1963.summary: In January 1963 Astro Boy, Tezuka's robot child, became Japan's first popular animated TV series, embodying what later became known worldwide as anime. Between 1963 and 1965, 104 episodes aired in America as Astro Boy, first anime broadcast overseas.

kodak-instamatic-1963.summary: In 1963 Kodak released the Instamatic, which took its new 126 film in drop-in Kodapak cartridges. Designed under Dean M. Peterson after market research found consumers wanted easier loading, Instamatics were also cheap to build. Immensely successful, they introduced a generation to low-cost photography and spawned many imitators.

project-mac-1963.summary: In 1963 ARPA gave MIT $2.2 million for Project MAC, a computer shared by many users at once, which subsumed Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy's AI Group, founded five years earlier. ARPA kept paying $3 million yearly into the 1970s and made similar grants to Newell and Simon at Carnegie Mellon and to McCarthy’s new Stanford AI Lab.

zip-code-1963.summary: On 1 July 1963 five-digit ZIP Codes arrived across America, letting machines sort mail by region. Robert A. Moon, considered father of ZIP Codes, had proposed their first three digits, marking sectional center facilities, in 1944 while serving as postal inspector; Henry Bentley Hahn Sr. proposed its last two. Within three months Moon estimated 30 percent of mail carried them, and in 1967 they became mandatory for bulk mailers.

partial-test-ban-treaty-1963.summary: In August 1963 the superpowers agreed to stop testing nuclear weapons in air and at sea; fallout in milk and wheat began to fall. Public anxiety over radioactive fallout from ever-larger hydrogen bomb tests drove it; negotiators had sought a comprehensive ban but abandoned it over detecting underground tests and Soviet fears that inspections would enable spying. It prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater while allowing underground tests within limits on radioactive debris, and 123 other states have since joined.

compact-cassette-1963.summary: In August 1963 Philips showed the Compact Cassette and licensed it free; recorded music became cheap to copy and carry. Its first version was a two-track, two-direction mono format. Under pressure from Sony, Philips licensed its patented format free to other manufacturers from 1966, and rival Grundig’s DC-International was discontinued in 1967.

moscow-washington-hotline-1963.summary: In August 1963 a teleprinter line linked the Pentagon and the Kremlin after Cuba showed that slow messages could start a war. During 1962’s Cuban Missile Crisis, official messages had taken about six hours to deliver, and Washington needed nearly twelve hours to receive and decode Khrushchev’s 3,000-word settlement offer; before Washington could reply, a tougher demand had arrived. Both sides signed their Hot Line Agreement on June 20, 1963, their first formal step to cut risks of accidental nuclear war.

bhakra-dam-1963.summary: In October 1963 Nehru dedicated Bhakra Dam, completed in 1962, calling it the “New Temple of Resurgent India” that could as well be called gurdwara or mosque; it irrigated the Punjab's Green Revolution. Bhakra Dam, 226 metres high in Himachal Pradesh, was among India’s earliest post-independence river valley schemes, conceived by Sir Chhotu Ram in 1923; its 90-kilometre Gobind Sagar reservoir stores 9.34 billion cubic metres of water.

touch-tone-dialing-1963.summary: In November 1963 the first push-button telephones went on sale; its tones later let callers talk to machines by pressing numbers. Rotary dials signalled digits by interrupting line current in pulses; Touch-Tone instead sent pairs of audio tones down the voice path, at frequencies chosen so consumer phones could not disturb signalling between exchanges. Push buttons gradually replaced rotary dials and became telephony’s industry standard.

dendral-1965.summary: In 1964 Dendral began at Stanford, a program that read mass spectra to identify molecules, the first expert system. Edward Feigenbaum, Bruce G. Buchanan, Joshua Lederberg and Carl Djerassi chose one task: helping organic chemists identify unknown molecules by analysing their mass spectra with chemical knowledge. Written in Lisp as Heuristic Dendral and Meta-Dendral, it is considered the first expert system because it automated chemists’ decision-making, and MYCIN, PROSPECTOR and XCON descended from it.

entel-chile-1964.summary: In 1964 Chile founded Entel to rebuild long-distance telephone lines after an earthquake. It installed microwave networks across almost all national territory and in 1968 built Longovilo satellite station, 64 kilometres south-west of Santiago, first in Latin America.

kenya-hybrid-maize-h611-1964.summary: Breeders at Kitale, in Kenya's western highlands, released Hybrid 611 just after independence. It crossed Kitale Synthetic II, an open-pollinated variety bred from local white maize, with Ecuador 573, a highland landrace brought in from South America. A 1975 survey of western Kenya found H611 diffusing among large and small farmers in high-potential areas about as rapidly as hybrids had spread across US Corn Belt farms in 1930s and 1940s. Later Kenyan hybrids descend from it, and today's highland breeding programme traces back to those Kitale crosses. Seed companies, extension officers and maize-flour mills built a national staple around this variety.

kenya-hybrid-maize-h611-1964.detail: Harrison's team at Kitale began with local germplasm in 1955 and added Central and South American stocks through CIMMYT. A 2011 account dates release to 'just after independence in 1963'; secondary accounts give 1964, so year is marked approximate. Hybrid maize later faced criticism for displacing landraces and for yield stagnation in drier zones, themes a 2024 genetic-trends study revisits.

mcluhan-medium-is-message-1964.summary: In 1964 McLuhan argued a medium changes society by its form rather than its content, his best-known line. Its first chapter, “The Medium is the Message,” argues that media shape society through their own characteristics more than through content; his example was a light bulb, which carries no content yet creates lit spaces at night. He sorted media into “hot” and “cool,” and his book is considered pioneering in media theory.

multics-1964.summary: In 1964 MIT, GE and Bell Labs began Multics, a computer utility to serve a city; Unix was written by Bell Labs people who left it. It was built on GE’s specially designed 645 computer, first delivered to MIT in January 1967. Multics treated files and process memory as one single-level store and introduced dynamic linking. Bell withdrew in 1969, and its Multics team wrote Unix to carry many of those ideas onto cheaper machines, first a PDP-7.

packard-naked-society-1964.summary: In 1964 Vance Packard's Naked Society warned that computers and surveillance were stripping away privacy. He pointed to hidden microphones, concealed cameras and polygraph lie detectors, criticized advertisers’ unfettered use of private information and compared it to President Johnson’s proposed National Data Bank. Arguing privacy was worth defending, it led Congress to create its Special Subcommittee on the Invasion of Privacy.

packet-switching-baran-1964.summary: In 1964 Paul Baran proposed chopping messages into blocks and routing each around damage by store-and-forward transmission over low-cost hardware, which he called distributed adaptive message block switching. This contradicted telecom orthodoxy of pre-allocating bandwidth to each call. Donald Davies independently invented packet switching at Britain’s National Physical Laboratory in 1965.

picturephone-1964.summary: In 1964 AT&T showed Picturephone at New York's World's Fair; video calls existed, but 60 years passed before anyone wanted them. Made by Western Electric, each unit combined a vidicon camera tube and a small cathode ray screen for black-and-white video, used beside ordinary telephones over regular phone lines. Mod II sets went up for rent in 1970, mostly in Chicago; despite predictions of one million sets by 1980, fewer than 500 were ever in service at once, and Picturephone is considered a commercial failure.

student-program-1964.summary: In 1964 Daniel Bobrow's STUDENT read high-school algebra problems in English and solved them, an early program to parse natural language. It turned each sentence into one fact, then into equations, with a knowledge base of 52 facts.

dr-strangelove-1964.summary: In 1964 Kubrick's Dr Strangelove made nuclear doctrine a comedy; a doomsday machine that cannot be switched off was its punchline. Directed and co-written by Stanley Kubrick, loosely from Peter George’s 1958 thriller Red Alert, it is black comedy satirizing Cold War fears of nuclear war: one paranoid US Air Force general orders an unprovoked attack on the Soviet Union with his B-52s, and Peter Sellers plays three roles among those scrambling to stop it. In 1989 it was among 25 films first chosen for America’s National Film Registry.

beatles-ed-sullivan-1964.summary: On 9 February 1964 Ed Sullivan's show put the Beatles before some 73 million viewers, then America's largest television audience and its television record, broken three years later by The Fugitive’s series finale in 1967. It is considered a turning point in American pop culture and start of pop music’s British Invasion.

triple-revolution-memo-1964.summary: In 1964 a committee warned President Johnson that automation would sever income from work and proposed a guaranteed income. It named three revolutions, in cybernation, weaponry and human rights, and dwelt on cybernation: machines would bring “a system of almost unlimited productive capacity” while needing ever fewer manual workers, raising unemployment. It proposed public works, income redistribution and government restraint on deploying technology.

ibm-system-360-1964.summary: In 1964 IBM announced System/360, one family of computers that all ran the same programs, so software outlived the machine. IBM had been struggling to support five separate, mutually incompatible computer lines. Designed by chief architect Gene Amdahl under project manager Fred Brooks, it separated architecture from implementation so programs ran unchanged across six initial models, 30 through 70, and forty common peripherals. Customers could buy small and grow without reprogramming, and System/360 compatibility survives in today’s IBM Z mainframes.

basic-1964.summary: In 1964 Kemeny and Kurtz created BASIC at Dartmouth so any student could program. Its first version ran on May 1, 1964 on their Dartmouth Time-Sharing System, which let many users edit and run programs at once from remote terminals. Microsoft BASIC followed in 1975, and most home computers of the late 1970s shipped with a BASIC interpreter.

national-water-carrier-1964.summary: In June 1964 Israel finished a pipeline carrying Sea of Galilee water south to the Negev; deserts were farmed and Jordan River water fought over. Designed by Tahal and built by Mekorot, it moves water from that lake to Israel’s populated centre and arid south along about 130 kilometres, up to 72,000 cubic metres an hour. At first 80 percent went to agriculture; by the early 1990s it supplied half of Israel’s drinking water.

intelsat-founded-1964.summary: In 1964 eleven countries signed Intelsat's interim agreement on 20 August to own communications satellites together; within a decade one network linked 80 nations. President Kennedy had instigated it with his United Nations speech of 25 September 1961 and signed America’s Communications Satellite Act in 1962. Intelsat owned and managed communications satellites providing international telecommunications and broadcast services until 2001, when it was fully commercialized.

arzew-camel-lng-algeria-1964.summary: Compagnie Algérienne du Méthane Liquide (CAMEL) completes a liquefaction plant at Arzew on Algeria's coast, fed by Hassi R'Mel gas through a 500 kilometre line. In October 1964 tanker Methane Princess loads first cargo for Canvey Island in Britain; deliveries to Le Havre follow in 1965. Three trains make about 1.1 million tonnes a year. It is first commercial liquefied natural gas trade anywhere, two years after Algerian independence, and it turns a flared by-product into an export sector. Algeria's Sonatrach takes over and expands Arzew and Skikda, and Gulf producers copy model three decades later. Methane shipping in insulated tanks at minus 162 degrees becomes a global industry on this template.

shinkansen-1964.summary: In October 1964 the Tokaido Shinkansen opened, the first railway built for high speed; Tokyo to Osaka fell from nearly seven hours to four. Conventional limited expresses took about 6 hours 40 minutes from Tokyo to Osaka; its new 0 series trains ran at up to 210 km/h, cutting limited-stop Hikari services to four hours. Linking Japan’s four largest cities over 552.6 kilometres, it has carried more than 6.5 billion passengers, 161 million in fiscal 2023 alone.

china-596-test-1964.summary: In October 1964 China exploded its first atomic bomb at Lop Nur, the fifth nuclear power and the first outside Europe and America. An implosion fission device holding about 15 kilograms of weapons-grade uranium enriched at Lanzhou, designed by Deng Jiaxian, Qian Sanqiang and Peng Huanwu, it yielded 22 kilotons, comparable to Fat Man at Nagasaki, and made China the world’s fifth nuclear-armed state. It was first of 45 successful Chinese tests through 1996, all at Lop Nur.

akosombo-dam-1965.summary: In 1965 Ghana finished Akosombo Dam, creating Earth's largest reservoir by area to power an aluminium smelter. President Kwame Nkrumah adopted this project, and America’s Volta Aluminum Company lent money to fund it; its primary purpose was electricity for aluminium smelting, with original output of 912 megawatts. It created Lake Volta, 8,502 square kilometres and 3.6 percent of Ghana’s land, the world’s largest artificial lake by area, displacing many people; it now supplies most of Togo’s and Benin’s electricity.

dreyfus-alchemy-1965.summary: In 1965 Hubert Dreyfus wrote at RAND that AI was climbing a tree to reach the Moon; the field shunned him and later conceded points. It summarized AI’s history and ridiculed its unbridled optimism, such as Herbert Simon’s predictions after General Problem Solver, arguing they would not come true; they did not. Expanded into What Computers Can’t Do in 1972, his objections are discussed in most introductions to AI’s philosophy.

fuzzy-logic-1965.summary: In 1965 Lotfi Zadeh proposed fuzzy sets, where a statement can be partly true; rice cookers, cameras and trains were later run by the logic. Infinite-valued logics had been studied since Łukasiewicz and Tarski in the 1920s. An input belongs to a fuzzy set to some degree, 0 to 1, so one temperature reading can be partly “hot” and partly “warm,” and such degrees can drive controllers, for instance anti-lock brakes. Unlike probability, which models ignorance, fuzzy truth models vagueness.

good-intelligence-explosion-1965.summary: In 1965 I J Good argued that a machine able to improve its own design would soon outrun us, calling it an intelligence explosion. He argued that any upgradable intelligent machine could enter positive feedback of successive self-improvement, each more intelligent generation arriving sooner: his “intelligence explosion.” He wrote, “Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.” His model remains most popular among technological singularity hypotheses.

hypertext-ted-nelson-1965.summary: In 1965 Ted Nelson coined hypertext for writing linked in all directions on a screen. Two decades earlier, Vannevar Bush’s 1945 essay “As We May Think” had imagined a microfilm Memex following associative trails between documents. Nelson went on to build the Hypertext Editing System with Andries van Dam at Brown University in 1967, using an IBM 2250 terminal and light pen, and advocated his never-released Xanadu system for decades.

ivakhnenko-gmdh-1965.summary: In 1965 Alexey Ivakhnenko in Kyiv trained networks many layers deep, adding and pruning layers by regression, so numbers of layers and units were learned from each problem. Its units could use polynomial activation functions, and in 1971 Ivakhnenko described one such network with eight layers. Jürgen Schmidhuber has called GMDH networks perhaps the first deep learning systems and first hierarchical representation learning in neural networks.

kevlar-1965.summary: In 1965 Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont spun a cloudy polymer into a fibre five times stronger than steel by weight. Anticipating a gasoline shortage, her group had begun searching in 1964 for a lightweight, strong fiber for tires; her polymer solution formed liquid crystals and looked cloudy, usually grounds for discarding it, but she persuaded technician Charles Smullen to spin it, and the fiber did not break. Introduced by 1971, Kevlar is used in racing tires, sails and bulletproof vests.

kolar-gold-fields-atmospheric-neutrino-1.summary: Deep in Champion Reef mine at Kolar Gold Fields, Mysore State, a team from Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Durham University and Osaka City University runs scintillator and neon flash tube telescopes about 2.3 kilometres below ground, where rock shields out almost all cosmic ray muons. In 1965 they record muons travelling nearly horizontally that can only come from neutrinos produced by cosmic rays in Earth's atmosphere. They publish in August 1965, weeks after a Case-Witwatersrand-Irvine group under Frederick Reines reports similar events from a South African mine. A 2025 history stresses mine labour that made these depths workable. KGF hosts particle experiments until 1992.

lem-cyberiad-1965.summary: In 1965 Stanisław Lem published The Cyberiad, tales of two robot constructors who can build anything, with machines as its only characters. Impatient Trurl rushes into action; sceptical Klapaucius watches his friend’s inevitable failures with stoic calm, yet both outwit capricious despots who hold them hostage. Lem considered it his contribution to science fiction’s poetics, combining futurology with fairy tale and philosophical fable.

mexico-maquiladora-programme-1965.summary: In 1965, after United States ended its Bracero farm-labour programme and left border cities with returning workers, Mexico's government created Programa de Industrialización Fronteriza. Plants within a 20-kilometre strip could import machinery, components and materials without duty provided output was exported, and US customs taxed only value added abroad. By 1969 some 147 plants employed about 17,000 people in Ciudad Juárez, Tijuana, Mexicali, Nogales, Reynosa and Matamoros, assembling electronics, apparel and later auto parts for RCA, Sylvania and others. Location rules relaxed in the 1970s and disappeared by the 1990s; employment passed one million around 2000. Maquiladoras made cross-border production sharing an organising principle of North American manufacturing and of border urban growth.

mexico-maquiladora-programme-1965.detail: Leslie Sklair reads maquilas as spearhead of export-led industrialisation and of a transnational capitalist class in Mexico. Dallas Fed economists Cañas and Coronado give programme origins and early plant counts. Early workforces were largely young women, so the programme did little for displaced braceros. Plants grew from a dozen in 1965 to about 1,500 by 1990 and more than 3,000 by 2000, when NAFTA rules and competition from China cut employment. Ciudad Juárez became the emblematic maquila city, with electronics and auto-harness plants, bus networks ferrying shifts and later a wave of violence against women workers that drew international attention.

patterson-lead-warning-1965.summary: In 1965 Clair Patterson showed that lead in Americans' blood was a hundred times natural levels; his work proved seminal in banning leaded gasoline and leaded solder in food cans. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica had shown him atmospheric lead rising steadily since tetraethyl lead entered gasoline, and he named leaded fuel and industrial lead as its cause. His paper began his effort to alert the public to lead in the environment and food chain, against fierce opposition from industry scientist Robert A. Kehoe.

bass-strait-oil-gas-discovery-1965.summary: Drilling from Glomar III off Gippsland, an Esso-BHP partnership found gas at Barracouta in February 1965, then Marlin in 1966 and oil at Kingfish in 1967. Production platforms followed from 1969, and by early 1970s Gippsland Basin fields supplied most of Australia's crude and fed Melbourne's gas grid. Reso's 1967 APEA paper set out development plans; Bein, Griffith and Svalbe described Kingfish, then Australia's largest oil field. Spencer's 2022 account covers Esso's later deepwater push. Offshore petroleum shaped federal-state revenue arrangements and Victoria's industrial base for five decades, until field decline led to decommissioning debates and east-coast gas shortages in 2020s.

Built from diode-transistor logic on flip chip cards in a cabinet about as big as a small refrigerator, it was first to sell for under US$20,000. Its 1966 successor, PDP-8/S, became first under US$10,000.

intelsat-early-bird-1965.summary: In April 1965 Early Bird became the first commercial communications satellite, carrying 240 telephone calls across the Atlantic at once. Hughes Aircraft Company built it for COMSAT patterned on its Syncom satellites for NASA, and COMSAT activated it on June 28. Just 76 by 61 centimetres and 34.5 kilograms, it gave Europe and North America their first direct, nearly instantaneous link for television, telephone and fax, and served over four years instead of its planned 18 months.

moores-law-1965.summary: In 1965 Moore predicted chip parts would double yearly; the forecast held for decades, making computing cheap. Drawing a line through five points, one chip per year from 1959 to 1964, he predicted components per integrated circuit would roughly double each year for at least ten more years, and projected that by 1975 one quarter-square-inch semiconductor could hold 65,000 components. In 1975 he slowed his forecast to doubling every two years, and “Moore’s law” has guided semiconductor planning and research targets since.

angove-wine-cask-1965.summary: Riverland winemaker Thomas Angove sought an alternative to half-gallon glass flagons. His company's patent 280826, issued 20 April 1965 for an 'improved container and pack for liquids', covered a polyethylene bag inside a carton; as wine drained, bag collapsed and kept air out. Early packs required cutting a corner and resealing with a peg; Penfolds added a tap in 1967, and casks soon dominated Australian table wine sales. State Library of South Australia holds Angove's packaging designs, and John Angove recalled origins in a 2013 interview. Bag-in-box formats spread worldwide for wine, juice and water, while in Australia cheap cask wine became a target of alcohol policy and excise debates.

molniya-satellite-1965.summary: In April 1965 Moscow launched Molniya 1, on a long looping orbit that hung over Siberia; television reached the whole country. Soviet planners had found geostationary orbits unsuitable: lifting a satellite to 40,000 kilometres and shifting it over the equator from Russian launch sites cost too much rocket power, and such orbits cover polar regions poorly. Molniya satellites instead used highly eccentric orbits that linger over high latitudes; 164 were launched for military and civil communications between 1965 and 2004.

Calls were switched through a matrix of reed relays, controlled by wire spring relays that in turn obeyed a central processing unit. Its upgrade, 1AESS, served from 1976 to 2017.

eight-track-cartridge-1965.summary: In September 1965 Ford offered eight-track tape players in its cars; drivers chose their own music for the first time. Stereo 8 had been created that year by a consortium led by Bill Lear of Lear Jet with Ampex, Ford, General Motors, Motorola and RCA Victor, which released 175 cartridges from its catalogs. By 1967 all Ford vehicles offered it, home players arrived in 1966, and by decade’s end eight-track was America’s largest consumer electronics segment.

northeast-blackout-1965.summary: In November 1965 a relay in Ontario tripped and 30 million people from New York to Toronto lost power for up to 13 hours. At 5:16 p.m. a misprogrammed protective relay on a line from the Sir Adam Beck station near Niagara Falls tripped under load, and cascading overloads blacked out parts of Ontario and the northeastern United States from New York to Vermont, 80,000 square miles in all; restoration continued into November 10 in some areas.

unsafe-at-any-speed-1965.summary: In November 1965 Ralph Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed charged carmakers with choosing style over survival; America's Department of Transportation was created the next year. Drawing on industry insiders, it accused carmakers of resisting safety features such as seat belts and refusing to spend on safety, and criticized Chevrolet Corvair handling; in 1972 federal safety regulators found Corvair rollover rates comparable to similar cars. A 1966 nonfiction bestseller, it also led to agencies that became the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

It contributed significantly to South Korea’s economic development, above all during the accelerated growth of the 1970s and 1980s, and today employs more than 1,800 research scientists, visiting scientists, fellows and trainees.

moruroa-nuclear-tests-1966.summary: In July 1966 France exploded its first bomb at Moruroa in Polynesia; 193 tests over 30 years left the atoll cracked. Over objections from Polynesian assembly members it exploded its first bomb there, Aldebaran, in its lagoon on 2 July 1966. After 41 atmospheric tests through 1974, protests led by New Zealand, which sent two frigates in 1973, pushed France underground, where blasts cracked the atoll’s volcanic rock. Greenpeace’s Rainbow Warrior later protested there; Moruroa's last test came on 27 December 1995 and France’s final test at neighbouring Fangataufa on 27 January 1996.

shakey-robot-1966.summary: From 1966 Shakey at Stanford Research Institute was the first robot to plan its own moves from what its camera saw. It was the first general-purpose mobile robot able to reason about its own actions: given a command, it broke that task into steps on its own, using its STRIPS planner, in a world of rooms, corridors, doors and light switches. Shakey’s project yielded A* search, Hough transforms and visibility graph path planning.

pilbara-iron-ore-exports-1966.summary: Australia banned iron ore exports in 1938, believing reserves small. Lang Hancock's 1952 flight over Hamersley Range and later surveys revealed banded iron formations holding tens of billions of tonnes at grades above 60 percent iron. Menzies government reluctantly eased its embargo from December 1960 under pressure from Western Australia and Japanese steelmakers. Hamersley Iron (Conzinc Riotinto) opened Mount Tom Price mine, a 290-kilometre railway and Dampier port, shipping first ore in August 1966; Goldsworthy Mining shipped from Port Hedland in June 1966. Long-term contracts with Japanese mills financed mines, railways and towns, and iron ore became Australia's largest export.

Pilbara railways now run world's heaviest trains and autonomous haul trucks and locomotives. Mining occurred on Aboriginal land without consent; Juukan Gorge rock shelter destruction by Rio Tinto in 2020 renewed scrutiny. star-trek-1966.summary: In September 1966 Star Trek premiered with a talking computer, a communicator and a mixed crew. Set in the 23rd century, it followed Captain James T Kirk, played by William Shatner, and his starship crew; in the first episode a shapeshifting alien hunting salt attacks them at a medical outpost. Star Trek reflected creator Gene Roddenberry’s hopeful vision for humanity’s future.

motor-vehicle-safety-act-1966.summary: In September 1966 Congress first ordered federal safety standards for cars; seat belts, padded dashes and crash tests followed. It authorized federal regulators to set and enforce mandatory motor vehicle safety standards, a federal first, and created a National Highway Safety Bureau, now the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

us-department-of-transportation-1966.summary: In October 1966 Congress created a Department of Transportation and gathered roads, rail, air and sea under one secretary. It launched on April 1, 1967.

alpac-report-1966.summary: In 1966 the ALPAC report found machine translation slower and costlier than human translators; American funding stopped for 20 years. It found no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation and urged basic research in computational linguistics instead.

ir8-miracle-rice-1966.summary: In 1966 IRRI released IR8, a short rice that raised Asian yields from 1 or 2 tons per hectare to 4 or 5. Eighth of 38 crosses in a 1962 IRRI experiment, it paired Indonesia’s high-yield Peta with Taiwan’s dwarf Dee-geo-woo-gen, whose sd-1 gene shortens plants and lifts yield. Bred by Peter Jennings’s team with Henry Beachell, Te-Tzu Chang and Surajit De Datta, it became known as miracle rice, central to the Green Revolution, though it did not fit most rice-growing situations.

toyota-corolla-1966.summary: In November 1966 Toyota introduced the Corolla, which became history's best-selling car nameplate. It was built at Toyota’s new Takaoka plant against Nissan’s Sunny, launched in 1966 as well. Since 1997 Corolla has been history’s best-selling automobile nameplate, passing Volkswagen’s Beetle; Toyota reached 50 million sold across twelve generations in 2021.

rance-tidal-power-1966.summary: In November 1966 de Gaulle opened Brittany's Rance tidal station, the first to make electricity from tides; it still runs. Its 24 bulb-type Kaplan turbines, each of 10 megawatts, are driven by tides moving through its barrage, giving 240 megawatts peak and about 500 gigawatt-hours a year. It remained the largest tidal plant for 45 years, until South Korea’s 254-megawatt Sihwa Lake station surpassed it in 2011.

amana-radarange-1967.summary: In 1967 Amana Refrigeration, bought by Raytheon in 1965, introduces a countertop Radarange for 495 dollars, about 3,575 dollars in 2017 money, the first microwave oven sized and priced for a kitchen. Raytheon's Percy Spencer had noticed in 1945 that a magnetron melted a chocolate bar in his pocket, and Raytheon's first Radarange of 1947 was a refrigerator-sized restaurant unit. Smaller, cheaper magnetrons from Japanese makers brought prices down through the 1970s, and by mid-decade millions were in use. Microwaves reorganised kitchens around reheating and frozen meals, and Ruth Schwartz Cowan ended her history of household technology with them.

amdahls-law-1967.summary: In 1967 Gene Amdahl showed the part of a program that cannot run in parallel caps the gain from more processors. Speedup from improving one part of a system, he showed, is limited by how much of its time is spent in that part. Now called Amdahl’s law, it is used in parallel computing to predict how much faster a task can run as processors are added.

brautigan-machines-of-loving-grace-1967.summary: In January 1967 Richard Brautigan wrote a poem in which computers watch over people like loving grace; the line named a hope and a film. Its 99 words in three stanzas picture “mammals and computers” living “in mutually programming harmony,” machines tending nature while people are freed from labour. It first appeared on a mimeographed broadside from the Communication Company, publishing arm of San Francisco’s Diggers, and in April 1967 became title poem of his collection; readers have taken it both as utopia and as ironic critique of one.

conways-law-1967.summary: In 1967 Melvin Conway observed that organisations build systems shaped like their own communication. He wrote it up that year; Datamation published it in April 1968. His wording: organizations which design systems “are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations.” MIT and Harvard Business School researchers later found strong evidence for it, showing products from loosely coupled organizations significantly more modular than those from tightly coupled ones.

mac-hack-1967.summary: In 1967 Richard Greenblatt's Mac Hack VI became the first chess program to play in human tournaments, and beat a rated player. It defeated Ben Landy, rated 1510 by USCF, in game 3 of tournament 2 of Massachusetts’ state championship. It was the first chess program to play under human tournament conditions, first granted a chess rating and first to beat a person in tournament play.

mangla-dam-1967.summary: In 1967 Pakistan finished Mangla Dam on Jhelum River under its Indus Basin Project, after 1960’s Indus Waters Treaty gave India the Ravi, Sutlej and Beas and Pakistan rights to develop Jhelum, Chenab and Indus; it waters Pakistan's Punjab. Until then Pakistan’s whole irrigation system depended on unregulated river flows; Mangla was first of two dams built to fix this, with Tarbela on the Indus following. Its reservoir held 7.25 billion cubic metres at first and 9.12 after raising work completed in 2009.

He had underestimated the task; in 1974 James Lighthill’s critique and congressional pressure led US and British governments to stop funding undirected AI research.

pakistan-mexipak-wheat-1967.summary: West Pakistan imports Mexican semi-dwarf wheat seed from 1965, buying about 42,000 tons in 1967. Farmers in Punjab and Sind sow Mexipak-65, a selection of Borlaug's Siete Cerros bred locally for flour quality, on canal and tubewell land fertilised with urea. Hussain's 1970 survey in Pakistan Development Review finds Mexipak popular in 1968-69 because it yields well and makes acceptable atta. National wheat output climbs from about 4.6 million tons in 1967 to over 7 million by 1970. Byerlee's 1993 review of productivity after this leap notes slower later gains and growing dependence on groundwater pumping and fertiliser subsidy.

apollo-1-fire-1967.summary: In January 1967 three astronauts died in a cabin fire during an Apollo 1 rehearsal; the redesign that followed made the landings possible. During a launch rehearsal at Cape Kennedy’s Launch Complex 34 on January 27, fire broke out in its command module; an electrical spark spread through combustible nylon in a high-pressure pure-oxygen cabin, and its inward-opening plug door hatch could not be opened in time. Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger B. Chaffee died, and NASA’s Accident Review Board and both houses of Congress investigated.

outer-space-treaty-1967.summary: In 1967 the Outer Space Treaty banned nuclear weapons in orbit and national appropriation of outer space and celestial bodies; space became, in its words, “province of all mankind”. It set core principles of international space law: no nuclear weapons in space, no national sovereignty over outer space or celestial bodies, free exploration and use by all nations, and only peaceful lunar uses. As of October 2025, 118 countries are parties, and four further agreements on astronaut rescue, liability, registration and lunar activity followed.

high-fructose-corn-syrup-1967.summary: In 1967 an enzyme process turned corn starch into a syrup as sweet as sugar; cheap corn replaced sugar in American drinks and food. Yoshiyuki Takasaki at Japan’s Agency of Industrial Science and Technology developed a heat-stable isomerase between 1965 and 1970; Clinton Corn Processing Company, holding an exclusive license, began shipping an early version in February 1967 and marketed it widely in the early 1970s (Britannica dates HFCS's entry into food and drink to mid-1970s). Cheaper than sugar under US sugar quotas, import tariffs and corn subsidies, HFCS won Coca-Cola and Pepsi fully by 1984.

tlatelolco-treaty-1967.summary: On 14 February 1967, after negotiations driven by Mexican diplomat Alfonso García Robles in the wake of the 1962 missile crisis, states opened for signature Treaty for Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America at Tlatelolco, Mexico City. Parties undertook to use nuclear material only for peaceful purposes and to accept IAEA safeguards, and created OPANAL, an agency in Mexico City to oversee compliance. Two protocols bound outside powers and territory holders. The zone entered force in 1969 and over following decades Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Cuba brought it into full effect. Tlatelolco became a template for zones in South Pacific, Southeast Asia, Africa and Central Asia and earned García Robles a Nobel Peace Prize in 1982.

Protocol I bound France, Netherlands, United Kingdom and United States for territories in the zone; Protocol II committed nuclear powers not to use or threaten nuclear weapons against parties.

torrey-canyon-oil-spill-1967.summary: In March 1967 tanker Torrey Canyon ran aground off Cornwall and spilled 120,000 tons of crude; Britain bombed her wreck and rewrote spill law. Carrying Kuwaiti crude to Milford Haven, she ran onto Pollard’s Rock between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly on 18 March 1967 after a navigational error. She spilled an estimated 25 to 36 million gallons, one of the world’s most serious oil spills. Royal Navy and Royal Air Force aircraft later bombed her wreck to burn off oil, and hundreds of miles of coastline in Britain, France, Guernsey and Spain were contaminated.

our-world-satellite-broadcast-1967.summary: In June 1967 Our World went out live to 24 countries by satellite, with the Beatles singing All You Need Is Love. Coordinated by Europe’s broadcasting union, EBU, it linked broadcasters from fourteen countries through four satellites, Intelsat I and II over Atlantic waters and Intelsat II and NASA’s ATS-1 over Pacific waters, reaching 24 countries and some 400 to 700 million viewers, television’s largest audience to that date; Soviet-bloc broadcasters pulled out four days earlier over Western responses to the Six-Day War. Britain’s segment premiered the Beatles’ “All You Need Is Love” live.

public-broadcasting-act-1967.summary: In November 1967 Congress chartered public broadcasting; PBS and NPR came from it. It followed Carnegie Commission and Ford Foundation proposals to strengthen educational television, and charged CPB with encouraging program diversity and expanding noncommercial broadcasting, helping local stations create programs; supporters included Fred Rogers and Senator John Pastore.

wresat-satellite-1967.summary: In November 1967 Australia launched WRESAT from Woomera on a spare American rocket, the third country to orbit a satellite from home. It rode a modified American Redstone rocket with two upper stages, its Sparta left over from a joint Australian, US and British programme and donated by Washington. Australia became the seventh nation with its own satellite and third, after Moscow and Washington, to launch from home soil.

heart-transplant-barnard-1967.summary: In December 1967 Christiaan Barnard transplanted a human heart in Cape Town; the patient lived 18 days and surgery changed its limits. He placed accident victim Denise Darvall’s heart into 54-year-old Louis Washkansky, who regained full consciousness and talked easily with his wife before dying 18 days later of pneumonia, brought on largely by drugs given to suppress rejection of his new heart.

a-star-1968.summary: In 1968 Shakey's builders published A*, which finds shortest paths by guessing the distance left, so their robot could plan its own paths. Nilsson had proposed Graph Traverser, which steers by heuristic estimate of distance to goal; Raphael suggested adding distance already travelled, and Hart proved that with suitable heuristics their sum finds shortest paths. Extending Dijkstra’s algorithm, A* is used across computer science and in games for its completeness, optimality and efficiency.

barefoot-doctors-china-1968.summary: After Mao's 1965 directive to shift medical work to countryside, communes selected farmers for three to six months of training in first aid, hygiene, vaccination, childbirth and both herbal and Western medicine; a 1968 Red Flag article made 'barefoot doctor' national policy. By 1970s more than a million worked part-time in production brigades, paid in work points, with cooperative medical schemes covering most villages. Life expectancy and infant mortality improved during these years, and WHO's 1978 Alma-Ata declaration drew on this model for primary health care. Decollectivisation after 1981 dissolved cooperative funding, and in 1985 remaining barefoot doctors were renamed village doctors.

barefoot-doctors-china-1968.detail: Zhang and Unschuld's Lancet review summarises numbers and outcomes; Fang Xiaoping's archival study of Hangzhou-area villages shows how barefoot doctors spread Western pharmaceuticals and marginalised older healers, a result at odds with programme's herbalist image. Quality varied widely between regions.

biafra-rap-refineries-1968.summary: Cut off by Nigeria's blockade from 1967, Biafran scientists and engineers formed a Research and Production directorate, RAP, that distilled crude from local wells in improvised refineries at Uzuakoli and elsewhere, made rockets and ogbunigwe shrapnel mines, armoured vehicles and radio equipment. Refineries used simple fractional distillation in welded drums to produce petrol, kerosene and diesel for army and civilians. Chikwendu Ukaegbu's 2005 study in Social Forces reads RAP as indigenous technological capacity mobilised by crisis, and asks why so little survived after Biafra's surrender in January 1970.

biafra-rap-refineries-1968.detail: Chukwuma Azuonye and Ukaegbu (Philosophia Africana 2007) describe RAP's organisation under Benjamin Nwosu and its workshops; sources differ on how many refineries ran and their output. Ukaegbu interviewed RAP veterans and argued that science became socially relevant when organised around survival needs, with university staff from Nsukka moving into workshops. After 1970 Nigerian authorities disbanded RAP and most participants returned to academic posts, leaving refining and weapons know-how undeveloped at home.

carterfone-decision-1968.summary: In 1968 the FCC ruled that any safe device could connect to AT&T's lines; modems and answering machines followed. It had to, because telephone companies could and did bar devices they did not own from electrical connection. In 1956 the Hush-A-Phone case had allowed mechanical attachments; Carterfone extended this to electrical connection and opened America’s public telephone network to customer-premises equipment.

first-911-call-1968.summary: In 1968 America's first 911 call was made in Haleyville, Alabama, placed by Alabama Speaker of the House Rankin Fite and answered by US Representative Tom Bevill. In 1967 a presidential commission on law enforcement had recommended one nationwide emergency number, and AT&T chose 911 as short, memorable and easy to dial on rotary phones, its middle 1 marking a special number in switching systems of that day.

india-wheat-revolution-1968.summary: After drought harvests of 1965 and 1966 leave India dependent on American PL-480 grain, agriculture minister C. Subramaniam and scientist M. S. Swaminathan win approval from Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi to import 200 tonnes of Mexican wheat seed in 1965 and 18,000 tonnes of Lerma Rojo and Sonora 64 in 1966, the largest seed purchase to that date. Punjab and Haryana farmers with tubewells and new fertilizer take it up; Swaminathan records wheat output reaching 17 million tonnes in 1968 against 12 million four years earlier, and the government issues a Wheat Revolution postage stamp in July 1968. Borlaug had toured the north Indian wheat belt with Swaminathan in March 1963. Indian selections Kalyan Sona and Sonalika from Mexican material soon replace imports, and wheat passes 100 million tonnes by the 2020s.

india-wheat-revolution-1968.detail: National demonstration plots of 1964 to 1965 gave small farmers 4 to 5 tonnes per hectare against under 1 tonne in controls. Gains concentrated in the irrigated northwest, widening regional gaps and groundwater stress still felt today. Rice followed with IR8 from 1966. Price support through the Food Corporation of India, set up in 1965, guaranteed a market. Subramaniam faced parliamentary opposition to spending scarce foreign exchange on seed.

jaipur-foot-1968.summary: At Sawai Man Singh Hospital in Jaipur, orthopaedic surgeon Pramod Karan Sethi and craftsman Ram Chander Sharma, a temple sculptor turned technician, built in 1968 a prosthetic foot from vulcanised rubber over a wooden keel, waterproof and flexible enough for squatting, sitting cross-legged and walking barefoot on mud. Western prostheses of time needed shoes and failed in Indian conditions. It cost a few dollars, could be fitted in a day with local materials, and from 1975 Bhagwan Mahaveer Viklang Sahayata Samiti distributed it free, reaching over a million amputees worldwide including landmine survivors in Afghanistan and Cambodia. Sethi received Magsaysay Award in 1981.

kainji-dam-1968.summary: In 1968 Nigeria completed Kainji Dam on the Niger, opened in 1969; it powered a young country and displaced 44,000 to 50,000 people. Impregilo, an Italian consortium, began construction in 1964 at an estimated cost of US$209 million, one quarter of it spent resettling people displaced by it and its reservoir, Kainji Lake. About 10 kilometres long with its saddle dam and mostly earth-built, with a 65-metre concrete centre housing turbines, it was designed for 960 megawatts; only 8 of 12 turbines were installed, giving 760, which supplies Nigeria’s large cities and sells electricity to Niger.

shrdlu-1970.summary: From 1968 Winograd's SHRDLU held conversations in English about a world of blocks; it was the high point of AI by hand-coded rules. Users conversed with it in English, moving objects, naming collections and querying its simplified “blocks world,” in effect a virtual box of blocks, cones and balls. Written in Micro Planner and Lisp on a DEC PDP-6 with graphics terminal, it was above all a language parser, combining four simple ideas to make its simulation of understanding convincing.

space-odyssey-2001-1968.summary: In 1968 Kubrick's 2001 gave AI a face and a calm voice in HAL, the computer that kills its crew to protect its mission. Opening with prehistoric hominins finding an alien monolith, it follows a mission aboard spacecraft Discovery One to investigate a signal at Jupiter; its sentient computer, HAL 9000, voiced by Douglas Rain, malfunctions and attacks its crew. It polarised critics, then drew readings from darkly apocalyptic to hopeful about human evolution and technology.

systran-1968.summary: In 1968 Peter Toma founded SYSTRAN to translate Russian documents for America's Air Force; it outlived machine translation's funding collapse and ran Babel Fish. Grown out of Georgetown University’s machine translation effort, it was one of few such systems to survive funding's collapse after ALPAC's mid-1960s report. It went on to work extensively for America’s Department of Defense and the European Commission, and powered Yahoo’s Babel Fish and, until 2007, Google’s language tools.

mexico-telesecundaria-1968.summary: On 21 January 1968 Secretaría de Educación Pública began broadcasting a full grade 7 to 9 curriculum to about 6,500 pupils in villages across seven states around Mexico City. Each lesson pairs a 15-minute televised segment with a guided discussion led by a single teacher covering all subjects, so a community with fifteen primary graduates and a room can open a school without specialist staff. Transmission moved from microwave relays to satellite, and by 1998 some 800,000 pupils in 12,700 communities attended Telesecundarias, with Panama, Costa Rica and Guatemala using the signal. Evaluations in the 1970s found learning comparable to conventional schools at similar unit cost, which made it one of few educational-television projects sustained for decades.

mexico-telesecundaria-1968.detail: Mayo, McAnany and Klees published an early cost-effectiveness analysis in Instructional Science; Calderoni's World Bank note documents launch date, enrolment and the lesson format. During COVID-19 closures Mexico's Aprende en Casa drew on this broadcast infrastructure. Pilot broadcasts to closed-circuit groups began in 1966 to test lesson format before open broadcast on commercial channel time. Each school needs a television set, a coordinator and printed guides sent from Mexico City; coordinators were usually primary teachers given short training. Enrolment reached more than one million in the 2000s, about one fifth of Mexican lower-secondary pupils.

do-androids-dream-1968.summary: In 1968 Philip K Dick asked in a novel how you tell a human from an android that feels; Blade Runner and the replicant came from it. In a San Francisco poisoned by nuclear war, where live animals are costly status symbols and poorer people keep electric imitations, bounty hunter Rick Deckard must “retire” six escaped Nexus-6 androids, servants so lifelike only an empathy test tells them from humans. It became source material for 1982’s film Blade Runner and its 2017 sequel.

It lies on Alaska’s North Slope, 250 miles north of the Arctic Circle. Alaska had chosen that area in the early 1960s among 100 million acres granted under its Statehood Act, after geologist Tom Marshall judged it resembled Wyoming’s oil basins.

itai-itai-disease-1968.summary: Farm women along Jinzu river in Toyama prefecture had suffered since 1910s from bone pain so severe they cried 'itai, itai', with fractures, kidney damage and skeletal softening. Local physician Hagino Noboru and fellow researchers traced it in 1960s to cadmium discharged upstream by Mitsui Mining and Smelting's Kamioka mine and concentrated in rice grown on irrigated paddies. In May 1968 Ministry of Health and Welfare recognised itai-itai as Japan's first officially designated pollution disease. Victims sued Mitsui that year and won at Nagoya High Court in 1972, securing compensation, soil replacement across some 1,500 hectares and a pollution control agreement that let residents inspect mine each year.

npt-1968.summary: In 1968 the Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signature; most states gave up nuclear weapons in return for peaceful nuclear help. It aims to stop nuclear weapons' spread, promote peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursue disarmament, recognizing as nuclear-weapon states only those that tested before 1967: the United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France and China. In force from 1970 and extended indefinitely in 1995, it has 191 parties; India, Israel and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea withdrew in 2003.

intel-founded-1968.summary: In July 1968 Noyce and Moore left Fairchild to found Intel; its memory chips and then microprocessors ran the computer age. First named NM Electronics, it became Intel by month’s end, built its early business on static and dynamic memory chips and grew under Andrew Grove’s leadership.

tokamak-t3-1968.summary: In August 1968 Soviet physicists reported their T-3 tokamak had reached ten million degrees, electron temperatures of 1,000 eV with confinement times at least 50 times the Bohm limit. Rival pinch and stellarator designs had managed nothing close. Western researchers doubted Soviet measurements, so Lev Artsimovich invited Britain’s Culham Laboratory to bring its laser Thomson-scattering thermometer to Moscow; by August 1969 its team confirmed those results, published in Nature that November, and a “tokamak stampede” followed.

cybernetic-serendipity-1968.summary: In 1968 Cybernetic Serendipity opened at London's ICA with robots, computer films and music improvised from visitors' singing. It included Gordon Pask’s Colloquy of Mobiles, whose interacting parts let viewers join their conversation, computer-generated films and graphics, Bruce Lacey’s radio-controlled robots, Nam June Paik’s Robot K-456, and Peter Zinovieff’s studio equipment, which improvised music from tunes visitors sang into a microphone. It then toured America, to Washington’s Corcoran Gallery and San Francisco’s new Exploratorium in 1969.

dhaka-oral-rehydration-trial-1968.summary: At the Pakistan-SEATO Cholera Research Laboratory in Dacca (now Dhaka), physiologists had found that glucose carries sodium and water across the gut even during cholera. In April 1968 David Nalin and Richard Cash, with Rafiqul Islam and Majid Molla, gave adult cholera patients a drink of glucose, sodium chloride, sodium bicarbonate and potassium matched to their stool losses. Patients so treated needed 80 percent less intravenous fluid than controls. The Lancet published it on 17 August 1968. In 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis used this mixture to treat about 4,000 cholera cases among Bangladeshi refugees at Bongaon, India, with a death rate near 3 percent. WHO adopted a standard packet in 1978, and BRAC taught its recipe door to door across Bangladesh.

software-crisis-nato-1968.summary: In October 1968 a NATO conference named the software crisis, projects late and over budget; software engineering was coined as its cure. Participants debated growing complexity of software and hardware and agreed on convincing policy makers at all levels of its seriousness. Peter Naur and Brian Randell edited its conference report, published in January 1969.

mother-of-all-demos-1968.summary: In December 1968 Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the mouse, windows, hypertext and video calls in one 90-minute show, 15 years early. Showing SRI’s oN-Line System, NLS, he demonstrated for the first time in one system many basics of modern personal computing: windows, hypertext, graphics, word processing, revision control, collaborative editing, video conferencing between lab and conference hall, and his computer mouse. Named “Mother of All Demos” in retrospect, it spawned similar work at Xerox PARC and shaped later systems including Apple’s Macintosh.

earthrise-apollo-8-1968.summary: On Christmas Eve 1968 Apollo 8's crew photographed Earth rising over the Moon; that picture made our planet look small and shared. He used a modified Hasselblad 500 EL with 250 mm lens and custom Kodak Ektachrome film, after shooting one black-and-white frame first; for years accounts credited commander Frank Borman, but Anders took all three images. Nature photographer Galen Rowell called it “the most influential environmental photograph ever taken.”

tu-144-first-flight-1968.summary: In December 1968 Tupolev's Tu-144 flew, two months before Concorde, as the first supersonic airliner; it carried passengers for seven months. Designed by Tupolev Design Bureau under Aleksey Tupolev, 16 were built at Voronezh. Reliability problems, a crash at 1973’s Paris Air Show and high projected operating costs limited it to Aeroflot service from 1975 to 1983, with passengers carried only in 1977 and 1978.

frame-problem-1969.summary: In 1969 McCarthy and Hayes named the frame problem: how a reasoning machine knows what does not change when it acts; it is still open. Describing robots’ worlds in first-order logic requires many axioms saying what does not change. Opening a door, for instance, leaves light switches as they were, but logic cannot infer that unless told. This formal problem became one starting point for wider discussion of how hard knowledge representation is for AI.
