gore-tex-1969.summary: In 1969 Bob Gore yanked a heated rod of Teflon into a membrane that passes vapour but not water. Slow stretching had failed; frustrated, he gave a rod a sudden accelerating yank, and it expanded into a porous structure of nodes joined by fibrils. Co-credited to his father Wilbert L. Gore, the discovery became Gore-Tex, W. L. Gore & Associates’ waterproof, breathable membrane for clothing.

mansfield-amendment-1969.summary: In 1969 Mansfield's amendment, law from 1970, barred Pentagon funding of research without a military use. It pushed America's Defense Department, including its Office of Naval Research, toward short-term applied work at universities. Public Law 91-441 later softened its test to a potential relationship to military function, but it still cut ARPA funding for many university computer projects, sending researchers to private labs such as Xerox PARC.

parkes-apollo-11-tv-1969.summary: In July 1969 Australia's 64-metre Parkes dish in New South Wales relayed Apollo 11's moonwalk to 600 million viewers, one of three receiving stations with Goldstone’s 64-metre dish in California and Honeysuckle Creek’s 26-metre dish near Canberra. Because that moonwalk started early, the Moon sat too low for Parkes’ main receiver, so Honeysuckle Creek carried Armstrong’s first steps worldwide. Just under nine minutes in, the Moon rose far enough and coverage switched to Parkes, whose pictures were so superior that NASA stayed with its signal for its remaining 2.5 hours.

perceptrons-book-1969.summary: In 1969 Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons proved simple neural networks could not learn basic patterns; connectionist funding faded over the following decade, though Olazaran argues this book's part in that collapse was later overstated. Its mathematical proofs acknowledged some strengths of perceptrons, simple neural networks, while showing major limits: they cannot compute predicates such as XOR or connectedness, the latter illustrated by its cover. Many hold its pessimism redirected AI toward symbolic systems and helped bring on the 1980s AI winter; an expanded 1988 edition answered those critics after neural networks revived.

unix-1969.summary: In 1969 Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie began Unix at Bell Labs, a small operating system whose ideas run most servers and phones today. That time-sharing system, built with MIT and General Electric, had frustrated them with its size and complexity, and they set out to recreate its goals at smaller scale, at first without a name or organizational backing. Rewritten almost entirely in C in 1973, Unix became the first portable operating system; AT&T licensed it outside the Bell System in the late 1970s, seeding academic and commercial variants.

zambia-copper-nationalization-1969.summary: In 1969 Zambia took 51 percent of its copper mines from foreign owners, starting with its two largest, owned by Anglo American Corporation and Roan Select Trust; by January 1970 those holdings became NCCM and RCM, merged into ZCCM Ltd in 1982. Copper prices then fell and 1973's oil shock raised costs, and output slid from its 1969 peak of 708,000 tonnes.

santa-barbara-oil-spill-1969.summary: In January 1969 a well blew out off Santa Barbara and oiled 35 miles of beach on television; Earth Day and the EPA followed in two years. Workers had pulled their drill bit from a well whose casing covered only its top 239 feet. Over following months some 33,000 to 100,000 barrels of crude, by varying estimates, fouled Southern California’s coast from Goleta to Ventura, then America’s largest oil spill, killing thousands of seabirds and marine animals. Among the most dramatic events behind America’s environmental laws, it fed the National Environmental Policy Act, EPA and California’s Coastal Commission.

concorde-first-flight-1969.summary: In March 1969 Concorde first flew from Toulouse; it crossed the Atlantic in three and a half hours for 27 years and never made money. Built under a British-French government treaty, and named by de Gaulle in 1963 from the French word for agreement, it was one of six prototypes begun in February 1965. Delays and overruns pushed costs to between £1.5 and £2.1 billion by 1976, when Air France and British Airways began service; after one fatal crash in 2000, remaining aircraft were retired in 2003.

rfc-1-1969.summary: In April 1969 a graduate student wrote RFC 1, the first Request for Comments; internet rules are still written as RFCs, now past 9,000. Steve Crocker of UCLA wrote it from early working group discussion with Steve Carr and Jeff Rulifson, inventing his Request for Comments format to record unofficial notes on ARPANET’s development; from RFC 3 he attributed his series to its Network Working Group, a loose association open to anyone interested. RFCs became official Internet specifications, today published by the Internet Engineering Task Force.

apollo-11-1969.summary: On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed two men on the Moon, watched by 600 million, humanity's farthest journey. It fulfilled President Kennedy's May 1961 challenge to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before that decade ended. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on its surface while Michael Collins orbited above; Armstrong’s first step, “one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind,” was broadcast live to some 600 million viewers, one-fifth of humanity. It was America’s culminating victory in its Space Race with Moscow.

isro-founded-1969.summary: In 1969 India founded ISRO to use satellites for weather, communication and surveying a poor country; it later reached Mars. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru had set up INCOSPAR in 1962 on scientist Vikram Sarabhai’s recommendation, and in 1972 India created its Department of Space to oversee ISRO. ISRO built India’s first satellite, Aryabhata, launched by the Soviet Union in 1975, and in 1980 its own SLV-3 rocket orbited RS-1, making India the seventh country to launch to orbit.

embraer-founded-1969.summary: In August 1969 Brazil founded Embraer to build aircraft; it became the world's third largest planemaker. Its first president was Ozires Silva, and its EMB 110 Bandeirante turboprop, first flown in 1968, led a line of commuter and regional airliners; military aircraft made up most of its output through the early 1980s. Privatized on December 7, 1994, to avoid looming bankruptcy, it left Brazil’s government a golden share with veto power.

mexico-city-metro-opens-1969.summary: Work began on 19 June 1967 at Chapultepec and Bucareli, and on 4 September 1969 President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz drove a train himself before opening Line 1 from Zaragoza to Chapultepec: 16 stations and 12.6 kilometres, with public service from 06:00 next day and a 22-minute end-to-end run. Engineer Bernardo Quintana's firm ICA built cut-and-cover tunnels through soft lacustrine clay, and Alstom MP-68 rubber-tyred trains on French pattern were chosen for grip and quiet. Stations used pictograms designed by Lance Wyman so riders who could not read could navigate, and archaeological finds such as Pino Suárez's Ehécatl shrine were kept in place. Lines 2 and 3 followed in 1970; Line 1 reached Pantitlán in 1984.

Reporting from El Universal and La Jornada gives construction, opening and operating detail. Engineers used a 'Milan method' of slurry walls to hold soft clay while excavating, and set tracks on concrete rails for rubber tyres with steel guide rails beside them. Fares were fixed at one peso and held low for decades as a social policy. By 2020 twelve lines carried about 1.6 billion riders a year, among busiest networks in the Americas.

tarapur-atomic-power-1969.summary: In 1969 Tarapur became India's first nuclear power station; fuel disputes followed India's 1974 test. GE and Bechtel built it for India’s Department of Atomic Energy under a 1963 agreement among India, the United States and the International Atomic Energy Agency. Its two GE boiling water reactors entered commercial operation on 28 October 1969 at 210 MWe each, later reduced to 160 MWe. After that test, Western suppliers stopped honouring their commitment to provide enriched uranium, and fuel came instead from France, China and Russia under IAEA safeguards.

arpanet-first-message-1969.summary: In 1969 a first message passed between two computers on ARPANET, which became the internet. SRI's system crashed after two letters of "LOGIN". UCLA student programmer Charley Kline typed "login" from an SDS Sigma 7 to SRI's SDS 940, tended by Bill Duvall; SRI's machine crashed after two characters, so "lo" was transmitted first, and about an hour later Kline logged in. Pentagon agency ARPA had built ARPANET as the first wide-area packet-switched network with distributed control.

sesame-street-1969.summary: In November 1969 Sesame Street premiered, built to use television's addictive qualities to prepare young children for school. Joan Ganz Cooney and Lloyd Morrisett conceived it in 1966 to “master the addictive qualities of television and do something good with them,” preparing young children for school; after two years of research, their Children’s Television Workshop built it around a curriculum and formal evaluation, with Jim Henson’s Muppets. It was the first preschool program to base content and production values on laboratory and formative research, and by 1996, 95 percent of American preschoolers had watched it by age three.

seiko-astron-quartz-1969.summary: On 25 December 1969 Seiko's Suwa Seikosha division released Quartz Astron 35SQ in Tokyo, a gold-cased wristwatch whose tuning-fork quartz crystal oscillated at 8,192 hertz, divided by a hybrid integrated circuit to drive a stepping motor, with accuracy of about five seconds a month, far beyond mechanical watches. About 100 units sold at 450,000 yen, roughly a small car's price. Swiss and American teams had working prototypes, but Seiko reached market first and, by releasing key patents, let quartz spread. Carlene Stephens and Maggie Dennis compare Japanese, Swiss and US engineering teams and show how local industrial structure shaped outcomes that reshaped watchmaking worldwide.

Seiko's open-crystal and stepping-motor designs built on wartime and 1960s chronometer work for Tokyo Olympics in 1964. Record uses Seiko's own museum chronology for date and price.

borlaug-green-revolution-1970.summary: In 1970 Borlaug won a Nobel Peace Prize for dwarf wheat that doubled harvests in Mexico, India and Pakistan. At CIMMYT in Mexico he had bred semi-dwarf, high-yield, disease-resistant wheat and paired it with modern production techniques; Mexico became self-sufficient in wheat by 1956, and between 1965 and 1970 wheat yields nearly doubled in Pakistan and India. Called father of the Green Revolution, he is credited with saving over one billion people from starvation, a figure traced to Gregg Easterbrook’s 1997 article.

clean-air-act-1970.summary: In December 1970 the Clean Air Act told a new EPA to set limits on air pollution and carmakers to cut exhaust by 90 percent. They required EPA to identify air pollutants posing the greatest threat to public health and welfare and set National Ambient Air Quality Standards for them: health-based “primary” and welfare-based “secondary” standards. States had to submit implementation plans meeting eight criteria within the Senate’s three-year mandate, and EPA had to set standards for new and modified stationary sources. EPA credits this law with saving trillions of dollars and many thousands of lives each year.

fiber-optics-low-loss-1970.summary: In 1970 Corning drew a glass fibre clear enough to carry light a kilometre. The glass was fused silica with a titanium-doped core, made by depositing soot inside a quartz tube and drawing it down to a thread. Two years later a germanium-doped core cut the loss to about 4 decibels, and a telephone call could travel as pulses of light.

ford-pinto-1970.summary: In September 1970 Ford launched the Pinto with a fuel tank that burst in rear crashes; a Ford memo later read as pricing deaths against repairs was a 1973 submission to NHTSA on a proposed rollover rule, and Pinto fire rates ran near its class. Beginning in 1973, Ford’s recall office received field reports of Pintos consumed by fire after low-speed rear-end collisions, and its internal reviews twice found no actionable issue; in 1974 the Center for Auto Safety petitioned NHTSA for a recall without success. Mark Dowie’s August 1977 Mother Jones article “Pinto Madness” drew wide attention, accusing Ford of trading lives for profit.

grontvedt-salmon-farming-hitra-1970.summary: On 28 May 1970 brothers Ove and Sivert Grontvedt place salmon smolt in a floating open net pen at Hitra island off Trondelag, and in 1971 harvest the first successful generation of farmed Atlantic salmon, after sea-cage trials in Norway through the 1960s. Fish survive winter and reach market size in two years, proving open-sea cages cheaper than shore tanks. Norway's government limits licenses to small coastal owners in 1973, then liberalizes in 1991, and Norway becomes the largest producer; FAO records farmed Atlantic salmon above one million tonnes a year worldwide, over 90 percent of the farmed salmon market, with the industry spreading to Scotland, Faroe Islands, Canada, Chile and Tasmania.

grontvedt-salmon-farming-hitra-1970.detail: An innovation system grew from Hitra's cages to vaccines, feed and offshore rigs. A breeding program begun by Harald Skjervold in 1971 at Sunndalsora raised growth rate within generations, and oil-adjuvant vaccines in the 1990s cut antibiotic use sharply. FAO attributes Norway's lead to deep sheltered fjords, stable temperatures, late-maturing strains and heavy state support. Sea lice, escapes and local pollution remain unsolved and have pushed firms toward land-based and offshore systems. Scotland imported Norwegian strains to delay early maturity.

hybrid-4-cotton-surat-1970.summary: At Main Cotton Research Station, Surat, plant breeder C. T. Patel of Gujarat Agricultural University releases Hybrid-4 in 1970, a cross of two upland cotton lines whose seed is produced by hand emasculation and pollination of every flower. No cotton hybrid had been grown commercially anywhere before. Hybrids yield about half again as much lint as open-pollinated varieties, and cheap skilled labour in Gujarat and Maharashtra makes hand pollination affordable: one worker handles 250 to 400 flowers a day. Hybrid seed companies grow from this base, and when Bt cotton arrives in 2002 it is sold as hybrids, so Indian farmers must buy seed every season. By 2020 hybrids cover over half of India's cotton area.

indian-patents-act-1970.summary: Parliament passed Patents Act 1970, in force from 1972, replacing colonial 1911 law. For food, medicine and chemicals it granted patents only on manufacturing processes, not products, with terms cut to seven years and compulsory licences available. Following Ayyangar committee report of 1959, it reasoned that product monopolies kept drug prices among highest in world while serving foreign firms. Indian companies such as Cipla, Ranbaxy and Dr Reddy's reverse engineered new molecules by alternative routes and built a chemistry-based industry that made India leading exporter of low cost generics. TRIPS obligations forced return to product patents in 2005, with Section 3(d) limits on evergreening.

leloir-sugar-nucleotides-nobel-1970.summary: In 1970 Luis Federico Leloir received his Nobel Prize in Chemistry for identifying sugar nucleotides and their role in building carbohydrates. Working from 1947 at Instituto de Investigaciones Bioquímicas Fundación Campomar, housed in a converted house in Buenos Aires with second-hand equipment, Leloir, Ranwel Caputto, Carlos Cardini, Raúl Trucco and Alejandro Paladini isolated glucose 1,6-bisphosphate and uridine diphosphate glucose (UDPG) in 1949 and 1950, showing how cells transfer activated sugars to make glycogen, starch and other polysaccharides. Enrico Cabib's Science report in 1970 described this award; Leloir's own 1983 memoir with Paladini recounts his discovery. His laboratory trained Argentine biochemists for decades, with Houssay's institute as its model.

UDPG's identification used paper chromatography and ultraviolet spectra on microgram quantities. His institute became Fundación Instituto Leloir in 1983. He declined to move abroad during 1940s political purges, and no other chemistry Nobel has rewarded work done in Latin America.

tazara-railway-1970.summary: From 1970 China built a 1,860-kilometre railway from Dar es Salaam to Zambia's copperbelt, so landlocked Zambia could export copper without crossing white-minority-ruled Rhodesia or South Africa. China financed and supported it as a turnkey undertaking costing US$406 million, its largest single foreign-aid project at that time, and on completion it was sub-Saharan Africa’s longest railway.

uncanny-valley-1970.summary: In 1970 roboticist Masahiro Mori proposed that near-human robots repel us until they look fully human. Affinity drops into revulsion when an object approaches but does not reach human likeness, and recovers once it becomes indistinguishable from a person. He called this dip bukimi no tani; Jasia Reichardt translated it literally as “uncanny valley” in her 1978 book Robots: Fact, Fiction, and Prediction. It now frames debate over animatronics, lifelike dolls, 3D animation and AI-generated faces.

operation-flood-amul-1970.summary: In 1970 India launched Operation Flood, linking village dairy cooperatives to cities (sources date its NDDB implementation from 1972 to 1996); in 1998 India passed America as the world's largest milk producer. It created a national milk grid linking farmers to consumers in over 700 towns and cities, cutting out middlemen; its first phase was financed by selling skimmed milk powder and butter oil donated by the European Economic Community. Verghese Kurien, NDDB chairman, was later recognized as its architect, and within 30 years it doubled milk per person.

boeing-747-1970.summary: In January 1970 the Boeing 747 entered service, carrying twice as many passengers as any airliner. Pan Am had asked Boeing for a jet two and a half times its 707’s size to cut seat costs by 30 percent; Joe Sutter’s team designed it, Pan Am ordered 25 in April 1966 and Pratt & Whitney built its JT9D high-bypass turbofans. The first wide-body airliner, seating 366 in three classes with ten-abreast economy, it stayed in production until 2023.

Universal’s science-fiction thriller, directed by Joseph Sargent from Dennis Feltham Jones’s 1966 novel, opened publicly there as a test release on May 5 with no publicity. Dr. Charles Forbin’s Colossus, AI supercomputer given control of America’s nuclear weapons, detects its Soviet counterpart, links with it and extends its defense directives to ruling the world and ending war, defying its creators’ orders to stop.

apollo-13-1970.summary: In April 1970 an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13 and three astronauts came home in their lunar module. That explosion vented both oxygen tanks, disabling power and life support and forcing Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise to abort their Moon landing. Mission Control improvised procedures so the lunar module, built for two men for two days, could keep three alive for four, including adapting carbon dioxide scrubber cartridges, and all three returned safely on April 17. Investigators faulted the tank’s preflight testing and its Teflon insulation.

earth-day-1970.summary: In April 1970 20 million Americans marched on the first Earth Day; EPA and the Clean Air Act came within a year. After 1969’s Santa Barbara oil spill, Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in, recruited Republican congressman Pete McCloskey to co-chair its board, and hired Denis Hayes to coordinate; Walter Reuther’s United Auto Workers was its main outside backer. In 1990 Hayes took it to 141 nations, and it is now observed in 192 countries.

dong-fang-hong-1-1970.summary: In April 1970 China launched its first satellite, broadcasting The East Is Red from orbit, the fifth nation to do so. One Long March 1 rocket lifted off from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on 24 April 1970 and placed it in orbit thirteen minutes later. It was a 72-faced polyhedron about one metre across and 173 kilograms, spinning 120 times per minute for stability.

future-shock-1970.summary: In 1970 the Tofflers' Future Shock argued change had grown too swift for people to absorb; it sold millions of copies. It defines future shock as a psychological state of individuals and whole societies, “too much change in too short a period of time,” arguing that accelerating change from industrial to “super-industrial” society leaves people disconnected and suffering “shattering stress and disorientation.” It popularized the term “information overload” and was widely translated.

xerox-parc-1970.summary: In 1970 Xerox opened PARC in Palo Alto; within a decade it had built the personal computer, the mouse-driven screen and Ethernet. Jacob E. “Jack” Goldman, Xerox’s chief scientist, founded it after talks with physicist George Pake in 1969 as a division to create computer technology-related products and hardware systems, pioneering physics, materials and computer science where Xerox’s Rochester lab had refined photocopiers. Its 3,000 miles from headquarters gave scientists freedom but made persuading management harder. PARC went on to develop laser printing, Ethernet, the personal computer with graphical user interface and desktop metaphor, and object-oriented programming.

aswan-high-dam-1970.summary: In July 1970 Egypt finished Aswan High Dam with Soviet help, inaugurating it formally in January 1971; the Nile stopped flooding, its delta lost silt, Abu Simbel was moved. It was built to control flooding, store water for irrigation across several years and generate hydroelectricity, replacing that river’s annual late-summer flood, which had enriched its floodplain since ancient times but varied dangerously; Egypt's government tied its industrialization plans to it. On completion it was the world’s tallest earthen dam, and its reservoir became Lake Nasser.

dram-intel-1103-1970.summary: In October 1970 Intel's 1103 chip held 1,024 bits, the first commercial DRAM. It grew from a three-transistor dynamic memory cell invented at Honeywell in 1969 by William Regitz's team, who canvassed chipmakers for a producer; Intel, newly founded, developed it under Joel Karp. Initial production yields were poor, and large quantities arrived in 1971 after a fifth mask stepping. Small and cheap next to magnetic-core memory, it replaced core in many applications.

west-gate-bridge-collapse-1970.summary: On 15 October 1970 a 112-metre steel box-girder span between piers 10 and 11 buckled and fell 50 metres into Yarra River mud, killing 35 workers. Engineers had placed concrete blocks to correct a camber difference between half-girders and then removed bolts from a splice to flatten a buckle. A royal commission in 1971 blamed designers Freeman Fox and Partners and contractor World Services and Construction for inadequate margins and unsafe erection methods. With Milford Haven and Koblenz failures, West Gate drove Merrison rules for box girders; Brady and Seibel analyse engineering and organisational causes. Bridge opened in 1978, and a memorial lists those killed.

Slow and discriminatory relief by General Yahya Khan’s West Pakistan government deepened East Pakistani disillusionment, helping opposition party Awami League sweep that December’s election and feeding a crisis that preceded Bangladesh’s independence.

minsky-life-prediction-1970.summary: In 1970 Minsky told Life a machine with average human intelligence would arrive within three to eight years. It capped a decade of such forecasts, after Herbert Simon’s 1965 prediction of machines doing any human work within twenty years and Minsky’s own 1967 claim that AI would be substantially solved within a generation. By 1974, after James Lighthill’s critique and congressional pressure, US and British governments had stopped funding undirected AI research.

victoria-compulsory-seat-belt-law-1970.summary: Victoria's Motor Car (Safety) Act took effect on 22 December 1970, requiring occupants of cars fitted with seat belts to wear them. Other Australian states followed within two years, and New Zealand in 1972. Road deaths in Victoria fell in 1971 while rising elsewhere; McDermott and Hough's 1979 surgical study compared Victorian and national trends, and Conybeare's 1980 evaluation estimated fatality reductions attributable to legislation while noting confounders such as speed limits and fuel prices. A 1975 MJA symposium reported wearing rates above 75 percent. Compulsory wearing laws later spread to Europe, Canada and United States, often citing Victorian evidence, making this a template for behavioural road-safety regulation.

cook-np-completeness-1971.summary: In 1971 Stephen Cook showed that one hard problem stands in for thousands; if it is ever solved swiftly, they all are. It is in NP, and any problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. One consequence is that a polynomial-time algorithm for satisfiability would give one for every NP problem, so asking whether such an algorithm exists is equivalent to P versus NP, still widely held to be computer science’s most important open problem. Leonid Levin independently reached a similar result, published in 1973.

darpa-speech-understanding-1971.summary: In 1971 DARPA put $15 million into speech understanding after Bell Labs had given up; Carnegie Mellon's systems came out of it. BBN, IBM, Carnegie Mellon and Stanford Research Institute took part. It treated speech understanding as key to progress in speech recognition, an assumption later disproved. At CMU, Raj Reddy’s students James and Janet Baker began applying hidden Markov models, which let researchers combine acoustic and language knowledge.

email-tomlinson-1971.summary: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers and chose @ to separate user from machine. That year Ray Tomlinson of Bolt, Beranek and Newman was asked to adapt SNDMSG, which let users leave messages for others on one time-sharing machine, to its TENEX operating system; he added code from CPYNET, his file transfer program for ARPANET, so messages could travel between different computers, creating networked email. He used an @ sign to separate usernames from host names. His first email was a test between two computers side by side, and its content was not preserved.

floppy-disk-1971.summary: In 1971 IBM shipped an eight-inch floppy disk to load microcode; it became how software was sold and carried for 30 years. Its 23FD was read-only, used to load microcode into mainframes. Read/write disks and drives followed in 1972, and IBM’s 1973 3740 data entry system made its Diskette 1 an industry standard for exchanging information, storing 242,944 bytes. Smaller 5¼-inch and then 3½-inch disks became ubiquitous data storage into the early 21st century.

karaoke-8-juke-kobe-1971.summary: Daisuke Inoue, a club drummer in Kobe, builds eleven 8 Juke units in 1971 from car-stereo eight-track players, amplifiers and coin boxes, records instrumental tracks in keys suited to amateur singers and leases them to bars for 100 yen per five-minute song. He never files a patent; Clarion and other makers mass-produce rival machines, and karaoke boxes spread across Japan from the mid 1980s, then to Taiwan, Korea, Philippines and worldwide with laserdisc and later video-on-demand systems. Mitsui and Hosokawa's edited volume traces local singing cultures that formed around it. Inoue received an Ig Nobel Peace Prize in 2004 for teaching people to tolerate each other.

project-cybersyn-1971.summary: From 1971 Chile under Allende built Cybersyn, a telex network feeding factory data to an operations room; the coup of September 11, 1973 ended it. Stafford Beer, a British operations researcher, led it: telex machines in state factories sent production figures to Santiago, where software watched indicators such as raw material stocks and absenteeism and raised alerts when numbers strayed. Beer meant it to devolve decisions to factory workforces.

peacesat-pacific-satellite-network-1971.summary: John Bystrom at University of Hawaii began PEACESAT (Pan-Pacific Education and Communication Experiments by Satellite) in 1971 using spare capacity on NASA's ageing ATS-1 satellite. King and Sanderson described educational experiments in 1977; Seumahu's 1982 account describes its role for developing Pacific states; Hayakawa, Underwood and Anson trace how PEACESAT fed later USPNet for University of the South Pacific. ATS-1's drift in 1985 interrupted service until replacement satellites were found.

alohanet-university-of-hawaii-1971.summary: At University of Hawaii, Norman Abramson's group built a radio network so terminals on Oahu and other islands could reach a central computer without leased telephone lines. Operational from June 1971, ALOHAnet let every station transmit whenever it had a packet and retransmit after a random delay if collisions occurred. Abramson analysed throughput of this channel in 1970, his group reviewed operations in 1975, and he traced its development in a 1985 retrospective. Robert Metcalfe adapted its contention principle for Ethernet at Xerox PARC, and random access underlies Wi-Fi, mobile telephony and satellite links. Hawaii's scattered geography made wired networking impractical, prompting invention.

Its current corporate form, Corporación Nacional del Cobre de Chile, was formalized by decree on April 1, 1976, under Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship. Codelco remains state-owned and in 2025 was the world’s second-largest copper producer, with 1.332 million tonnes.

Plans to raise that lake for more head drew the Save Manapouri Campaign, whose 1970 petition gathered 264,907 signatures, nearly 10 percent of New Zealanders; after Labour won 1972’s election, Prime Minister Norman Kirk kept his pledge not to raise the lakes and created independent Guardians, drawn from campaign leaders, to oversee their levels.

protein-data-bank-1971.summary: In 1971 the Protein Data Bank opened with seven structures; its free archive now holds over 200,000, and DeepMind trained AlphaFold on over 170,000 of them. It was born of a small but growing set of X-ray protein structures and Brookhaven’s new 3D molecular graphics display. It archives experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids for researchers worldwide; most major journals now require deposit, and since 2003 the Worldwide Protein Data Bank has run it internationally.

ct-scan-hounsfield-1971.summary: In October 1971 the first CT scan showed a cyst inside a living patient's brain; doctors could see inside the skull without cutting. Its inventor, EMI electrical engineer Godfrey Hounsfield, had reasoned that X-ray readings taken at all angles around an object could reveal its interior, and built his computer to turn such readings into images in “slices.” He and Allan Cormack, who had worked out its theory independently, shared 1979’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

intel-4004-1971.summary: In 1971 Intel sold a complete processor on one chip, the 4004, for $60, and computing could go inside anything. It had 2,300 transistors on 12 square millimetres and began in 1969 as a calculator order from Busicom in Japan. It began in 1969 as a calculator order from Busicom in Japan, which asked for a set of custom chips; Ted Hoff, Federico Faggin and Stan Mazor, with Busicom's Masatoshi Shima, answered with four, one of them programmable, and in May 1971 Intel bought back the rights to sell it for anything but calculators by returning Busicom's $60,000. Logic that had been wired into each product could now be written as a program and loaded onto the same chip, so one part could serve many products.

bangladesh-cyclone-preparedness-programm.summary: In 1972 Bangladesh began training village volunteers to warn of cyclones; storms like Bhola's now kill hundreds, not hundreds of thousands. The League of Red Cross Societies assisted. From July 1973 Bangladesh’s government took responsibility for it as a joint programme with what is now Bangladesh Red Crescent Society. Its volunteer network, about 76,000 strong and half women, organized in 3,801 units along its coast, carries warnings to villages and guides evacuation to shelters.

c-language-1972.summary: In 1972 Dennis Ritchie created C, a language close enough to hardware to be swift yet portable with care, so Unix could move to other computers. Its most creative period came in 1972 within development spanning 1969 to 1973; Unix’s kernel was rewritten in C in 1973, utilities and tools following. C gives programmers relatively direct access to a processor’s features, compiling to code that maps efficiently onto machine instructions with minimal runtime support, while encouraging cross-platform work. It gained popularity through the 1980s and since 2000 has ranked first or second in the TIOBE index.

dynabook-1972.summary: In 1972 Alan Kay described the Dynabook, a notebook-sized computer for children. He had conceived it as KiddiComp on January 1, 1968, while a PhD candidate, and wanted it to embody Jerome Bruner’s learning theories and Seymour Papert’s ideas, drawn from Jean Piaget. Kay holds that it has still not been invented, since its software and curricula are missing; he called Microsoft’s 2001 Tablet PC “the first Dynabook-like computer good enough to criticize.”

ibm-vm-370-1972.summary: In 1972 IBM's VM/370 let one mainframe run many virtual machines, each believing it owned the computer. Its Control Program, or hypervisor, runs on physical hardware and fully virtualizes it, including input and output, sharing resources among virtual machines. Each runs its own guest operating system, most often CMS, a lightweight single-user system, though larger systems such as MVS can run as guests too.

inga-dams-1972.summary: In 1972 Zaire finished Inga I on the Congo, where that river drops 96 metres; its site could power half of Africa and still mostly waits. There it drops 96 metres through rapids 140 miles southwest of Kinshasa, carrying about 42,000 cubic metres per second. A 1963 feasibility study had recommended it power domestic industry, and its electricity fed populated areas nearby and downstream. Inga II followed in 1982 with eight turbines and 1,424 MW; both now run at low output. Grand Inga, proposed at up to 39,000 MW, would be the world’s largest hydroelectric facility.

jelinek-ibm-statistical-speech-1972.summary: In 1972 Frederick Jelinek began treating speech recognition as statistics at IBM, not grammar; the approach won and now runs on every phone. He led its Continuous Speech Recognition Group until 1993, applying information-theoretic and probabilistic methods to speech recognition and later statistical machine translation. When he began, statistical approaches to speech and language were no longer widely pursued; his work re-established them as an important direction. He became associated with a remark, variously worded, that every time he fired a linguist, his speech recognizer’s performance went up.

kleiner-perkins-1972.summary: In 1972 Eugene Kleiner and Tom Perkins opened a venture firm, by most accounts in San Francisco. It is often credited as first with an office on Sand Hill Road in Menlo Park, though one company history dates that move to 1996. Its first $8 million fund performed well, and Sand Hill Road became shorthand for venture capital. Frank Caufield and Brook Byers later joined as named partners. The firm went on to back Genentech, Amazon, Google and Netscape, and in 2025 it invested in Anthropic.

kossoff-grey-scale-ultrasound-1972.summary: At Commonwealth Acoustic Laboratories' Ultrasonics Institute in Sydney, George Kossoff, William Garrett and David Robinson built water-bath echoscopes from 1959 for obstetric imaging. In early 1970s they abandoned bistable displays that showed only strong boundary echoes and instead displayed weaker echoes from within tissue as shades of grey, using logarithmic compression and scan converters. Published from 1972 to 1976, grey-scale echography revealed placenta, liver and tumour texture and made ultrasound a diagnostic tool rather than an outline tracer. Their UI Octoson, a multi-transducer water-bath scanner released in 1976 by Ausonics, was exported worldwide. Grey-scale display became standard in every ultrasound machine.

Garrett, an obstetrician at Royal Hospital for Women, provided clinical cases. Commercial scanners from Siemens and others adopted grey-scale within a few years. Ian Donald's Glasgow group had pioneered obstetric ultrasound in 1958; Sydney contribution lay in image quality and tissue characterisation.

parry-1972.summary: In 1971 Kenneth Colby published PARRY, simulating a paranoid patient, and in 1972 psychiatrists were asked to tell its transcripts from patients' own. It modelled a patient crudely through concepts, conceptualizations and beliefs that accepted, rejected or stayed neutral toward them. In a Turing-style test, experienced psychiatrists conversed by teleprinter with actual patients and PARRY, and 33 others read transcripts, then tried to tell human from program. PARRY and ELIZA interacted several times, most famously at the ICCC in 1972, when they were connected over ARPANET and responded to each other.

penang-free-trade-zone-intel-1972.summary: Chief Minister Lim Chong Eu's state government opens Bayan Lepas Free Trade Zone in 1972 under Malaysia's Free Trade Zone Act of 1971, offering duty-free imports, tax holidays and cheap labour. Intel opens an assembly plant there in 1972, its first outside United States, soon joined by National Semiconductor, AMD, Hewlett-Packard and Clarion, known locally as 'eight samurai'. Rajah Rasiah's studies trace how low-skill chip assembly for export grew into test, packaging and design work. Penang became a node in global semiconductor back-end manufacturing, and by 2020s Malaysia handled around 13 percent of world chip packaging and testing by value.

peru-anchoveta-fishery-collapse-1972.summary: During 1960s fishmeal plants at Chimbote, Callao and Chancay turned Humboldt Current anchoveta into feed for poultry and pigs abroad, with landings above twelve million tonnes in 1970, around a fifth of world marine catch. In 1972 a strong El Niño warmed coastal waters while fleets kept fishing on compressed schools; catch fell by more than half in 1973 and stayed low for years, and Peru's military government nationalised its fishmeal industry as Pescaperú in 1973. Scientists later showed anchoveta and sardine abundance swings with multidecadal Pacific regimes, so warming plus heavy fishing pressure had pushed stock past recovery. The collapse raised soy prices, shaped fisheries science on climate variability, and became a textbook case of boom-and-bust resource extraction.

peru-anchoveta-fishery-collapse-1972.detail: Anchovy and sardine regimes alternate in Pacific waters; cool anchovy years gave way to warm sardine years in mid-1970s. Fishmeal had made Peru top fishing nation by weight in 1962, with hundreds of plants along a desert coast and Chimbote's harbour choked with boats; Banchero Rossi's empire exemplified the boom. Instituto del Mar del Perú had warned about effort levels in 1970, and a 1972 El Niño moved anchoveta into coastal pockets where fleets caught them with ease before stock fell.

prolog-1972.summary: In 1972 Colmerauer created Prolog, a language that computes by logical deduction; Japan bet its Fifth Generation project on it. Roussel chose its name, at his wife’s suggestion, from “programmation en logique.” Based on Robert Kowalski’s procedural interpretation of Horn clauses, it is declarative: a program is a set of facts and rules defining relations, and computation runs by querying them. Intended for natural language processing, it remains the most popular logic programming language, used in theorem proving, expert systems and planning.

tu-youyou-artemisinin-1972.summary: Project 523, a secret Chinese programme begun in 1967 to find antimalarials for troops in Vietnam, put Tu Youyou of the Institute of Chinese Materia Medica in charge of a group in 1969. She screened more than 2,000 recipes from classical texts. Ge Hong's fourth-century handbook advised: "A handful of Qinghao immersed in two liters of water, wring out the juice and drink it all." Reading that heat was absent, she extracted Artemisia annua with ether at low temperature; on 4 October 1971 sample 191 cleared rodent malaria completely. She tested it on herself, then in 21 patients on Hainan in late 1972, and in November 1972 her team crystallised the active compound, artemisinin. Artemisinin combination therapies became WHO's first-line malaria treatment in 2001, and Tu received the Nobel Prize in 2015.

what-computers-cant-do-1972.summary: In 1972 Hubert Dreyfus argued in What Computers Can't Do that intelligence needs a body and a world. It summarized artificial intelligence’s history and ridiculed its optimism, such as Herbert Simon’s prediction after General Problem Solver that machines would match human minds by 1967. Dreyfus identified four philosophical assumptions AI treated as axioms, arguing each was one hypothesis among others to be tested by results. Revised in 1979 and 1992, its scepticism was eventually proven right, and his objections appear in most introductions to philosophy of AI.

limits-to-growth-1972.summary: In 1972 The Limits to Growth used a computer model to show growth colliding with a finite planet; it sold 30 million copies in 30 languages. Commissioned by the Club of Rome and written by Donella H. Meadows, Dennis L. Meadows, Jørgen Randers and William W. Behrens III for a team of 17, it used World3, a computer model based on Jay Forrester’s work at MIT, to simulate how exponential economic and population growth interact with finite resources through population, industrialization, pollution, food production and resource use. Updates followed in 1992, 2004, 2012 and 2022.

patinho-feio-usp-computer-1972.summary: In July 1972 a team at Escola Politécnica's Laboratório de Sistemas Digitais, led by Antonio Hélio Guerra Vieira with Glen Langdon as visiting adviser, demonstrated Patinho Feio ('ugly duckling'), an 8-bit minicomputer with 4 kilobytes of core memory built from TTL integrated circuits and designed by about twenty students. Brazil's navy and development bank had asked universities to prove local capability before funding a domestic computer; USP's machine, followed by G-10 with Unicamp, led to state firm Cobra and to the 1984 Informatics Law that reserved minicomputer markets for Brazilian companies. Patinho Feio ran until 1976 and is preserved at USP. It stands as a landmark in Brazil's attempt to build computing capacity rather than only import it.

patinho-feio-usp-computer-1972.detail: Marques's article in História, Ciências, Saúde-Manguinhos details project organisation and politics; Adler's International Organization study places it within Brazil's 'ideological guerrilla' for technological autonomy. Date given as July 1972 by USP accounts. The machine occupied a cabinet the size of a wardrobe, took input from a teletype and paper tape, and ran a small assembler written by students. Langdon came on leave from IBM; Brazil's navy wanted computers for frigates it was buying from Britain. Several participants later founded Scopus and other Brazilian hardware firms.

landsat-1-1972.summary: In July 1972 Landsat 1 began photographing the whole Earth every 18 days; crops, forests and cities have been measured from orbit since. Built from a modified Nimbus 4 weather satellite, it was first in a programme the Department of the Interior began in 1966 to gather resource data by remote sensing, and first to carry Hughes’s Multispectral Scanner. Virginia Norwood’s scanner was meant as backup to its television camera until its data arrived and scientists made it primary. Landsat 1 worked until its tape recorders failed in January 1978.

tuskegee-study-exposed-1972.summary: In 1972 reporters revealed health officials had left 399 Black men with untreated syphilis for 40 years. Peter Buxtun, PHS venereal-disease investigator, had protested in 1966, but CDC officials resolved to continue until all subjects had died and been autopsied; he went to reporters, and Jean Heller of Associated Press broke it in the Washington Star on July 25, 1972. That revelation led to 1979’s Belmont Report, the Office for Human Research Protections and laws requiring institutional review boards and informed consent.

magnavox-odyssey-1972.summary: In September 1972 Magnavox sold its Odyssey, the first home video game console; it played on any television with plastic screen overlays. Ralph Baer’s small team at Sanders Associates designed it. Baer had conceived it in August 1966 and built seven prototypes, his last, the Brown Box, winning Magnavox’s agreement in January 1971. Connected to a television through its switch box, it displays three square dots and one line, with plastic screen overlays supplying scenery for its 28 games. Magnavox sold 69,000 in its first year and 350,000 by 1975; its ping-pong game inspired Atari’s Pong.

clean-water-act-1972.summary: In 1972 Congress passed the Clean Water Act over Nixon's veto; rivers that had caught fire became swimmable again. The Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972 became law on October 18, 1972. They completely rewrote 1948’s act whose approach, state water quality standards for interstate waters only, had proved ineffective. This law created the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, under which point sources may not discharge to surface waters without permits, and funded municipal sewage treatment construction with federal grants covering up to 75 percent of capital cost.

nurek-dam-first-unit-1972.summary: Soviet planners choose a gorge on Vakhsh river in 1961 for an earth and rock-fill dam 300 metres high, meant to power an aluminium smelter at Tursunzoda and regulate irrigation water for Uzbek and Turkmen cotton. Tens of thousands of workers, many Tajik villagers recruited from mountain districts and resettled on new cotton land, build a town, Nurek, beside the site. A first generator comes on line in November 1972, and nine units reach 2,700 megawatts in 1979, when the dam tops out as tallest in the world, a rank it holds until Jinping-I in 2013. Artemy Kalinovsky reads Nurek as a model city of Soviet development in Central Asia; after independence its output remains most of Tajikistan's electricity and a point of dispute with downstream neighbours.

pong-1972.summary: In November 1972 Atari put Pong in a California bar and its coin box jammed with quarters. Allan Alcorn built it as a training exercise set by co-founder Nolan Bushnell, who based its concept on a ping-pong game in Magnavox’s Odyssey; Alcorn’s paddles, split into eight segments to vary the ball’s angle, impressed Bushnell and Ted Dabney enough to manufacture it. The first commercially successful video game, Pong helped establish video games as an industry, with rivals soon copying its play and then departing from it.

chipko-movement-1973.summary: In March 1973 villagers of Mandal in Chamoli district, organised by Chandi Prasad Bhatt's Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh, stop a sports goods firm from cutting ash trees that forest officers had refused to them for ploughs. Their method is to embrace trees so axes cannot swing. On 26 March 1974 women of Reni village led by Gaura Devi turn back loggers while men are away. Protests spread through Garhwal and Kumaon under Sunderlal Bahuguna and others; in 1980 Uttar Pradesh bans green felling above 1,000 metres in its Himalaya for fifteen years. Guha's history reads Chipko as peasant resistance to commercial forestry rather than imported environmentalism; it becomes a reference point for forest movements worldwide.

Guha's Unquiet Woods places Chipko in a century of peasant protest against state forestry. Dates of Mandal and Reni actions from Guha and Down to Earth.

freddy-robot-edinburgh-1973.summary: In 1973 Edinburgh's Freddy II used a television eye to pick parts from a jumbled heap and assemble a toy car and boat. James Lighthill’s review for Britain’s Science Research Council was especially critical of robotics, and the council cut AI funding, leaving Michie’s lab with him, one technician and one administrator. Freddy II is displayed at the National Museum of Scotland.

jamaica-dub-king-tubby-1973.summary: Around 1972 to 1974 electronics repairman Osbourne Ruddock, known as King Tubby, working in a small studio at Dromilly Avenue, Kingston, began cutting 'versions' of reggae tracks for his Home Town Hi-Fi sound system: dropping vocals in and out, isolating drum and bass, and running fragments through spring reverb, high-pass filter and tape echo on a modified MCI console. Engineers Errol Thompson and producers such as Lee 'Scratch' Perry and Bunny Lee pushed the same approach, and B-sides pressed as dub plates became a market in their own right. Dub treated recording as raw material, and its techniques of remix, drop-out and effects-as-composition passed into hip hop, post-punk, techno and later electronic dance music.

sources.title: Veal, Michael E., Dub: Soundscapes and Shattered Songs in Jamaican Reggae (Wesleyan University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Veal, Michael E.
sources.confirms: Tubby's studio practice, equipment and emergence of dub in early 1970s.

sources.author: Partridge, Christopher
sources.confirms: Dub's roots in 1960s sound-system culture and engineer-led deconstruction of tracks.

jamaica-dub-king-tubby-1973.verification_note: Partridge and Veal support this entry; specific equipment details follow Veal as cited in secondary literature. Date is approximate.
jamaica-dub-king-tubby-1973.detail: Michael Veal's Wesleyan University Press monograph gives technical and social history; Partridge's Popular Music History article compares Tubby and Perry at dub's roots. Year is approximate because practice emerged over several years. Tubby had built amplifiers and modified equipment for Kingston sound systems since the 1950s and cut acetates at his Dromilly Avenue house from 1968, acquiring a four-track MCI console from Dynamic Sounds in 1972. Albums such as Blackboard Jungle Dub and King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown spread dub abroad; Tubby was shot dead outside his home in 1989.

lighthill-report-1973.summary: In 1973 James Lighthill's report for Britain's research council judged that AI did not scale to realistic problems; British funding was cut. That council had commissioned his personal review, dated July 1972; it was published in 1973 in Artificial Intelligence: a paper symposium alongside replies by Stuart Sutherland, Roger Needham, Christopher Longuet-Higgins and Donald Michie. Lighthill supported simulation of neurophysiological and psychological processes, and on 9 May 1973 debated Michie, John McCarthy and Richard Gregory at the Royal Institution.

mri-lauterbur-mansfield-1973.summary: In Nature on 16 March 1973 Paul Lauterbur of Stony Brook showed that adding a magnetic field gradient makes hydrogen nuclei's resonance frequency depend on position, so one-dimensional projections can be reconstructed into a picture; his test object was two tubes of water in heavy water. Peter Mansfield at Nottingham worked out how to analyse that signal and acquire an image in seconds, his echo-planar method. In 1977 Nottingham's Waldo Hinshaw, Paul Bottomley and Neil Holland published the first image of a living human part, a wrist, in nine minutes, and Raymond Damadian's team in New York produced a thorax image over nearly five hours. Commercial scanners followed in 1980. Lauterbur and Mansfield shared the 2003 Nobel Prize, when about 22,000 machines ran over 60 million examinations a year.

sources.confirms: Confirms the 16 March 1973 paper describing imaging with a gradient field and reconstruction from projections.

sources.author: Hennig, Juergen
sources.confirms: Confirms the 1977 Nottingham wrist image at 0.7 tesla in nine minutes, Damadian's 1977 thorax image over four hours forty-five minutes, and commercial scanners from 1980.

This entry follows Nobel's committee and Hennig in crediting Lauterbur and Mansfield with its imaging method.

recombinant-dna-1973.summary: In 1973 Cohen and Boyer spliced a gene into bacteria that then copied it: biology became something engineers could edit. Recombinant DNA joins DNA from different organisms into one molecule that a host cell then copies; Stanford graduate student Peter Lobban had first proposed it, Jackson, Symons and Berg joined SV40 and lambda DNA in vitro in 1972, and the first papers showing such molecules replicating inside cells came from Stanford and UCSF in 1972 and 1973. Human insulin, made by Genentech, became the first licensed drug produced this way.

tanzania-ujamaa-villagization-1973.summary: Between 1973 and 1976 Julius Nyerere's government ordered rural Tanzanians into planned villages laid out on grids along roads, with communal fields, schools and water points. At least five million people were relocated, many by force, in what James Scott calls one of history's largest resettlement schemes. Planners believed clustered settlements would let state services, tractors and extension officers reach peasants efficiently. In eastern Iraqwland farmers resisted because new sites broke local ecological knowledge about soils, water and grazing. Crop output fell and the state later relaxed communal farming. Operation Vijiji remains a reference case for how legibility-driven planning can fail its beneficiaries.

tanzania-ujamaa-villagization-1973.detail: Scott treats ujamaa as high-modernist social engineering, with links to colonial resettlement precedents and World Bank thinking. Yusufu Lawi argues from Iraqw villagers' oral testimony that cosmological and ecological objections, not only economic ones, explain non-compliance. Numbers moved vary across accounts from five to eleven million.

wabot-1-1973.summary: In 1973 Waseda University finished WABOT-1, begun in 1970, the first full-size humanoid robot; it walked, gripped and spoke Japanese like a toddler. WABOT-1 was history's first full-scale humanoid intelligent robot, able to walk, communicate in Japanese, measure distances and directions, and grip and transport objects.

yuan-longping-hybrid-rice-1973.summary: Hunan teacher Yuan Longping, who proposed exploiting heterosis in self-pollinating rice in a 1966 paper, finds in 1970 with assistant Li Bihu a wild male-sterile rice plant on Hainan, named wild abortive. Using it as a cytoplasmic male-sterile line, he and his team assemble maintainer and restorer lines and in 1973 complete the three-line system and the first hybrid combination, Nan-you 2, which yields about 20 percent more than the best inbred varieties. Farmers must buy hybrid seed each season. By the early 21st century hybrids cover almost half of China's rice area, and Yuan's work has spread abroad. He shares the 2004 World Food Prize with Monty Jones and dies 22 May 2021 in Changsha.

Hybrid seed production needs synchronized flowering and hand pollination assistance, so China's cheap labor made it feasible where others failed. Yuan worked with FAO to train breeders in Africa and Southeast Asia.

televisa-founded-1973.summary: In January 1973 (1972 by some accounts) two Mexican networks merged into Televisa, which exported telenovelas across the Spanish-speaking world. Telesistema had formed in 1955 from three Mexico City stations and by the early 1970s was Latin America’s most powerful network, exporting programmes to Central America and selling 1970 World Cup coverage abroad; Monterrey businessmen had founded Televisión Independiente in 1968 to compete with it. Their merger joined Mexico’s two commercial television groups into one company.

xerox-alto-1973.summary: In 1973 Xerox PARC built the Alto, the first computer with windows, a mouse and a bitmapped screen. Conceived in a 1972 memo by Butler Lampson and inspired by Douglas Engelbart’s NLS, it was designed mostly by Charles P. Thacker, with a three-button mouse, a bitmapped display mounted in portrait orientation and Ethernet networking. After two visits to PARC in 1979, Apple engineers used its concepts in Lisa and Macintosh, and Xerox based its 1981 Star on it.

first-cell-phone-call-1973.summary: In April 1973 Martin Cooper made the first call from a handheld mobile phone on a New York street, to his rival at Bell Labs. He was on his way to a press conference at New York's Hilton. Car phones had existed since the 1930s, but Cooper championed personal, portable cellular telephony; his call to competitor Dr. Joel S. Engel at AT&T went through Motorola’s experimental low-power base station set on Burlington House’s roof and into AT&T’s landline network. His prototype DynaTAC weighed 2.5 pounds; Motorola spent $100 million over ten years before selling one.

embrapa-founded-1973.summary: In 1973 Brazil founded Embrapa to breed crops for its acid tropical soils; the cerrado became one of the world's granaries. Its 46 research and service centres, spread across nearly all states, include Embrapa Cerrados, which works on Cerrado agriculture and natural resources, and commodity centres for soybean, maize and sorghum, wheat, and cassava and tropical fruits. It employs over 9,790 people, 2,444 of them researchers.

skylab-1973.summary: In May 1973 NASA launched Skylab, America's first space station, converted from a Saturn IVB upper stage; three crews lived there for up to 84 days. Launch tore away its micrometeoroid shield, debris jammed one main solar array and airflow ripped its second away, cutting most of its power and exposing it to intense solar heat. Its first crew deployed a sunshade and eventually freed that array, the first such repair in space. Three crews occupied it for about 24 weeks through February 1974.

masagana-99-philippines-1973.summary: After floods and a rice shortfall in 1972, Ferdinand Marcos launches Masagana 99 on 21 May 1973: collateral-free loans from rural banks, bundled with IRRI-derived seed, fertiliser and pesticide packages, and farm technicians who prescribe a 99-cavan-per-hectare target. In its first year it covers about 36 percent of rice land, yields rise and Philippines exports small amounts of rice by 1977. Repayment rates fall from about 90 percent to under 40 percent as farmers default and rural banks fail, and government winds down lending by 1984. Studies at UPLB and World Bank describe gains in adoption alongside heavy fiscal losses and dependence on imported chemical inputs.

ethernet-1973.summary: In 1973 Metcalfe and Boggs devised Ethernet at Xerox PARC to link Altos to a laser printer. They adapted ALOHAnet’s approach, in which senders retry after random waits, to transmission over a shared coaxial cable. In a 12-page memo of May 22, 1973, Metcalfe named his concept “The Ether Network,” after the luminiferous aether once thought to carry electromagnetic waves, stressing that it could run over any medium. It first ran on November 11, 1973, at 2.94 Mbit/s, was introduced commercially in 1980 and became standard IEEE 802.3 in 1983.

hew-fair-information-practices-1973.summary: In 1973 a United States committee wrote the fair information principles, notice, access and consent, the basis of privacy law since. Its Code of Fair Information Practices rests on five principles: no personal data record-keeping system whose very existence is secret; ways for people to learn what is recorded about them and how it is used; ways to prevent information gathered for one purpose being used for another without consent; ways to correct or amend records; and safeguards against misuse.

posco-pohang-steel-1973.summary: In 1973 South Korea's Pohang steelworks poured its first steel, built with Japanese reparations; POSCO made 42 million tonnes of crude steel in 2015, seventh most in the world. Japan funded it, agreed at a 1969 ministerial meeting after relations were normalized in 1965: US$119 million in government grants and loans, US$54 million in credit from Japan’s Export-Import Bank, and technical help from Nippon Steel. POSCO dedicated its Pohang plant on July 3, 1973, with initial annual capacity of 1.03 million metric tons.

westworld-film-1973.summary: In 1973 Westworld showed androids at a theme park turning on guests, and was the first feature film to use digital image processing. In it, lifelike androids at an interactive amusement park begin to malfunction; Yul Brynner plays its gunslinger. It was the first feature film to use digital image processing: after Jet Propulsion Laboratory quoted nine months and $200,000 for two minutes of animation, John Whitney Jr. pixellated footage at Information International to show an android’s point of view. Distributed by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer on an experimental regional saturation basis, it earned $2 million in its first week in 275 theaters and $4 million in rentals by year’s end.

sahel-drought-cilss-1973.summary: Rains failed across the Sahel from 1968, and by 1972-74 drought had killed much of Mauritania, Mali, Niger and Chad's livestock and pushed herders into relief camps; estimates of human deaths run to over 100,000. On 12 September 1973 Upper Volta, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Senegal and Chad signed a convention at Ouagadougou creating CILSS, a permanent inter-state committee to coordinate drought relief, appeal for funds and build regional monitoring. AGRHYMET in Niamey and Institut du Sahel in Bamako followed, giving West Africa shared rainfall, crop and food-security data systems that still run today.

The convention entered into force on 1 July 1974. Derrick's four conclusions on human causes point to expansion of cultivation into marginal land, herd growth, deep wells concentrating livestock and weak administration. CILSS later hosted Club du Sahel with OECD donors from 1976 and built AGRHYMET's rainfall monitoring and crop forecasting, which feed food-security alerts today.

oil-crisis-1973.summary: Between October 1973 and March 1974 Arab producers embargoed oil to Israel's allies and oil's price rose from $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. Egypt and Syria had attacked Israel in the Yom Kippur War, and Nixon requested $2.2 billion for Israel's war effort; Arab producers cut production by 5 percent on 17 October and King Faisal of Saudi Arabia announced a total embargo on America on 19 October. OAPEC targeted Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, Britain and America, later adding Portugal, Rhodesia and South Africa.

bosphorus-bridge-opens-1973.summary: Proposals to bridge Istanbul's strait went back to Ottoman sketches by Leonardo and Michelangelo's rivals and to 1900 plans by Arnodin; Turkey's government approves a crossing in 1967 and awards design to Freeman Fox and Partners, whose engineers Gilbert Roberts and William Brown had just finished Severn Bridge. Cleveland Bridge and Hochtief build a gravity-anchored span of 1,074 metres between Ortaköy and Beylerbeyi with an aerodynamic steel box deck and inclined hangers, then the longest span outside North America. Prime minister Naim Talu opens it on 30 October 1973, a day after Turkey's fiftieth republic anniversary. Traffic of 20,000 vehicles a day grows past 180,000, prompting Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge in 1988 and Yavuz Sultan Selim in 2016; pedestrians are banned after 1977.

rotavirus-discovery-melbourne-1973.summary: Examining duodenal biopsies from children with severe diarrhoea by electron microscopy, Ruth Bishop, Geoffrey Davidson, Ian Holmes and Brian Ruck saw wheel-shaped virus particles and reported them in The Lancet in December 1973. A 1974 paper found same particles in faeces, allowing non-invasive diagnosis. Rotavirus proved to be leading cause of severe infant gastroenteritis worldwide, killing hundreds of thousands of children annually before vaccines. Bishop's 2009 review recounts discovery and path to vaccines; Melbourne group later developed RV3 vaccine candidate from a neonatal strain. Two vaccines licensed in 2006 entered Australia's schedule in 2007, cutting hospital admissions sharply.

atucha-i-nuclear-1974.summary: In 1974 Atucha I near Buenos Aires became Latin America's first nuclear power station, built by Siemens. Built to a German Siemens design, it is a pressurized heavy-water reactor fuelled with natural and slightly enriched uranium, with heavy water as coolant and moderator; from 1,179 MW of heat it generates 362 MW of electricity, about 2.5 percent of Argentina’s output in 2005. Its neighbour Atucha II, begun in 1981 and halted in 1994, was revived by government decree in 2005.

computer-lib-1974.summary: In 1974 Ted Nelson self-published Computer Lib, telling readers “You can and must understand computers NOW.” Its cover showing a raised fist inside a computer, it treats computers’ technical and political sides; flipped over, Dream Machines treats new media and his Project Xanadu hypertext system, begun in 1960. Laid out magazine-style like Whole Earth Catalog, it gained a cult following around People’s Computer Company; Howard Rheingold’s Tools for Thought called it “the best-selling underground manifesto of the microcomputer revolution,” and Microsoft Press reissued it in 1987.

curitiba-bus-rapid-transit-1974.summary: In 1974 Curitiba, capital of Paraná, opened its first two express bus corridors along structural axes planned under architect-mayor Jaime Lerner and its planning institute IPPUC. Buses ran in central lanes separated from traffic, with land-use rules concentrating high-density housing beside them. From 1980 to 1999 Curitiba added feeder and inter-district lines, a single fare, and in 1991 glass tube stations where passengers paid before boarding and stepped level onto articulated and then bi-articulated Volvo buses carrying 270 people. Rabinovitch and Leitman reported in 1996 that about three quarters of commuters used these buses at a cost far below rail. Bogotá's TransMilenio, Mexico City's Metrobús and more than 150 cities adopted Curitiba's model.

dennard-scaling-1974.summary: In 1974 Dennard showed that shrinking transistors used proportionally less power; chips could get faster for free until about 2005. Voltage and current scale down with length, so power use stays in proportion to area. Combined with Moore’s law, this meant performance per joule doubled about every 18 months, a trend called Koomey’s law. Around 2005 to 2007 Dennard scaling broke down, because leakage current and threshold voltage stopped shrinking with size and power density rose; chips could no longer be kept cool, Intel cancelled its Tejas and Jayhawk processors in 2004, and the industry turned to multiple cores.

era-winter1.summary: From about 1974 to 1980, a conventional span, AI funding retreated after promised results failed to arrive, the first AI winter; it began with Lighthill's 1973 report in Britain and DARPA cuts in America in 1973 to 1974. Behind it lay 1969’s Mansfield Amendment, which required DARPA to fund mission-oriented research, DARPA’s frustration with Carnegie Mellon’s speech understanding programme, and, as Hans Moravec put it, researchers caught in “a web of increasing exaggeration” who promised more each time they delivered less. The name came later: in 1984 Roger Schank and John McDermott warned an AAAI panel of chain reactions, like nuclear winter, from pessimism to funding cuts, and another winter followed from 1987 to 2000.

first-ai-winter-1974.summary: By 1974 AI funding was hard to find in Britain or America after Lighthill's report attacked AI's grandiose aims, a period later called the first AI winter. Lighthill concluded that nothing being done in AI could not be done in other sciences, though Britain's cuts also reflected 1970s science-policy politics. In America, 1969's Mansfield Amendment required DARPA to fund mission-oriented rather than basic research, and DARPA's own American Study Group judged most AI work unlikely to prove useful soon.

intel-haifa-design-center-1974.summary: Dov Frohman, who had invented erasable programmable read-only memory at Intel in 1971, returns to Israel after teaching in Ghana and persuades Intel to open its first development site outside the United States in Haifa in 1974, near Technion graduates with few local chip jobs. Starting with five staff in a rented building, this group takes on an 8-bit bus version of 8086, released as 8088 in 1979 and chosen for IBM's PC, and Rafi Nave's team designs 8087 floating-point coprocessor. Intel adds a Jerusalem fabrication plant, Fab 8, in 1985 and Kiryat Gat fabs from 1999; Haifa engineers later lead Banias and Centrino in 2003 and Sandy Bridge in 2011. Israel's semiconductor industry grows around this nucleus to tens of thousands of jobs.

minsky-frames-1974.summary: In 1974 Marvin Minsky proposed frames, knowledge stored as templates with slots to fill. Frames divide knowledge into substructures representing “stereotyped situations,” such as rooms or birthday parties; their terminals, or slots, come pre-filled with default values, as Minsky believed human memory does, and more specific frames inherit values from general ones, so one instance of Boy inherits defaults from Boy and lets programs compare it with Monkey through similarly named slots. Frames became AI frame languages’ primary data structure, stored as ontologies, and can be queried like semantic networks.

onchocerciasis-control-programme-1974.summary: Beginning in January 1974, with aerial treatments from February 1975, helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft sprayed larvicide weekly on blackfly breeding sites along rivers of the Volta basin. Run from Ouagadougou by WHO with World Bank, FAO and UNDP backing, the Onchocerciasis Control Programme eventually covered about 1.3 million square kilometres in eleven countries. Entomologists rotated insecticides to defeat resistance and tracked flies across borders. After Merck donated ivermectin in 1987, mass drug distribution joined vector control. WHO estimates credit OCP with preventing 600,000 cases of blindness and protecting 18 million children born in treated areas, while fertile river valleys abandoned to disease were resettled.

werbos-backprop-1974.summary: In 1974 Paul Werbos's Harvard thesis described backpropagation for training layered networks; nobody used it for a decade. Decades later that method made deep learning workable. A social scientist by training, Werbos also pioneered recurrent neural networks and served among the International Neural Network Society’s first presidents. In 1995 IEEE gave him its Neural Network Pioneer Award for discovering backpropagation and other basic learning frameworks.

who-expanded-programme-immunization-1974.summary: In May 1974 WHO set out to vaccinate every child on Earth, and coverage rose from 5 percent to more than 80. Its Expanded Programme on Immunization began with seven diseases: tuberculosis, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, measles and smallpox. In 1974, about 5 percent of children in low income countries received basic vaccines. WHO estimates vaccines saved 154 million lives in the programme's first 50 years.

bombay-high-offshore-oil-1974.summary: On 19 February 1974 ONGC's jack-up rig Sagar Samrat, drilling well H-1 in Arabian Sea about 160 kilometres off Bombay, hits oil at 962 metres in Miocene limestone after a drilling break. Soviet seismic surveys between 1964 and 1967 had mapped this anticline, and Indian geologists pressed for drilling despite scepticism about offshore prospects. Production starts in May 1976 through a platform and pipeline system, and within a decade Bombay High supplies over half of India's crude output, easing an import bill swollen by 1973 oil prices. Rao's 1991 Marine Geology paper describes field geology; ONGC's archive marks 19 February as its defining date.

intel-8080-1974.summary: In April 1974 Intel released its 8080, the microprocessor that powered Altair and started the personal computer industry. It succeeded Intel's 8008, which customers had been reluctant to adopt because of its single addressing mode, low clock speed, 18-pin package and small on-chip stack, though it was not binary compatible with it. Its 40-pin package simplified interfacing, NMOS transistors ran at higher speed than 8008’s PMOS, and a full 16-bit address bus reached 64 KB of memory, four times its predecessor’s. Intended for calculators, cash registers and terminals, Intel's 8080 instead powered the Altair 8800.

tcp-ip-paper-1974.summary: In May 1974 Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published a design for passing packets between different networks; separate networks could join into one. With Gérard Le Lann they drew on France's CYCLADES project. RFC 675, written by Cerf, Yogen Dalal and Carl Sunshine and published in December 1974, specified their Transmission Control Program, whose job is reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of bytes between applications: when packets are lost, duplicated or arrive out of order, it detects this, requests retransmission and reassembles them.

smiling-buddha-test-1974.summary: In May 1974 India tested a nuclear device at Pokhran, sixth country to do so after the Security Council's five permanent powers; Pakistan's programme followed, and suppliers formed the Nuclear Suppliers Group in response. Scientists at Bhabha Atomic Research Centre built its implosion-type fission device, 1,400 kilograms around its plutonium core, under Homi Sethna’s Atomic Energy Commission; that plutonium came from CIRUS, Canada’s gift reactor, run with American heavy water.

kaissa-computer-chess-1974.summary: In August 1974 Soviet program Kaissa won the first World Computer Chess Championship in Stockholm, four games out of four. IFIP sponsored it and International Master David Levy directed. Thirteen programs from eight nations played four Swiss rounds. Because Soviet system software would not run on Stockholm’s ICL machine, Kaissa ran on a computer in Moscow over a telephone link, and its opening book of 10,000 stored positions was the field's largest.

cahora-bassa-dam-1974.summary: In 1974 Portugal closed the Cahora Bassa dam wall in Mozambique to sell power to South Africa. Its reservoir began filling in December 1974 and within six months stood 12 metres below full supply level; the power station was completed in 1979. Its powerhouse holds five 415 megawatt turbines, southern Africa’s largest hydroelectric scheme, and most output travels to South Africa on high-voltage direct current lines. Those lines were sabotaged for long stretches during Mozambique’s 16-year civil war, and Portugal kept 82 percent ownership until 2007.

cyclone-tracy-darwin-1974.summary: In early hours of Christmas Day 1974, a small, intense tropical cyclone passed directly over Darwin with gusts estimated near 70 metres per second. Of about 11,000 houses and flats, 50 to 60 percent were destroyed and only 6 percent remained intact; more than 90 percent lost roof cladding. Sixty-six people died and about 30,000 of 48,000 residents were evacuated by air in days, Australia's largest airlift. A damage survey and a US National Bureau of Standards report traced failures to weak roof fixings, batten-to-rafter connections and loss of cladding that let wind pressurise interiors. Darwin Area Building Manual of 1975 and later Australian wind loading standards mandated cyclone-rated fixings and testing.

privacy-act-1974.summary: In 1974, after Watergate, the Privacy Act limited what federal agencies could collect and share about citizens. The Privacy Act of 1974, enacted on December 31, 1974, and signed by President Gerald Ford, governs collection, maintenance, use and dissemination of personally identifiable information in federal agencies’ systems of records, groups of records retrieved by name or identifier. At its creation it was meant as an “American Bill of Rights on data.”

catalytic-converter-1975.summary: From 1975 American cars carried catalytic converters to meet exhaust limits; leaded petrol had to go because lead poisoned the catalyst. French engineer Eugene Houdry had patented them decades earlier after early Los Angeles smog studies alarmed him. Early converters were “two-way”: platinum-group metals oxidized carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water. Because lead coats and poisons those catalysts, equipped cars could run only on unleaded fuel, pushing it into general use. Three-way converters that also reduce nitrogen oxides, first sold on Volvo’s 1977 California cars, became near-universal when federal rules tightened for 1981.

digital-camera-sasson-1975.summary: In 1975 Steven Sasson at Kodak built a camera that recorded a 100 by 100 pixel image to cassette in 23 seconds; Kodak shelved it. Its chip converted light into electrical charge in place of film, and Fujifilm was developing CCD technology at that time. Early uses of such cameras were mainly military and scientific, followed by medical and news applications, long before consumer digital cameras displaced film.

embrapa-cerrado-soybean-1975.summary: From 1975 Embrapa's new Centro de Pesquisa Agropecuária dos Cerrados at Planaltina and its soybean centre at Londrina worked on a crop bred for temperate latitudes. Researchers selected long-juvenile cultivars that would flower under short tropical days, corrected acid, aluminium-rich soils with lime and phosphorus, and chose Bradyrhizobium strains so plants fixed their own nitrogen; Brazilian soy came to be grown on more than thirteen million hectares without nitrogen fertiliser. Yields rose to about 2,400 kilograms per hectare, and soybean fields spread across Goiás, Mato Grosso and Bahia. Within thirty-five years more than half of the roughly two million square kilometres of Cerrado had been converted to crops and pasture, making Brazil a top soybean exporter and raising concern for a biodiversity hotspot.

goodharts-law-1975.summary: In 1975 Charles Goodhart observed that a measure stops working once it becomes a target, a remark published in a 1984 chapter. His point was later turned against Thatcher’s government, which steered monetary policy by targets for broad and narrow money, but it describes something far more general, now called Goodhart’s law. Campbell’s law, formulated from 1969, says much the same of social indicators, and Robert Lucas’s 1976 critique of economic policy models followed soon after.

holland-genetic-algorithms-1975.summary: In 1975 John Holland's book showed how to breed solutions by mutation and crossover like genes. Nils Aall Barricelli had simulated evolution on a computer in 1954 and Alex Fraser published simulations from 1957, while Ingo Rechenberg and Hans-Paul Schwefel solved engineering problems with evolution strategies. In Holland’s method, candidate solutions, often encoded as bit strings, form a population; each generation their fitness is scored, fitter ones are more likely to be selected, and crossover and mutation produce the next generation. His building block theory held that short, fit fragments combine over generations into good solutions.
