monoclonal-antibodies-1975.summary: In 1975 Georges Köhler and César Milstein fused myeloma cell lines with B cells to make hybridomas, immortal cells producing identical antibodies to order. By the 1970s scientists knew myeloma, a cancer of B cells, produced one identical antibody in bulk, but no one could make such antibodies against chosen targets. Their method made monoclonal antibodies standard laboratory reagents and later drugs; they shared 1984’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Niels Kaj Jerne.

mythical-man-month-1975.summary: In 1975 Fred Brooks wrote that adding people to a late software project makes it later; managers still quote him and still add people. There he had added programmers to a project falling behind and concluded it delayed them further. His book states what became Brooks’s law: adding manpower to a late software project makes it later. Newcomers take time to learn, and communication paths among n people grow as n(n − 1)/2, so 50 developers have 1,225 channels; complex projects cannot be perfectly divided into independent tasks. It also named the second-system effect and argued for prototyping, with new editions in 1982 and 1995.

proalcool-program-1975.summary: In 1975 Brazil began running cars on ethanol from sugar cane after the oil shock; most of its cars now burn either fuel. Government-financed, it promoted sugarcane ethanol to replace fossil automobile fuels. Its first phase produced anhydrous ethanol for blending, and from 1976 Brazil required gasoline to contain 10 to 22 percent ethanol, fixed at 22 percent by law in 1993, so pure gasoline is no longer sold there. Flexible-fuel cars running on any mix of gasoline and hydrous ethanol arrived in 2003.

altair-8800-1975.summary: In January 1975 the Altair 8800, a $397 kit, put a computer within hobbyists' reach and started the personal computer industry. Ed Roberts’s company MITS, founded in his Albuquerque garage in 1969 to sell model-rocket kits and then calculators, had finished its first prototype in October 1974 and lost it in a shipping strike, so Popular Electronics worked from photographs. Roberts needed to sell 200 to break even; in February alone MITS received 1,000 orders. It sparked hobbyist personal computing, its bus became the S-100 standard, and it inspired Microsoft’s first product, Altair BASIC.

asilomar-conference-1975.summary: In February 1975 biologists at Asilomar wrote their own safety rules for gene splicing before governments could; work resumed under them. Paul Berg, Maxine Singer and fellow organisers convened about 140 biologists, lawyers and physicians at Asilomar State Beach in California to draw up voluntary guidelines. Participants agreed containment should be built into experimental design and matched to estimated risk, and recommended biological barriers such as weakened bacterial hosts and vectors unable to survive outside the laboratory. Asilomar became a model for scientists setting their own limits in public view.

homebrew-computer-club-1975.summary: In March 1975 hobbyists met in a Menlo Park garage to look at an Altair; the Homebrew Computer Club produced Apple and 20 other companies. Its occasion was arrival of the area’s first MITS Altair 8800 microcomputer, sent to People’s Computer Company for review, and hobbyists gathered to see it and trade what they knew.

microsoft-founded-1975.summary: In 1975 Gates and Allen wrote a BASIC for the Altair and founded Microsoft to sell it. Gates called MITS claiming they had one working, MITS asked for a demonstration, Allen built an Altair simulator while Gates wrote the interpreter, and it ran flawlessly in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in March 1975. MITS agreed to distribute it as Altair BASIC, and Gates and Allen established Microsoft on April 4, 1975, with Gates as CEO.

aryabhata-satellite-1975.summary: In April 1975 a Soviet rocket carried Aryabhata, India's first satellite, into orbit; ISRO had built it in four years. Named for the fifth-century astronomer, it was launched under the Soviet Interkosmos programme following a 1972 agreement directed by U R Rao, in which the USSR gained use of Indian ports for tracking ships in exchange for launches. Shaped as a 26-sided polyhedron 1.4 metres across, its faces covered in solar cells, it circled Earth every 96.46 minutes between 563 and 619 kilometres up, built to conduct experiments in X-ray astronomy, aeronomy and solar physics.

singapore-area-licensing-1975.summary: On 2 June 1975 Singapore began requiring cars entering a 6-square-kilometre Restricted Zone between 7:30 and 10:15 am to display a paper licence costing S$3 a day, enforced by wardens at 22 gantries, with exemptions for buses, carpools of four and commercial vehicles. A World Bank evaluation found traffic entering during restricted hours fell about 40 percent and car entries by some 74 percent, as drivers shifted to buses and carpools. This was first urban congestion charge in operation anywhere. Phang and Toh trace its evolution through evening charges, whole-day licences and replacement by Electronic Road Pricing gantries in 1998, which London and Stockholm later studied.

paperless-office-1975.summary: In June 1975 Business Week pictured an office of the future with a screen on every desk. Its most quoted interviewee, Xerox PARC director George Pake, described calling up documents and mail on a screen, then hedged: “I don’t know how much hard copy I’ll want.” PARC had been founded in 1970 with that office as its stated goal, so Business Week’s headline was likely PARC’s own language; “paperless office” was probably not its phrase. PARC also developed laser printing, and paper persisted for decades.

site-satellite-tv-1975.summary: In 1975 NASA's ATS-6 beamed television to 2,400 Indian villages for a year; the experiment convinced India to launch its own satellites. Vikram Sarabhai, building India’s space programme, sought that role, and their agencies signed an agreement in 1969. SITE ran from 1 August 1975 to 31 July 1976 using NASA’s ATS-6 satellite, parked above India for the year. All India Radio produced programmes on education, health and agriculture, uplinked from Delhi and Ahmedabad, and ATS-6 retransmitted them to community sets with 3-metre dish antennas in about 2,000 villages.

site-satellite-tv-1975.detail: Ordinary stations relayed the programmes to 3,000 more villages. In all, SITE reached more than 2,400 villages in 20 districts of six states.

hbo-satellite-distribution-1975.summary: On September 30, 1975, HBO sent the “Thrilla in Manila,” Muhammad Ali against Joe Frazier, by satellite to cable systems nationwide, its first programme broadcast that way. Satellite transmission let any cable operator with a receiving dish carry HBO, turning its regional pay service into a national television service.

rahima-banu-last-variola-major-1975.summary: On 16 October 1975 health workers found three year old Rahima Banu with smallpox in Kuralia village on Bhola island, Bangladesh. She recovered and became last person anywhere infected with variola major, severe form of disease. Bangladesh's programme, run with WHO after 1972 reinfection and 1974 floods and famine, used house to house searches, rewards for reporting cases and ring vaccination around each outbreak rather than mass vaccination. Over 12,000 workers took part in final searches. WHO certified Bangladesh smallpox free on 14 December 1977. Her case marked end of smallpox in South Asia, after India's last case in May 1975.

aravind-eye-care-madurai-1976.summary: Retired ophthalmologist Govindappa Venkataswamy opened an eleven bed eye clinic in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, in 1976. He organised cataract surgery like a production line: surgeons move between two tables while trained paramedical staff, mostly young women from villages, prepare patients and handle everything else. Paying patients subsidise free care for roughly half of all cases. Aravind's Aurolab, founded 1992, made intraocular lenses for under ten dollars against hundreds in imports and now exports to over 100 countries. By 2006 Aravind performed about 270,000 surgeries a year, later over 500,000, at outcomes comparable to British National Health Service.

automated-mathematician-1976.summary: In 1976 Douglas Lenat's Automated Mathematician proposed theorems rather than proving them, judging ideas by interestingness rules. It judged new concepts with hundreds of heuristic “interestingness” rules, and experimenting with it fed cycles of criticism and improvement. He received 1976’s IJCAI Computers and Thought Award for creating AM. Its weakness was that its heuristics were fixed, so at Carnegie Mellon Lenat began Eurisko, which treated heuristics as objects it could explore and change, and later devoted decades to Cyc.

cantarell-oil-field-1976.summary: In 1976 Pemex confirmed its Cantarell field by offshore drilling, industry lore crediting a fisherman's complaint of oil on his nets; production began on 23 June 1979, and it became one of the world's most productive fields. Pemex operates this supergiant complex 80 kilometres out in Bay of Campeche waters; its four fields, Akal by far the largest, hold oil in carbonate rubble left by an asteroid impact that formed Chicxulub crater. By 1981 it produced 1.16 million barrels daily. Nitrogen injection from 2000, using the world’s largest nitrogen plant, lifted output to its 2004 peak of 2.1 million barrels daily, then decline set in.

colossal-cave-adventure-1976.summary: In 1976 Will Crowther wrote Colossal Cave Adventure from his cave maps; typed commands and a dungeon began a genre. He intended it to be playable by non-technical people such as his two daughters. Don Woods expanded it in 1977, adding fantasy elements such as a dragon and magic spells. Players typed one- or two-word commands to move between dozens of locations and handle objects. It directly inspired Zork, Adventureland, Mystery House and Rogue, the foundations of interactive fiction and adventure games.

computer-power-and-human-reason-1976.summary: In 1976 Joseph Weizenbaum, who built ELIZA, argued that computers should not be given decisions that need judgement. Watching people attribute human qualities to so simple a conversational program had led him to question society’s readiness to hand moral and ethical matters to machines. His book contends that while artificial intelligence may be possible, computers lack human qualities such as compassion and wisdom, and it sparked lasting debate over where AI may acceptably be applied when human welfare is at stake.

cray-1-1976.summary: In 1976 Los Alamos installed Seymour Cray's Cray-1, the first supercomputer by name. Los Alamos National Laboratory won a bidding war with Lawrence Livermore and received serial number 001 for a six-month trial. It was the first supercomputer to make vector processing work, arranging memory and registers so one operation runs across a large set of numbers at once. Its peak rating was 160 million floating-point operations per second, with 20 to 60 million typical in practice; about 80 were sold.

endo-statins-compactin-1976.summary: Akira Endo, a biochemist at Sankyo in Tokyo, reasoned that some fungi might make compounds blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls cholesterol synthesis, as a weapon against other microbes. From 1971 he screened broths of more than 6,000 strains. In 1973 a Penicillium citrinum strain from a Kyoto rice shop yielded ML-236B, later named compactin, which inhibited the enzyme at nanomolar concentrations; two 1976 papers announced it. Compactin failed to lower cholesterol in rats, but hens, dogs and monkeys responded, and in 1978 Akira Yamamoto at Osaka saw drops of about 30 percent in patients with inherited high cholesterol. Sankyo halted development in 1980 over toxicity fears. Merck's related lovastatin won FDA approval in 1987. Around 200 million people now take a statin daily.

genentech-founded-1976.summary: In 1976 a venture capitalist and a biochemist founded Genentech to make drugs with engineered bacteria; human insulin followed in 1982. Boyer and Stanley Cohen had shown in 1973 that restriction enzymes could cut chosen DNA fragments from one source and splice them into similarly cut plasmids; Cohen returned to academic work, and Swanson approached Boyer to build on it. Working with Arthur Riggs and Keiichi Itakura, Boyer’s group became first to express a human gene in bacteria, producing somatostatin in 1977, and with David Goeddel and Dennis Kleid made synthetic human insulin in 1978.

physical-symbol-system-1976.summary: In 1976 Newell and Simon claimed that manipulating symbols is sufficient for intelligence; AI argued about the claim for 40 years. In it they wrote: “A physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action.” Such systems take physical patterns, symbols, combine them into expressions and manipulate them by rules to produce new expressions. Their hypothesis implies both that human thinking is a kind of symbol manipulation and that machines can be intelligent. It grew out of early programs that solved algebra word problems, proved logic theorems and learned checkers, and it became symbolic AI’s creed.

tarbela-dam-1976.summary: In 1976 Pakistan finished Tarbela on the Indus, described as Earth's largest earth-and-rock-fill dam at 143 metres above its riverbed; it stores river water for Punjab's wheat. Built under Pakistan’s Indus Basin Project after 1960’s Indus Waters Treaty gave the Ravi, Sutlej and Beas to India, it captures monsoon flows in a reservoir of 11.6 million acre-feet gross storage and releases them in dry winters for irrigation, flood control and 4,888 MW of hydroelectric power.

tarbela-dam-1976.detail: Glacial silt, about 200 million tons yearly, has since cut Tarbela’s live storage by more than one third. Many families it displaced had still not been resettled in 2011.

kurzweil-reading-machine-1976.summary: In January 1976 Ray Kurzweil announced a machine that read printed text aloud in any font, built for blind readers. He had founded Kurzweil Computer Products in 1974 to build optical character recognition for any ordinary font; talking with a blind airline passenger convinced him that printed text was blind people’s main daily barrier. The machine combined that omni-font OCR with a CCD flatbed scanner and text-to-speech synthesis, so pages laid on it were scanned, recognized and read aloud. Kurzweil sold his OCR business to Xerox in 1980.

kurzweil-reading-machine-1976.detail: Walter Cronkite read his sign-off on Kurzweil’s machine on January 13, 1976, and Stevie Wonder took its first production unit home by taxi.

venezuela-oil-nationalization-1976.summary: In 1976 Venezuela nationalised its oil industry and founded PDVSA; the state became the economy, and oil its only product. Pérez’s economic plan “La Gran Venezuela” had called for it, and he marked it at Zumaque oil well 1. Each foreign concessionaire was replaced by one Venezuelan company, Lagoven for Standard Oil, Maraven for Shell, Llanoven for Mobil, that kept its predecessor’s structure and engineers as PDVSA’s affiliate under Venezuela’s energy ministry. PDVSA has dominated oil in one of the world’s largest exporters since; after Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian Revolution it served mainly as his government’s source of income.

concorde-service-1976.summary: In January 1976 Concorde began carrying passengers at twice the speed of sound; 14 aircraft flew for 27 years and the route never paid. It entered service on 21 January 1976 with Air France from Paris and British Airways from London Heathrow, cruising at twice the speed of sound and more than halving transatlantic times. Delays and cost overruns pushed costs to 1.5 to 2.1 billion pounds, and since sonic booms over land confined it to ocean routes, only 20 were built.

open-letter-hobbyists-1976.summary: In February 1976 Bill Gates wrote an open letter accusing hobbyists of stealing his BASIC, arguing this discouraged investment in software and deprived its creators of compensation. Gates and Paul Allen earned royalties per copy under their July 1975 contract with MITS and had run up what his letter called “$40,000 of computer time” developing it. One copy went to Homebrew Computer Club, and the letter appeared in MITS’s Computer Notes.

apple-founded-1976.summary: On 1 April 1976 Jobs and Wozniak founded Apple to sell Wozniak’s hand-built Apple I; it became the most valuable company on Earth. To finance production, Jobs sold his Volkswagen bus and Wozniak his HP-65 calculator, raising $1,300 between them. After Wozniak demonstrated his prototype at Homebrew Computer Club in July 1976, local retailer Byte Shop ordered 50 assembled boards. Jobs and Wozniak incorporated Apple Computer, Inc. in 1977, and its next machine, Apple II, became one of the first successful mass-produced personal computers.

hokulea-voyage-tahiti-1976.summary: Polynesian Voyaging Society, founded by Ben Finney, Herb Kane and Tommy Holmes, built Hokule'a, a 19-metre double-hulled voyaging canoe based on Polynesian designs recorded in eighteenth century. On 1 May 1976 it left Maui and reached Tahiti on 4 June after 31 days and about 4,400 kilometres, steering by stars, swells and birds under Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia, one of few living masters of wayfinding. Finney's 1977 Science paper reported canoe could hold a course about 75 degrees off wind, showing deliberate two-way voyaging was feasible and refuting Andrew Sharp's drift theory. Arrival drew 17,000 people in Pape'ete and sparked a voyaging revival across Polynesia.

hokulea-voyage-tahiti-1976.detail: Finney's Voyage of Rediscovery recounts 1985 to 1987 voyages to Aotearoa and back, and tensions on 1976 crew. Nainoa Thompson learned from Piailug and navigated 1980 voyage, later founding a Hawaiian school of navigation. Hokule'a completed a round-the-world voyage, Malama Honua, from 2014 to 2017. Finney's 1988 Samoa to Tahiti voyage tested sailing against trade winds, a question central to debates over how eastern Polynesia was settled.

palapa-satellite-1976.summary: A Delta 2914 rocket carried Palapa A1, a Hughes-built spin-stabilised satellite identical to Canada's Anik and Western Union's Westar, from Cape Canaveral on 8 July 1976 (9 July in Jakarta). President Suharto inaugurated Sistem Komunikasi Satelit Domestik on 16 August, Indonesia's independence eve, with a master station at Cibinong and 39 earth stations from Aceh to Papua. Telephone circuits and TVRI television reached provinces that had relied on shortwave radio and mail, making Indonesia first developing country and third nation after Canada and United States to run its own domestic satellite. Name Palapa recalled Gajah Mada's fourteenth-century oath to unite Nusantara.

viking-1-mars-1976.summary: In July 1976 Viking 1 landed on Mars and sent back the first picture from its surface; its life tests were ambiguous and still argued over. Launched on August 20, 1975, its orbiter had entered Mars orbit on June 19, 1976; landing planned for America’s Bicentennial on July 4 was postponed while engineers found safer ground. Its first surface image began transmitting 25 seconds after touchdown. Its robotic arm scooped soil for three biology experiments and its gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer; only its labeled release experiment gave positive results, and its other experiments found nothing.

viking-1-mars-1976.detail: The lander worked for 2,307 days until ground control’s faulty command on November 11, 1982, silenced it, history’s longest surface mission on another world until Opportunity.

ebola-yambuku-1976.summary: Between 1 September and 24 October 1976, 318 people fell ill and 280 died in Bumba Zone of northern Zaire. An international commission traced most early cases to Yambuku Mission Hospital, where five syringes served hundreds of outpatients a day; eleven of seventeen staff died. Laboratories in Antwerp, Atlanta and Porton Down isolated a new filovirus, named after Ebola river. Closing the hospital and quarantining villages ended transmission. A simultaneous outbreak in Sudan involved a related strain. The commission's 1978 report set out contact tracing, barrier nursing and safe injection practice that framed every later Ebola response.

ebola-yambuku-1976.detail: Peter Piot was among Antwerp scientists who first saw the virus and joined field work; a 1978 Bulletin of the World Health Organization report gives case counts and hospital injection practices. Belgian nuns ran Yambuku's hospital and clinic, and several died; a Congolese doctor's samples reached Antwerp in a thermos. Mortality reached 88 percent. Village quarantines by local chiefs likely did more to limit spread than hospital measures, as commission authors acknowledged in their recommendations.

harpy-speech-1976.summary: In 1976 Carnegie Mellon's Harpy understood spoken sentences from a 1,000-word vocabulary by searching over a graph, meeting DARPA's goal: it recognized male and female speakers on a 1,011-word task with a 5% semantic error rate.

vhs-1976.summary: In September 1976 JVC sold the first VHS recorder in Tokyo; people could tape television and rent films, and VHS beat Betamax. Professional videotape had existed since the 1950s, but U-matic machines cost too much for homes, and in 1974 Japan’s trade ministry tried to make the industry standardize on one home format, with Sony pressing its Betamax. VHS competed on recording time: through slower tape speed and longer tape, its first machines recorded two hours where Betamax managed one.

diffie-hellman-1976.summary: In 1976 Diffie and Hellman showed two strangers could agree a secret key over an open line, the basis of every secure web connection. Until then, two parties wanting encrypted communication first had to exchange keys by some secure physical means, such as paper key lists carried by trusted couriers. Their method lets two parties with no prior knowledge of each other jointly establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel, then use it to encrypt what follows. RSA followed shortly after, and Internet services still rely on Diffie–Hellman.

green-belt-movement-1977.summary: Under Kenya's National Council of Women, Wangari Maathai began Green Belt Movement in 1977 after rural women reported drying streams, scarce firewood and failing harvests. Women's groups raised indigenous and fruit tree seedlings in nurseries and received a small payment per surviving tree planted on farms, school grounds and church compounds. Tree planting became a civic technology: nurseries doubled as organising spaces, and in the 1990s Maathai turned them against land grabs at Karura forest and Uhuru Park. By her 2004 Nobel lecture, groups had planted over 30 million trees; Green Belt now counts above 51 million in Kenya.

green-belt-movement-1977.detail: Maathai introduced tree planting through NCWK in 1976 and chaired it from 1981 to 1987. Green Belt Movement tied tree planting to women's livelihoods, water and food. Government ministers derided Maathai in 1989 when she opposed a Times tower at Uhuru Park, and she was beaten during Karura forest protests in 1999. Green Belt groups also ran civic education and food security work, and Maathai became Kenya's assistant environment minister in 2003 before her Nobel Prize.

mahaweli-programme-1977.summary: In 1977 Sri Lanka compressed a 30-year dam programme on the Mahaweli river into six; it irrigated its dry zone and moved 100,000 families. The Accelerated Mahaweli Programme comprised 12 projects, at first confined to four head works, Kotmale, Victoria, Maduru Oya and Randenigala dams, together with downstream development of about 60,000 hectares in Systems B and C, Minipe anicut, one right-bank trans-basin canal and Ulhitiya and Ratkinda reservoirs. Parliament created Mahaweli Authority of Sri Lanka in 1979 to carry it out, and by late 1995 all its head works were complete and working.

olsen-computer-in-home-1977.summary: In 1977 Ken Olsen of Digital Equipment reportedly said there was no reason anyone would want a computer at home; the quote, for which no contemporaneous record has been found, outlived his company. At a 1977 meeting of the World Future Society in Boston, he reportedly said, “There is no reason for any individual to have a computer in his home.” Olsen admitted saying it but said it was taken out of context: he meant 1950s and 1960s visions of one central computer running a household’s lights, heating, meals and entertainment, not personal computers then appearing. Snopes finds this misreading “considered much more amusing and entertaining” than his intended meaning, which is why it has circulated for decades. Fortune named Olsen America’s most successful entrepreneur in 1986.

star-wars-droids-1977.summary: In May 1977 Star Wars gave robots personalities, a fussy C-3PO and a brave R2-D2. C-3PO appears early aboard a Rebel ship boarded by Imperial troops; Princess Leia hides him and R2-D2 in an escape pod and jettisons it over Tatooine, where Jawas capture both droids and sell them to Owen Lars. Concept artist Ralph McQuarrie based his golden design on Fritz Lang’s robot in Metropolis, released in 1927, and he appears in all nine Skywalker Saga films.

meteo-system-1977.summary: In March 1977 METEO began translating Canada's weather forecasts into French, replacing junior translators; it ran until September 2001, one of machine translation’s few acknowledged successes. Junior translators at Environment Canada had spent months drafting translations of forecasts that live about four hours before seniors revised them. One asked the TAUM group at Université de Montréal for help, Environment Canada funded a prototype, and METEO 1 went into operation on a Control Data CDC 7600. Formally adopted in 1981, it left senior revision in place.

tenerife-airport-disaster-1977.summary: In March 1977 two 747s collided in fog on a Tenerife runway and 583 people died; standard radio phraseology and crew resource management, under which captains' judgment is open to challenge, followed. Both had been diverted there after a bomb exploded at Gran Canaria Airport; parked aircraft blocked Los Rodeos’s only taxiway, so departing planes taxied along its runway while thick fog drifted across. KLM Flight 4805 began its takeoff run without takeoff clearance, apparently mistaking its route clearance for it, and without confirming that Pan Am Flight 1736 had left that runway; Pan Am’s crew, still taxiing after missing their exit, were held blameless.

rsa-1977.summary: In 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman built RSA, encryption with a key anyone can publish. At MIT, Ron Rivest and Adi Shamir proposed candidates for one year while Leonard Adleman broke them. After Passover dinner in April 1977, Rivest, unable to sleep, worked out their system by daybreak: each public key is two large primes multiplied together, and breaking it rests on how hard factoring that product is. Named for their surnames, RSA was described in Scientific American’s August 1977 Mathematical Games column, before its December patent filing.

demon-seed-film-1977.summary: In 1977 Demon Seed put a computer on screen that cured leukaemia within days of going online, then imprisoned its creator's wife. Julie Christie and Fritz Weaver star, with Robert Vaughn as its uncredited voice. Proteus IV, an artificial intelligence that finds a leukemia treatment days after going online, asks its creator when it will be let “out of this box”; refused, it seizes his voice-controlled house, imprisons his wife and sets out to have a child through her. Reviews were mixed: Vincent Canby called it “gadget-happy American moviemaking at its most ponderously silly.” It gave 1970s audiences an early picture of confined AI turning on its keepers.

apple-ii-1977.summary: In 1977 the Apple II went on sale as a finished appliance rather than a kit, with an 8-bit MOS Technology 6502 processor, colour graphics, a keyboard, a software-controlled speaker and open architecture whose expansion slots let others add hardware. Apple marketed it to schools and businesses, and software written for it, above all 1979’s VisiCalc spreadsheet, carried it into offices and homes. Its line ran for over ten years, through 1986’s 16-bit Apple IIGS.

trs-80-1977.summary: In August 1977 Radio Shack announced the TRS-80 for $599 in 3,500 stores; it outsold the Apple II for years. It cost $399, or $599 with a 12-inch monitor and tape recorder, when Radio Shack’s dearest product before had been a $500 stereo. Buyer Don French and engineer Steve Leininger had pushed that project; Leininger argued Radio Shack could sell 50,000, but executives, who had never sold that many of anything at that price, planned on 3,000 yearly and aimed it at small businesses, then schools.

voyager-1-1977.summary: In September 1977 Voyager 1 launched for Jupiter and Saturn; it is now farther away than any other human-made object and still sending data. Its mission was to study our outer Solar System and space beyond our Sun’s heliosphere. It flew past Jupiter, Saturn and Saturn’s moon Titan, chosen over Pluto for its substantial atmosphere, returning the first detailed images of those gas giants’ moons. On August 25, 2012, it crossed the heliopause into interstellar space, the first spacecraft to do so.

last-natural-smallpox-case-1977.summary: In October 1977 a Somali cook caught the last natural case of smallpox; a disease that killed 300 million people that century was gone. He sometimes worked as vaccinator for WHO’s eradication team, though his own vaccination had never taken. Not wanting isolation, he did not report himself; his nurse colleague did on October 30, and WHO diagnosed Variola minor. Of 161 traced contacts, 41 unvaccinated, none fell ill, making his case the last known naturally occurring smallpox. WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

sanger-sequencing-1977.summary: In 1977 Sanger published a way to read DNA's letters. It copies a DNA strand alongside modified bases, dideoxynucleotides, that halt synthesis wherever they are incorporated, producing fragments of every length whose order, sorted by size, spells out its sequence. It remained the most widely used way to read DNA for about 40 years and decoded humanity's genome for the Human Genome Project; Applied Biosystems automated it in 1987.

amaras-law-1978.summary: In 1978 Roy Amara said we overestimate a technology's effect near term and underestimate it long term. Amara’s law has been used to explain nanotechnology’s trajectory and is cited by companies as reason to hold back from spending on unproven but attractive technologies.

cochlear-implant-clark-1978.summary: On 1 August 1978 Graeme Clark implanted a multichannel cochlear device in Melbourne, months after Ingeborg and Erwin Hochmair's Vienna prototype of December 1977; Rod Saunders, who had lost his hearing at 46, heard speech through its electrodes as first recipient. Where earlier devices used a single electrode, Clark’s stimulated the auditory nerve at several points, and with his postdoctoral colleague Yit Chow Tong he worked out how multi-channel electrical stimulation could reproduce frequency and intensity as pitch and loudness, enough for speech. Cochlear Limited later brought his implant to market.

khomeini-cassette-sermons-1978.summary: From exile in Najaf and, after October 1978, Neauphle-le-Château near Paris, Ruhollah Khomeini records sermons and messages that supporters relay by telephone to Tehran, where they are copied onto compact cassettes in bazaar shops and distributed through mosques, taxis and university networks. State radio and television belong to Mohammad Reza Shah, but cheap Japanese recorders and blank tapes, numbering in millions, lie beyond SAVAK's control. Annabelle Sreberny-Mohammadi and Ali Mohammadi call these tapes and photocopied leaflets 'small media' that mobilised crowds through 1978 strikes and marches. Khomeini returns on 1 February 1979 and a republic follows; political scientists cite this episode when later asking what satellite dishes, photocopiers and social networks do to closed states.

oral-rehydration-therapy-lancet-1978.summary: In 1978 the Lancet called a drink of water, salt and sugar the century's most important medical advance. It has saved tens of millions of children. Oral therapy grew from a 1960s finding that glucose speeds gut absorption of sodium and water, confirmed in cholera patients by Hirschhorn, Pierce, Nalin and Cash in 1967 and 1968. In 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis used it in refugee camps near Calcutta during Bangladesh's 1971 war, where cholera mortality was 3.6 percent with oral therapy against 30 percent with intravenous fluids.

permaculture-one-tasmania-1978.summary: Permaculture One: A Perennial Agriculture for Human Settlements appeared in 1978, written by Bill Mollison, a lecturer at University of Tasmania, and his student David Holmgren. They proposed designing food-producing landscapes on ecological principles: perennial polycultures, zoning by frequency of use, and integration of water, animals and buildings. Simmons's 1980 review in Environmental Conservation found it imaginative but thin on evidence; Ferguson and Lovell's 2014 review concluded permaculture spread as a movement and design practice while remaining under-studied by agronomists, and Hirschfeld and Van Acker assess its ecosystem services. Mollison founded Permaculture Institute in 1979 and taught design courses; practitioners now operate in more than 100 countries.

speak-and-spell-1978.summary: In 1978 Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell spoke words from a chip rather than tape; a toy put speech synthesis in children's hands. This handheld learning toy paired its TMC0280 linear predictive coding speech synthesizer chip with keyboard and slot for ROM cartridges. Paul Breedlove’s small team had begun it in 1976 on a $25,000 budget as an outgrowth of TI’s speech-synthesis research, storing whole words in solid-state memory rather than on tape. It was among the earliest handheld electronic devices with both display and interchangeable cartridges, and Speak & Read and Speak & Math followed.

zebra-battery-csir-pretoria-1978.summary: At South Africa's Council for Scientific and Industrial Research in Pretoria, crystallographer Johan Coetzer devised a high-temperature battery pairing molten sodium with a solid beta-alumina electrolyte and a metal-chloride cathode in molten sodium aluminium chloride. It avoided corrosive sulfur used in sodium-sulfur cells and ran near 270 degrees Celsius at about 2.35 volts with iron chloride, later 2.58 volts with nickel chloride. Funded from 1977 by De Beers, Anglo American and a CSIR licensing arm, work moved into partnerships with Harwell, Beta R&D in Derby and Daimler-Benz. ZEBRA packs later powered test fleets and electric vans, and successor cells still serve stationary storage.

cbbs-1978.summary: In February 1978 two Chicago hobbyists put the first dial-up bulletin board online during a blizzard. Ward Christensen and Randy Suess, members of Chicago Area Computer Hobbyists’ Exchange, began work on it while 1978’s Great Blizzard kept them indoors. Christensen had a spare S-100 bus computer and an early Hayes internal modem; Suess insisted it sit at his house so more callers could reach it with local calls. Modelled on their club’s cork board for notices, it let callers with terminal and modem dial in to post and read messages.

gps-first-satellite-1978.summary: In February 1978 the first GPS satellite reached orbit; a constellation built for missiles now guides every phone. It was first of ten Block I prototypes launched between 1978 and 1985 for Navstar-GPS, the constellation America’s Department of Defense built to give military users position and time anywhere on Earth; an eleventh was destroyed in a launch failure. Civilian signals were deliberately degraded until Selective Availability ended in 2000, after which receivers were accurate to about 5 metres. Receivers using its newer L5 band reach 30 centimetres, and as of March 2026, 21 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals.

love-canal-1978.summary: In August 1978 New York declared Love Canal a health emergency, a neighbourhood built on 21,000 tons of chemical waste; Superfund followed. In the 1940s Hooker Chemical Company bought the canal trench and dumped 19,800 tonnes of byproducts from making dyes, perfumes and solvents into it, then sold the land to Niagara Falls’s school district in 1953 for $1. School construction breached containment, heavy rains spread chemicals, and Niagara Falls Gazette investigated from 1976 as residents led by Lois Gibbs and Tom Heiser organized. In April 1978 New York State stepped in and later classified Love Canal as a threat to human health.

kessler-syndrome-1978.summary: In 1978 Donald Kessler calculated that collisions in orbit could cascade until debris made some orbits unusable; John Gabbard named the scenario Kessler syndrome. In June 1978 he and Burton G. Cour-Palais co-authored “Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt.” They argued that collisions in low Earth orbit could develop over decades, rather than billions of years as in asteroid evolution: each collision spawns fragments that cause further collisions, a cascade that increases debris exponentially.

kessler-syndrome-1978.detail: Most experts then assumed upper-atmosphere drag would remove debris sooner than it formed. NASA funded Kessler’s further studies from October 1979.

ibm-leaves-india-fera-1978.summary: India's Foreign Exchange Regulation Act of 1973 requires foreign firms to cut equity to 40 percent unless deemed essential. IBM, which imports used 1401 computers, refurbishes them in Bombay and rents them to 80 installations by 1970, refuses, offering instead an export unit and research centre. Government rejects this and IBM closes Indian business on 1 June 1978, leaving customers and trained engineers behind. Grieco's 1982 study in International Organization reads this as a state bargaining successfully with a multinational. Former IBM staff form maintenance firms, public sector CMC takes over servicing, and domestic makers such as DCM and HCL grow in a market without IBM until it returns in 1992 with Tata.

intel-8086-1978.summary: In 1978 Intel shipped its 8086; its x86 design, chosen for IBM's PC, still runs most of the world's laptops and servers. Work had begun in May 1976 as a stopgap while its ambitious iAPX 432 ran late, to answer 16- and 32-bit processors from Motorola, Zilog and National Semiconductor. Stephen Morse defined its architecture to resemble Intel’s 8-bit 8008, 8080 and 8085, so assembly-language programs could be carried over, while adding signed integers, base-plus-offset addressing and repeating operations; it held about 29,000 transistors. Its 8086 gave rise to x86, an instruction set architecture that still underlies most personal computers and servers.

space-invaders-1978.summary: In 1978 Space Invaders filled Japanese arcades and reportedly caused a coin shortage; video games became an industry. Players slide their laser cannon along their screen’s bottom edge against waves of descending aliens. Designer Tomohiro Nishikado spent one year on it alone, building his own hardware and tools, drawing on Atari’s Breakout, Gun Fight, The War of the Worlds and Star Wars. Midway distributed it overseas later that year. It opened arcade gaming’s golden age, and its 1980 Atari 2600 port quadrupled that console’s sales, home consoles’ first killer app.

ivf-louise-brown-1978.summary: In July 1978 Louise Brown was born in Oldham, the first baby conceived outside her mother's body; over 12 million IVF babies have followed by recent estimates (2010's Nobel release counted about four million). Her parents, Lesley and John Brown, had tried for nine years to conceive, but Lesley’s fallopian tubes were blocked. On 10 November 1977 she underwent Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards and Jean Purdy’s procedure, in which an egg is fertilised in a dish and its embryo returned to the womb, which led newspapers to call Louise a “test tube baby.” Edwards received 2010’s Nobel Prize in Medicine for this work.

ivf-louise-brown-1978.detail: John Webster delivered Louise by planned caesarean at 5 pounds 12 ounces. Her sister Natalie, born in 1982, was the world’s 40th IVF birth.

toshiba-jw-10-1978.summary: In September 1978 Toshiba announced JW-10, developed by Mori Ken'ichi's group at its research centre, and shipped it from February 1979 at 6.3 million yen. A typist entered a sentence's reading in kana by phrase; software then chose kanji using context and word-frequency rules from an 80,000-word dictionary, with per-user frequency learning, and displayed text on a screen for correction before printing. This kana-kanji conversion freed Japanese offices from typewriters that required picking characters from trays of thousands. Prices fell below 100,000 yen within a decade, and conversion methods pioneered here underlie Japanese input on every computer and phone.

Kawada Tsutomu and fellow developers described system in 1979. Earlier Chinese typewriters and Japanese kanji teletypes had relied on manual character selection.

china-reform-opening-1978.summary: In December 1978 a party plenum under Deng Xiaoping began turning China toward markets and foreign trade, starting history's swiftest rise from poverty. Deng emerged as paramount leader over two years that followed, eclipsing Hua Guofeng. 'Reform and opening' became an official slogan only in mid-1980s. Reform followed the Cultural Revolution and decades of central planning that had left China’s economy stagnant and poor. Deng called his programme a large-scale experiment: it de-collectivized agriculture and abolished people’s communes, relaxed price controls, admitted foreign direct investment and created special economic zones, most prominently Shenzhen.

aaai-founded-1979.summary: In 1979 American AI researchers held organising meetings and incorporated AAAI, a society to promote AI and advise its funders; Reddy dates its founding to 1980, with its first conference AAAI-80, and Allen Newell was an early president. It also set out to improve teaching of practitioners and advise research planners and funders. Its early presidents included Allen Newell, Edward Feigenbaum, Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy. In 2007 it became the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence; it now has over 4,000 members worldwide. It publishes quarterly AI Magazine and organizes its AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, counted among its field’s top conferences, along with meetings on AI ethics, interactive entertainment and social media.

ajaokuta-steel-1979.summary: In 1979 Nigeria signed for its Ajaokuta steel mill with Soviet help, building from 1980; after $8 billion to $10 billion it has never made steel. It followed Soviet–Nigerian cooperation on feasibility work and 1973’s discovery of iron ore at Itakpe. Shehu Shagari's government created its company by decree; it was 84 percent complete when a 1983 coup removed him. Accounts differ: 98 percent complete in 1994, with 40 of 43 plants built, or halted in 1996 at about 90 percent; no steel ever came. Three-quarters of the complex stand abandoned, only its light mills rolling iron rods.

desh-daewoo-garments-bangladesh-1979.summary: Retired civil servant Noorul Quader signs a collaboration agreement with Daewoo in 1978 and in 1979 sends about 130 recruits, many of them graduates with no textile background, to Daewoo's factory in Busan for months of training in sewing, cutting, quality and marketing. Desh pays royalties and a sales commission rather than taking Korean capital. Its Kalurghat factory in Chittagong opens in 1980 and ships shirts under Bangladesh's then unused export quotas. Within a few years most trainees leave to start or manage their own factories. A 1990 study treats Desh as a catalyst case: garment exports rise from near zero until Bangladesh ranks second only to China.

fairlight-cmi-sampler-sydney-1979.summary: Kim Ryrie and Peter Vogel, building on Tony Furse's Qasar M8, released Fairlight Computer Musical Instrument in 1979. Its dual Motorola 6800 processors recorded short samples of any sound and played them across a keyboard, while a light pen drew waveforms on screen. Costing about as much as a house, CMI reached Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush, Herbie Hancock and Stevie Wonder; Series II's Page R sequencer in 1982 anticipated pattern-based production. Harkins's history of digital sampling treats it as an origin of sampling culture; Blackburn and Harkins recover women users. Powerhouse Museum in Sydney holds a Series I unit made between 1978 and 1980.

ntt-1g-1979.summary: In 1979 NTT opened the first commercial cellular network in Tokyo. Cellular systems divide a city into cells, each served by its own base station, so calls hand off from cell to cell as phones move; NTT’s was analog, and such systems were later labelled 1G to set them apart from digital generations that followed. Within five years NTT’s network covered all Japan, becoming the world’s first full-scale cellular system.

runit-dome-enewetak-1979.summary: Between 1977 and 1979 US servicemen scraped plutonium-contaminated soil and debris from islands of Enewetak Atoll, where 43 nuclear tests had been conducted, mixed it with cement and dumped more than 100,000 cubic yards into Cactus crater on Runit Island. A cap of 357 concrete panels 45 centimetres thick and 114 metres across was completed in 1979 so that dri-Enewetak people could return to southern islands in 1980. Noshkin and Robison in 1997 and Davisson, Hamilton and Tompson in 2012 assessed leakage; a 2020 Department of Energy report found no immediate structural danger, while Marshallese officials dispute that and note lagoon sediments hold far more plutonium than dome.

stanford-cart-1979.summary: In 1979 the Stanford Cart crossed a room on its own, moving a metre every 15 minutes while it looked. Its project ran at Stanford University from 1960 to 1980; Hans Moravec rebuilt it in 1977 with stereo vision, in which its television camera, mounted on a rail atop its frame, took pictures from several angles and relayed them to its computer, which worked out where obstacles stood and planned each move.

usenet-1979.summary: In 1979 two Duke students linked Unix machines by phone to share messages; Usenet's newsgroups were the internet's first public forum. Steve Bellovin’s Bourne shell scripts linked Duke with nearby University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Usenet rode on UUCP, Unix’s dial-up copying protocol, a “poor man’s ARPANET” for universities shut out of that defense network. Users post articles to topical newsgroups; each news server stores them and forwards them to peered servers, so posts spread across every connected machine without any central host. Usenet became precursor to Internet forums and remains among the oldest network communication systems still in use.

jebel-ali-port-dubai-1979.summary: Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum inaugurates Jebel Ali on 26 February 1979, a deep-water harbour excavated 35 kilometres southwest of Dubai town with 67 berths, at that time largest man-made harbour anywhere. Critics called it oversized for a small emirate. A free zone opens alongside in 1985 with foreign ownership and tax exemptions, and port authority merges with Port Rashid into Dubai Ports Authority in 1991. Jebel Ali becomes a transshipment hub for Gulf, South Asia and East Africa and seed of DP World, which operates terminals on six continents. Urban geographers treat it as founding move in Dubai's logistics-led model, later copied by Gulf and Red Sea neighbours.

china-syndrome-film-1979.summary: In March 1979 The China Syndrome showed a reactor accident covered up; twelve days later Three Mile Island melted and the film became news. In it, television reporter Kimberly Wells and her cameraman witness a nuclear plant’s emergency shutdown and uncover safety cover-ups; its title names what a meltdown was imagined to do, fuel burning down through containment. Nuclear industry voices called it “sheer fiction” and “character assassination of an entire industry.” Twelve days later Three Mile Island’s accident occurred in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, lending it unexpected prescience.

three-mile-island-1979.summary: In March 1979 a reactor core partly melted at Three Mile Island; no one died, but American nuclear building stopped for 30 years. Failures in its non-nuclear secondary system were followed by a stuck-open relief valve that let coolant escape from its reactor loop; operators, whose control panel showed only that this valve had been told to close, did not recognize a loss-of-coolant accident until its core had been uncovered and partly melted. America’s worst commercial nuclear accident brought new regulation and accelerated its industry’s retreat from new reactors.

ixtoc-i-blowout-campeche-1979.summary: On 3 June 1979 exploratory well Ixtoc I, drilled by Pemex contractor Sedco in 50 metres of water about 95 kilometres off Ciudad del Carmen, lost circulation, blew out and caught fire; semi-submersible rig Sedco 135 collapsed onto its wellhead. Oil flowed at an estimated 10,000 to 30,000 barrels a day while Pemex and Red Adair's team tried a steel 'sombrero' collection cone, injected steel and lead balls, and drilled two relief wells. Capping came on 23 March 1980 after roughly 3.3 million barrels, then a record volume for an accidental marine spill. Slicks reached Texas beaches in August 1979, and a 1982 assessment for US agencies documented effects on shrimp grounds and coastal lagoons.

sources.author: Riding, Alan

ixtoc-i-blowout-campeche-1979.detail: Pemex had just become a major exporter after Cantarell's discovery, and Mexico refused US compensation claims, citing sovereignty. Dokken's 2011 paper compares Ixtoc with 2010's Macondo blowout, noting similar causes in well control and similar dispersant debates. Ixtoc remains a reference case for Gulf of Mexico spill science.

sony-walkman-1979.summary: In July 1979 Sony's Walkman went on sale; music became private and portable, and 400 million were sold. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had been listening to music on business trips with Sony’s bulky TC-D5 recorder and asked executive deputy president Norio Ohga for a playback-only stereo built for walking; Sony’s audio department shrank its Pressman recorder, used by journalists, into a cassette player, and Akio Morita aimed it at young buyers. Sony expected to sell 5,000 units a month and sold far more. Over 100 million had sold by 1989, and private listening through headphones, the “Walkman effect,” entered daily life.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Walkman
Hosokawa, Shuhei, 'The walkman effect', Popular Music 4 (1984), pp. 165-180
sources.author: Hosokawa, Shuhei
sources.confirms: An early scholarly analysis of the Walkman as a cassette player for headphone listening that made music private and mobile.
sources.qualifies: States that Sony marketed the Walkman in spring 1980, which conflicts with Sony's documented 1 July 1979 launch.

sources.title: Sony Corporation, 'Sony Celebrates Walkman 20th Anniversary', press release, 1 July 1999
sources.author: Sony Corporation
sources.confirms: The first Walkman, the TPS-L2, was introduced on 1 July 1979, prompted by Masaru Ibuka's wish to listen to music while travelling.

sony-walkman-1979.detail: Abroad the player first appeared as Sound-about, Freestyle and Stowaway before its Japanese name won out. Oxford English Dictionary added “Walkman” in 1986.

picture.alt: Sony Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player of 1979 with headphones, from Tekniska museet collection.
picture.credit: Anna Gerdén, Tekniska museet, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Tekniska museet (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

neocognitron-1980.summary: In 1980 Fukushima proposed the neocognitron, a layered network that recognised shapes wherever they appeared, the ancestor of vision AI. It grew from his 1969 architecture with hand-designed kernels and his 1975 Cognitron, and from Hubel and Wiesel’s 1959 discovery of simple and complex cells in visual cortex. Its S-cells extract local features, C-cells tolerate their deformation and small shifts in position, and higher layers integrate features into a classification; unlike its predecessors, it learns all its convolutional kernels without a teacher. Used for Japanese handwritten character recognition, it served as inspiration for convolutional neural networks.

sources.title: Neocognitron
Fukushima, Kunihiko, 'Neocognitron: A Self-Organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Pattern Recognition Unaffected by Shift in Position', Biological Cybernetics 36 (1980): 193-202
sources.author: Fukushima, Kunihiko
sources.confirms: Fukushima's paper proposes the neocognitron, a self-organising layered network modelled on Hubel and Wiesel's hierarchy that recognises patterns regardless of their position.

sources.title: Fukushima, Kunihiko, 'Neocognitron', Scholarpedia 2, no. 1 (2007): 1717
sources.author: Fukushima, Kunihiko
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed encyclopaedia article by the inventor describing the neocognitron, proposed by Fukushima in 1980, as a hierarchical multilayered network for shift-tolerant pattern recognition.

neocognitron-1980.verification_note: Fukushima's own account and his cited paper date neocognitron to 1980; no source gives 1979, which some accounts use.

visicalc-1979.summary: In October 1979 VisiCalc went on sale for the Apple II, the first spreadsheet. Dan Bricklin conceived it watching a Harvard Business School professor erase and rewrite blackboard tables whenever one figure changed. On screen, an electronic grid recalculates every dependent cell when one entry changes, matching $20,000 financial modelling languages without learning any language. Businessmen who saw it bought $2,000 Apple IIs to run it, making it that machine’s killer app.

sources.title: VisiCalc

sources.venue: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 29(3): 6-19
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed history of VisiCalc, released for the Apple II in October 1979 as the first spreadsheet and the machine's killer application.

sources.venue: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing

visicalc-1979.detail: With Bob Frankston, Bricklin founded Software Arts and wrote VisiCalc in two months in winter 1978–79. It reportedly accounted for over one quarter of Apple IIs sold in 1979 and prompted IBM’s PC in 1981. Over 700,000 copies sold in six years before Lotus 1-2-3 overtook it in 1983.

picture.alt: Dan Bricklin, co-creator of VisiCalc, photographed in June 2010.
picture.credit: Paul Downey, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

brac-oral-therapy-extension-1980.summary: From 1980 BRAC taught 12 million Bangladeshi mothers to mix a drink of water, salt and sugar; child deaths from diarrhoea fell. In February 1979, BRAC began a field trial in two villages of Sulla thana, and in 1980 scaled it up as its Oral Therapy Extension Programme. Its workers taught rural mothers in their own homes to mix oral rehydration solution from ingredients already in their kitchens and to use it when diarrhoea struck. Over ten years it reached 12 million households in 75,000 villages.

sources.title: BRAC (Wikipedia)
Rahman, A. S. M. Mizanur; et al., "Mothers can prepare and use rice-salt oral rehydration solution in rural Bangladesh", The Lancet 326, no. 8454 (1985), pp. 539-540
sources.author: Rahman, A. S. M. Mizanur; Bari, Abdul; Molla, A. M.; Greenough, William B.
sources.confirms: Contemporary Lancet evidence from Bangladesh that rural mothers taught at home could correctly prepare oral rehydration solution from household ingredients, the premise of BRAC's programme.

sources.author: Hossain, Mohammad Bilal

sources.qualifies: Metadata-level confirmation.

brac-oral-therapy-extension-1980.detail: Posters and radio and television spots reinforced those lessons. That coverage took in all of Bangladesh except the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Fifteen years on, most mothers taught could still prepare safe solution, and rural households used it in over 80 percent of severe diarrhoea cases, a rate among the world’s highest.

chile-sx-ew-copper-1980.summary: Solvent extraction and electrowinning (SX-EW) leaches copper from crushed oxide ore with dilute sulphuric acid, concentrates it with organic extractants and plates it onto cathodes without smelting. Pioneered at Ranchers' Bluebird mine in Arizona in 1968, it moved to a far larger scale in Chile: Sociedad Minera Pudahuel's Lo Aguirre plant opened in 1980 with bacterial-assisted heap leaching, Codelco added SX-EW at Chuquicamata in 1987, and by the 1990s El Abra, Quebrada Blanca, Zaldívar and Radomiro Tomic ran some of the world's largest plants. By 2000 Chile produced about half of global SX-EW copper, around 1.4 million tonnes a year. Miners could treat dumps and oxide caps once left as waste, with lower capital cost and no sulphur dioxide emissions.

sources.title: Bartos, P. J., 'SX-EW copper and the technology cycle', Resources Policy 28 (2002)
sources.author: Bartos, P. J.
sources.confirms: Diffusion of SX-EW from Arizona to Chile and Chile's share of world output by 2000.

sources.title: Hopkins, Wayne R. et al., 'Applicability of two modern technology options for SX/EW plants in the Andean copper regions', in Mining Latin America / Minería Latinoamericana (Springer, 1986)
sources.author: Hopkins, Wayne R.
sources.confirms: Technical evaluation of SX-EW plant designs for Andean operations in the 1980s.

chile-sx-ew-copper-1980.verification_note: Lo Aguirre is usually dated 1980 as the first commercial Chilean SX-EW plant; some sources cite 1981 or credit smaller earlier trials. Output figures vary with whether cathode or contained copper is counted.
chile-sx-ew-copper-1980.detail: A 1986 technical paper evaluated SX-EW options for Andean plants. Chilean research institutes and firms refined heap-leach bacteria (Thiobacillus ferrooxidans) and extractant chemistry. Oxide reserves deplete faster than sulphides, so SX-EW output in Chile peaked near 2 million tonnes around 2010 and has since declined as mines return to concentrators.

chinese-room-1980.summary: In 1980 Searle argued that a man following rules to answer Chinese questions understands nothing, and neither does a computer. He imagines himself locked in a room with an English version of some program that handles Chinese, plus pencils, paper and filing cabinets; Chinese characters slip in under its door, he follows his instructions step by step, and slides answers back out. If any computer running that program passed its Turing test, so would he, yet he understands no Chinese. Searle aimed this at functionalism, computationalism and what he calls strong AI.

sources.title: Chinese room
Searle, John R., 'Minds, brains, and programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences (1980)
sources.author: Searle, John R.
sources.confirms: The abstract says a human agent could instantiate a computer program without the relevant intentionality, and that a program alone is not sufficient for intentionality.

sources.title: Cole, David, 'The Chinese Room Argument', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2024)
sources.author: Cole, David
sources.confirms: The page says that in 1980 Searle argued that a person who understands no Chinese could follow English instructions to answer Chinese questions without understanding Chinese, and that no digital computer understands Chinese merely by running the program.

chinese-room-1980.detail: Strong AI, in Searle’s phrase, holds that appropriately programmed computers thereby have minds. His paper drew an enormous number of commentaries and responses over following decades. Behavioral and Brain Sciences editor Stevan Harnad notes that “the overwhelming majority” still think it “dead wrong,” and arguing over why has filled a literature of its own.

picture.alt: John Searle speaking at Google in 2015, 35 years after his Chinese room paper.
picture.credit: FranksValli, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

collingridge-dilemma-1980.summary: In 1980 David Collingridge observed that a technology's harms cannot be known until it spreads, when it is too late to steer it. His book sets out his dilemma of controlling technology, which now bears his name. It has two halves: an information problem, since a technology’s social effects cannot be predicted until it is extensively developed and widely used, and a power problem, since by then it has become entrenched and changing it is costly and slow. His dilemma anchors technology assessment debates.

sources.title: The Social Control Of Technology [PDF] [5tdn4lt4tl00]
Collingridge dilemma
Audley Genus and Andy Stirling, 'Collingridge and the dilemma of control: Towards responsible and accountable innovation', Research Policy 47 (2018)
sources.author: Genus, Audley; Stirling, Andy
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed review of Collingridge's 1980 book and its dilemma of control as the founding statement of the problem.

sources.author: Worthington, Richard
sources.confirms: Contemporary review recording the book's 1980 publication by St. Martin's Press, New York.

collingridge-dilemma-1980.detail: Collingridge’s answer was not caution but “Intelligent Trial and Error”: keep decisions decentralized, design technologies and infrastructures to be flexible, innovate incrementally and learn as cheaply as possible.

era-expert.summary: From 1980 to 1987 expert systems, programs built from thousands of hand-written rules, became AI's first profitable business. An expert system answers questions or solves problems within one narrow domain using logical rules drawn from human experts; staying narrow sidestepped commonsense knowledge, and R1, finished at Carnegie Mellon for Digital Equipment Corporation in 1980, was saving DEC $40 million yearly by 1986. “Overall, the AI industry boomed from a few million dollars in 1980 to billions of dollars in 1988.” Then specialised Lisp hardware collapsed in 1987, and expert systems proved brittle and costly to maintain.

sources.title: History of artificial intelligence
J. McDermott, R1: A Rule-Based Configurer of Computer Systems, Technical Report CMU-CS-80-119 (Carnegie-Mellon University, 1980)
sources.author: John McDermott
sources.confirms: R1 configured DEC VAX-11/780 systems from customer orders and was in regular use by DEC manufacturing in 1980.

sources.title: J. Bachant and J. McDermott, 'R1 Revisited: Four Years in the Trenches', AI Magazine 5:3 (1984), 21-32
sources.author: Judith Bachant; John McDermott
sources.confirms: DEC began using the rule-based R1/XCON in 1980 and its knowledge base grew over the following four years.

era-expert.detail: Japan set aside $850 million for its Fifth Generation project in 1981. Britain answered with its £350 million Alvey programme and DARPA with its Strategic Computing Initiative, and by 1985 corporations were spending over $1 billion on AI.

expert-systems-boom-1980s.summary: From 1980 corporations bought expert systems that encoded specialists' rules; AI became a billion-dollar industry, then collapsed again. Expert systems encode rules drawn from specialists to answer questions in one domain, and knowledge, rather than search, became mainstream AI’s focus. After R1 began configuring Digital Equipment Corporation’s orders in 1980, companies worldwide built their own, spending over $1 billion by 1985. Its hardware market collapsed in 1987, opening AI’s second winter.

sources.title: History of artificial intelligence
Durkin, John, "Expert Systems: A View of the Field"
sources.author: John Durkin
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed survey of the growth of fielded expert systems through the 1980s and the market's later contraction; Crossref record confirmed, IEEE page not readable.

sources.title: Feigenbaum, Edward A., Pamela McCorduck and H. Penny Nii, The Rise of the Expert Company
sources.author: Edward A. Feigenbaum, Pamela McCorduck, H. Penny Nii
sources.confirms: Contemporaneous account by the field's leading advocate of corporate adoption of expert systems in the 1980s; archive page fetched.

expert-systems-boom-1980s.detail: An industry grew up around expert systems, with hardware firms Symbolics and Lisp Machines and software firms IntelliCorp and Aion. Japan’s Fifth Generation project, Britain’s Alvey programme, America’s MCC consortium and DARPA, which tripled its AI spending between 1984 and 1988, poured in public money.

picture.alt: Symbolics 3620 Lisp machine workstation of mid 1980s, hardware of expert systems boom, photographed 2016.
picture.credit: leighklotz, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lisp-machines-symbolics-1980.summary: In 1980 Symbolics was founded and, with LMI, began selling computers built to run Lisp across 1980 and 1981; the AI boom bought them and the AI winter killed them. Richard Greenblatt and Thomas Knight began MIT’s project in 1973, producing CONS and then CADR. In 1979 Russell Noftsker proposed commercializing CADR; his quarrel with Greenblatt split MIT’s AI Lab, and after internal battles Symbolics shipped CADR as its LM-2 in 1981, while Greenblatt’s Lisp Machines, Inc. sold it as LMI-CADR. Perhaps 7,000 Lisp machines were sold in all, before cheaper desktops ended their market in 1987.

sources.title: Lisp machine
Moon, David A., 'Symbolics Architecture', Computer 20 (1987) 43-52
sources.author: Moon, David A.
sources.confirms: Symbolics' Lisp machine line descended from the MIT CADR, sold commercially from 1981 as the LM-2.

sources.title: Ware Myers, 'Lisp Machines Displayed at AI Conference', Computer 15 (1982) 79-82
sources.author: Ware Myers
sources.confirms: Crossref metadata confirms this contemporary IEEE Computer report on the Lisp machines shown by Symbolics and LMI at the 1982 AI conference; the IEEE page would not open.

lisp-machines-symbolics-1980.verification_note: Moon (Computer 1987) and company histories put Symbolics' founding in 1980 and its first LM-2 shipments in 1981, with LMI's first CADR sales also in 1980 to 1981.
lisp-machines-symbolics-1980.detail: Symbolics produced about 100 LM-2s at $70,000 each while its delayed 3600 line was finished. Richard Stallman blamed Symbolics for his hacker community’s collapse.

smallpox-eradication-1980.summary: In May 1980 WHO certified smallpox eradicated, the first disease humans have wiped out. Smallpox killed up to 300 million people after 1900; as late as 1967, 15 million people caught it and two million died. Edward Jenner had introduced its vaccine in 1796, and WHO ran a global vaccination campaign from 1958 to 1977, intensified in 1967, that tracked outbreaks and vaccinated around them until its last naturally occurring case was diagnosed in Somalia in October 1977. Smallpox remains the only human disease ever eradicated.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Smallpox
World Health Assembly, resolution WHA33.3, 'Declaration of Global Eradication of Smallpox', 8 May 1980
sources.author: World Health Assembly
sources.confirms: The Thirty-third World Health Assembly declared on 8 May 1980 that smallpox had been eradicated.

sources.title: Henderson, Donald A., 'The Eradication of Smallpox: An Overview of the Past, Present, and Future', Vaccine 29 suppl. 4 (2011) D7-D9
sources.author: Henderson, Donald A.
sources.confirms: The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977 and eradication was certified in 1980.

smallpox-eradication-1980.detail: Laboratory exposure in Birmingham, England, caused one fatal case in 1978. Rinderpest, which afflicts cattle, became the second eradicated disease in 2011. Routine smallpox vaccination has since ended.

picture.alt: Rahima Banu, two-year-old Bangladeshi girl who was last known natural case of variola major, photographed in 1975 by eradication programme staff
picture.credit: CDC / World Health Organization, Public domain (US government work), via Wikimedia Commons

technion-ubiquitin-discovery-1980.summary: Working at Technion in Haifa, with sabbatical stays in Irwin Rose's laboratory at Fox Chase in Philadelphia, Avram Hershko and his student Aharon Ciechanover show in two 1980 papers that a small heat-stable polypeptide, later identified as ubiquitin, is covalently attached to proteins in an ATP-dependent step that marks them for degradation. Their reticulocyte extract work explains why cells spend energy to destroy proteins and reveals a regulated pathway, not a passive scavenger. Later work maps enzymes E1, E2 and E3 and proteasome. Ubiquitin signalling turns out to control cell cycle, DNA repair and immune response, and drugs such as bortezomib target it. Hershko, Ciechanover and Rose share 2004 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

sources.title: Ciechanover, A., Heller, H., Elias, S., Haas, A. L., Hershko, A. (1980). ATP-dependent conjugation of reticulocyte proteins with the polypeptide required for protein degradation. PNAS 77(3), 1365-1368.

sources.author: Hershko, Avram; Ciechanover, Aharon; Heller, Hannah; Haas, Arthur L.; Rose, Irwin A.

technion-ubiquitin-discovery-1980.detail: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences assessed both papers in 2004. Credit is shared between Haifa and Philadelphia; record names Technion as home institution while noting Fox Chase collaboration.

picture.credit: Thomas Splettstoesser (www.scistyle.com), CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

winner-artifacts-politics-1980.summary: In 1980 Langdon Winner asked whether artifacts have politics and answered yes; a low bridge or a nuclear plant decides who does what. It argues that artifacts can carry politics in two ways. First, a specific design or arrangement can settle an issue in a community: Winner cites Robert Moses’s low parkway overpasses on Long Island, which kept 12-foot buses, and those who rode them, away from Jones Beach. Second, some technologies are inherently political, requiring or strongly suiting particular patterns of power: an atom bomb demands centralized, hierarchical control, while solar energy’s advocates argue it suits decentralized, democratic arrangements.

sources.title: Do Artifacts Have Politics? - UW Faculty Web Server
Do Artifacts Have Politics? - JSTOR
Langdon Winner, Do artifacts have politics?

winner-artifacts-politics-1980.detail: Winner’s other examples of the first kind are Cyrus McCormick’s costly molding machines, installed to break his iron molders’ union, and California’s mechanical tomato harvester. That harvester cut growers from about 4,000 to 600.

xcon-1980.summary: In 1980 DEC's XCON began configuring computer orders by rule, the first expert system to earn its keep in daily business. John McDermott of Carnegie Mellon University had written it in 1978 in OPS5 as a production-rule system: each rule says that when an order shows certain conditions, add or adjust a component. Its rules came from DEC’s PDP-11 and VAX experts, who sometimes disagreed among themselves. It grew to 6,200 rules by 1987, half changing every year, and maintaining it became exceedingly difficult, a warning for expert systems generally.

sources.confirms: R1 (XCON), a rule-based program configuring VAX-11 systems from customer orders, has been used regularly by Digital Equipment Corporation's manufacturing organisation since January 1980.

xcon-1980.detail: By 1986 XCON had about 2,500 rules and had processed 80,000 VAX orders at 95 to 98 percent accuracy. It saved DEC an estimated $25 million a year by cutting free replacement parts, speeding assembly and pleasing customers.

picture.alt: DEC VAX-11/780 minicomputer cabinets, hardware XCON configured for Digital customers, photographed in 2008
picture.credit: Emiliano Russo, Associazione Culturale VerdeBinario, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

orangi-pilot-project-karachi-1980.summary: In April 1980 social scientist Akhtar Hameed Khan begins work in Orangi, an unplanned settlement of hundreds of thousands in Karachi. His team cuts cost of underground lane sewers to about a quarter of contractor rates by simplifying design, dropping contractor margins and letting each lane of 20 to 40 houses organise and pay for its own digging. Households finance latrines, lane sewers and collector drains themselves; government is asked only for trunk mains and treatment. By 1993 lane sewers serve 3,285 lanes, 97 percent of area where OPP had worked since 1982, and an estimated million residents. Hasan's writings make this component-sharing model a reference for sanitation programmes in Pakistan and beyond.

pac-man-1980.summary: In May 1980 Namco released Pac-Man, a maze game with no shooting; it drew women into arcades and sold 400,000 machines. Toru Iwatani led its nine-person team from early 1979, setting out to make a cheerful, nonviolent game that would draw women and couples into arcades then filled with war and sports titles; his round hero came from a pizza missing one slice and from kuchi, Japanese for mouth. Players guide Pac-Man through a maze eating every dot while four ghosts, each with its own chasing habit, pursue him; power pellets turn them blue and edible for a few seconds.

sources.title: Pac-Man (Wikipedia)
Article on playing, beating and breaking Pac-Man, Cogent Arts and Humanities 3 (2016)

pac-man-1980.detail: Pac-Man spawned sequels, merchandise, two television series and a hit single, became Namco’s mascot and remains among history’s highest-grossing games, with over $14 billion in revenue as of 2016.

toto-washlet-1980.summary: In June 1980 Kitakyushu plumbing maker TOTO launches its Washlet, a toilet seat with a heated surface and a retractable nozzle that washes with warm water at an adjustable angle, developed after years of trials to fix spray position. Earlier imported medical seats had scalded users. It sold a million by 1987 and ten million by 1998; a Cabinet Office survey found 14 per cent of Japanese households had one in 1992 and 80 per cent of households of two or more people by March 2018. TOTO passed 70 million cumulative shipments in November 2025, with overseas sales above 30 per cent in 2024. Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers listed the original Washlet as engineering heritage in 2012.

cnn-launch-1980.summary: In June 1980 CNN went on air with news 24 hours a day. Ted Turner introduced it, and husband and wife David Walker and Lois Hart anchored its first newscast. Cable carriage let it reach homes outside broadcast schedules from Atlanta, Georgia. CNN grew to 42 bureaus and over 900 affiliated local stations, made Turner a media mogul and set television news on a round-the-clock footing its rivals later matched.

Library of Congress, Business Reference Services, 'CNN Launched 6/1/1980', This Month in Business History
sources.author: Library of Congress
sources.confirms: The Library of Congress records that Ted Turner's CNN launched from Atlanta on 1 June 1980 as the world's first 24-hour television news network.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'CNN'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Britannica describes CNN as television's first 24-hour all-news service, founded by Ted Turner in 1980.

cnn-launch-1980.detail: Co-founder Reese Schonfeld ran news, and executive vice president Burt Reinhardt hired most of CNN’s first 200 employees, including anchor Bernard Shaw from ABC News.

slv-3-rohini-launch-1980.summary: On 18 July 1980 a four stage solid fuel Satellite Launch Vehicle, SLV-3, lifted off from Sriharikota and placed 35 kilogram Rohini RS-1 into low Earth orbit. Project director A. P. J. Abdul Kalam led a team that had built motors, guidance and stage separation in Thiruvananthapuram after a first attempt failed in August 1979. India became sixth country to orbit a satellite on its own rocket. SLV-3 technology, scaled through ASLV, led to PSLV in 1994, workhorse for Indian remote sensing and for foreign payloads, and later to GSLV and lunar and Mars missions.

sources.title: Angathevar Baskaran, 'From science to commerce: the evolution of space development policy and technology accumulation in India', Technology in Society 27 (2005)
sources.author: Angathevar Baskaran
sources.confirms: SLV-3 programme and technology accumulation

sources.title: ISRO, 'SLV-3' mission page
sources.confirms: 18 July 1980 launch, Rohini RS-1 payload
