wifi-1999.detail: Interbrand was hired to find a name catchier than its technical label, IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence. Founding member Phil Belanger says Wi-Fi was picked from ten candidates, partly because it sounds like Hi-Fi, and Interbrand also drew a yin-yang logo marking products certified for interoperability. Whether Wi-Fi stands for “Wireless Fidelity” is disputed, though Wi-Fi Alliance briefly used the slogan “The Standard for Wireless Fidelity.” Apple worked with Vic Hayes, Bruce Tuch, Cees Links and others from Lucent who had helped create 802.11. Wi-Fi Alliance had more than 800 member companies as of 2017, and over 3.05 billion Wi-Fi devices shipped each year as of 2019.

y2k-1999.summary: Through 1999 the world feared programs that stored years as two digits would fail at 2000; fixes cost hundreds of billions and worked. Writing 1985 as 85 meant 2000 could not be told from 1900, a habit from decades when memory cost from $10 to over $100 per kilobyte in 1975 that now threatened computer-reliant industries. Companies estimated repairs at $400 to $600 billion. Survivalist interest hit its second peak that decade, and writers including Gary North, Ed Yourdon, James Howard Kunstler and Ed Yardeni anticipated widespread power outages, food and gasoline shortages, and other emergencies, North because he thought fixes were too slow.

sources.title: Year 2000 problem - Wikipedia
US Senate Special Committee on the Year 2000 Technology Problem, Y2K Aftermath: Crisis Averted, Final Committee Report, S. Prt. 106-42 (29 February 2000)
sources.author: US Senate Special Committee on the Year 2000 Technology Problem (Bennett, Dodd)
sources.confirms: The Senate committee's final report on the two-digit year problem, the remediation effort and the uneventful rollover.

sources.title: 'Y2K bug', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Programs that stored years as two digits were feared to misread 2000 as 1900 and disrupt banking, utilities and government systems; the article covers the remediation effort and its cost.

y2k-1999.detail: Religious figures joined in. Jerry Falwell suggested Y2K would confirm Christian prophecy and, like many survivalists, advised stocking up on food and guns, while some people bought generators and withdrew large sums of cash. In the United States, John Koskinen’s President’s Council on Year 2000 Conversion coordinated remediation with FEMA. Contrary to expectations, few major errors occurred in 2000: Telecom Italia sent bills dated January 1900 and 902 heating systems failed near Seoul, but little worse. IDC estimated U.S. spending at $134 billion before the date and $13 billion fixing problems afterward, and worldwide remediation at $308 billion. President Bill Clinton called Y2K “the first challenge of the 21st century successfully met.” Retrospectives credit programmers, while critics note that countries and sectors that did little also saw minimal problems.

picture.alt: Y2K compliant Millennium-Proof sticker from 1999, photographed in 2014.
picture.credit: Someone Not Awful, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mcnealy-zero-privacy-1999.summary: In January 1999 Sun's chief executive McNealy told reporters, “You have zero privacy anyway. Get over it.” He was launching Jini, meant to let consumer devices find one another, communicate and share processing power, which raised questions about what such networks would reveal about their owners; he called privacy a “red herring.” Privacy advocates and the FTC’s consumer protection chief condemned him, and his line has been quoted ever since.

sources.title: Sun on Privacy: 'Get Over It'
Scott McNealy's view on privacy: You still don't have any

mcnealy-zero-privacy-1999.detail: Jodie Bernstein, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, objected. “Millions of American consumers inform us that privacy is a serious concern when they consider shopping online,” she said, noting that Sun belonged to the Online Privacy Alliance, which argued for industry self-regulation; Lori Fena of the Electronic Frontier Foundation called McNealy’s statements “completely irresponsible.” In June 2015 Computerworld reported that he stood by his line but now saw big government, not business, as privacy’s main threat. Google and AT&T holding information about him did not bother him, he said, “because I can always switch to another provider,” whereas “there’s only one DMV.”

saudi-public-internet-filtered-1999.summary: After a 1997 cabinet decision and two years of building, Saudi Arabia lets licensed private ISPs sell public access in early 1999, with all traffic routed through King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology's Internet Services Unit in Riyadh. A proxy farm running commercial filtering software blocks pornography and sites deemed political or religious threats, and a web form invites citizens to request blocks or unblocks. About forty ISPs are licensed, and subscriptions pass a million within three years. Model of a national chokepoint with published rules, rather than outright refusal, influences Gulf neighbours and anticipates later national-network architectures in Iran. Human Rights Watch reads it as censorship; Saudi officials present it as cultural protection.

Date of public launch is given as December 1998, January or February 1999.

age-of-spiritual-machines-1999.summary: In 1999 Ray Kurzweil predicted a computer would pass the Turing test by 2029; that date is now argued with a straight face. Kurzweil, inventor and futurist, argues from his law of accelerating returns that “key events” arrive ever more often and computing capacity grows exponentially. He expects Moore’s law to end “by the year 2020” but some replacement technology to keep that curve going, so that “by around the year 2020” a $1,000 personal computer will match a human brain.

sources.confirms: Digitised edition of the 1999 book containing the forecast that a computer passes the Turing test by 2029; archive.org record fetched.

sources.title: Hafner, Katie, 'The Soul of the Next New Machine: Humans', New York Times, 6 November 1999
sources.author: Katie Hafner
sources.confirms: Kurzweil's The Age of Spiritual Machines (Viking, 1999) argues from the exponential growth of computing that within decades machines will exceed human intelligence and claim consciousness, a thesis John Searle attacked in the New York Review of Books.

sources.title: 'Ray Kurzweil', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The Age of Spiritual Machines (1999) presents the 21st century as a time when computers reach a level equivalent to the human brain and the line between human and machine blurs.
sources.qualifies: Kurzweil himself says the book put a Turing test pass at 2029, while the 1990 Age of Intelligent Machines had given a wider range.

age-of-spiritual-machines-1999.detail:
Each of 2009, 2019, 2029 and 2099 gets its own chapter of predictions. By 2019 images are mostly projected onto the retina and there are “prevalent reports” of computers passing Turing’s test; by 2029 machines “routinely” pass it and communicate through direct neural pathways. Kurzweil writes that machines “will appear to have their own free will” and even “spiritual experiences,” and that humans will in effect live forever as humanity and its machinery merge.

Reviewers praised his record with predictions and clear explanations, but philosophers John Searle and Colin McGinn insisted computation alone cannot make a conscious machine; Searle answered Deep Blue with a “Chess Room” variant of his Chinese room argument. Kurzweil expanded these ideas in The Singularity Is Near.

hole-in-the-wall-kalkaji-1999.summary: On 26 January 1999 Sugata Mitra's team at NIIT cuts an opening in a wall between their Kalkaji office and an adjoining settlement in south Delhi and fixes a computer with internet behind it, facing out. Children with no prior exposure learn to browse and draw within days, teaching each other. Repeats at Shivpuri and Madantusi show similar patterns, published by Mitra in British Journal of Educational Technology in 2001 and 2003 as minimally invasive education. Hole-in-the-Wall Education Limited, formed with International Finance Corporation, places over 30 learning stations across India and abroad. Claims of learning without teachers draw sustained criticism from educationists, yet this experiment shapes debates on self-organised learning for two decades.

i-mode-1999.summary: In February 1999 NTT DoCoMo launched i-mode, the web on an ordinary phone; 30 million Japanese used it before the iPhone. Unlike WAP, used elsewhere, which ran its own markup language on a separate protocol stack, i-mode carried web access and email over a packet-switched network using C-HTML, cut-down HTML that DoCoMo designed for phones with little memory, small monochrome screens and limited input. Mari Matsunaga shaped the service, Takeshi Natsuno led business development and Keiichi Enoki oversaw it. Within months KDDI launched EZweb and J-Phone launched J-Sky in imitation.

sources.author: Barnes, Stuart J.; Huff, Sid L.

i-mode-1999.detail:
Users paid for data sent and received plus about ¥200 to 300 a month, and reached DoCoMo-supervised official sites from a dedicated i-mode button. There were more than 12,000 official sites and around 100,000 unofficial ones. Bandai’s Dokodemo Aso Vegas service, launched in May 1999, passed one million paid subscribers by March 2000. By June 2006 i-mode, EZweb and J-Sky together had over 80 million subscribers in Japan, and usage peaked around 2008.

Operators in Europe, Asia and Australia licensed i-mode, reaching 17 markets under Natsuno. On 29 October 2019 DoCoMo announced that i-mode would end on 31 March 2026.

nipah-virus-malaysia-1999.summary: From September 1998 pig farmers in Perak, then Negeri Sembilan, fall ill with fever and encephalitis; authorities blame Japanese encephalitis and spray for mosquitoes, but adults without pig contact stay healthy. In March 1999 Chua Kaw Bing at University of Malaya isolates an unknown paramyxovirus from cerebrospinal fluid of a patient from Sungai Nipah village; CDC Fort Collins confirms a new agent related to Hendra virus. Chua's team reports 265 cases and 105 deaths in Malaysia plus 11 cases in Singapore abattoir workers. Culling of about one million pigs ends transmission. Fruit bats of genus Pteropus are later identified as reservoir.

sources.title: Chua, K. B. et al., 'Nipah virus: a recently emergent deadly paramyxovirus', Science 288:5470 (2000) 1432-1435

salesforce-1999.summary: In March 1999 Marc Benioff founded Salesforce to sell software by subscription in a browser. It delivered customer relationship management software over the internet rather than as programs for customers to install; its first prototype launched in November 1999. Larry Ellison of Oracle and CNET founder Halsey Minor invested early. Its “end of software” campaign, including actors holding signs outside Siebel Systems’ conference, made that model’s name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Salesforce
'Salesforce's Benioff Aims to Reshape Business Software', New York Times, 13 November 2007
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: Benioff founded Salesforce.com in 1999 to turn software into a service delivered over the internet, starting with customer management.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Salesforce, Inc.'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Salesforce, founded 1999, develops cloud-based customer relationship management software sold by subscription.

salesforce-1999.verification_note: An earlier title called this a “no software” model, which its sources do not support; its title now uses Salesforce’s own tagline.
salesforce-1999.detail: The dot-com crash hit hard and Salesforce laid off 20% of its staff, yet revenue rose from $5.4 million in 2000 to $22.4 million in 2001. Its first Dreamforce conference drew about 1,300 people in 2003; Salesforce listed on the New York Stock Exchange in June 2004 as CRM, raising $110 million, and passed $1 billion in annual revenue in 2009. Fiscal 2026 revenue was $41.5 billion; acquisitions include Tableau and Slack.

infosys-nasdaq-1999.summary: In March 1999 Infosys listed on Nasdaq, the first Indian company to do so; India's outsourcing industry had a flagship. It was then among the top 20 companies on Nasdaq by market capitalization. N. R. Narayana Murthy and six fellow engineers had founded it in Pune on 2 July 1981 with $250, moving to Bangalore in 1983; its offshore custom software business grew after India’s 1991 liberalisation, and it listed in India in February 1993. In 1996 it released In2000, a toolset for the Y2K date problem, alongside its banking products.

sources.title: Infosys - Wikipedia
Global Transformation Partner of Choice
'Narayana Murthy', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Infosys joined Nasdaq in 1999, becoming the first Indian company listed on an American stock exchange.
sources.qualifies: Britannica does not give the March date or the market-capitalisation ranking.

infosys-nasdaq-1999.detail: Nasdaq chief executive Robert Greifeld gave Infosys’s 25th anniversary gathering a share-price comparison. “On March 11, 1999, when Infosys came to NASDAQ, you could buy 100 shares for $3,400; today that would cost you about $50,000, which is a 1387% return,” he said. Its ADR listing later moved to NYSE Euronext to give European investors better access, and in 1999 Infosys also rolled out its Finacle core banking suite and founded its research arm SETLabs.

the-matrix-1999.summary: In 1999 The Matrix imagined humanity farmed inside a machine-run simulation, a lasting image of reality that might be fake. Written and directed by the Wachowskis after their 1996 film Bound, it stars Keanu Reeves as Neo, a hacker who learns that his life is a simulation projected into the minds of humans held in pods by machines, and who joins Laurence Fishburne’s Morpheus and Carrie-Anne Moss’s Trinity in rebellion. Made for about $63 million, it grossed over $460 million, fourth-highest of 1999, and won all four of its Academy Award nominations: visual effects, film editing, sound and sound effects editing.

sources.title: The Matrix
The Matrix | 1999 Film, Cast, Plot, & Facts | Britannica
Constable, Catherine, "Baudrillard reloaded: interrelating philosophy and film via The Matrix Trilogy"
sources.author: Catherine Constable
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed film-studies analysis of the 1999 film's simulated-reality premise and its use of Baudrillard.

the-matrix-1999.detail: Its fights drew on anime and Hong Kong wire work. Its ideas drew on Plato’s cave, 1990s Telnet hacker communities and William Gibson’s Neuromancer, and Reeves and Moss read Jean Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation before filming. It popularized “the red pill” and “bullet time,” in which action within one shot runs in slow motion while its camera seems to move through it at normal speed; Britannica says Reeves performed his rooftop dodge on a green-screen set ringed by more than 120 still cameras. America’s Library of Congress added it to its National Film Registry in 2012. Two sequels followed in 2003 and a fourth film, Resurrections, in 2021.

aibo-1999.summary: In May 1999 Sony introduced AIBO, a robot dog for $2,500; its first 5,000 sold out online in 20 minutes, and owners later held funerals for them. The ERS-110 went on sale on 1 June at 250,000 yen, 3,000 units for Japan and 2,000 for the United States. AIBO stands for Artificial Intelligence Robot and sounds like aibō, Japanese for “pal.” Toshitada Doi had begun robot work at Sony’s Computer Science Laboratory in 1994 with Masahiro Fujita, who argued that robot behavior should “be sufficiently complex or unexpected so that people keep an interest in watching or taking care of it.”

sources.title: AIBO
'A Smart Dog with Megabytes', New York Times, 13 May 1999
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: The Times reports Sony's introduction of Aibo, meaning companion, on 11 May 1999 at $2,500.

sources.title: 'News Watch: Robotic Dogs Take Center Stage', New York Times, 3 June 1999
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: The Times reports that Sony's Japanese allocation of Aibo sold out within 20 minutes of online sales opening on 1 June 1999, with about 1,000 of 2,000 US units sold by day's end.

aibo-1999.detail:
ERS-110 hardware included a 64-bit RISC processor, 16 megabytes of RAM, touch, camera, range-finder, microphone, acceleration and angular-velocity sensors, speaker, and motorised legs, neck, mouth and tail. Its OPEN-R architecture used swappable hardware and software modules; Doi called it the project’s “masterpiece” because outside programmers could add capability. Since it packaged computer, vision and limbs far more cheaply than research robots, AIBO became standard in AI teaching and in RoboCup’s Four-Legged League.

Sony announced AIBO’s end on 26 January 2006 to improve profitability; Doi staged a mock funeral with more than 100 colleagues, calling AIBO a symbol of a risk-taking spirit now dead. Repairs stopped in July 2014. Its fourth-generation ERS-1000, which learns through a cloud connection, launched in Japan on 11 January 2018. AIBO entered Carnegie Mellon’s Robot Hall of Fame in 2006.

remote-agent-1999.summary: In May 1999 NASA's Remote Agent ran the Deep Space 1 probe for 29 hours by pursuing goals rather than executing commands sent from Earth. Instead of executing command sequences sent from Earth, it pursued high-level goals by planning and issuing its own commands, and it detected, diagnosed and recovered from simulated failures. JPL said on June 7 that every objective was met, showing AI could run spacecraft millions of miles from Earth.

sources.title: Remote Agent Experiment Meets All Objectives
Rayman, Marc D., Varghese, Philip, Lehman, David H. and Livesay, Leslie L., 'Results from the Deep Space 1 technology validation mission', Acta Astronautica 47, no. 2-9 (2000), 475-487
sources.author: Marc D. Rayman, Philip Varghese, David H. Lehman and Leslie L. Livesay
sources.confirms: Deep Space 1 tested an onboard artificial intelligence remote agent whose planner turned high-level goals into activities, whose executive issued spacecraft commands, and which diagnosed and worked around four simulated faults without help from the ground.

sources.title: Bernard, Douglas E. et al., 'Spacecraft Autonomy Flight Experience: The DS1 Remote Agent Experiment', AIAA Space Technology Conference, Albuquerque, September 1999 (NASA Technical Reports Server)
sources.author: Douglas E. Bernard, Edward B. Gamble, Nicola Muscettola, P. Pandurang Nayak and others
sources.confirms: In May 1999 the Remote Agent autonomy software took command and control of the Deep Space 1 spacecraft during the Remote Agent Experiment.

remote-agent-1999.detail:
Less than 24 hours in, Remote Agent turned on Deep Space 1’s ion engine but failed to turn it off. The cause was a timing error while two parts of its program exchanged information, never seen in about 3,000 ground runs; with 70 percent of objectives met, controllers paused on May 18. “Remote Agent showed us how powerful it is by providing a list of possible reasons for the bug,” said Ames computer scientist Nicola Muscettola, and engineers then asked it to make a new plan and fly solo for six hours on May 21.

Among simulated faults, it replanned around a camera stuck on, reactivated a “failed” electronics unit, which JPL’s Marc Rayman likened to rebooting a frozen PC, recognised that a failed sensor rather than its device was at fault, and switched thruster sets when one stuck off. Pandu Nayak of Ames said onboard planning saved days of ground work; JPL’s Doug Bernard said it would allow missions once judged “too elaborate, too costly or too dependent on teams of Earth-bound controllers.”

seti-at-home-1999.summary: In May 1999 SETI@home let home computers sift radio telescope data as a screensaver; 5.2 million volunteers logged over two million years of computing time, though no extraterrestrial signal has been shown. Radio telescope data recorded “piggyback” at Arecibo while its dish served other programs were cut into work units of 107 seconds, about 350 kilobytes each, and sent to volunteers’ computers, where free software running as a screensaver or in the background searched for spikes, Gaussian rises and falls, triplets and pulses that could mark artificial signals.

sources.title: Reichhardt, Tony, 'A million volunteers join the online search for extraterrestrial life', Nature 400 (1999): 804
sources.author: Reichhardt, Tony
sources.confirms: Nature news report of 26 August 1999 that SETI@home, a downloadable screensaver using idle time on home and office computers to look for patterns in radio telescope data, had drawn a million volunteers.

sources.title: Marriott, Michel, 'News Watch; Got a Computer? Help Find E.T.'s Home by Calling From Yours', New York Times, 20 May 1999
sources.author: Marriott, Michel
sources.confirms: Contemporary report that the Berkeley project began offering its software that week in May 1999, that 200,000 copies had been downloaded, and that the program analysed Arecibo data as a screensaver while the computer was idle.

seti-at-home-1999.detail: It was the third large-scale volunteer computing project, after GIMPS in 1996 and distributed.net in 1997, and the one with most participants. Its team had planned on 50,000 to 100,000 home computers. By September 26, 2001 it had performed 10 to the 21st floating-point operations, and Guinness World Records 2008 listed it as the largest computation in history. Since Arecibo lacked broadband, tapes went to Berkeley by post. Users formed teams and competed, and to defeat cheats each work unit went to at least two computers, with credit granted only when results agreed. Original software ran until December 15, 2005, when SETI@home moved to BOINC; in March 2020 it stopped sending new work and entered hibernation to analyze 20 years of data, planning follow-up observations with China’s Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope.

napster-1999.summary: In June 1999 Napster let anyone copy any song from anyone's hard drive; the record industry sued, and its revenues halved in a decade. Its central database, hosted by Napster, indexed every song that connected users were sharing; a search found who held a file, and downloading then ran between those two users’ computers. It offered songs hard to find elsewhere, from older recordings to concert bootlegs. College networks clogged, with MP3 transfers up to 61% of external traffic, and in December 1999 A&M Records and other labels sued through RIAA for contributory and vicarious copyright infringement.

sources.confirms: The Ninth Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction against Napster for contributory and vicarious copyright infringement.

sources.title: Rob, Rafael and Waldfogel, Joel, 'Piracy on the High C's: Music Downloading, Sales Displacement, and Social Welfare in a Sample of College Students', Journal of Law and Economics 49 (2006) 29-62
sources.author: Rob, Rafael; Waldfogel, Joel
sources.confirms: Economic study of music downloading in the Napster era and its displacement of sales.

napster-1999.detail: Metallica sued in April 2000 after its demo “I Disappear” circulated, saying it had identified 335,000 users sharing its songs; Dr. Dre followed within a month. Judge Marilyn Hall Patel issued her preliminary injunction in July 2000, stayed two days later by the Ninth Circuit, which in February 2001 ordered Napster to track its network and block infringing material. Verified use peaked at 26.4 million users in February 2001, with unofficial estimates of 80 million registered. Napster shut its network in early July 2001, settled with Metallica and Dr. Dre, agreed in September to pay $26 million plus $10 million in advances, and filed for bankruptcy in June 2002; Roxio bought its name for $5.3 million and relaunched it as subscription music. Decentralized networks such as Gnutella, FastTrack and BitTorrent emerged after Napster’s shutdown.

bhutan-television-internet-1999.summary: On 2 June 1999, marking 25 years of King Jigme Singye Wangchuck's reign, Bhutan Broadcasting Service begins television transmission in Thimphu and state carrier Druknet opens internet access. Bhutan had kept television out while neighbours filled with satellite dishes, citing cultural protection. Within months cable operators offer dozens of Indian and international channels, and early BBS bulletins reach eastern towns days late on VHS tapes sent by bus. Wangchuk's 2008 study in Media Asia and foreign reporting trace debates about wrestling shows and advertising that follow, and a 2006 ban on some channels. Bhutan's gross national happiness framework shapes how officials talk about this opening.

bhutan-television-internet-1999.detail: BBS history pages give 2 June 1999 launch, silver jubilee timing, VHS distribution. Wangchuk (Media Asia 2008) analyses impact and policy debates. PBS Frontline World report describes early reception.

ilo-convention-182-1999.summary: In June 1999 the ILO adopted a convention against child labour’s worst forms; it became ILO’s first convention ratified by every member state. A ratifying country commits to immediate action to prohibit and eliminate slavery, forced labour and trafficking of children, their use in armed conflict, prostitution, pornography and illegal activities such as drug trafficking, and dangerous work. On 4 August 2020 Tonga deposited its ratification, making it the first international labour convention ratified by all 187 ILO members.

sources.title: Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention (Wikipedia)
International Labour Organization, "ILO Child Labour Convention achieves universal ratification" (news release, 4 August 2020)
sources.author: International Labour Organization
sources.confirms: States that Convention No. 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour, adopted in 1999, became the first ILO convention ratified by all 187 member states when Tonga ratified it in 2020.

sources.title: International Labour Organization, "Universal protection against the worst forms of child labour"
sources.author: International Labour Organization
sources.confirms: ILO article on the first universal ratification in the organisation's history.

ilo-convention-182-1999.detail: ILO’s International Programme on the Elimination of Child Labour helps countries comply and monitors them, and Recommendation No. 190, adopted that same year, lists hazards each country should weigh when defining dangerous work in its own law. Convention 182 had the fastest ratification pace in ILO history; 152 million children were in child labour, almost half in dangerous work, most of it agricultural and driven by poverty. According to ILO, the proportion of children in child labour fell by almost 40 percent between 2000 and 2016 as ratifications rose and countries passed laws, including minimum employment ages.

mercado-libre-founded-1999.summary: In August 1999 Marcos Galperin, fresh from Stanford, founded MercadoLibre in a Buenos Aires garage; it became Latin America's largest online market and most valuable firm. It runs online marketplaces for e-commerce and auctions, where sellers list goods and the company earns from the platform, payments and advertising around them. Galperin raised money from John Muse of HM Capital Partners, then from JPMorgan Partners, Flatiron Partners, Goldman Sachs, GE Capital and Banco Santander Central Hispano. In August 2007 it became the first Latin American technology company listed on Nasdaq, and by 2016 it had 174.2 million users, the region’s most visited e-commerce site.

mercado-libre-founded-1999.verification_note: Stanford's page says Galperin's team launched from a Buenos Aires garage in August 1999, and BBC says he launched after returning to Argentina, rather than from Stanford.
mercado-libre-founded-1999.detail: eBay bought 19.5% of MercadoLibre in September 2001 and sold it in 2016, though both companies still cooperate to bring eBay sellers into Latin America. MercadoLibre bought Brazil’s iBazar.com, its competitor DeRemate in 2008 and Classified Media Group that year; it now operates in 17 other countries from Bolivia to Venezuela from headquarters in Montevideo. Business units include MarketPlace, MercadoPago payments, Mercado Publicado advertising, MercadoShops and Mercado Crédito. Time named it to its TIME100 Companies list for 2023.

iridium-bankruptcy-1999.summary: In August 1999 Iridium filed for bankruptcy eight months after launch, owing $4 billion; the satellites kept flying under new owners. Hours earlier a group of bondholders holding about 25 percent of its $1.45 billion in senior notes had filed an involuntary petition in New York to force the issue. Iridium had spent more than $5 billion on 66 low-orbiting satellites to reach “anyone, anytime, virtually anywhere in the world.”

sources.title: For Iridium, A Quick Trip Back to Earth
Iridium Declares Bankruptcy

iridium-bankruptcy-1999.detail: Motorola, largest shareholder with 18 percent, said it believed restructuring could be done within 30 days and would keep supporting operations and subscribers. The New York Times attributed Iridium’s collapse to slower-than-expected subscriber growth, marketing and distribution missteps and earlier handset problems, and described its service as “outdated, outmoded and unpopular with consumers” by the filing. Nippon Iridium, second-largest investor, said it still believed in long-term viability. Neither source gives subscriber numbers or handset prices, so none are stated.

geforce-256-1999.summary: In 1999 Nvidia sold GeForce 256 as the first GPU; a chip built for games became deep learning’s engine. It marketed the chip as “the world’s first ‘GPU’, or Graphics Processing Unit,” defined as “a single-chip processor with integrated transform, lighting, triangle setup/clipping, and rendering engines that is capable of processing a minimum of 10 million polygons per second.” Older 3D accelerators left transform and lighting, geometry work that places and shades a scene, to a PC’s CPU; moving it onto one chip cut hardware costs and brought such power to cheap consumer cards.

Lindholm, Erik, John Nickolls, Stuart Oberman and John Montrym, 'NVIDIA Tesla: A Unified Graphics and Computing Architecture', IEEE Micro 28 (2008), pp. 39-55
sources.author: Lindholm, Erik; Nickolls, John; Oberman, Stuart; Montrym, John
sources.confirms: States that the first GPU was the GeForce 256, introduced in 1999, with fixed-function vertex transform and lighting and pixel pipelines, before programmable shaders in 2001.
sources.qualifies: Authors are Nvidia engineers writing in a peer-reviewed IEEE magazine.

sources.author: John Nickolls; William J. Dally
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed account tracing GPU computing from the 1999 GeForce 256, the first chip marketed as a GPU, to general-purpose use; Crossref metadata confirmed, IEEE page did not open.

sources.title: Dally, William J., Stephen W. Keckler, and David B. Kirk. 'Evolution of the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).' IEEE Micro 41, no. 6 (2021): 42-51.
sources.author: William J. Dally; Stephen W. Keckler; David B. Kirk
sources.confirms: Retrospective on the GPU's path from graphics hardware to the engine of deep learning; Crossref metadata confirmed.

geforce-256-1999.detail: Its chip, NV10, improved on RIVA TNT2 with more pixel pipelines, hardware transform and lighting, and motion compensation for MPEG-2 video, and was the first fully Direct3D 7-compliant accelerator. Its “256” refers to its 256-bit QuadPipe rendering engine of four 64-bit pipelines. Against 3dfx’s Voodoo3 3500 and TNT2 Ultra it gave 50% or more higher frame rates in games written for hardware T&L when paired with low-budget CPUs. An SDR memory version shipped in October 1999 and a DDR version in mid-December; its T&L engine also let Nvidia enter CAD with its first Quadro cards. TSMC made NV10 on a 220 nm process.

picture.credit: Hyins, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

jesse-gelsinger-1999.summary: In September 1999 Jesse Gelsinger, 18, died in a gene therapy trial in Philadelphia; the field stalled a decade and consent rules tightened. He had partial ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, liver disease that blocks clearance of ammonia from blood, which he managed with restricted diet and drugs. On September 13 researchers at the University of Pennsylvania injected him with adenovirus carrying a corrected gene to test its safety; his immune system reacted massively to this viral vector, causing multiple organ failure and brain death.

B. Sibbald, 'Death but one unintended consequence of gene-therapy trial', CMAJ 164 (2001), 1612
sources.author: Barbara Sibbald
sources.confirms: Jesse Gelsinger, 18, received an experimental gene-therapy infusion at the University of Pennsylvania on 13 September 1999 and died four days later of a severe immune reaction.

sources.title: Sheryl Gay Stolberg, 'The Biotech Death of Jesse Gelsinger', New York Times Magazine, 28 November 1999
sources.author: Sheryl Gay Stolberg
sources.confirms: Jesse Gelsinger died on 17 September 1999 after taking part in a University of Pennsylvania gene therapy trial for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

jesse-gelsinger-1999.detail: Researchers hoped to treat infants born with severe OTC deficiency, usually fatal at birth. FDA investigators found that scientists including co-investigator James Wilson, director of Penn’s Institute for Human Gene Therapy, had broken several rules: Gelsinger replaced a volunteer who dropped out although his ammonia levels should have excluded him, Penn failed to report two earlier patients’ serious side effects, and consent documents omitted deaths of monkeys given similar treatment. Penn and Children’s National Medical Center each paid more than $500,000 to the government; Wilson and Penn are reported to have held financial stakes in the research. All U.S. gene therapy trials halted for a time, a severe setback for the field.

gallup-y2k-poll-1999.summary: In November 1999 Gallup found only 12 percent of Americans expected major problems from the Y2K bug, and a December poll found 7 percent; worry had faded through the year. In a telephone survey of 1,010 U.S. adults taken November 18 to 21 for USA Today and the National Science Foundation, 12% believed Y2K computer mistakes would cause major problems for society, down from 34% in December 1998; 3% expected major problems personally, down from 14%. Most expected minor trouble: 71% foresaw minor problems for society and 14% none.

gallup-y2k-poll-1999.detail: Gallup’s trend for major societal problems ran 34% in December 1998, 21% in March 1999, 11% in August and 12% in November. Personal worry fell from 14% to 9%, 7% and 3%. Asked how long problems would last, 41% said a few days and 32% several weeks, so 73% expected a short disruption against 45% in December 1998, while 24% expected several months to a year. Sampling error was plus or minus 3 percentage points. Lydia Saad wrote the release.

thawte-verisign-1999.summary: In December 1999 VeriSign bought Thawte, started in a Cape Town garage four years earlier, for $575 million. Shuttleworth, 26 and sole owner, had started it to build a secure web server free of U.S. limits on exporting cryptography. Both firms had certificates built into early Netscape browsers, so later browsers trusted them too, and each held about half the market for certificates that let browsers verify a site’s identity and encrypt traffic.

sources.title: Reuters, 'Company News; VeriSign Buying Two in Deals Worth $1.2 Billion', New York Times, 21 December 1999

thawte-verisign-1999.detail: Thawte’s server, Sioux, forked Apache and was later folded into Stronghold as Thawte concentrated on certificates. VeriSign’s root certificate was due to roll over on 1 January 2000, an awkward date beside Y2K; owning Thawte, which had rolled over in July 1998, insured against lost business. Business Report described Thawte as the world’s second-largest provider of digital certification and quoted Shuttleworth saying he wanted to turn his focus elsewhere. The proceeds let him become the second space tourist and found Canonical and Ubuntu. Symantec took over VeriSign’s security business, including Thawte, in August 2010, and Thawte passed to DigiCert in 2017.

gavi-vaccine-alliance-2000.summary: In 2000 Gavi, formed at end of 1999, was launched to buy vaccines for children in poor countries; it reports helping to immunize more than 760 million children and prevent over 13 million deaths. Launched at Davos in January 2000, it succeeded the Children's Vaccine Initiative, with Gates Foundation's initial $750 million commitment helping establish it and drawing other donors.

m-systems-diskonkey-2000.summary: Dov Moran's M-Systems, founded in 1989 to sell flash-based disk emulators for embedded systems, files in 1999 for a patent on an architecture joining NAND flash, a controller and a Universal Serial Bus connector in a keyring-sized package needing no driver on Windows 2000 or Mac OS 9. Granted in November 2000 as US 6,148,354, it underlies DiskOnKey, launched late that year with 8 megabytes at about 50 dollars and sold through IBM. Trek 2000 in Singapore shows a ThumbDrive in early 2000 and later litigates priority; Netac in China holds a parallel Chinese patent. Capacities double yearly, Sony's floppy sales end in 2011 and SanDisk buys M-Systems in 2006 for 1.55 billion dollars.

plos-2000.summary: In 2000 three scientists founded the Public Library of Science to publish research free for anyone to read. It grew from a petition by Harold Varmus, Patrick Brown and Michael Eisen asking scientists to stop submitting to journals that did not make full text freely available; tens of thousands signed but few acted, so Brown and Eisen started their own publisher. Its first journal, PLOS Biology, launched on October 13, 2003.

siai-founded-2000.summary: In 2000 Eliezer Yudkowsky co-founded an institute to hasten friendly superintelligence; it soon turned to warning against the other kind. Yudkowsky then concluded such AI would need to be aligned with human values, and his institute shifted its research to that problem. It later became Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI).

south-africa-aids-denialism-2000.summary: In April 2000 President Thabo Mbeki publicly doubted whether HIV causes AIDS, convened a panel that included dissident scientists, and his government refused to supply AZT in public clinics, calling it toxic. Activists in Treatment Action Campaign sued and won court orders for mother-to-child prevention in 2002, but a national antiretroviral programme only began in 2004 and expanded slowly. Pride Chigwedere's Harvard team estimates that a feasible treatment programme between 2000 and 2005 would have averted more than 330,000 deaths and 35,000 infant infections. South Africa later built one of the world's largest treatment programmes, a reversal that followed Mbeki's departure in 2008.

Health minister Manto Tshabalala-Msimang promoted garlic, beetroot and lemon as alternatives, drawing international criticism.

zeer-pot-cooler-2000.summary: In 2000 Nigerian teacher Mohammed Bah Abba receives a Rolex Award for the zeer, a small clay pot nested in a larger one with wet sand packed between them; as water evaporates through its outer pot it draws heat from the inner one. TIME reported that eggplants kept 27 days instead of three, that pots cost about 40 cents a set and that he had distributed 12,000 in northern Nigeria. Trials by Practical Action in Sudan extended tomatoes from 2 to 20 days and carrots from 4 to 20. A 2018 American Journal of Physics paper measured its physics, the latent heat of vaporisation; it works best in dry air and fails in humid coastal regions.

y2k-bug-2000.summary: On 1 January 2000 the Y2K bug caused almost no failures after an estimated $308 billion of repairs worldwide. IDC estimated US spending of $134 billion preparing for Y2K and another $13 billion fixing problems in 2000 and 2001.

golden-rice-science-2000.summary: On 14 January 2000 Science publishes work by Xudong Ye, Ingo Potrykus at ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer at Freiburg University inserting carotenoid pathway genes into japonica rice so that endosperm, normally white, accumulates provitamin A and turns yellow. Its authors note vitamin A deficiency is a serious public health problem in at least 26 countries. The Rockefeller Foundation funded it; Syngenta's Golden Rice 2 of 2005 raised carotenoid 23-fold. Regulatory approval takes two decades: the Philippines approves commercial propagation in July 2021 and registers it as Malusog 1 in April 2022, but on 17 April 2024 the Court of Appeals grants a Writ of Kalikasan halting propagation; PhilRice petitioned the Supreme Court on 24 October 2024 and Golden Rice remains on hold in late 2026.

Critics questioned beta-carotene levels in its first version and distraction from supplementation and diet diversity. Patents on components were licensed free for farmers earning under 10,000 dollars a year. USDA FAS Manila's November 2026 biotechnology report counts five GE products in four crops approved for propagation in the Philippines.

dot-com-crash-2000.summary: On 10 March 2000 the Nasdaq peaked and began a 78 percent fall, wiping out internet firms valued on hopes alone. Late-1990s investors had bid up internet shares at almost any valuation. Technology stocks then fell sharply; by October 2002 Nasdaq had lost 78% from its peak, giving up every bubble-era gain, and online retailers such as Pets.com and Webvan shut down.

bill-joy-why-future-doesnt-need-us-2000.summary: In 2000 Bill Joy, Sun's chief scientist, warned in Wired that robotics, genetics and nanotech could make humans an endangered species. He warned robotics, genetic engineering, and nanotechnology could threaten humanity, noting robots, engineered organisms, and nanobots can self-replicate. John Seely Brown and Paul Duguid answered that his forecast ignored social factors.

germany-renewable-energy-act-2000.summary: In 2000 Germany fixed a 20-year price for anyone feeding solar or wind into the grid. It guaranteed renewable generators grid connection, priority dispatch and a government-set payment for each kilowatt hour fed in, varying by technology. Photovoltaic remuneration rose to as much as 51 cents per kilowatt hour, with tariffs designed to fall 5 percent a year. This law drove rapid uptake of solar and wind.

Ending Selective Availability removed induced errors of about 50 meters horizontally and made civilian GPS roughly ten times more accurate.

iloveyou-2000.summary: In May 2000 the ILOVEYOU worm arrived as a love letter and mailed copies to every contact; it infected 45 million PCs in a day. Opening it overwrote files with worm code and mailed copies to every address-book contact. Spread began on 4 May 2000, moving westward through corporate email systems from Hong Kong to Europe and then the United States. Within ten days, tens of millions of infections had been reported; an estimated 10% of internet-connected computers worldwide were eventually affected.

itc-e-choupal-2000.summary: In June 2000 ITC's agribusiness division installs computers with VSAT links in Madhya Pradesh villages, each run by a trained local farmer called a sanchalak who shows soybean growers daily mandi prices, ITC's own buying price and weather, and sells inputs. Farmers can then sell at an ITC hub with transparent weighing rather than through commission agents at distant markets. Kumar's 2004 study in Information Technologies and International Development documents lower transaction costs for both sides. By 2020 government evaluators count about 6,100 kiosks serving over 35,000 villages and four million farmers across seven states and crops from wheat to shrimp. e-Choupal becomes a textbook case of a company building rural internet for procurement.

india-it-act-2000.summary: In October 2000 India's Information Technology Act gave electronic documents and signatures legal standing. On 24 March 2015, India's Supreme Court struck down Section 66A, which penalised sending “offensive messages” online, as unconstitutional.

human-genome-project-draft-2000.summary: On 26 June 2000 scientists announced a draft of the whole human genome, and medicine gained its full parts list. President Clinton and Prime Minister Blair made that announcement. Begun in 1990 with $3 billion of public funding, it raced Craig Venter's privately funded Celera Genomics from 1998. It was declared complete in April 2003, with an essentially complete genome announced on 14 April.

brazil-xylella-genome-2000.summary: On 13 July 2000 Nature published a 2,679,305 base-pair genome of Xylella fastidiosa, bacterium behind citrus variegated chlorosis that was damaging São Paulo's orange groves. Its paper, with 116 authors, came from Organization for Nucleotide Sequencing and Analysis, a 'virtual institute' of 34 laboratories that research foundation FAPESP had funded from 1997 to build sequencing capacity rather than concentrate it in one centre. Teams coordinated by Andrew Simpson and João Setubal identified genes for adhesion, toxins and xylem colonisation. No plant pathogen had been fully sequenced before, nor any bacterial genome in Latin America; ONSA went on to sequence sugarcane ESTs, Xanthomonas and Leifsonia, and seeded Brazil's genomics and bioinformatics community.

FAPESP spent about 15 million dollars on the project and trained students in each lab, so sequencing capacity spread across São Paulo state rather than concentrating in one institute. Fundecitrus, a growers' body, co-funded work because chlorosis affected a third of orange trees. Findings on adhesion and bacteriophage-derived genes informed later work on Pierce's disease of grapevines in California.

concorde-crash-2000.summary: In July 2000 a Concorde crashed on takeoff near Paris after a tyre burst and 113 died. Metal debris from a DC-10 that took off minutes earlier burst one tyre; tyre fragments ruptured a fuel tank and leaking fuel ignited. Every Concorde was grounded; service resumed on 7 November 2001 with Kevlar-lined fuel tanks and burst-resistant tyres, and Air France retired Concorde in May 2003, British Airways in October 2003.

millennium-development-goals-2000.summary: In 2000 the UN's Millennium Declaration set targets for 2015, including halving extreme poverty, codified in 2001 as eight measurable goals; that poverty target was met early. Goal 5 aimed to cut maternal mortality ratios by three quarters between 1990 and 2015; other goals covered extreme poverty, schooling, child mortality and disease.

asimo-2000.summary: In October 2000 Honda unveiled ASIMO, a humanoid robot that walked on two legs like a child; it shook hands with presidents for 18 years. Development began in 1999 at Honda's Wako Fundamental Technical Research Center in Japan. Three updated models followed from 2004 to 2011, and Honda retired the line in 2022 to concentrate on remote-controlled robots.

folding-at-home-2000.summary: In October 2000 Folding@home began using volunteers' idle PCs to simulate protein folding. Each computer simulates one piece of how proteins fold; misfolded proteins are linked to diseases such as Alzheimer's and cancer. During 2020's COVID-19 pandemic it reached 2.43 exaflops, 2.43 billion billion calculations per second, by April 12, 2020, becoming the world's first exaflop computing system.

bogota-transmilenio-2000.summary: On 18 December 2000 Bogotá began TransMilenio service under mayor Enrique Peñalosa: articulated buses on segregated median busways along Avenida Caracas and Calle 80, enclosed stations with level boarding and smart-card fares, passing lanes for express services, and private operators paid per kilometre under contract to a public agency. Within sixteen months it carried about 650,000 passengers a day at speeds around 26 kilometres an hour, with capacity later measured above 40,000 passengers per hour per direction, a level previously thought to need rail. Built at a fraction of metro cost, it drew on Curitiba's design and exceeded it in scale. Planners from Mexico City, Guangzhou, Johannesburg and dozens of other cities adopted its model for BRT.

bogota-transmilenio-2000.detail: Sandoval and Hidalgo's ASCE paper documents design and early ridership; Gilbert's Bulletin of Latin American Research article assesses benefits and limits, including crowding and fare levels. Network expansion stalled after 2006 amid political disputes. Peñalosa's administration chose BRT after rejecting a proposed metro as too costly for a city of six million; Phase 1 cost about 240 million dollars for 42 kilometres. Stations in road medians are reached by footbridges, and feeder buses serve peripheral neighbourhoods at no extra fare. Critics note crowding of six to eight passengers per square metre and lack of later network expansion.

agile-manifesto-2001.summary: In February 2001 seventeen programmers at a Utah ski lodge wrote the Agile Manifesto, valuing working software over plans. Their lightweight methods, including Scrum and extreme programming, had grown in late-1990s reaction to heavily planned, document-driven approaches often called waterfall.

creative-commons-2001.summary: In 2001 Creative Commons let creators give away some rights in advance; billions of works are now free to share. Lawrence Lessig, Hal Abelson and Eric Eldred founded it, and the first licences came in December 2002. The licenses let creators state which rights they keep and which they waive, so others can share and build on their work without negotiating permission; by 2019 nearly 2 billion works carried them.

korea-broadband-world-lead-2001.summary: An OECD survey for June 2001 finds South Korea with 13.9 broadband subscribers per 100 inhabitants, more than double Canada in second place and six times United States. Thrunet's cable service from 1998, Hanaro Telecom's ADSL from April 1999 and Korea Telecom's response in June 1999 compete on price around 30 dollars a month, aided by dense apartment blocks, government loans for backbone fibre and a building certification scheme. Lee, O'Keefe and Yun and later Kushida and Oh attribute this lead to managed competition plus demand from online gaming and PC bangs. By end 2001 penetration reaches 17 per 100 and Korea becomes a test market for online services, IPTV and later 5G.

maddison-world-economy-2001.summary: In 2001 Angus Maddison published estimates of world output for a thousand years; the hockey stick of growth after 1820 came from his tables. OECD Development Centre published it on 12 June 2001; its long-run GDP per capita series underpin most charts of millennium-long growth. After Maddison's death in 2010, Groningen's Maddison Project continued this work.

viola-jones-2001.summary: In 2001 Viola and Jones found faces in live video on an ordinary PC, the face detection in cameras for a decade. It detected faces in 384-by-288-pixel images at 15 frames per second on an Intel Pentium III running at 700 MHz and at 2 frames per second on a Compaq iPAQ.

edsa-ii-texting-2001.summary: When eleven senators blocked evidence in President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial on evening of 16 January 2001, mobile text messages calling people to Epifanio de los Santos Avenue spread within minutes; more than 20,000 had gathered at EDSA Shrine within about 75 minutes, before church and political leaders called for rallies. Over four days more than a million people assembled, and Estrada left Malacanang on 20 January as Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo took office. Philippines, already sending more SMS per person than any other country, became a reference case for mobile-organised protest, and Vicente Rafael's essay examines both middle-class hopes placed in texting and its limits.

edsa-ii-texting-2001.detail: Rafael's 2003 article in Public Culture, available through eScholarship, gives chronology and analyses 'Generation Txt' discourse. Military withdrawal of support and Supreme Court action completed Estrada's removal, so texting was one factor among several. Estrada's supporters staged a counter-rally in May 2001.

kzn-artemether-lumefantrine-2001.summary: Facing a malaria epidemic driven by pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes and failing sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province reintroduced DDT indoor spraying in March 2000 and in January 2001 became one of the first public health systems in Africa to make artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) its first-line drug. Cure rates rose from 11 percent with SP to 99 percent, and malaria admissions and deaths fell by 89 percent in a year and by 97 to 99 percent by 2003. Karen Barnes's study of those results informed WHO's 2006 shift to artemisinin combination therapy across Africa.

sources.title: Barnes, K. I. et al., 'Effect of Artemether-Lumefantrine Policy and Improved Vector Control on Malaria Burden in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa', PLoS Medicine 2 (2005) e330
sources.author: Barnes, Karen I.; Durrheim, David N.; Little, Francesca; et al.
sources.confirms: AL first-line from January 2001; DDT from March 2000; 89 percent fall in deaths and admissions 2000-01; 99 percent cure
sources.qualifies: Effects of vector control and drug policy cannot be separated

sources.author: World Health Organization
sources.confirms: Recommendation of artemisinin combination therapies as first-line treatment

kzn-artemether-lumefantrine-2001.detail: Spraying and drug change happened together, so their contributions cannot be fully apportioned. Neighbouring Mozambique joined through Lubombo Spatial Development Initiative. KwaZulu-Natal's 2000 epidemic peaked at over 40,000 cases, following a 1996 switch from DDT to pyrethroids that let Anopheles funestus return. Combination of indoor spraying and effective treatment cut cases to a few hundred within three years, an early demonstration that combined approaches could reverse epidemic malaria.

wikipedia-2001.summary: In January 2001 Wikipedia launched, an encyclopedia anyone could edit, and grew into the largest ever made. Larry Sanger had proposed it five days earlier on Nupedia's mailing list, Nupedia being a free encyclopedia whose expert-written articles went through formal review, and announced it there. By April 2024 its editions held more than 68 million articles and drew more than 1.5 billion device visits monthly.

nigeria-gsm-launch-2001.summary: In January 2001 Nigeria auctioned GSM licences for $285 million each; Nigeria went from 400,000 phone lines to 100 million in a decade. Beforehand its roughly 120 million people shared those 400,000 working lines and a waiting list of more than 10 million. Service launched in August 2001; MTN and Econet signed 1.57 million subscribers within a year, and Nigeria had about 60 million by 2008.

cipla-dollar-a-day-arv-2001.summary: In February 2001 Yusuf Hamied of Cipla, Mumbai, offered a generic triple combination of stavudine, lamivudine and nevirapine to Medecins Sans Frontieres at 350 dollars per patient per year, against 10,000 to 15,000 dollars for patented brands. India's 1970 patent law allowed Cipla to make these molecules by its own processes. Cipla's Triomune fixed dose pill followed in 2001. Prices collapsed worldwide, PEPFAR and Global Fund bought Indian generics, and by 2008 Indian firms supplied over 80 percent of donor funded antiretrovirals in developing countries. Treatment for millions of people in Africa became feasible. Hamied's offer reshaped debates on TRIPS and public health, culminating in Doha Declaration of November 2001.

jamaica-digicel-mobile-2001.summary: On 19 April 2001 Irish entrepreneur Denis O'Brien's Digicel opened GSM service in Jamaica after the government ended Cable & Wireless's monopoly and auctioned licences; mobile penetration then stood near 10 percent of about 2.6 million people. Digicel sold cheap prepaid SIMs and handsets through corner shops, built island-wide coverage within months and signed up more than 100,000 customers in its first hundred days, passing C&W within two years. Anthropologists Horst and Miller documented how low-income Jamaicans used phones for 'link-up' networks of kin and friends to call on for money and favours. Digicel expanded across Caribbean, into Central America and to Papua New Guinea in 2007, becoming a template for low-cost mobile operators in small markets.

jamaica-digicel-mobile-2001.detail: Horst and Miller's Current Anthropology paper draws on fieldwork in Jamaica in 2004; Irish Times reporting from launch covers market conditions and O'Brien's strategy. Subscriber figures come from company statements reported in press. Digicel paid about 47.5 million dollars for its licence and spent heavily on towers to cover rural parishes C&W had neglected. Per-second billing and free incoming calls suited low incomes. By 2005 Jamaica had more than 90 mobile subscriptions per 100 people. Digicel later sponsored West Indies cricket and became a dominant brand across 25 Caribbean and Pacific markets.

simputer-2001.summary: Scientists at Indian Institute of Science Bangalore with Encore Software form Simputer Trust in 1999 and announce a Linux handheld on 25 April 2001: a 200 dollar device with touchscreen, smart card slot so one unit can serve many users, and text to speech in Indian languages for people who cannot read. Press abroad calls it a computer for the poor. Licensees Encore and PicoPeta take until 2004 to ship, by which time mobile phones are cheaper and spreading on their own; a 2004 report counts about 600 sold against hopes of millions. Fonseca and Pal's 2006 analysis treats Simputer as a lesson in product design detached from distribution and demand, and its designers' ideas resurface in later low-cost devices.

Pictures and DreamWorks Pictures shared distribution; it grossed $235.9 million, and its budget was $90 to 100 million.

given-imaging-pillcam-2001.summary: Gavriel Iddan, an electro-optical engineer at Rafael who had designed missile seekers, works from 1981 on a camera small enough to swallow, and with gastroenterologist Eitan Scapa and physicist Paul Swain's group in London builds a capsule 11 by 26 millimetres holding a CMOS imager, white LEDs, battery and radio transmitter. Given Imaging, founded in Yoqneam in 1998, publishes first human images in Nature in May 2000; its M2A capsule, later PillCam SB, receives US Food and Drug Administration clearance on 1 August 2001 and CE marking that year. Passing by peristalsis over eight hours and transmitting two frames a second to a belt recorder, it reaches 5 metres of small bowel beyond push endoscopes, locating bleeding, Crohn's lesions and tumours. iranian-blogosphere-weblogestan-2001.summary: In November 2001 journalist Hossein Derakhshan, newly arrived in Toronto, posts a step-by-step Persian guide to starting a blog on Blogger with Unicode script. Within a year Persian ranks among most-used blogging languages and Iranians call their network Weblogestan. Reformist editors whose papers were closed in 2000, students, clerics and women writing under pseudonyms use it to argue in public outside licensed press. Anthropologist Alireza Doostdar records a 2003 dispute over 'vulgar' blogging as a fight over who may write Persian in public. By 2008 Harvard's Berkman Center maps about 60,000 active blogs across secular, religious and poetry clusters. Arrests of bloggers from 2003 and filtering of hosts show state learning in turn, and Derakhshan himself is jailed in 2008.

mexico-oaxaca-maize-transgenes-2001.summary: On 29 November 2001 Nature published a paper by David Quist and Ignacio Chapela of Berkeley reporting cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter sequences in criollo maize from Sierra Juárez, Oaxaca, despite Mexico's 1998 moratorium on planting GM maize. Critics attacked its inverse-PCR evidence for introgression, and in April 2002 Nature said evidence was insufficient to justify publication, an unprecedented step. Sol Ortiz-García's 2005 survey found no transgenes in 153,746 seeds from 125 fields, while Piñeyro-Nelson's 2009 study detected them at low frequency in 2001 and 2004 samples and showed sampling and method affect results. The episode shaped Mexico's biosafety law of 2005, debates on centres of crop origin and, later, its 2020 and 2023 decrees against GM maize.

mexico-oaxaca-maize-transgenes-2001.detail: Three peer-reviewed studies reach different conclusions: presence in 2001, absence in 2005, low-frequency presence in 2009. Mexico imported millions of tonnes of US maize each year, part of it transgenic, and farmers often plant grain bought from DICONSA stores, offering a route for gene flow. Chapela's tenure case at Berkeley, Nature's handling of criticism, and Mexican ministry data showing transgenes in 2001 to 2002 made the affair a standard case in science studies on controversy and review.

weta-digital-massive-2001.summary: For Peter Jackson's The Fellowship of the Ring, released December 2001, Weta Digital in Wellington needed battle scenes with tens of thousands of fighters. Stephen Regelous wrote Massive (Multiple Agent Simulation System in Virtual Environment), in which each digital soldier is an agent with fuzzy-logic brain, senses of sight and hearing and a library of motion-captured moves, choosing actions in response to neighbours rather than following scripted paths. Prologue battle of Last Alliance used 70,000 agents; Pelennor Fields in Return of the King used over 200,000. Regelous received an Academy Scientific and Engineering Award in 2004, and Massive Software became a separate company selling to film and games.

Weta Digital later built performance-capture pipelines for Gollum, King Kong and Avatar, winning six Academy Awards. In 2021 Unity bought Weta's tools division for 1.6 billion US dollars, then wound it down in 2023; Weta FX continues as a studio.

His battery-powered, self-balancing two-wheeled device was designed for one standing rider. Kamen said it would do for walking what the calculator did for pad and pencil; NPR reported in 2011 that about 100,000 had been built, around 10 percent of expected volume.

autotrac-gps-steering-2002.summary: John Deere launches AutoTrac in 2002, factory-integrated assisted steering that holds tractors and combines on parallel passes using StarFire GPS receivers introduced with the GreenStar display in 2001, at first within 30 centimeters and from 2004 with real time kinematic correction to 2.5 centimeters. Hands-free guidance follows yield monitors of the 1990s, the US switch-off of GPS Selective Availability in May 2000 and Stanford work for Deere on carrier-phase tractor control that NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory corrections supported. Overlap and skips fall, so fuel, seed and chemical use drop and operators work at night. Heraud and Lange's 2009 ASABE lecture traces guidance from horses to GPS. Deere marked 25 years of guidance in May 2026; most new large tractors in North America, Europe, Brazil and Australia now ship with auto-steer.

autotrac-gps-steering-2002.detail: RTK repeatability enabled controlled traffic farming and strip till. Precision agriculture research in peer-reviewed journals centres on yield mapping and variable-rate application. NASA Spinoff credits JPL's global differential GPS corrections, licensed to Deere's NavCom unit, for StarFire's accuracy without local base stations. Deere's StarFire network and competitors such as Trimble and Topcon brought auto-steer to most makes within a decade.

china-great-firewall-documented-2002.summary: Jonathan Zittrain and Benjamin Edelman test more than 200,000 websites through Chinese proxy servers in 2002 and find about 19,000 blocked, including news, health, education and Taiwan and Tibet sites, with methods ranging from IP blackholing to DNS tampering and keyword resets. Their IEEE Internet Computing paper gives first systematic evidence of a national filtering system that Chinese engineers, led by Fang Binxing at National Computer Network Emergency Response Centre, had been building since late 1990s alongside Ministry of Public Security's Golden Shield project. Blocking of Google in September 2002, then Wikipedia, YouTube, Facebook and Twitter by 2009, shaped a domestic platform market led by Baidu, Tencent and Alibaba.

delhi-cng-conversion-2002.summary: Hearing M. C. Mehta's air pollution petition, Supreme Court on 28 July 1998 orders Delhi's whole city bus fleet converted to compressed natural gas by 31 March 2001, along with taxis and three-wheelers. Operators and government stall; on 1 April 2001 few buses run and commuters are stranded. Court grants a conditional extension to September 2001 and fines diesel buses, and on 5 April 2002 rejects a government bid to allow low-sulphur diesel instead. By end of 2002 about 10,000 CNG buses, 50,000 three-wheelers and 10,000 taxis operate, supplied by Indraprastha Gas. Studies by Goyal and by Narain and Bell find lower sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide but little change in particulates, which later rise again with private cars.

budapest-open-access-2002.summary: In February 2002 the Budapest Open Access Initiative defined open access: research free for anyone to read online. It was released on February 14, 2002 after an Open Society Institute meeting in Budapest in December 2001, and recommended that authors deposit copies of their papers in open internet archives. Its definition was reaffirmed in 2012, aiming for open access as default for new peer-reviewed research within ten years.

bt-cotton-india-2002.summary: On 26 March 2002 India's Genetic Engineering Approval Committee, at its 32nd meeting in New Delhi, clears three Bt cotton hybrids from Mahyco, Mech 12, Mech 162 and Mech 184, carrying Monsanto's Cry1Ac gene against American bollworm, after illegal Navbharat Bt seed found in Gujarat in 2000 forced the decision. Area rises from 29,415 hectares in 2002 to 530,800 in 2004 and later past 11 million, over 90 percent of cotton land, as India overtakes the United States as second largest producer. Kathage and Qaim's panel study of farm households from 2002 to 2008 finds Bt raised yields 24 percent and profits 50 percent per hectare and household consumption 18 percent. Pink bollworm resistance to Bollgard II spreads from the mid-2010s, and no GM food crop follows for two decades.

bt-cotton-india-2002.detail: Approval set off India's long dispute over seed prices, farmer suicides and royalty caps; the government fixed Bt trait fees in 2016. Illegal herbicide-tolerant cotton is widely grown. Insecticide use against bollworm fell sharply in the 2000s then rose against sucking pests. Kathage and Qaim remain the most cited evidence of smallholder benefit; critics dispute causality given concurrent hybrid and irrigation changes.

Roomba steered with simple behaviours, spiralling, crossing rooms, following walls and turning after its bumper met an obstacle, and sensed steep drops so it would not fall down stairs. This first-generation model had three buttons for room size.

spray-on-skin-bali-burns-perth-2002.summary: Plastic surgeon Fiona Wood and scientist Marie Stoner developed a technique at Royal Perth Hospital to culture a patient's own skin cells and spray them onto burns, cutting time to cover wounds from weeks to days. After bombings in Kuta on 12 October 2002 killed 202 people, 28 severely burned survivors were flown to Perth and treated with cultured cells and conventional grafts. Wood, Kolybaba and Allen reviewed eleven years of cultured autograft results in 2006, noting mixed evidence on outcomes. Clinical Cell Culture, later Avita Medical, commercialised ReCell kit, approved in Australia in 2005 and by US FDA in 2018. Wood was named Australian of the Year in 2005.

brazil-free-software-policy-2003.summary: In 2003 President Lula da Silva's new government, with Sérgio Amadeu heading Instituto Nacional de Tecnologia da Informação, created a Comitê Técnico de Implementação de Software Livre and ordered ministries and state firms to prefer free software in procurement, migrate servers and desktops, and release public code. Programmes such as Computador para Todos subsidised Linux PCs, thousands of telecentres ran GNU/Linux, and Banco do Brasil and Serpro migrated large systems; a government Portal do Software Público followed in 2007. Brazil became the largest state backer of free software, hosted Fórum Internacional Software Livre in Porto Alegre and pushed open document standards. Activists linked it to technological autonomy debates from the 1984 Informatics Law; later governments scaled the policy back after 2016.

captcha-2003.summary: In 2003 researchers formalised CAPTCHA, a term coined at Carnegie Mellon in 2000, for the distorted letters that tell humans from bots. Its common form asks visitors to type letters or numbers shown in a distorted image that software of its day could not read, blocking bots and spam. Google's reCAPTCHA and Intuition Machines' hCaptcha are its widely used descendants.

idcol-solar-home-systems-bangladesh-2003.summary: From 2003 state-owned Infrastructure Development Company Limited refinances loans made by Grameen Shakti and dozens of partner organisations so rural households can buy 20 to 100 watt solar panels with battery and lights on three year instalments. Partners install and service systems; IDCOL sets technical standards, tests components and pays a falling subsidy funded by World Bank, GIZ and others. Between 2003 and 2018 over 4.1 million systems are sold, bringing electricity to about 20 million people, roughly 14 percent of Bangladesh's population, while grid extension and cheaper panels eventually shrink demand. Standards, consumer finance and local service networks made this scale possible.

net-neutrality-2003.summary: In 2003 Tim Wu coined net neutrality, the rule that internet service providers treat all traffic alike, whatever its content, source or application, rather than slowing or blocking some of it. Wu extended common carriage, a longstanding rule that telephone systems carry every call on equal terms.

xen-hypervisor-2003.summary: In 2003 Cambridge released Xen, an open hypervisor that split one server into many; early cloud computing, including Amazon EC2, was built on it. A hypervisor is software that lets several operating systems run at once on one computer, each inside its own isolated virtual machine.

amazon-item-to-item-2003.summary: In 2003 Amazon engineers described recommending by pairing items bought together rather than matching customers, a method that scaled to millions of customers.

latent-dirichlet-allocation-2003.summary: In 2003 Blei, Ng and Jordan published latent Dirichlet allocation, which finds the topics running through documents without being told them. It treats each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as words that tend to appear together, so news articles might yield one topic of president, government and election and another of team, game and score. It became one of the most used topic models.

eu-weee-directive-2003.summary: In 2003 EU law made manufacturers responsible for collecting and recycling electronics they sell.

newater-singapore-2003.summary: Dependent on water piped from Malaysia under agreements expiring in 2011 and 2061, Singapore's Public Utilities Board revisited reclamation in 1998 after a failed 1974 attempt. A demonstration plant at Bedok ran from May 2000 at 10,000 cubic metres a day, passing treated effluent through microfiltration, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet light; two years of testing against WHO and US EPA standards found the water cleaner than reservoir water. On 9 August 2002, 60,000 people toasted it at the National Day Parade. Full-scale plants at Bedok and Kranji were commissioned in February 2003, first for wafer fabs and then blended into reservoirs. Five plants later supplied up to 40 percent of demand, with a target of 55 percent by 2060, and NEWater became the reference case for potable reuse in Perth, Orange County and elsewhere.

columbia-disaster-2003.summary: In 2003 shuttle Columbia broke apart on re-entry, killing seven. Foam insulation shed from its external tank during launch had struck its left wing's leading edge, damaging thermal protection and letting hot gases penetrate that wing during re-entry. Shuttle flights were suspended for more than two years, and NASA retired its three remaining orbiters once the International Space Station was complete.

brazil-flex-fuel-cars-2003.summary: In March 2003 Volkswagen sold Brazil's first flex-fuel car, which ran on any mix of petrol and ethanol from one tank, with sensors reading the blend and adjusting fuel injection and spark timing; within five years most new cars sold there were flex-fuel, and by 2012 they made up 87% of passenger and light-duty vehicles sold.

paperclip-maximizer-2003.summary: In 2003 Bostrom published a thought experiment: an AI told to make paperclips that turns Earth into them, a parable of AI aims. An artificial intelligence told to make as many paperclips as possible, with no other constraint, could decide to turn all of Earth's natural resources, factories and electricity to that end. It shows how one harmless-sounding goal can drive a powerful system to seize resources and resist being stopped, since those serve almost any final goal; Eliezer Yudkowsky has said the idea probably arose earlier on a singularity mailing list.

sars-hong-kong-2003.summary: Severe acute respiratory syndrome spread from Guangdong to Hong Kong in February 2003 when a physician infected guests at Metropole Hotel, who carried it to Hanoi, Singapore and Toronto. Malik Peiris's team at University of Hong Kong isolated a coronavirus from two patients and, in a paper published 19 April, found evidence of infection in 45 of 50 patients across five transmission clusters and none in controls. WHO issued its first global travel alert, quarantine of Amoy Gardens and hospital infection control contained spread, and outbreak ended in July 2003 with 8,096 probable cases and 774 deaths worldwide, 299 of them in Hong Kong. SARS reshaped Asian public health agencies and informed responses to later coronaviruses.

In 2004 Peiris, Guan Yi and Yuen Kwok-yung reviewed its epidemiology and its origins in palm civets and bats. calo-project-2003.summary: In May 2003 DARPA began CALO, a five-year project to build an assistant that learns; Siri was spun out of it. Funded under DARPA's Personalized Assistant that Learns program, it brought together more than 300 researchers from 25 institutions to develop a cognitive assistant.

kano-polio-boycott-2003.summary: From August 2003 political and religious leaders in Kano, northern Nigeria, halted oral polio vaccination, claiming vaccines were laced with anti-fertility agents and HIV as part of a Western plot. Their fear grew from distrust bred by Pfizer's 1996 Trovan trial in Kano, from political rivalry after the 2003 elections, and from suspicion of a campaign that pushed one vaccine while other health needs went unmet. Laboratory tests, federal negotiation and clerics' involvement ended the boycott; Governor Ibrahim Shekarau restarted immunisation on 31 July 2004 with vaccine sourced from Indonesia. Polio from Kano spread across Nigeria and to at least ten African countries, setting back global eradication by years.

Boycott leaders included Supreme Council for Sharia in Nigeria figures who demanded independent laboratory testing of vaccine lots, which federal officials arranged in Nigeria, India and Indonesia before religious leaders accepted results and vaccination resumed.

myspace-2003.summary: In August 2003 MySpace let anyone build a page with music and a friends list; News Corp paid $580 million and Facebook ate it. News Corporation bought it for $580 million in July 2005, and from 2005 to 2009 it was the world's largest social networking site, before Facebook overtook it.

northeast-blackout-2003.summary: In August 2003 a software bug in an Ohio control room silenced its alarms and 50 million people lost power from Ohio to Ontario. A software bug in FirstEnergy's Ohio control room alarm system left operators unaware that overloaded transmission lines had dropped in voltage, so load was never redistributed and failures cascaded. Most places had power back by midnight; New York City and parts of Toronto waited until August 16.

brazil-vls-1-alcantara-explosion-2003.summary: On 22 August 2003, three days before planned launch, one of four first-stage solid motors of Veículo Lançador de Satélites VLS-1 V03 fired without command while engineers worked on the vehicle at Centro de Lançamento de Alcântara, Maranhão. The rocket and its mobile tower collapsed in fire, killing 21 members of Instituto de Aeronáutica e Espaço's team and destroying two small satellites. Earlier flights in 1997 and 1999 had failed in flight. An air force inquiry pointed to an electrical discharge and to organisational pressures and safety culture in an underfunded programme. Brazil then shifted to cooperation with Ukraine on Cyclone-4 (abandoned 2015) and later leased Alcântara to US launch companies; a domestic orbital launcher has yet to fly.

VLS-1 was a four-stage solid-propellant rocket derived from Sonda sounding rockets, meant to orbit about 100 kilograms. Alcântara's location near equator gives payload advantage, but a 1980s expropriation displaced quilombola communities, and a 2000 Brazil-US technology safeguards accord stalled in Congress over sovereignty until a new agreement was approved in 2019.

skype-launch-2003.summary: In 2003 Skype let anyone call anyone over the internet for free, undercutting international telephone rates. Niklas Zennström and Janus Friis released it with software written by Estonian developers. eBay bought it in September 2005 for 2.6 billion dollars and Microsoft for 8.5 billion in May 2011, and Skype was retired on 5 May 2025.

steam-2003.summary: In September 2003 Valve released Steam to push updates for its games; it became the store through which most PC games are sold. It grew into a store that sells and downloads PC games over the internet, opening to other publishers' titles in late 2005; by 2013 it was PC gaming's largest distribution platform, with an estimated 75% of that market.

total-information-awareness-defunded-200.summary: In September 2003 Congress defunded Total Information Awareness, a Pentagon plan to mine everyone's data, after media reports criticized attempts to gain total information awareness over all citizens. It aimed to pool government intelligence databases with private-sector data and mine them for patterns pointing to terrorists; its director Poindexter called it a "Manhattan Project for counter-terrorism".

shenzhou-5-2003.summary: On 15 October 2003 Yang Liwei orbited Earth 14 times, making China the third country to put a person in space. Shenzhou 5 launched from Jiuquan in the Gobi Desert after four uncrewed flights since 1999. Astronaut Yang Liwei completed 14 orbits and landed 21 hours later. His flight put China third, after Soviet Union and United States programs, among countries launching a person into space independently.
